News.title: Three sisters die as fire rips through shopping centre forcing panicked customers to jump from windows to escape inferno
News.content:
Next

THREE sisters were killed as a fire ripped through a shopping centre -forcing panicked customers to leap from windows to escape.

Shoppers leapt from heights of up to 35ft to flee the inferno, which also killed a fourth woman and injured at least five others.



Trapped shoppers begged people on the street below to help them as black smoke billowed from the shopping complex in Russia.

Footage from the scene shows shoppers jumping from windows into outstretched sheets held by locals.



Sisters Elena Egorova, 45, Viktoria Samigullina, 34, and Elizaveta Musina, 29, were among those killed in the blaze.



They were shopping for a birthday present for their mum when they were caught in the flames.

A truck driver moved his vehicle under a 25ft-high window, to allow two women to clamber down a ladder to safety.



“I heard cries for help seconds after parking to unload goods at a nearby shop,” he said.

“There were torchlights in the third-floor windows.”

“Firefighters had not arrived”.

A 17-year-old girl was left in a coma after she suffered severe carbon monoxide poisoning and fractures, while helping others to escape.

A 35-year-old woman was also in a coma after suffering severe smoke inhalation.



Another 17 people were evacuated from the shopping centre.

One witness described how a woman clambering down the ladder on top of the truck stumbled and fell onto a man.

“It was horrific. A woman fell from a ladder onto a man right in front of me,” they said.

Those on the scene said there was a major delay in firefighters arriving at the scene.

A chronic lack of firefighters stemming from Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine is speculated to have contributed to the delay.



Russia‘s federal fire service is about 203,750 personnel short of the number it needs to operate effectively, the country’s Emergency Situations Ministry said.

Minister Alexander Kurenkov said the units were only staffed to 65.5 per cent of the level needed.

It’s understood firefighters from the region have been recruited to the Ukraine frontline.

Poor pay has also contributed to the shortage.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An investigation is underway to establish the cause of the blaze.

News.title: How Ukraine can stop Putin’s 800,000 troops with ‘wrecking ball’ masterplan as tyrant ‘burns through 2,000 men a day’
News.content:
Next

UKRAINE has unleashed a wave of lethal tactics as it faces Russia on the battlefield, with Vladimir Putin’s troops suffering unprecedented losses.

The desperate tyrant has held onto power through “sham” elections – used as evidence of public support to continue his meat grinder war.



But as Russian commanders call up 800,000 additional troops, Ukraine has developed a series of lethal tactics to meet them on the front line.

In the latest edition of Battle Plans Exposed, former intelligence officer Philip Ingram breaks down the astonishing Ukrainian operations crippling Russia.



Watch the latest episode of Battle Plans Exposed here…

From the collapse of Moscow’s Donetsk strategy to Kyiv’s defensive buildup along the Belarus border and deep-strike drone campaign, Ingram reveals how Kyiv‘s resilience could shift victory in their favour.

Ingram said: “Ukraine has developed an unseen level of lethality in combat.

“There are reports of a 60 per cent fatality rate on the Russian side.



“A new call up or draft escalation in late autumn seems likely, but Russia’s capability to train, equip, feed, mobilise and integrate a new wave of recruits is under question on the ground.”

Kyiv is rapidly developing long-range and ballistic missiles to overwhelm Russia’s air defences with unrelenting attacks.

Volodymyr Zelensky said his forces unleashed the largest attack on Moscow since the start of war on Sunday – on the final day of Russia’s election.



Russian officials were left reeling after 450 drones swarmed the capital followed by a volley of state-of-the-art missiles.

The strikes left two dead, with gaping craters in apartment blocks and huge plumes of smoke filling the sky.

Ingram said: “What we’re seeing here is a devastating long range strike campaign catching the Russian Aerospace Forces entirely off guard.”

Just last week Ukrainian long range drones hit Russia’s military airfield at Rostov on Don and an oil refinery in Yaroslavl.

The blitz sparked a series of explosions which left an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three left 12 transport plane and three military helicopters completely destroyed.



Ingram said: “Kyiv is systematically wiping out Moscow’s air defence radar and aviation assets across the southern theatre before they can even get off the ground.

“This is crippling Putin’s logistics and creating vital breathing room for his frontline troops.”

He also said Ukraine were using SAS-style strikes to hit Russian airpower.

Ingram said: “What we’re witnessing is a 21st century evolution of David Stirling’s SAS airfield raids in North Africa back in 1942, a handful of men in armed jeeps wrecking hundreds of axis planes on the tarmac, forcing Rommel to pull vital troops off the frontline to guard his rear airfields.

“Ukraine is doing exactly the same thing today, not with jeeps but with long range strike drones by crushing Russian transport planes and fighters on the ground.”



For more than a year, Moscow’s strategic goal in Donetsk has been to surround the fortress belt.

This is the chain of heavily fortified cities including Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Zhukovsky and Kostiantynivka.

Unable to break through directly, Russian generals planned a massive pincer movement to bypass the cities – swinging round from the south down through the Lyman Salient.

“That plan has completely collapsed”, Ingram said.

As part of what it calls Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine cut Russian supply lines, blew up fuel depots and pushed Moscow’s logistics back across the border into the Voronezh Oblast.



Ingram explained: “This isn’t just a minor tactical win. It’s a strategic wrecking ball.

“Ukraine has completely severed the northern pincer of that grand encirclement plan.

“Russian commanders are still throwing meat wave attacks at the fortress belt from the south.

“But without that northern arm to close the trap, Moscow simply burning through men and armor for no strategic gain.”

He also said Ukraine were taking down Russian drones by using interceptors.



Describing dramatic footage of a UAV take-down, he said: “A high speed interceptor drone locks on and detonates right alongside it, triggering a violent mid-air explosion.

“This… is how Ukraine is preserving its multi-million dollar Western missile stockpiles, whilst neutralising Moscow’s relentless aerial swarms.”

Russia has suffered catastrophic losses in its bid to capture territory whilst trying to keep pressure on the rest of the front line.

Ingram said: “It’s costing Russians over 1200 troops a day. And we’ve seen on some days 2000 troops a day.

“That’s 35,000 to 42,000 troops each month.”



A Putin burns through his army, Russian generals have reportedly asked for an additional 800,000 troops.

But even at the lowest rate of fatalities on the front line, this new call up will be taken out within two years.

Ingram said: “Putin has put a timeline of the whole of the Donetsk Oblast being captured by the 31st of December, 2026. It’s not going to happen.

“And when the Ukrainians hold him back for that one more cycle, what he’s going to do after that is anybody’s guess.”

The cornered despot is also relying on Trojan horse-style tactics to save its crumbling war machine, Ingram said.



He detailed one example where a Russian supply vehicle was painted as a civilian car in a desperate bid to have it blend in with its surroundings.

Moscow is also hiding its critical vessels thousands of kilometres away from the frontline – proving that no target is safe from Ukraine’s cutting-edge UAVs.

Ingram showed how Russia warships were being protected with drone netting as far as the Caspian Sea by Dagestan – roughly 1,000km away from Ukraine.

Meanwhile the Ukrainian military is expanding its defensive networks.

Zelensky’s troops have cut vast swathes of forest to constructing multi-layered fortification lines to blunt armoured assaults and covert infiltration forces.



Ingram said: “There is no immediate threat of a Russian ground invasion towards Kyiv or western Ukraine from the north right now.

“What we’re seeing is classic forward planning by Kyiv.”

Ingram also showed how local defiance in Ukraine was still resisting Russian oppression.

In one clip, an elderly Ukrainian woman was seen disarming a Russian drone with her bare hands by casually removing its fiber optic cable.

Ingram said: “While it shows breathtaking individual defiance, it also reveals a fascinating technical detail – Russia is increasingly relying on tethered fiber optic guided drones to beat Ukrainian signal jamming.”



As part of Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine is also airlifting so-called kamikaze ground robots and dropping them behind enemy lines on the battlefield for the first time.

Robots are sent ahead of infantry to harass Russian forces from behind – controlled by pilots hidden in bunkers tens of kilometers away.

They carry ammunition and can capture enemy positions, trudging across rugged terrain and bombed-out streets up at a speed of up to 12km per hour.

The fresh operation has also allowed Kyiv to shatter Russia’s pincer movement to capture the Ukrainian city of Lyman.

But Ingram warned there is still a northern threat near the Suwalki Gap and the border with Belarus that Putin could look to exploit.



“In the coming weeks and months, watch out for Russian troops being trained in Belarus to try and threaten into that north [region],” he said.

It comes after Ukraine this summer relentlessly blitzed oil depots with state-of-the-art drones, before shifting to a series of strikes that have crippled Russia’s largest e-commerce platform.

The attacks have tanked Russia’s already reeling economy – wiping out businesses, suffocating trade and sparking nationwide fuel shortages.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Russians are now trying to flee the country in increasing numbers amid fears of a new military mobilisation.

News.title: Sinister Green Party plan to track punters with personal ID & ban all sports betting ads
News.content:
SNOOPING GREENS Sinister Green Party plan to track punters with personal ID & ban all sports betting ads







Next

A SINISTER Green gambling proposal is considering banning all betting adverts in sport and tracking punters through a personal ID.

Madcap plans include tougher restrictions on under-25s placing bets and deposit limits across online and in-person gambling, enforced if necessary through “mandatory player tracking”.



The policy has been put forward by the party’s health working group, which would rewrite the party’s health policy if members vote it through.

Strong bans on advertising in sport could potentially cut off millions of pounds for football clubs across the Premier League and Football League.



The paper admits that enforcing deposit limits will “require loss of privacy” for ordinary Brits wanting to place a bet.

Grainne Hurst, CEO of the Betting and Gaming Council, said the plans showed how “out of touch” the Greens are with the millions of ordinary adults who enjoy a bet safely and responsibly.



Ms Hurst said: “Forcing people to gamble under a personal ID would be a huge intrusion into their privacy and will drive customers straight into the arms of the illegal black market.

“That means fewer protections for consumers, more business for illegal operators and less tax for the Treasury.”

Some Greens are also toying with banning introductory betting offers and VIP schemes as well as stopping companies from offering payments or gifts to politicians.

New taxes on gambling companies’s profits would be used to offset the “social and economic cost” of the gambling industry.



Meanwhile children would be taught in schools about the damage of gambling harms.

A Green Party Spokesperson: “These proposals are not currently Green Party policy. They are contained in one of a large number of motions proposed for our Autumn conference.

“All motions go through a prioritisation process, and few will actually be debated. Only motions passed by conference become Green Party policy.”

News.title: Exact date Brits will enjoy last rays of summer sunshine with temperatures to hit 26C this week
News.content:
Next

Parts of the UK will reach highs of 26 degrees this week as Brits are set to enjoy a final dose of summer.

With September nearly drawing to a close, chilly autumn weather will no doubt follow soon after.



The Met Office predicts that parts of the country will enjoy highs of 26 degrees later this week, with a map confirming the exact date and time.

The Met Office map shows that London and the South East of England could enjoy temperatures as high as 26 degrees at around 4pm on Friday.



Meanwhile, the South West of England will remain pleasantly mild, with temperatures of around 19 degrees predicted.

Parts of South Wales look set to reach as high as 20 degrees.

However, areas as far North as Manchester are predicted to only get as high as 15 degrees while experiencing rainy spells, while parts of Scotland will peak at 16 degrees.

While London and the South of the UK look set to avoid wet weather this week, other parts of the country are in for a rainy Wednesday.

The Met Office’s deputy chief forecaster, Tony Wisson said: “There remains some uncertainty over the exact track of a frontal system on Wednesday which could bring a spell of heavy rain, particularly across eastern and south-eastern Scotland, and potentially parts of northern and north-eastern England.

“We’re closely monitoring this development and would encourage people to keep up to date with the latest forecasts over the coming days. It’s likely that many southern areas will remain largely dry,” he added.

News.title: Tax hikes ‘inevitable’ as Chancellor John Healey hit by £8bn borrowing nightmare
News.content:
Next

TAX hikes are “inevitable” at next month’s Budget after the Chancellor was dealt a fresh borrowing headache, experts say.

John Healey was given a “trickier” hand after Britain borrowed £8 billion more than expected so far this financial year.



The warning comes as Downing Street ally Lord O’Neill warned that the government’s pledge of “growth in every postcode” was unrealistic.

Figures reveal net borrowing in August rose to £18.3 billion which was £3.5 billion more than the Budget watchdog expected in March.



But Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”



Mr Healey may have to find up to £15 billion through tax hikes or spending cuts to standstill and maintain the government’s financial cushion of around £24 billion.

Rising borrowing costs and higher inflation from the fall-out of the Middle East conflict have helped wipe out a huge chunk of the buffer.

But Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, said: “The PM and chancellor will be feeling quite claustrophobic today as the walls close in around them.

“Borrowing costs keep climbing, while borrowing itself is outpacing the teeny rise in tax receipts.”



The borrowing woes come as an Andy Burnham adviser said the PM’s pledge to bring “good growth to every postcode” was unrealistic.

Lord O’Neill said: “I’m not a huge fan personally of the growth in every postcode. As I’ve actually said to them privately, recently.”

He told the Centre for Cities think tank: “Most of us take that to mean they are going to try and directly support growth in every postcode.

“And let’s just say, good luck with that strategy, if that’s it … it would almost definitely result in some wasted taxpayers’ money.”

Andy Burnham last week said that “difficult decisions” will need to be made at the Budget.



Capital losing out on nearly £3billion, report says ANDY Burnham has been warned that the capital is losing out on nearly £3 billion a year over planning rules, a new report says The Prime Minister has been warned that £7.4 million is being lost in economic output a day as rules force mobile sites offline without a replacement. A new study reveals that those living and working in the capital in “functional not spots” after Notice To Quit measures are issued. Landowners issue the measure when buildings are renovated, redeveloped or demolished but they take five years on average to be replaced. High Streets and train and underground stations across the capital are in such a not-spot area. The warning comes in the report Lost Sites, Lost Signal: The Impact of Notices to Quit on Londoners, commissioned by VodafoneThree. Andrea Dona, Chief Networks Officer at VodafoneThree said: “London’s strength has always rested on its ability to connect people: to jobs, ideas, markets, culture, transport and each other. “In the 21st century,that connectivity is digital as well as physical. Mobile networks are critical national infrastructure. “When that infrastructure is removed before replacements are in place, local communities can face years of reduced connectivity which ultimately costs London billions in economic output.”

Treasury Minister Emma Reynolds said: “Britain has huge potential to deliver good growth in every postcode, creating jobs, raising living standards and investing in the services people rely on.

“But we can only deliver that growth with fiscal discipline.”

News.title: Cops foil suspected UK terror plot to target Jewish community – as two men arrested following raids
News.content:
HIGH ALERT Cops foil suspected UK terror plot to target Jewish community – as two men arrested following raids







Next

COPS have foiled a suspected UK terror plot targeting the Jewish community, as two men have been arrested following raids.

The men, who are in their 30s, were arrested on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000.

The investigation relates to a suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.



Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.



“Counter Terrorism policing continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities.

“We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy day period.

“I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester Police and partners to ensure we’re doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe.

“And more broadly, across the country CTP is working with local police forces to provide protective security support and advice for areas with Jewish communities, and particularly during the High Holy Day period.

“As we have shown with these arrests, where we suspect there could be a threat to the public, then we will not hesitate to investigate and take action.

“We are pursuing a number of lines enquiry and we anticipate these will continue over the coming days as this investigation continues.

“Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns.”



The two men were arrested in Newton Street, Manchester and were subsequently taken to a London police station, where they currently remain in police custody.

On September 22, officers obtained warrants of further detention for both men, meaning they can be detained in police custody up until September 27.

It was Yom Kippur from Sunday to Monday, which is seen as the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

News.title: Friends of twisted mum, 38, ‘caught performing vile sex act with dog by husband’ launch shock fundraising campaign
News.content:
SHOCK APPEAL Friends of twisted mum, 38, ‘caught performing vile sex act with dog by husband’ launch shock fundraising campaign







Next

PALS of a mum accused of performing depraved sex acts with her family dog have launched a fundraising campaign to help cover legal costs.

Malia Nummerdor, 38, was hit with charges after her husband allegedly caught her engaging in sexual contact with her family dog, Ranger.



The fundraiser, created on SupportNow, says the donations will be used to cover “significant legal costs” as the mother of two battles the allegations – which she denies.

Florida cops claim Malia was captured on home CCTV “partially nude” with her family dog “positioned in a manner consistent with sexual activity”.



Her husband, Erik Nummerdor, originally stumbled upon the footage while reviewing security cameras aimed at catching a coin jar thief, according to PEOPLE.

Erik shared the disturbing allegations on Facebook after which he was contacted by detectives who launched an investigation.

Malia – from Punta Gorda, Florida – was arrested on charges of Sexual Activity Involving Animals, a serious crime that carries a maximum penalty of up to 15 years behind bars.

It is understood she has since been freed on bail from Charlotte County Jail.



After the charges became public, a fundraiser was launched to support Malia.

It says that Malia and her children’s lives have been “turned upside down” by the allegations, with the post adding that the trio are currently “displaced from their home”.

The post said: “Funds raised will help with Malia’s legal expenses and immediate living needs while she navigates this disruption and the legal processes affecting her family.



“This fundraiser is not asking anyone to decide the facts of the case. It is about helping a mother and her children get through an extraordinarily difficult period and making sure Malia has access to appropriate legal representation.

“Our hope is simply to give Malia one less thing to carry right now and remind her and her boys that they are not facing this alone.”

Sheriff Bill Prummell from the Charlotte County Sheriff’s Office, previously said he simply cannot comprehend the mother’s “disgusting” behaviour.

He said: “There are only a few times in my career that I have been at a loss for words.

“No animal should ever be subjected to this kind of conduct, and you can be sure that we will take action when we learn about it here in Charlotte County.”



When police interviewed Malia last week she acknowledged the video showed her with the dog but denied there was any sexual contact and that she was simply petting it.

When posed for her mugshot on the day of her arrest on September 15, Malia flashed a toothy grin.

Sheriff Prummell said: ” I don’t know what there is to smile about when you’ve been arrested for something as disgusting as this.”

She is scheduled to appear in court on October 19.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She denies all charges.



At the time of publication the fundraiser has raised £11.20 ($15) of its £22,450 ($30,000) goal.

News.title: Trump blasts ‘terrible’ Chagos deal in first meeting with Burnham at UN – before President takes swipe at Starmer
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump has rebuked Andy Burnham over the “terrible” deal to surrender the Chagos Islands.

But the US President stopped short of letting rip at the new PM – and even said he preferred him to Sir Keir Starmer.



The two leaders came face-to-face for the first time at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Despite their political differences, a nervous Mr Burnham emerged from the meeting relatively unscathed as Mr Trump hailed him as a “natural businessperson”.



But he took a slap from the US President over his continued support to give the Chagos Islands away to Mauritius.

Mr Trump said: “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. They [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership.

“Somebody [Mauritius] has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.”

He said the islands are “strategically very important” and that Mr Burnham is going to be looking at it.”



Mr Trump said the US Air Force had been forced to fly B-2 bombers back to Kansas after strikes on Iran.

Under a deal signed by his predecessor Sir Keir, Britain is set to cede sovereignty of the Indian Ocean territory while keeping the joint US-UK Diego Garcia military base.

It will also see UK taxpayers pay Mauritius tens of billions of pounds to lease back the base.

After the giveaway was approved by Joe Biden, Mr Trump has since withdrawn American support and put the handover on ice.

Mr Burnham said last night he was committed to finding a “resolution” to push the deal over the line.



Following Mr Trump’s broadside over the deal, Reform boss Nigel Farage said: “The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God.”

What is the Chagos deal? UNDER the Chagos deal, Britain will hand sovereignty of the island to Mauritius while leasing back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years at a potential cost of £34billion. Sir Keir Starmer sparked a sell-out row when he originally announced the plans. It will cost the UK £90million a year to rent the strategically vital base. The surrender agreement, spurred on by human rights lawyer colleagues, has repeatedly been slammed by Donald Trump. He has frequently called the giveaway deal one of “great stupidity”.

But Mr Burnham survived a lashing from his US counterpart despite previously butting heads and earlier goading from Labour MPs for the PM to take a more combative stance.

Mr Trump said that US-UK relations were on the “up”, adding: “Based on my relations with your prime minister Andy. I think we’re doing very well.”

The President also said Mr Burnham was a “natural business person” who “understands what he needs to do”.



The PM even jibed Mr Trump about his previous dismissal of Manchester as “a town” but did not invite him to visit as was expected.

The pair did not publicly discuss the Falkland Islands after Mr Trump boasted he could “settle” any future conflict but Mr Burnham said he raised the President’s threat.

The comment came during a recent trip to Ireland where Mr Trump said a war between the UK and Argentina would be a “potential disaster”.

He went on to say he would love to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now” as it is “going to happen eventually”.

They also avoided flaring tensions over AI after Mr Burnham told business leaders this morning that he wants the tech to be regulated by global standards.



While Mr Trump rebuked calls for more tech regulation in his speech this afternoon.

During his address the President also pushed back any resolution to the Iran war until after the mid terms.

But the President threatened to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell” during his speech.

He also told world leaders the Ukraine war would “end more quickly than people understand” while Mr Burnham is expected to push for more support for Ukraine.

Burnham himself has made some inflammatory remarks about his US counterpart in the past, describing him as “poisonous.”



And, in 2021 he said: “any politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now.”

Despite this, last night the PM said: “Politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in.”

Indicating the tone Mr Burnham hopes to set at their crucial meeting today, No 10 said: “He is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation.”



The President and the Prime Minister have previously shared a phone call in the wake of Mr Burnham’s ascension to the top job.

But, the pair have never met in person with Mr Burnham warned he must keep Washington on side while trying to rebuild the UK.

And Mr Burnham did not meet Mr Trump at Trump Tower like French President Emmanuel Macron did during his trip to New York.

The two world leaders are understood to have discussed football, Manchester and the Iran war during their first phone call.

A Downing Street spokesperson added that they had also discussed defence and security.



Trump said the call was “interesting” and “went very well.”

Ahead of their meeting Mr Trump addressed the United Nations and met with Denmark and Greenland’s delegations to sign an “unprecedented agreement.”

This is understood to have come as a surprise to British officials who were hoping an end to the situation would lower bills back home with the opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The meeting follows Mr Burnham announcement that the RAF would help Saudi Arabia in their fight against the Iran-backed Houthi terrorists.

In his first major military intervention as PM, he confirmed he authorised a military jet to aid the Kingdom in repelling the Iran-backed militia who are causing havoc in the Gulf.

News.title: Plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community disrupted, say police
News.content:
A "suspected terrorist plot" to target the Jewish community in Manchester is believed to have been foiled after two men were arrested in the city on Sunday, police have said.

The men, both in their 30s, were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, according to the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said police were aware the news would cause "further concern" to the Jewish community "especially given the significant High Holy day period".

Yom Kippur - considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar - was marked this year from Sunday evening to Monday evening.

The two suspects remain in police custody after being taken to a London police station for questioning.

Police said the investigation related to a "suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area".

"This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area," said Evans.

"Counter-terrorism policing (CTP) continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities.

"Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns."

News.title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Burnham
News.content:
Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.

The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and would raise the subject with von der Leyen when he meets her during a UN summit in New York.

Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".

He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy.

The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains.

Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.

Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us.

"We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain.

"We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies hereâ¦ we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem.

"We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."

News.title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
News.content:
Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.

The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004.

These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape.

Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December.

Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support.

"Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line."

Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said.

A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027.

Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood.

"Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women.

"These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women.

"Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings.

"The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial."

News.title: Father admits causing death of his son in hotel fall
News.content:
Foster was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week for the plea hearing to take place.

His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.

Paphos District Court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.

Foster decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.

A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing.

"The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.

The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.

In a statement given to the BBC, Alexandrou, said: "This was a momentary lapse of attention, without any intention to cause harm, which had the most devastating and unimaginable consequences.

"We will now present to the court the relevant mitigating evidence and circumstances for consideration ahead of sentencing."

The family have suffered "unimaginable grief" since the "horrific events" and have asked for privacy during this time, added the lawyer.

News.title: Earl Spencer should pull Diana book from shelves, Piers Morgan says
News.content:
Piers Morgan has called for Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana to be pulled from the shelves over a factual error.

Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, apologised to Morgan for incorrectly describing him in the memoir as the editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group published "highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym" in 1993.

Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said he accepted the apology but that his lawyers would be "laying out that we want the offending pages to be removed from this book. And if that means they pulp the first edition, so be it".

The BBC understands Penguin, the publishers of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, will be amending this one point in future editions of the book.

The photographs of Princess Diana mentioned in relation to Morgan in Earl Spencer's book were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993.

At the time, Morgan was working at The Sun and did not join the Mirror as its editor until 1995.

Earl Spencer admitted "his assumption was incorrect" and "apologises to Mr Morgan for this error", a statement said.

On his YouTube show, Piers Morgan Uncensored, Morgan read out a section of the book, in which Earl Spencer wrote: "They realised they were unable to be rude to the brother of the much-mourned princessâ¦

"The only one who sounded surly, as opposed to merely confused or embarrassed, was Piers Morgan of the Mirror, who snarled with annoyance before he hung up.

"I assumed Morgan must be feeling particular guilt because, four years earlier, he and his Sunday Mirror counterpart had published photographs taken with hidden cameras by a gym owner. They were of Diana working out in a leotard.

"This was such an intolerable invasion of her privacy that Diana instructed lawyers to sue the Mirror Group and to block further use of the images."

A spokesperson for Princess Diana's brother said in a statement that "Earl Spencer's account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate. Mr Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister's funeral."

The statement admitted the factual error, and said that "as an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error."

Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said: "He's a historian. He should want it removed from the shelves. Why, if you're doing this for historical record, would you want such a completely untrue series of claims over several pages about a public figure to still be in that book.

"Now you've admitted it's untrue and apologised. He should pull the book."

In a post on social media on Tuesday, Morgan said he was "pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King's Trust".

News.title: Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
News.content:
The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his party conference.

The Lib Dem leader said that if he gained power, he would raise the annual tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000.

He would also raise the 40p income tax threshold from Â£50,270 to Â£56,000, in a Â£17bn package funded by the economic boost he says would come from the UK rejoining the EU single market and customs union.

He claimed the plan would mean a Â£680 cut for "most taxpayers" but it would not come into full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government - potentially up to eight years away.

The announcement was greeted with sustained applause by Lib Dem MPs and activists in the Brighton conference centre.

The Â£12,570 income tax allowance was frozen by the Conservatives in 2021, resulting in more people being dragged into paying the tax, and Labour has so far resisted calls from trade unions and some of its MPs to unfreeze it.

The Lib Dems said they would raise the threshold to Â£15,000 a year, and increase the starting point for paying employee National Insurance (NI) to the same level.

At their conference earlier this month, Reform UK promised to increase the income tax personal allowance to Â£15,000 within 100 days if they won power.

Sir Ed told the Lib Dem faithful "the difference between us and Reform" is that "their tax cut is paid for through cruelty."

He said "Reform's figures show they'd pay for it by ripping Â£22bn of crucial support away from disabled people."

Explaining his pledge to raise the 40p income tax threshold, Sir Ed argued that more and more people were being dragged into a tax bracket that had originally been intended for higher earners.

"A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses" he said, adding: "That's not fair, it's not right."

Under the Lib Dem plan, based on research by think tank Frontier Economics, external, the economic boost from rejoining the single market would allow the party to spend Â£17bn on tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament.

The party says it would unfreeze personal allowances in the second year of a Lib Dem government, allowing them to rise with inflation, before bringing in big tax cuts in year five when the economic benefits of closer trading with the EU had kicked in.

However, the move would depend on the party being able to negotiate a closer trading arrangement with the EU in just 12 months.

Stuart Adam, of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, told BBC Verify the Lib Dem package would cost "much more" than the Â£17bn quoted by the party.

Reform has estimated that its policy, to raise the starting threshold to Â£15,000 just for income tax, would cost Â£21bn by the fifth year.

The Lib Dems say their policy would be funded by an extra Â£27bn from its plans for a "growth and defence pact" with the EU.

News.title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular charged with rape in Massachusetts
News.content:
The online influencer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with rape, providing liquor to a person under the legal US drinking age, and drugging someone for sexual intercourse, court records show.

The alleged offences occurred in May 2025, according to the charges filed in the state of Massachusetts.

A spokesperson for Peters told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the charges are "bogus" and that the influencer has yet to be served with an arrest warrant.

Peters is facing a civil lawsuit filed by a woman earlier this year who alleged that he had served her several rounds of vodka and had nonconsensual sex with her at his parents' home on Cape Cod.

The woman said she was a minor at the time and also accused him of injecting her with a non-FDA approved substance. He denied the allegations.

The criminal charges filed this month do not identify the alleged victim.

Clavicular is known for his role in an online movement called "looksmaxxing", centred on maximising physical attractiveness.

His online account has amassed a large following, where he streams the lengths to which he goes to achieve physical perfection.

Peters has spoken openly about methods such as "bone smashing", which involves hitting his jawline with a hammer or other objects to get a more chiselled look.

Despite courting controversies for his "looksmaxxing" protocols, Peters has translated his online fame into broader cultural recognition. In June, he walked the runway at a fashion week show in Paris.

Peters has also had brushes with the law.

He was charged earlier this year in Florida after he filmed himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator, for which he pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public.

In March, he was arrested in Florida on suspicion of battery charges after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities later said in July they did not intend to file charges.

After the Massachusetts charges became public, Peters posted a video on X that appeared to show his accuser, as well as a handwritten note.

"Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money," he wrote.

News.title: Mum and three children die in Bootle house fire
News.content:
A mother and three children have died in a house fire on Merseyside.

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, at 03:45 BST.

Eight firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom who were showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

Another casualty, who was outside the property when crews arrived, was taken to hospital.

Officers from Merseyside Police were at the scene and a joint investigation with the fire service into the cause of the blaze is under way.

The North West Ambulance Service's hazardous area response team also attended the scene of the fire and confirmed the four fatalities.

Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle confirmed the "intense fire [had] spread very rapidly".

News.title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.

The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.

The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".

"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."

Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".

Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).

He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."

The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".

He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.

His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.

News.title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe suspends production at key UK plants blaming high gas prices
News.content:
Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe's industrial giant Ineos is pausing production at its three plants in Hull, blaming high UK gas prices.

The firm said gas prices in the UK are twelve times higher than in the US, and eight times more expensive than the coal-based processes used by Chinese competitors.

Sir Jim said: "We are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe, but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete."

Ineos Acetyls, part of the Ineos Group, is the only European producer of key chemicals used in a wide range of products from food and medicines to explosives. Gas is a key ingredient in production.

Ineos said the move will affect up to 1,000 of its staff, of whom 245 work directly at the site.

But the BBC understands workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from the US at lower prices - which could take up to a year - or waits for gas prices to go down.

Ineos is asking governments in the UK and the EU - where most of its products are exported to - to put in tariff protections against Chinese products.

Two plants on the site have already been turned off, and the third will follow in coming days.

One plant makes acetic acid, which is used in vinegar, paint and glue. Another makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin, and the third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and for decaffeinating tea and coffee.

The disruption of supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran has pushed up prices around the world.

The wholesale price of natural gas â used for heating homes and generating electricity â has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

Sir Jim said the current government's energy policy was "economic vandalism on an industrial scale".

Ineos says that its plants in Humberside are "among the most efficient in the world", producing materials with half the carbon footprint of US rivals, and only one eighth the footprint of Chinese equivalents.

It's the second time in less than a week that Sir Jim, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, has heavily criticised government policy.

He told BBC News last week that he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide", which he blamed on high taxes and high immigration.

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said it would be a "concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families".

A spokesperson said: "We've taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including Â£350 million for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis.

"We've also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our Supercharger and British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive."

Ineos Acetyls company cut a fifth of its workforce last year, citing high energy costs and "dirt-cheap" competition from China. It called for tariffs - or taxes on imports - to protect the industry.

News.title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
News.content:
The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek a rapid review of their care if they want.

It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule.

Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being taken on board.

The nationwide expansion should be complete by March 2028, after a trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out in all inpatient wards.

Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern.

News.title: Inquest opens into 'Putney Pusher' suspect's death
News.content:
A man suspected of knocking a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge was found dead by his brother-in-law after missing a family meal, his inquest has heard.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick on 15 September, West London Coroner's Court was told.

He had been arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident of May 2017, when a woman was shoved into the road by a jogger. His family say he was not involved.

Opening and adjourning the inquest, West London coroner Melanie Lee said she had been told of a referral to the Independent Office of Police Conduct and was suspending the hearing pending the outcome of its inquiry.

News.title: Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor
News.content:
An unexpected surge in government borrowing in August, driven by persistently higher inflation, has added to pressure on Chancellor John Healey as he prepares to deliver his first Budget at the end of October.

Borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was Â£18.3bn in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

That figure was Â£3.5bn more than official forecasters expected.

Inflation rose to its highest rate in five months in August in the UK, driven up by higher petrol and diesel prices.

Although tax receipts were higher in August compared with a year ago, spending on public services, benefits, and other costs grew more as the pace of price rises increased.

The interest the government is paying on its debt rose to Â£8.8bn, its highest August level since records began in 1997.

The cost of servicing that debt comes as the government is under pressure to spend more on defence and cost-of-living support to households, said Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy.

He said it was important not to "overinterpret a single month given the volatility in the numbers", but added that there were some "concerning elements".

He said the cost of paying the interest on government debt is likely to rise in the coming months.

News.title: No regular contact with pair held in Iran, family say
News.content:
A British couple who have been detained in Iran for more than 20 months have not had regular contact restored with their family, despite assurances, their family say.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman, who were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges which they deny, were promised family contact after they ended hunger strikes, but there had not been regular calls since, they said.

The family of the couple, who are from East Sussex, is calling for an urgent meeting with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to discuss what action can be taken.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said the couple's welfare was its "top priority" and officials had been working to provide assistance.

It said this included the ambassador visiting the pair in prison and facilitating calls with their family back in the UK.

The couple began hunger strikes earlier this year, after claiming that prison authorities had began to prevent them from speaking to their families. The hunger strikes lasted 93 and 84 days respectively.

The family is now calling for the government to provide regular consular visits and implement a focused strategy to secure the couple's release.

A spokesperson for the family says a British consular visit is planned for 5 October, which they say will be just the second visit of 2026.

They said the length of time it took to arrange the meeting, particularly following the hunger strikes, was "extremely concerning".

The FCDO said the family met with Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty and the UK's envoy for complex consular detentions Alistair Burt in August.

A spokesperson for the office said Doughty "set out how unjustified and appalling we consider Lindsay and Craig's incarceration to be, and the action that the UK Government is taking to try and secure their release".

News.title: 'Lego-type blocks' anger woman who was fenced in
News.content:
A council has placed two "concrete Lego-type" blocks at the rear access to the home of an 81-year-old just one week after she won a legal wrangle over access.

Retired teacher Helene Ball won a three-year battle against Derbyshire County Council after it fenced off a 98cm gated gap between her garden and a council car park in April 2023.

As well as being fenced in, dozens of concrete blocks were laid on the access road leading to the car park, off Cavendish Road in Matlock, after it was put on the market.

After a first-tier tribunal ruled in Ball's favour on 27 August, she said the council was "a law unto themselves" after two new concrete blocks were laid at the rear of her home.

The BBC understands the two additional blocks were to protect the grassed area and trees from unauthorised parking and damage once the car park entrance is opened.

The council has acknowledged it was "unreasonable" to erect the original green fence at the heart of the dispute, adding it had "apologised for any distress caused".

A right of way has now been established, while the council has been ordered by the courts to pay Â£50,000 costs and to ensure Ball's access is not impeded again.

News.title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
News.content:
Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-in appointments too, external.

Two doses offer the best protection. First doses are available until 31 December 2026, with second doses available until 31 March 2027.

Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA, said: "This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change.

"The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place."

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer.

Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before.

These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added.

Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period.

Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham.

The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students.

It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening.

Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes.

Economists are warning Andy Burnham that tax rises will be almost certain in this month’s Budget – a worry for the prime minister just as he prepares for his first face-to-face meeting with the famously brusque Donald Trump.

The prime minister said he was hoping to find “common ground” with the US president when they hold talks in the margins of the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York.

He said: "We've found a connection. So I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find.”

Mr Burnham also insisted he personally trusted Mr Trump, telling reporters: “When you come into this job, you realise how deep this relationship is.

“We trust our allies. Of course we do.”

The talks will involve discussions on wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and the rapid development of AI.

Economists say tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after government borrowing rose in August to the second-highest level for the month on record.

Official figures also showed the Treasury had borrowed £8bn more than expected this year.

News.title: Trump’s UN speech went from campaigning to denial — and then it took a dark turn
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Nobody had high hopes for Trump’s speech at the UN General Assembly, and as the president ambled out to the lectern and tiredly began ranting about how “I can report to you with pride that America is back and our country is better than ever before,” most diplomats and journalists alike settled in for a proto-rally.

The vintage Trumpian claims came thick and fast. “Our economy is the envy of the world,” he told the gathered world leaders, who looked decidedly unenvious. “We are leading in virtually everything,” he added, as though the prime ministers and presidents of Canada and France and the U.K. and South Korea were actually going to applaud it, much less believe it.

It took less than five minutes for Trump to get into his own personal achievements: how many jobs he took credit for creating, how Washington, D.C., has “bustling restaurants” again, how “I sent our crime-busters into Memphis, Tennessee and New Orleans, Louisiana.” The previous administration got a kick in the pants from him, of course, during a long aside that ended with: “Two years ago, our country was dead, and now we have the hottest country in the world.”

The childish word choice felt strange and out-of-place among the pomp and ceremony of the flag-draped United Nations building, the gathered leaders with their interpreter headphones, the seriousness of the occasion. But who cares about that, because America is risen from the dead and hot as hell — a steaming, boiling reanimated corpse! Hell yeah!

Or perhaps we might’ve said, “hell yeah,” if only the president hadn’t looked like he was about to fall asleep.

open image in gallery It took less than five minutes for President Donald Trump to get into his own personal achievements as he spoke before the UN General Assembly in New York Tuesday ( AFP/Getty )

Needless to say, turning up to the UNGA to boast about having “the hottest country in the world” is a bit like turning up the PTA to boast about how, in your unbiased opinion, your kid is the cleverest kid in the school, but emotional intelligence has never been one of Donald’s strong points. Superintelligence, however, was absolutely on the agenda — and that’s the new word for AI, by the way, which the president announced in a roundabout way during a conspiracy-laden couple of paragraphs about globalism.

Evil people have tried to “construct a globalist scheme” to control AI, the president said, which by the way isn’t even called AI now because he’s “changing the name” to super intelligence. “In other words,” he added, “welcome to the new world of super intelligence — SI.” He said the “dash” part out loud, presumably reading too faithfully from the piece of paper in front of him.

There was no explanation provided for why we’re now supposed to call the technology SI instead of AI; or rather, the only explanation Trump offered was “Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do and maybe I don’t.” Unfortunately, even he didn’t seem entirely comfortable with the new label, later adding that “whoever wins AI, you have to remember — uh, whoever wins SI” will lead the world. And by the way, “we’re leading over China by a lot and everyone else… We’re going to keep it very straight and very strong.”

This ramble about AI/SI was punctuated by occasional nods to a “Ukraine hoax,” climate change, “open borders” and “transgender mutilization,” a strange combination of both mangled English and uneasy bedfellows that were presumably mentioned because they comprise the Republicans’ midterms attack strategy. But at the UN, the whole thing seemed like word soup. Slipping in transgender culture wars points while talking about keeping AI “very straight” gave the bizarre impression that he was hoping to keep the coming super intelligence revolution heterosexual.

On the side of the word soup came the regular stuff about how faceless bureaucrats and their grand conspiracies will never stop America (these include the “evil” globalists of the International Criminal Court who conduct “show trials by an anti-American tribunal”, activists seeking a carbon tax, and UNESCO) and promises that he won’t bring in any regulation on AI — sorry, SI — because that would “stifle growth.”

open image in gallery Trump took time out to praise first lady Melania Trump’s global children’s efforts for a moment of applause on the world stage that relied largely on members of his cabinet for the actual clapping ( Reuters )

In between, we were treated to a too-long, surprisingly gushing bit about Melania, where he paused for applause once and then tried unsuccessfully to get the room to applaud again.

In this way, Trump’s speech trundled on, ending around 45 minutes in, which is short by the standards of his usual efforts. It had the flavor of a State of the Union speech, although he did stop to thank the UN Security Council twice for some resolutions that had gone his way in the past year. He offered up some fairly subdued words about Gaza, for which he thanked the gathered countries for helping usher through America’s peace plan.

There was only one moment which drew sharp intakes of breath, and that was when he mentioned Iran. “They were the bully of the Middle East but they’re the bully no more,” he began, which was fairly standard; he then boasted a little about military triumphs and pointed out that Iran is now suffering from out-of-control inflation. But now, the president intimated, “I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran” that would make them “one of the greatest countries in the world”? He paused for effect, before taking a suddenly dark turn: “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly?”

As the gathered heads of state took stock of this wording, Trump added, “Do I drive them to hell with no chance of survival?” and murmurs started up in the room.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm elections,” the president claimed of Iran, as if what’s top-of-mind for him might be top-of-mind for another country that’s being summarily decimated. He quickly added another revealing tidbit: “The Republican party is running… but I am not running.” And anyway, “the cowards and traitors love to say ‘The United States is low on munitions’ but that’s not true.” He did a funny voice for the cowards and the traitors.

It was a strange digression, from which the U.S. president then moved swiftly on and returned to what passes for statesmanlike when it’s him talking: he thanked the UN a couple of times, he didn’t threaten the organization with its own destruction, and he didn’t belligerently storm through an hour and a half of extra content. He seemed tired throughout; he gripped the lectern, leaned on it at times, and his energy seemed to be ebbing even at the beginning. He called out Mark Rutte by name, but seemed to be aware that he was not especially among friends.

The fact that he was not as combative as he could have been seems to imply that he’s realized he needs more allies. Approval of the war in Iran is at an all-time low, with Republicans in particular getting sick of the conflict and nobody buying the “I wouldn’t call it a war” rhetoric currently popular among Trump administration officials. The midterms are just around the corner, little more than six weeks away, and the president is already distancing himself from the results and the people who are running in them.

Efforts to redefine words as an exercise in ego-stroking are perhaps interesting to psychologists but uninteresting to anyone who actually wants to talk about AI and what it might do to the planet. They’re about as useful as renaming Lake Ontario and about as popular as the “Gulf of America”.

In other words, the bar is on the floor for Donald Trump. And so, considering the expectations, he didn’t entirely alienate people today. He also looked — under the bombast and the boasting, dredged up from clearly diminishing reserves of enthusiasm and verve — like he might, just might, be running scared.

News.title: About 2,000 church sex abuse victims have come forward for reparations in France
News.content:

About 2,000 people who reported being sexually abused by priests or other church representatives have sought reparations from a French independent body created to address decades of abuse, the organization said Tuesday as it prepares to end its five-year mission.

The Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation, or INIRR, said its work extended beyond financial compensation to include psychological support.

INIRR's report comes ahead of Pope Leo XIV's four-day visit to France, beginning Friday, during which he is expected to meet privately with seven survivors of sexual abuse by priests and other Catholic personnel.

France’s Catholic bishops’ conference agreed to provide reparations after a 2021 report estimated some 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials and urged the French Catholic Church to respect the rule of law in France.

Here's a look at the independent reparations program, by the numbers:

1,184 decisions

Over 1,184 decisions granting financial or other reparations from the church have formally been made by the INIRR.

Hundreds of other cases are still awaiting a decision. Some 183 people reached out to the independent body this year.

The INIRR closed to new submissions on Aug. 31, after completing its scheduled mandate, but is still accompanying victims until the end of next year.

It is to be replaced by another body, meant to be permanent and focusing on restorative justice, long-term guidance, and support for victims of sexual violence within the church.

1 letter

After completing the process, survivors receive a “letter of recognition” that formally acknowledges the sexual abuse and details the financial compensation.

“The letter was a shockwave for me,” said Cécile Reneaume, 34, who received reparations from INIRR after she was abused as a young child by the leader of a Catholic community, who has since died.

“I was expecting a very small amount of financial compensation — that’s how I had imagined it. But when I read the letter, it said: ‘The church acknowledges these specific failings'," she described.

“It meant that the little girl who once had been unable to speak was finally believed. It gave weight and credibility to what happened to me as a child,” Reneaume said.

The Associated Press generally doesn’t identify victims of sexual assault or abuse unless they come forward publicly or give their consent to be identified.

36,892 euros

Survivors who went through the process were awarded an average of 36,892 euros ($42,186) each.

Once the INIRR approves the financial compensation, the case is sent to a special fund financed by the church for payment.

“My first reaction was violent,” said Eric, 55, who didn’t want his last name to be public, when he was informed of the amount. “I felt anger, disbelief. Am I worth this?”

Eric was raped by a priest when he was between ages 8 and 14.

“It took me time to understand that it wasn’t me who was being assessed, nor was it about putting a price on what I had suffered, because you can’t put a price on a childhood," he said.

The compensation is intended to financially support the healing process.

56 years on average

People reaching out to INIRR last year were aged 56 on average, about two-thirds were men and one-third were women.

Among them, Philippe Gomes was 49 in 2023 when a session of therapeutic hypnosis helped him remember he had been a victim of sexual abuse by two priests from age 7 to 12. Survivors may experience complete or partial loss of memory due to the traumatic events.

“I reached out to the INIRR and that was a real shock, because the first thing I was told was: ‘I believe you,’" Gomes said.

Gomes said the therapy he is undergoing has helped him say he was raped without crying.

"I'm not ashamed, I'm not the one who should be ashamed," he said.

Reparations also may include nonfinancial support. Requests have included help for victims to write down their stories, organizing meetings with local church representatives, or installing a plaque in memory of victims.

Musician Rick Sollo was among four people on board a helicopter that has disappeared in Brazil, it has been reported.

The twin-engine Bell 430 aircraft had departed from Porto Belo heading towards Sao Joaquim on Monday afternoon when the pilot lost contact with air traffic control, according to G1 Globo.

The three passengers have been identified as Sollo, 59, from the country music duo Rick and Renner, influencer Bruno Avelar and videographer Paulo Soares, according to a statement shared on Avelar’s social media. The pilot has not yet been named.

“To date, there is no official confirmation of an accident involving the aircraft,” it added. A further post said there were five people on board, bit did not identify the fifth person.

open image in gallery Sollo had earlier posted a video on Instragram showing him boarding ( Facebook )

This came hours after Sollo posted a video on his Instagram story showing him boarding and landing an aircraft alongside Avelar.

A search and rescue operation has been launched in the mountainous region of Urubici, where air traffic last detected the helicopter.

In an appeal to residents, Avelar’s team urged them to listen out for “loud bangs and noises” and report any sightings of smoke and debris.

The Santa Catarina Fire Department first received a call about a possible aircraft crash at around 4pm on Monday.

open image in gallery Avelar's team shared a map of the search area on his social media ( Avelar's team )

At the time, a red weather alert for thunderstorms and heavy rainfall was issued for Urubici.

“Rainfall between 30 and 60 mm/h or 50 and 100 mm/day, strong winds (60–100 km/h), and hail. Risk of power outages, crop damage, fallen trees, and flooding,” said a downgraded weather warning issued at midnight.

The Brazilian Air Force (FAB) has deployed a Black Hawk military helicopter and an SC-105 Amazonas in the rural Vacas Gordas area to search for a possible wreckage, according to Sapicua Radio Agency.

Lieutenant Colonel Heloisa, commander of the 5th Military Fire Brigade Battalion of Santa Catarina, said about the search and rescue late last night: “The first search point is the point of the aircraft's last communication. A team has already arrived at the location, and nothing was found.

open image in gallery The search has been launched in the mountainous region of Santa Catarina ( Getty/iStock )

“We also have information on the last cell phone signal point of one of the people who were on that aircraft. At this moment, teams are moving to that location to carry out searches.”

Fire crews are expected to be carrying out searches in the area Tuesday, but the weather conditions are understood to be slowing down the operation.

The air forces added that "the priority of the operation is to locate the aircraft and its occupants in the shortest possible time, concentrating search efforts in the areas of highest probability and continuously adjusting the plan as new information is obtained."

The Independent has contacted the Brazilian Air Force for a comment.

Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials said Tuesday they plan to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging that the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program, or simply do not exist.

Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.

“We’re actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them,” Vance, who leads a government-wide task force to eliminate fraud, said in a public address at the White House, Tuesday. He was flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and other administration officials.

The Trump administration also announced a six-month suspension on new brokers who sign up enrollees for healthcare coverage, who officials say commit a disproportionate amount of the fraud they uncovered.

Tuesday's announcement is the latest in an administration-wide initiative to address fraud around the country, including in federal healthcare programs, which officials say is needed to rein in runaway spending and protect taxpayers.

The announcement comes as inflation and rising healthcare costs pressure the Trump administration to come up with a plan to bring down costs for Americans heading into the midterms.

The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many Americans during Trump’s second term, after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Biden’s term.

Premiums doubled or tripled for many enrollees, prompting millions to downgrade their plans or exit the program entirely after the Republican-led Congress allowed the subsidies to expire this year.

Roughly 19.2 million Americans are actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans as of early 2026, according to the HHS website.

The White House referred The Associated Press to the Vice President’s team for additional comment on bigger plans to address healthcare affordability.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news of the Trump administration’s plan to remove ACA enrollees from public exchanges.
