A woman and three children have died following a house fire in Merseyside.

Emergency services were called to the blaze at a semi-detached property in Stone Square, Bootle, in Sefton, at about 3.45am on Tuesday, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service confirmed.

A spokesperson said that four people had been found showing no signs of life in an upstairs bedroom.

“Two members of North West Ambulance’s Hazardous Area Response Team were subsequently committed into the incident and tragically confirmed that all four had lost their lives,” the spokesperson said.

A fifth person was outside the house when crews arrived, and was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

Speaking from the scene, Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle said described the fire as “intense” and said that it “spread very rapidly”.

open image in gallery Police officers on the scene after the fatal fire ( PA )

Police officers cordoned off the street on Tuesday morning, with fire crews seen knocking on the doors of neighbouring homes as fire engines arrived and departed from the area.

Fire service area manager Kevin Longshaw said: “This is a devastating incident and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured.

“We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident.”

At the height of the incident, six fire engines were at the scene.

Eight firefighters entered the property, which was well alight upon arrival, to search for occupants and tackle the blaze, a fire service spokesperson said.

open image in gallery Authorities are now working to ascertain the cause of the fire ( PA )

The fire service is now undertaking a joint investigation with Merseyside Police to establish the cause of the blaze.

One neighbour, who did not want to be named, said: “We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses.

“The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street.”

Another woman said: “I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines.”

A contract aircraft company has identified the second pilot killed in the weekend crash of a firefighting helicopter in Yosemite National Park as Ryan Cutter.

Cutter and pilot Greg King both worked for Precision and were conducting water drops on a wildfire inside the park. They were the only people aboard when the AS332 Super Puma helicopter went down near Ostrander Lake shortly before 2 p.m. Sunday.

“These two men brought honor to the mission,” Precision wrote in a social media post accompanying photos of the pilots. “Their dedication and service will never be forgotten.”

The lake is roughly 9 miles (14 kilometers) south of Yosemite’s iconic El Capitan and about 7 miles (11 kilometers) northeast of Wawona, California.

Details about the circumstances surrounding the crash were not immediately released. It will be investigated by the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board. Precision did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment.

On Monday, firefighters, law enforcement officers and other first responders took part in a procession honoring Cutter and King, lining the route to a local airport as the pilots' remains were transported home to their families.

The pilots were contracted to work with an Idaho-based wildland firefighting crew that specializes in using ropes to descend from helicopters to reach otherwise inaccessible terrain, known as helitack rappelling, and had recently been assigned to assist with the Dome Fire. The Super Puma helicopter can carry eight or more rappellers at one time, and can also be used to deploy water buckets or specially mounted tanks.

The Dome Fire started Sept. 15 near Wawona, according to the National Interagency Fire Center. It’s burning on about 4.7 square miles (12.3 square kilometers) and is about 15% contained.

At least 14 people have died while helping fight wildfires in the U.S. this year, the most since 2022 when 25 deaths were recorded, according to government reports.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

News.title: France releases infertile Asian tiger mosquitoes to fight dengue threat
News.content:
French cities are fighting the growing threat of diseases like dengue, chikungunya and Zika in mainland Europe by releasing millions of sterile male Asian tiger mosquitoes.

Terratis, a new company in the southern city of Montpellier, is breeding infertile males on an industrial scale as a long-term solution to the rapid spread of the disease-carrying insects.

The sterile males are bred at a factory in the southern city of Montpellier and then released in urban hot zones where the mosquitoes are most prevalent. After they have mated, females reproduce only empty eggs for the remainder of their lives.

“By using this technique, the mosquitoes will have no descendants and then, in theory, we can reduce the population with each generation,” said Clelia Oliva, the founder of Terratis.

“We are confident of being able to achieve a reduction of between 70 and 90 per cent in the towns in which we are releasing the sterile mosquitoes.”

The company, which started only two years ago, has experienced a dramatic surge in demand in the last few years as France tries to deal with the invasive species.

News.title: ‘42 surgeries in 48 hours’: Doctors face extreme pressure in South Sudan
News.content:
Dr Mathiang Agany had no idea what was coming.

On a humid morning in April, scores of patients were rushed into his basic hospital in rural South Sudan after a shoot out between rival gangs. As the most senior doctor, Dr Agany, a maternal health specialist, had to perform 42 surgeries in just 48 hours.

Working alongside a second surgeon, a nurse and an anaesthetist, Dr Agany, 44, carefully extracted bullets from the vital organs of nine patients.

In 22 cases, he glued together fractured bones; and in four others he clamped damaged tissues shut and repaired torn organs.

Over the same 48 hour period, he also delivered seven babies through emergency c-sections.

“You are tired... but you can relax later,” he told The Telegraph over a video call.

“My job [was] to keep people alive”.

Separate to the ruinous four-year civil war in neighbouring Sudan, the violence plaguing South Sudan is inter-communal, a self-perpetuating cycle of cattle raiding, territorial disputes and revenge attacks carried out by armed youth militias from pastoral communities known as Titweng (“cattle guard”).

Young children were among the victims, including a four-year-old boy, whose leg was fractured by a gunshot, and a nine-month-old baby girl whose chest was grazed by the same bullet that killed her father.

News.title: Afghan medical students face expulsion from Pakistan
News.content:
An educational lifeline for young Afghan women banned by the Taliban from training as doctors in their homeland is in jeopardy after Pakistan’s medical authorities tried to have them expelled.

Several hundred Afghan female students studying across the border in Pakistan have been threatened with removal, amid rising tensions and tit-for-tat exchanges between the neighbours.

The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) which regulates medical education earlier this month ordered medical and dental colleges with Afghan students to kick them out.

Within days, major institutions including King Edward Medical University (KEMU), Shaikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Medical and Dental College, and the Services Institute of Medical Sciences, had ordered Afghan students to leave.

The nationwide order was estimated to have affected around 1,000 Afghan students, with 35 per cent of those thought to be female students.

Provincial high courts have now temporarily halted the expulsion pending further hearings, but Afghan students told The Telegraph they were terrified their careers would be ended.

“The government’s decision aimed to send us to the Stone Age because the Taliban in Afghanistan have banned female education,” said Sabiha Daftani, one of the 22 Afghan students given orders on September 7 by KEMU in Lahore on to leave within 24 hours.

“The fear is constant and haunting us,” she said.

News.title: Michael Carrick will not survive unless Manchester United change
News.content:
But so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

It begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the plan to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.

He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

We now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

That still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

Sports.title: ‘This is not an apology’ – Roy Keane defends calling Andy Robertson a ‘baby’ in awkward chat with Spurs star
Sports.content:
Next

ROY KEANE has cleared things up with Andy Robertson after infamously calling him a “big baby” in 2023.

Keane scolded the left-back – then with Liverpool – after claiming he was elbowed in the throat by linesman Constatine Hatzidakis in a 2-2 draw with Arsenal.



The incident happened just after referee Paul Tierney blew for half time as Robertson angrily approached the linesman.

Hatzidakis reacted by moving his arm backwards towards Robertson’s face and the Scot was convinced he made contact.



But Keane wasn’t pleased with Robertson’s behaviour at the time and claimed he grabbed the official first.

He told Sky Sports: “Do you know what it is, that Robertson? I’ve watched him a number of times. He’s a big baby. That’s what he is.

“Just get on with the game and concentrate on your defending. He does grab the linesman first.”

Keane came face-to-face with Robertson – now with Tottenham – for the first time since the incident while appearing on Stick to Football.

Gary Neville brought up the row and said to Robertson: “[Keane] doesn’t remember how or why he called you a baby.”

Keane then appeared to defend his comments and refused to say sorry as co-hosts Jamie Carragher and Ian Wright were left in stitches.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The Irish pundit said: “Players have to remember sometimes – this is not an apology.”

Robertson immediately chimed in by saying: “I wasn’t expecting one.”

Keane continued: “In the studio, we can have long days, can’t we? It can get a bit flat.



“Sometimes a player might do something and you’re agitated by having a long day.”

There was more laughter in the studio as Robertson replied: “The first two babies were alright, the third one was too far.”

Keane then chuckled before adding: “In my defence, when I said it… right, OK. We get agitated with traffic all the way to the game.

“But then none of [the pundits] are saying anything and I’m looking thinking, ‘You gotta say something.’

“That’s why I threw the last ‘baby’ in. They’re all staring at me going… ‘Say something.'”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Robertson played 378 times for the Reds across nine years and won a host of trophies – including two Prem titles and the Champions League.

The Scotland international joined Tottenham on a free transfer this summer and has since played six games for the struggling North London club.

SIR ALEX FERGUSON’s Manchester United dynasty did not start with signs pointing to the unprecedented success he would have.

Instead, a 2-0 loss in Division One at Oxford United’s old stadium, The Manor Ground, is what kicked off the Ferguson era at United.



And the first casualty of Ferguson’s reign came in the aftermath of that game in the form of the team’s bus driver, Derek “Sooty” Sutton.

The tale is told in extracts from Fergie: the Lost Tapes, detailed by The Telegraph, which regales taped recordings of interviews between Ferguson and Tom Tyrell, the late United reporter for Piccadilly Radio.



Tyrell’s grandson had hours of interviews on tape and approached Wayne Barton when he was in the early stages of writing a book about Ferguson’s first steps at United following his arrival at Old Trafford in November 1986.

And Fergie opened up on the tapes in a way he never did with the written press, and stories of his early struggles can be looked at again with the benefit of hindsight.

Pre-Ferguson, when Ron Atkinson was United manager, bus driver Sutton would join the coaching staff on the bench during games and brew tea which he would hand out at half-time.

He was retained as the team still needed a bus driver, and after taking them to the Manor Ground he took up his spot on the coaches bench – which was swiftly stopped by an astonished Ferguson.

A famous picture of Ferguson on the bench at Manor Road during that 2-0 loss next to Sutton makes for an incredible memory.

Ferguson’s side of the story to Tyrell was: “I had done my team-talk and was going into the dugout when I saw the bus driver sitting there.

“Let’s say that quickly stopped.”

“He did that behind my back to my bosses at the coach firm… I hate the man – he is a very hateful person.

MAURO ICARDI has gone to war against Argentina’s government – after his girlfriend’s antics landed him a driving ban.

The Argentine striker, a free agent since leaving Turks Galatasaray this summer, has been linked with a move to Roberto de Zerbi‘s struggling Tottenham.



But the Inter Milan and Paris Saint-Germain star Icardi has meanwhile landed in hot water in his home country.

Formerly married to model and TV presenter Wanda Nara, the 33-year-old is now in a relationship with Maria Eugenia Suarez – nicknamed La China.



She posted footage on social media of herself hanging out of the window of Icardi’s car as he drove at high speed.

Argentina’s Ministry of Transport has since reacted by stripping the footballer of his driving licence.

“After the video was published, we established that Icardi’s driving licence had expired. For this reason we have declared him to be banned from driving.

“Before he gets a new permit he will have to be tested to determine his aptitude to drive. Road safety does not allow for any exceptions.”

A furious Icardi took to social media to hit back at the government department.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“Make sure to fix the roads, so our country’s traffic flows better, instead of spending your time tweeting and scratching your b***s.

Sports.title: Scotland's Pocognoli has 'good mix' as he eyes winning start to his reign
Sports.content:
New Scotland head Sebastien Pocognoli has told Sky Sports it was time for change, believing he has a "good mix" in his first squad.

The Belgian is meeting his players for the first time this week as they train in the La Manga sunshine ahead of their Nations League opener against Slovenia.

Five players were handed their maiden full Scotland call-ups in his initial squad, with Blackburn Rovers midfielder Kristi Montgomery drafted in following the withdrawals of Kieran Tierney and Kenny McLean.

Image: The Scotland players are training in La Manga ahead of their Nations League opener

The longer international break - with four Nations League matches - gives the new boss more time with his squad as he looks to make an impact as Steve Clarke's successor.

"We have plenty of experience in the team, there are some new faces and young lads, and I think we have a good mix," Pocognoli told Sky Sports News.

"We need to make sure that the balance stays right, and to keep what makes the Scotland team really strong, it was the cohesion and really proper DNA in the team, and this needs to stay.

Image: Kristi Montgomery has been added to the Scotland squad

"The needed change was at this moment, because we follow the timelines, and the change is just about the things that we want to create on the pitch.

"It's also performance in your club, injury, and at the same time you need to make the change.

"What was provided in the past is massive to use it for the future.

"It's to find the right balance, like I said, so the experienced players will be important to continue to take care of this, and on the coaching staff point of view, we need to be aligned about what we want to achieve together.

"I want to see a team who are just really together, it's quite basic, attack together, defend together, but that's part of the Scotland mentality."

Image: Oli McBurnie is included in the Scotland squad for the first time since 2021

The Pocognoli era officially gets underway in Ljubljana on Saturday, with a game against Switzerland at Hampden Park three days later.

The squad then fly to North Macedonia on October 3 before returning to Glasgow to face Slovenia again on October 6.

Scotland were demoted from Nations League A after a play-off defeat by Greece last year and return to the second tier for this year's competition.

"There are many ways to be successful," the 39-year-old added.

"For me, in the Nations League, it's to stay competitive and try to be as much as possible higher in the ranking to go to League A.

"But just to recognise some principles on the pitch, recognise who are the leaders on the pitch, see some young lads playing, see team cohesion on the pitch.

"Also, to get the supporters excited. If we can combine with the result, and that's why we do this job, I would be really happy."

Sports.title: Packer on Red Roses losing their winning run, responding vs NZ and motherhood
Sports.content:
England Red Roses back-row Marlie Packer chats exclusively to Sky Sports following the end of their 39-Test winning run, and ahead of Saturday's huge home Test against New Zealand's Black Ferns.

Last week, Canada took their first step towards avenging Rugby World Cup final defeat to England by ending the Red Roses' record winning streak - dating back to 2022 - in a gripping 26-26 draw in Exeter.

Eight days short of the one-year anniversary of England's 33-13 World Cup final triumph at Twickenham, the sides treated a sold-out Sandy Park to an absorbing WXV Global Series clash featuring eight tries that went down to the final play with the clock in the red.

Speaking to Sky Sports on Tuesday, experienced back-row Packer - 2023's World Player of the Year - said New Zealand can expect a Red Roses backlash at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday.

"For us, obviously, it's not what we wanted, but it wasn't a loss. It's a learning curve," Packer said.

"It's made us put even more work into this week and focus on New Zealand come Saturday.

"I think it sharpens the mind, but also just shows we are human.

Image: The Red Roses saw their 39-Test winning streak end in a draw with Canada in Exeter last week

"It was an arm wrestle, and Canada brought it to us. It was a great game. It was the World Cup final last year and we played again now. But it's a three-Test series. We're now going to play them out in Canada twice.

"For us, it's about making sure we learn from that draw. We'll learn, and we'll do better next time.

"Most definitely [no better way to respond than beating New Zealand]. Playing at the home of English rugby, every player wants to play there.

"There's literally a new pitch as well there for us, so I'm really excited for that. The girls are buzzing just to get back out there.

"New Zealand can expect a very strong Red Roses team coming at them.

"The fact is we're not a team that worries about what happened last week. We're looking forward and we're looking forward to this game.

"They're going to see a very happy, strong Red Roses team coming in to put on a show for the fans, but also a performance for ourselves.

"I think they're going to be a very strong, dynamic New Zealand team, but we're a very dynamic, strong Red Roses team.

"So for the fans and for the neutral, it's going to be another great game of rugby."

Image: Packer says New Zealand's Black Ferns can expect a Red Roses backlash at Twickenham

Also on the horizon for Packer is the arrival of her second child, with fiancée and Red Roses team-mate Rosie Galligan due to give birth at the end of next month.

Due to that fact, Packer confirmed she is planning to step away from rugby for a period once the baby arrives.

"I'm really excited. It's five weeks until Rosie [Galligan] has our little girl.

"We're so excited, but for me, it's head into New Zealand this week, and then I can start getting really excited for baby girl to come.

"I won't be going away to Canada for the away leg, I'll be staying here and supporting from the sideline.

"I'll be supporting and cheering on the girls and I'm sure I'll be back on the phone to Mitch [head coach John Mitchell] a couple of times."

Packer believes the appointment points to the progress women's rugby and the Red Roses specifically have made in recent years.

"He's [Edwards] been excellent," Packer said. "He's been in the last couple of days.

Sports.title: Great Britain out of Billie Jean King Cup Finals as Boulter, Kartal beaten
Sports.content:
Great Britain's stay at the Billie Jean King Cup Finals lasted only one match as they fell to Czechia in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen.

Anne Keothavong's side were bidding to reach the last four for the fourth time in five years but were considerable underdogs and defeats for Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter sealed their fate.

Led by Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, the whole Czech team is ranked higher than any of Britain's players, and it was Noskova who sealed victory with a 6-2 7-6 (7-3) win over Boulter.

That followed a lengthy struggle between Marie Bouzkova and Kartal lasting a minute short of three hours, which the Czech eventually took 7-6 (7-2) 4-6 6-4.

Keothavong said: "For both these players [Boulter and Kartal], it required their absolute best and a bit of luck for the result to go our way. I can't fault their efforts. I think the Czechs are the strongest team here. I'd be surprised if they don't go on to win this competition."

It was a fine effort from Kartal, who was playing her first match in six months after suffering a stress fracture in her back in Indian Wells in March and she will now hope to finish the season strongly.

The Czechs will bid for their seventh title in the competition since 2011 while Britain's hopes of lifting the trophy for the first time are over for another year.

Keothavong's team have over-performed in the Billie Jean King Cup in recent years and did so again by reaching the finals, with an under-strength team upsetting Australia in April.

Neither Kartal nor Boulter were available for that tie, with the former in the early stages of an injury break that would eventually see her miss the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open.

Kartal found her range immediately against 26th-ranked Bouzkova, who has had a very good season, but could not convert a 40-0 lead in the third game to make it 3-0 and was edged out in a first-set tie-break.

She fought back well in the second set, often dictating the play against Bouzkova, who was preferred to Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova.

When Kartal broke to lead 2-1 in the deciding set, she appeared to be in the ascendancy, but fatigue seemed to catch up with the 24-year-old as Bouzkova reeled off four games in a row.

Kartal, now ranked down at 127, hung on grimly, saving three match points and breaking the Bouzkova serve, but she could not quite get back on level terms.

Great Britain will play Alexander Zverev's Germany in the quarter-finals of the Davis Cup in November.

Britain booked their return to the eight-team Finals, this year held in Bologna, over the weekend with a 4-0 victory against Ecuador at London's Copper Box.

It is the first time Leon Smith's side have reached the eight-team end-of-season event since 2023, when they fell at the first hurdle to Novak Djokovic's Serbia.

The 2015 champions will have their work cut out to avoid the same fate given Zverev has shown a strong commitment to the competition, heading straight from winning his second Grand Slam title of the year at the US Open to Halle to help Germany defeat Croatia.

Sports.title: Why did Tom Brady want the Raiders? Maybe this is why
Sports.content:
As I walked out of Allegiant Stadium in the middle of last November, following the Las Vegas Raiders' miserable home defeat to the Dallas Cowboys, I looked at all the downcast fans trudging away and I thought, why does Tom Brady want to be involved with this?

As many of you know, the seven-time Super Bowl-winning quarterback has a top front office job with the Raiders, as well as being a TV commentator, and it's his job to try to build the silver and black back into a contender. But they felt miles away from contention on that night in November.

They'd just lost 33-16 to the Cowboys, Geno Smith was ineffective a quarterback and arguing with fans in the stands, star defensive end Max Crosby was so frustrated at the final gun that he launched his helmet about 40 yards across the field.

That stadium in Las Vegas is nicknamed the Death Star, and as I walked away that night, I was reminded of the very first Star Wars film and thought, like the original Death Star, this thing needs to be blown up. Not the stadium, but the football program.

Head coach Pete Carroll was in the final throes of his potentially Hall of Fame career, and it's kind of fitting that he was in Las Vegas. It's the place where legendary names go to sell tickets, and I felt like that was what was happening there with the Raiders last year with Pete Carroll at the helm.

But this team is now laying down what seem to be proper foundations. They had the first overall pick in the NFL draft, and they used it well with the obvious selection of Fernando Mendoza out of Indiana.

And then you think, well, that means they're going to throw him into the fire straight away. That's been the way it's been done in the NFL in recent years. There aren't many teams that take a patient approach anymore.

Rookie quarterbacks are thrown to the wolves occasionally. Look at Cam Ward last year with the Tennessee Titans. Beaten from start to finish of the season, then spends the first part of the offseason rehabbing a shoulder injury that he suffered in Week 18.

The last really patient approach of quarterback that was notable was probably the Kansas City Chiefs resisting the temptation to put Patrick Mahomes in as a rookie, having him sit and learn for a year under an unselfish proven veteran in Alex Smith. And the Raiders have replicated that model, and so far it's worked.

They brought in Kirk Cousins, and the relationship between Cousins and Mendoza is not only endearing and quirky, it's also going to be very valuable. Cousins will have some limitations as a quarterback, but he is a safe pair of hands, and he knows how to get you in and out of the huddle. He knows how to win games.

Even this past week, as the Raiders moved to 2-0 on the season, you saw some of the veteran smarts that are going to help the Silver and Black this year.

On one of his touchdown passes against the Chargers, pre-snap, Cousins was constantly looking behind, signaling to the running back time and time again. Now yes, he could have been calling out protections, but it's also a good chance he was trying to pull the defense into thinking a running play was coming, and then he tosses the ball into the end zone for a touchdown.

So the Raiders are 2-0, one of the surprising teams to be with that record in the early stages of this season, and they can now really take their time in bringing Mendoza along. I spoke to Cousins in the summer, and he talked about why he was excited for this opportunity in Las Vegas, and I got the impression it was because this is his job for this year if things go well.

I could see a scenario where we have a wire-to-wire Cousins situation with the Raiders, and how he works with Klint Kubiak, the new head coach, he's got it all laid out before him. It's going to be fascinating to see.

The thing with Kirk as well is he's one of the most unselfish and nicest guys in the NFL. So even if it's to his long-term detriment, he is going to bring Mendoza along. He is not going to close himself off in the quarterback room. He's never going to keep secrets and tips and advice to himself.

He will be an extra coach in effect for their franchise quarterback in waiting. So it feels like there's a newer approach with the Raiders, a more patient approach.

I think Kubiak has time now to build the program the right way. He's got young players who he can work with for many years. Ashton Jeanty at running back, Brock Bowers at tight end. If they can keep Maxx Crosby healthy and productive on the other side of the ball, then there are pieces in place.

But the most important piece for the Raiders this season is a quarterback that very few teams around the NFL wanted anymore, and that's Kirk Cousins. He has a mighty role to play for the Silver and Black this season, but how he operates in the coming months could set the stage for this team to be competitive in many, many years to come.

Sports.title: PL assessed: Spurs lack backbone and history repeating itself at Man Utd
Sports.content:
Are Manchester City really title contenders? Is history repeating itself at Manchester United? Why do big-spending Tottenham still lack a backbone? After just five games, a number of storylines are already emerging.

Here, Sky Sports' team of writers assess the early talking points across an eventful start to the 2026/27 season...

Are Man City genuine title contenders?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League match between Manchester City and Sunderland.

Enzo Maresca was asked in his press conference whether he considered Manchester City to be title contenders after his side beat Sunderland 5-3 in one of the Premier League's most frenetic encounters to date. He gave the standard answer. "Too early to tell".

There is a pragmatic truth in that response. Five games is a small sample size. But I've seen enough to stick my neck out and say they will be right up there.

Maresca has so far made this exciting, dynamic City squad work for him, partly by design, partly by luck. He's lucky he has Erling Haaland. He's lucky the club believe so heavily in his cause they were willing to spend £320m on an entirely new midfield department.

But there is no doubt this squad is packed with entertainers who are determined to win. I like that the burden of scoring responsibility has been more equally shared; both Antoine Semenyo and Rayan Cherki can boast as many goal involvements as Haaland.

Haaland will suffer his inevitable dip at some point. Injuries will occur because City's most explosive players, Jeremy Doku in particular, are prone.

The Premier League is an ever more demanding beast and City are no longer Pep Guardiola's possession-based puppets.

But this is a team that will also get better with time. Maresca can now spend the next three weeks polishing up the bits he doesn't like, ready to go again. Barring any major injuries, City can - very probably will - rival Arsenal in the race.

Spurs find money can't buy them everything

Inevitable expectations followed when Spurs went big this summer - bigger than they've ever gone before.

Their £334m outlay sat them only behind perennial big spenders Chelsea and Man City across the transfer window.

Of course, any dreams of a return to the halcyon days at the top were always going to be tough to reach in the short term, as many previous clubs have found after a significant turnover of players.

But even with the patience required, sitting bottom of the table, with just two goals and as many points from their opening five games is miles below-par.

Spurs and Roberto De Zerbi's greatest concern will be that his side's issues are more than just teething problems.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Tottenham Hotspur and Aston Villa.

"In my 14 years as a coach, I've never seen a team like us, so fragile and inconsistent," De Zerbi said after their 3-0 defeat to Aston Villa.

For all the money spent, there is still no sign of a Spurs backbone. They are approaching two years since they last conceded first and went on to win. The pressure of even playing at home remains a problem - their lavish stadium has seen more Beyonce concerts than home wins over that same period.

And given the £85m outlay on Savio and future £60m on Omar Marmoush, fans and De Zerbi would hope for far more than the worst xG per shot of any team in the Premier League, and just two consolation goals in that Villa loss.

With the quality brought in, and flashes of showing already, things will improve and three uninterrupted weeks on the training ground will do the likes of James Maddison the world of good.

But after comfortably the biggest spend in their history, he lingering worry that Spurs still have so many areas left to address is not a problem fans had anticipated facing just five games into this new era.

Ron Walker

Same old story for Man Utd as Carrick feels the heat

Statistically, Manchester United had the easiest start to the 2026-27 Premier League campaign. Five points from five games later, it feels like the Red Devils have turned the clock back a year and there are more questions than answers.

Michael Carrick’s reign began with an incredible level of intensity when his side beat Manchester City. Compared to now, United look like a shell of that team. Constantly outrun and outfought.

Having only strengthened in the midfield over the summer, the defence looks out of date and vulnerable, conceding fewer than two goals in the Premier League just once.

While their attacking overhaul in the summer of 2025 made them look a threat, they now appear disjointed. Injuries to Amad Diallo and Benjamin Sesko have clearly hurt, while Marcus Rashford’s reintegration has hardly led to on-field results.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On The Premier League show, Dave Reed breaks down Manchester United's running stats and distance covered in the Premier League this season.

As if that’s not bad enough, they are also being held to ransom by 15-year-old JJ Gabriel, with reports suggesting that the teenager’s representatives want him to be allowed to leave because United have fallen behind other European giants.

Carrick was part of the backroom staff when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer felt similar pressure. Five years on, the story is the same.

A cult hero returns on an interim basis, does the job asked of him, is given the keys to Old Trafford and is then almost immediately under scrutiny.

When will the rerun of the same programme finally come to an end? Before that, Carrick has to ensure that he doesn’t hand another one of his former clubs their first Premier League win after the international break when United host bottom-of-the-table Tottenham. Lose, and it's anyone’s guess where things go.

Callum Bishop

Are Arsenal really stronger than last season?

Many expected Arsenal to dominate the league this season, partly due to the lack of a competitive rival capable of taking their Premier League crown.

But the 3-0 loss to Brighton on Saturday, coupled with Man City continuing their perfect start to the campaign, has tested that theory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Brighton and Arsenal.

Yes, we're only five games in, and the jury is still out on whether Arsenal are truly better than the team that won the league last season in terms of quality.

The Gunners signed Ezri Konsa to bolster their defence but he has replaced the injured William Saliba in the team, so is not exactly seen as an improvement in that area, other than depth.

Bruno Guimaraes was another marquee signing and showed his worth against Sunderland. But his underwhelming performance at Brighton raised early questions about whether he too is an improvement on Myles Lewis-Skelly, who is perhaps better-skilled than the Brazilian in handling a high-pressing opponent.

Arsenal have won every Premier League game in which Lewis-Skelly has started in midfield.

Christos Tzolis has been a successful buy overall but he is yet to score for Arsenal. The goalscoring output that the now-departed Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli provided last season are yet to be replaced.

Other than those three players, Arsenal are pretty much the same squad that won the league last season.

The likes of Martin Odegaard and Bukayo Saka have found some early-season form that they lacked last term - but the next batch of fixtures post-international break will test the claims about whether Arsenal have improved. It will test their title defence.

Sam Blitz

Liverpool unbeaten but the real test is now coming

Liverpool's hard-fought 1-0 win at Bournemouth on Sunday maintained head coach Andoni Iraola's unbeaten record since taking charge of the club in the summer which when also taking into account pre-season friendlies, now stretches to 12 games.

In fact, the Basque is the first Reds boss to remain unbeaten in his first five league matches since Joe Fagan all the way back in September 1983.

However, do not let those statistics trick you into thinking Iraola has Liverpool back firing again, with the Reds having passed the eye test in only a handful of competitive contests so far this season, while at the same time needing late goals to rescue a point against bottom-half sides Newcastle United and Nottingham Forest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on a bonus podcast after Liverpool's win over Bournemouth, Jamie Carragher questioned Florian Wirtz's impact since arriving at Anfield and highlighted the challenge of fitting him into the team without disrupting the balance.

And despite having now kept three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League for the first time since September 2024, the back line still looks shaky, especially when defending set plays.

Meanwhile, the midfield is not clicking as the new man tries to find the right balance and £116.5m playmaker Florian Wirtz remains the elephant in the room, although less so after Jamie Carragher's analysis of his anonymous and error-strewn display at the Vitality.

Do not forget either that Iraola has been handed a relatively gentle start to this campaign, although that all changes after the international break when the Reds face far sterner tests at home to league leaders Man City and in-form Brighton, with a tricky-looking trip to high-flying Brentford in between.

Come through those examinations unscathed and we can start talking about a Reds revival under their new boss.

Rich Morgan

Chelsea playing catch-up in title bid after mixed start

Chelsea's mixed start is captured perfectly by their mid-table position. Their attack has dazzled but their defence has been disastrous as Xabi Alonso looks to find a balance with his 3-4-3 formation. They must do better.

There have been few issues with the 'JP Morgan' frontline which is living up to its billing. Morgan Rogers has made a fast start to his Chelsea career following his £117m move with three goals and an assist.

His partnership with Cole Palmer is blossoming, and his form earned him a recall to the England squad, while Joao Pedro's three goals and three assists got him back in with Brazil.

Entertainment hasn't been in short supply. Chelsea have won 3-2, 4-3 and 6-3 but their last two results, a 2-2 draw with Hull City and a 3-0 defeat at Brentford, have raised concerns that their leaky defence will prevent them from mounting a title challenge despite signing experienced goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.

Image: Chelsea have been struggling all season at the back

They were bullied against Brentford, overpowered in the second half and conceded from another set piece, the fourth time this season - taking their overall tally since the start of last season to 23, the joint-worst out of any Premier League side. Poaching set-piece coach Austin MacPhee from Aston Villa hasn't worked yet either.

Chelsea's lack of control has been highlighted, particularly compared to last season, when they could rely on midfielders Moises Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez. Caicedo hasn't played a minute due to injury and Fernandez departed on Deadline Day, with Chelsea unable to bring in a replacement.

It's meant untested duo Romeo Lavia and Reece James have mostly played in the middle. Ironically, in the two games when Chelsea have had more possession, against Brentford and Hull, they earned their two worst results. Chelsea had just 26 per cent of the ball in their 4-3 win over Brighton.

Alonso must achieve Champions League qualification at the very least, while going far in cup competitions, to make up for their lack of European football and make this season a success.

If they fix their defensive issues, then there's no reason why their attack can't put them in the title mix, but they're already seven points adrift.

David Richardson

Tension and stress lifted after Villa's slow start

Alarm bells were ringing at Villa Park following their worrying start to the Premier League season, but a 3-2 win against Tottenham before the international break has hinted that Aston Villa's rebuild could be slowly coming together.

Unai Emery's side had to wait until the 2-1 defeat to Nottingham Forest on September 12 to score their first goal, and the victory at Spurs marks their lone win across the first five games.

It was a summer of change after losing Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Emiliano Martinez, Ollie Watkins, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne. But the performance against Spurs, and the players that shone during it, offer an insight into what could be on the horizon from this side.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Tottenham Hotspur and Aston Villa.

Johan Manzambi announced himself to the fans perfectly with a goal and an assist on his first start for the club.

Zion Suzuki continued to impress with both his shot-stopping and passing ability, while Nicolas Jackson's finish and footwork to manufacture the chance hinted that Emery could be the one to get the best out of him once again.

The pieces of the rebuild - with Ibrahim Mbaye and Alejandro Garnacho also easing into their new surroundings - are slowly paying dividends.

The tension and stress of their poor start to the campaign has now been lifted. Emery is never one to panic, as the similar slow start to last season showed, but now the work can really begin.

Patrick Rowe

Brentford and Brighton's push for top four?

There would have been no prizes for predicting Man City and Arsenal would be first and second in the Premier League table heading into this extended international break. But who'd have guessed Brighton and Brentford would be in third and fourth?!

In fairness, these two teams are absolutely brilliant at finding an edge, hence why they make up two-thirds of the newly-coined 'Bermuda Triangle'. They don't have the same financial clout as the division's elite, but year after year, they trouble them regardless.

The weekend just gone was perhaps the best example of that.

On Friday night, Brentford took advantage of Chelsea's defensive woes to win 3-0 at the Gtech. That result ended an 88-year wait for a home win over the Blues - but also ensured Keith Andrews' side remain unbeaten in their opening five games of a top-flight season for the very first time (W2 D3).

On Saturday, Brighton beat reigning champions Arsenal by the same scoreline. The Gunners took 36 touches in the opposition box, but managed just two shots on target. The Seagulls had five and scored with three of them.

Fabian Hurzeler's side have scored three more goals than any other team in the Premier League (16) and their goal difference is something to behold (+11).

This hasn't come as a complete surprise, of course. Brighton and Brentford have been outsmarting those around them for several years now. But could this be the campaign the pair really set the cat among the pigeons?

Dan Long

Who are the early-season relegation candidates?

Newly-promoted teams always top the odds for relegation candidates, but heading into the first international break, only one is currently in the bottom three.

The biggest surprise package has been Hull City with only one loss so far - and an opening weekend win against Man Utd. Two wins for Ipswich have them above the likes of Aston Villa and Tottenham in mid-table.

Even Frank Lampard's Coventry City have impressed, despite sitting in 18th on goal difference.

Of course, after five games, it's hard to predict if these teams can sustain this over the next 33 matches - but eyes are also turning to some established Premier League sides who are already staring down a difficult season.

Sports.title: Webster: Littler won't walk away from darts over crowd treatment
Sports.content:
Sky Sports Darts' Mark Webster believes Luke Littler will not walk away from darts over crowd treatment, adding the PDC are determined to rid the sport of whistling but that boos will always remain.

Littler's bid for a clean sweep of all major PDC titles in 2026 was ended on Sunday after a crushing 10-4 defeat to Jonny Clayton in the last eight at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam, but the main talking point coming out of the event was Littler's continued fractious relationship with darts fans.

Indeed, earlier in the tournament Littler threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during victory over Nathan Aspinall.

The back-to-back world champion also faced a hostile environment during Friday's win over home favourite Danny Noppert and it escalated on Saturday night as referee Charlie Corstorphine had to intervene in the last-16 win over Aspinall.

Littler has taken a stance against volatile crowds before, refusing to travel to European Tour events in Germany as a result of his treatment from fans there, but Webster does not believe Littler will leave the sport entirely over it.

"No, I don't think he's [Littler] going to walk away from the sport over this," Sky Sports Darts' Webster said.

"He was obviously very upset about how he was treated in the Netherlands at the weekend, but some of the opponents he played - a home favourite in Danny Noppert - he was going to get some rough treatment there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Luke Littler's bid for a clean sweep of all major PDC titles in 2026 is over after defeat to Jonny Clayton at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam

"I'm not saying it's right, and the whistling, I know they're trying to take it out of the game.

"The booing, they won't be able to stop, but the whistling is something that's a bugbear to a lot of players at the minute. The PDC are trying to get rid of it.

"I spoke to a few of the security guys who are experimenting with stuff within the crowd, but obviously it got on top of Luke Littler this weekend.

"He was saying after games he wasn't happy with the treatment he got. I don't like saying it, but a lot of the booing is part of the game now.

"He kind of has drawn attention to it by speaking about it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look as a fired up Luke Littler was booed by the crowd in Amsterdam during his World Series of Darts win against Danny Noppert. Credit@OFFICIALPDC

"The whistling is annoying, and I think it's a bit sharper when the players are throwing and it puts them off. A constant boo, I think players can deal with. Luke has dealt with it in the past, and I'm sure he'll be okay.

"If he chooses to miss events in the Netherlands, that's his prerogative. There is a Premier League night there, which I think he'll play, but the European Tour, there's 15 events during the year. He doesn't really need to go to the Netherlands, so he can cherry-pick there.

"So if he does decide to boycott, he can still plan out his year, really.

"He's got a long time left in the sport. I don't think he'll leave the sport as early as people make out.

"He loves playing darts and he's brilliant at it, so I think he'll just bounce back. He'll get some more rough treatment and he'll try and deal with it the way he has done the majority of the time, and just win games and win tournaments. He was a little bit hurt at the weekend."

Darts in 2026 Event Winner Dates World Championship Luke Littler Dec 11-Jan 3 World Masters Luke Littler Jan 29-Feb 1 UK Open Luke Littler March 6-8 Premier League* Luke Littler Feb to May World Cup* Luke Littler and Luke Humphries June 11-14 World Matchplay Luke Littler July 18-16 World Series of Darts Finals* Ross Smith September 17-20 World Grand Prix Sept 28-Oct 4 European Championship October 22-25 Grand Slam of Darts November 14-22 Players Championship Finals November 27-29 *Non-ranking event

'Littler is the main draw in darts - he'll bounce back'

Webster added that Littler remains the main face of darts after the 19-year-old's incredible achievements over recent years.

"We're still in this boom on the back of what he [Littler] did," he said.

"There's other players, but he is the main draw. After that run to the World Championships final on debut, and he's backed up by winning back-to-back World Championships. People buy a ticket to watch him. They may boo him, they may whistle when he throws.

"He's the best player in the world, and we've got this sort of culture in our country where the best players receive a bit of rough treatment. They want them knocked off their perch.

"He gets fired up himself, and I'm sure he'll bounce back in the right way at the Grand Prix in Leicester.

Image: Littler's performance was purely down to 'pressure', according to Raymond van Barneveld

"It's easy to forget he's 19 because he's been around since he was 16, and he's done a lot in those three years. We're already talking about sort of holding every major. As good as he is, that's always going to be difficult.

"I don't think he should be too hard on himself about the weekend, he was beaten by the better man in Jonny. He acknowledged that. He was just a bit disappointed with the crowd.

"I fully expect him to win a few of the majors remaining. I think the European Championships will be a massive priority for him, because then he's ticked every box.

"And then obviously go on to Ally Pally and try and retain that, keep the streak going, and just keep cementing his place at world No 1.

"He's going to come away with some more major titles, that's for sure. I think these tournaments kind of favour him in terms of longer formats.

"Who's going to compete in there? It's going to be tough, but it's up to the other players and to see where his hunger is at in a minute."

What next for Littler?

Littler can still sweep the ranking events in 2026 - the World Series Finals, like the World Cup and Premier League, is non-ranked - if he wins the remaining four majors in Leicester, Dortmund, Wolverhampton and Minehead this autumn.

'The Nuke' has withdrawn from two Players Championship events in the Netherlands less than 24 hours after his bid for a PDC majors title clean sweep was dashed.

The teenager - currently £16,750 adrift of the final qualification spot - had hinted he may not try to reach the Players Championship Finals should his hopes of a major sweep end in the Netherlands.

What could the rest of Littler's year look like? Sports.title: Branthwaite reveals brain study helped him conquer injuries and earn England call
Sports.content:
Jarrad Branthwaite has credited a “complex” rehabilitation programme in Germany, which analysed links between his injuries and his brain and movement, with his return to the England squad.

The Everton defender’s fine start to the season has been rewarded with a place in Thomas Tuchel’s squad for the Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia. If selected, it will be Branthwaite’s second appearance for the England senior side having been blighted by hamstring and groin problems in recent years.

The centre-half has been ever-present in the Premier League after being restricted to 10 appearances last season by repeated hamstring issues. In the search for a solution to his injury problems, Everton sent the 24-year-old to the MYOS sports and health clinic in Munich at the start of the summer. Branthwaite believes that was a turning point.

“I sat down with the club after the three or four times where I was picking up the injuries,” he said. “It was to look at the wider picture, look at the holistic approach of the body essentially. I went over there for three or four weeks working with a team alongside the club, just to assess different things, and hopefully that has helped. There were a lot of different things looked at like movement patterns, the brain; it was quite complex, but fingers crossed it has worked.”

Branthwaite was carried off in tears after sustaining another hamstring injury in the Merseyside derby defeat by Liverpool in April. The setback ended his season and his prospects of making a late play for the World Cup squad, and Everton’s form also plummeted in his absence.

“It is probably the worst thing as a footballer not to be on the pitch and I think when it keeps happening it is mentally tough because you are sort of doubting your body and going on the pitch wary of what is going to happen. I think now I am in a position where I got managed throughout the pre-season, managed my load well and hopefully I can stay on the pitch this season.”

Branthwaite made his England debut as a substitute in a win against Bosnia and Herzegovina in June 2024, and a recall was a target this season alongside a return to full fitness.

“I found out when I was having breakfast – it was a good start to the day,” the Everton defender said of his call-up last week. “It is a proud moment. Over the last season or so it has been a target of mine. When I have been out and not on the pitch, I wanted to get back playing and give myself the best possible chance to be in and around the England squad after missing such a lot of time.

Sports.title: Mexican soccer banned promotion and relegation. Senators may bring it back
Sports.content:
The debate over the absence of promotion and relegation in Mexican soccer has reached the floor of the country’s Senate, where officials announced that a legislative reform to restore the system will be proposed on Tuesday.

Senator Clemente Castañeda of the Movimiento Ciudadano party put forward the proposal, backed by representatives from other party leaderships, including Ignacio Mier of the ruling Morena party.

Castañeda stated that the initiative is critical for “expressly incorporating sporting merit among the obligations that national sports associations must observe” and ensuring promotion and relegation are enshrined in Mexican law.

“When they closed off the possibility of promotion, they didn’t just change a sporting rule; they also restricted a path for players, staff, and sports projects to grow in a country that needs to open up opportunities,” Castañeda said.

The senator said that she invited the president of the Liga MX, Francisco Iturbide, and the commissioner of the Mexican football, Mikel Arriola, and they declined.

The Associated Press contacted the Mexican Federation for comment but did not receive a response.

Broken promises

Owners of Mexican top-flight teams eliminated promotion and relegation in April 2020, citing financial difficulties among second-division clubs that were exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic.

Under the original plan, the suspension was set for five years, with the system scheduled for reinstatement last year so that a team could earn promotion and another face relegation at the end of the most recent season in May of this year.

However, reinstatement never materialized. Starting last year, several second-division clubs began protesting to demand that authorities honor the agreement. At the time, the Mexican Football Federation stated that returning to the system was impossible because the necessary economic conditions did not yet exist.

“The whole pandemic thing was a sham; they always knew they were going to permanently shut down promotion and relegation,” said Alberto Castellanos, president of U de G Leones Negros, one of the protesting teams.

View image in fullscreen Senator Clemente Castañeda has led the introduction of legislation to reinstate promotion and relegation. Photograph: Luis Barron/Eyepix Group/LightRocket/Getty Images

High barriers and disillusioned investors

Liga MX imposed stringent requirements on second-division teams, mandating a certification process before they could aspire to play in the top tier. These rules included a venue capacity requirement of 30,000 seats – a standard not even met by all active first-division clubs.

The elimination of promotion directly affected new investors in Mexican soccer. Cancún FC was acquired in 2022 by an investment group led by figures like former Houston Astros general manager Jeff Luhnow on the premise that promotion would return.

“When we bought the team, we saw great potential – potential that often even Mexicans don’t see – but the current system fosters mediocrity; it’s very sad,” said Giovani Solazzi, the team’s president.

Facing pushback from some second-division owners, Mexican soccer authorities completely removed the promotion and relegation system from the regulations this year. Neither the Federation nor Liga MX provided an explanation for the decision.

Public outcry

The owner of Club América – one of Mexico’s most powerful clubs and arguably its most influential decision-maker – stated last month that he supports reinstating the system, provided the right conditions are met.

“I am in favor of promotion and relegation. Everyone makes comparisons, pointing out that it exists in Spain, England, or Portugal; however, those countries have very solid second divisions, whereas here, we haven’t managed to build that kind of solid second-division league,” he said.

Once promotion was officially scrapped, widespread protests broke out during second-division matches. Players responded on the pitch by standing motionless after the opening whistle or passing the ball passively without attacking.

“I arrived in Mexico on 8 June under the premise that there would be promotion – joining Morelia, a team contending for promotion – but then we were notified that it wasn’t happening,” said Spanish goalkeeper Roberto Galán. “That’s why we protested and the clubs were sanctioned, but the protests will continue because we have the right to make our voices heard.”

Fan groups have also shown up at stadiums wearing protest shirts to voice their discontent.

And last week, Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission (CNA) launched an investigation into potential monopolistic practices in the Mexican league centering on the absence of a promotion and relegation system.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Klopp, Xavi, Zidane, Mancini: big nations ready to unleash bigger dogs
Sports.content:
INTERNATIONAL SUPERSTARS

While Thomas Tuchel continues to gaslight his employers at the FA into believing he was in no way responsible for England’s comically shambolic semi-final exit at the hands of Argentina, not every head coach who underperformed at the Geopolitics World Cup is still in their job. A total of 17 different managers who took teams to North America have since left their roles, with safety-first’s Steve Clarke, failing-up’s Roberto Martínez and tyranny’s Marcelo Bielsa among them. In Europe, teams such as Portugal (Jorge Jesus), Croatia (Slaven Bilic), Scotland (Sébastien Pocognoli), Czechia (Santi Denia) and Belgium (Mark van Bommel) will go into the Nations League under new management, but it is towards the bigger dogs of the football pack where Football Daily wishes to turn today’s beady gaze.

Germany: Having been accused of using his role as a TV pundit to undermine Julian Nagelsmann during the GWC, it was no great shock to see Jürgen Klopp take over from the 39-year-old when he stepped down. Klopp immediately fired a volley across the bows of the German press pack and will begin his first role in international management with a trip to the Netherlands. Unlike his predecessor, the former Liverpool boss is unlikely to rock up to training on a skateboard and it will be intriguing to see how successfully he instils his ethos of heavy-metal football in a group of players he only gets into the rehearsal room three or four times a season. “This is the pinnacle, the absolute high point of my footballing career as coach,” he parped, raising sceptical eyebrows on Merseyside. “I will give everything I have got.”

Netherlands: Upon replacing Ronald Koeman, Xavi Hernández was eager to emphasise his deep connection with the Dutch. While it remains to be seen if the former Spanish midfield maestro is a bike-riding windmill enthusiast with a capacity for extreme bluntness, he was handed his Barcelona debut by Louis van Gaal and name-dropped club legends Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels during his unveiling. Third choice on a shortlist of four behind Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot, Xavi can at least sleep safe in the knowledge the Dutch FA considered him a slightly more glamorous candidate than Michael Reiziger, and will begin his international reign with a match against a fellow newbie. “I feel motivated because we are playing against Germany,” he cheered, before his opening game in Amsterdam. “So yeah, it’s a big challenge from the beginning, but I think we will be ready.”

Italy: Having suffered the indignity of failing to qualify for their third successive World Cup, Italian football suits didn’t so much go back to the drawing board, as back in time when it came to replacing Gennaro Gattuso. Roberto Mancini is back for his second spell in charge, having previously masterminded victory in the European Championship in 2021 and subsequent failure to get to the HRWC in 2022. “I believed that the best person to become head coach was ‌Roberto Mancini,” tooted FIGC top brass Giovanni Malagò, shortly after his organisation’s plot to install Andrea Pirlo in the role was foiled by the former midfielder’s commercial ties to a Russian betting firm. A famously patient people when it comes to their national football team, fans of the Azzurri are surely unlikely to get upset if early results against Belgium and Turkey don’t go their team’s way …

France: It was a matter of when, not if Zinedine Zidane took over the national team and despite his pedigree as a three-time Bigger Cup-winning coach of Real Madrid, he has extremely big boots to fill. After taking over from his former French water carrier, Didier Deschamps, Zizou played all the right notes. “I’ve been looking forward to this moment,” he cheered. “It’s a dream come true. The France national team has been the most beautiful thing that has ever happened to me. It’s a great adventure that I hope is just beginning.” Kylian Mbappé has already described the prospect of working under Zizou as being “like a film”. Its box-office success will almost certainly stand or fall on the chemistry – or lack of it – between two of French football’s most iconic leading men.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Will Unwin at 5.45pm (BST) for Women’s Bigger Cup updates on Bayern Munich 2-2 Manchester City.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Every time I see it, I’m cringing, I’m in disbelief. It’s horrible to watch back and to see what could have been. Thankfully I was fortunate I did manage to fall on to the floor at the right time, so nothing snapped as the roller went over me … I was able to get my left arm up and relieve some of the pressure, and then I was able to get my teammates around me who were able to lift it, and I was able to squeeze out but at that moment where it was crushing my left leg, it was quite terrifying, I must say” – Andros Townsend explains what it was like to be run over by that pitch roller in Thailand and just how much he thanks his lucky stars for not coming to more harm than suffering a few cuts and bruises.

As an Ipswich fan marooned in Sussex, I spent much of my teenage years at the Goldstone which, despite being a dump (I stood on the crumbling South Stand), held a certain magic for me. It still does, actually. Haven’t been to the Amex yet – hopeless nostalgia is undoubtedly a factor. The team weren’t much better than the ground for most of that time, but the 1987-88 promotion season was memorable. Garry Nelson was a bit special, Doug Rougvie had played under Fergie at Aberdeen and Gerry Armstrong had legendary status after *that* goal, but the rest of the team probably (and unfairly ) fall into the journeyman category. I loved them all. Keith Dublin dribbling his way into and then out of trouble, sleeves-up Kevin Bremner who grafted and worked the Albion into the promotion places, Deano (one of the Wilkins brothers) classy and, of course, Barry Lloyd, who never brought a sub on until the last four or five minutes, frustrating us beyond belief. And into this pantheon came teenage Johnny C who, to start with, was utterly hapless, hence the nickname football genius. Somehow, despite this, we took to him from the off and it was lovely to see how he grew into becoming an Albion legend in what were fallow years. Blimey, not sure where that all came from – you can probably tell I’m stuck out in the middle of the Fens on a slow-moving train. But thank you for bringing it all back to me!” – Jonathan Foulkes.
