EXTRADITION AND MUTUAL legal assistance agreements that actually function under pressure — so that an arrest made at a neighbor’s request, as Ghana made of a suspect wanted in Liberia, does not end in a suspect who “reportedly vanished” before he can be handed over.

A JOINT TASK FORCE tracking networks, not just shipments — built to follow people like Leijdekkers and his associates across the borders they cross freely, rather than waiting for each country to rediscover the same names independently.

NONE OF THIS IS EXOTIC. Regional bodies elsewhere have built exactly these tools. What West Africa has lacked is not the blueprint but the political will to treat trafficking as a shared emergency rather than each nation’s private scandal.

The Region’s Future Is What Is Actually at Stake

IT WOULD BE A MISTAKE to see this only as a drug story. Every scanner that gets overridden for cash, every police escort sold for $5,000, is a small transaction that adds up to something much larger: a generation of West African institutions being hollowed out from the inside, one bribed official at a time. Money on this scale does not stop at corrupting a customs post. It buys judges, financiers elections, and arms the same criminal networks it enriches. A region that cannot secure its own ports and highways against traffickers will find it just as hard to secure them against anything else.

JOS LEIJDEKKERS WILL eventually be caught, or he will not; that is, in the end, a matter for Dutch, Sierra Leonean and Interpol investigators. But whether West Africa produces the next Leijdekkers-scale network, and whether it takes years or weeks to unravel next time, is entirely within this region’s own hands. Liberia, Ghana, Sierra Leone and their neighbors have now each been handed unmistakable proof that their ports, their patrols and their own officials are being tested for weaknesses by organized crime on an industrial scale. The only responsible answer is to close that gap together, before the next shipment — and the next bribe — finds it first. The choice in front of West Africa’s governments is not complicated. Cooperate now, or explain later why they didn’t.

World.title: Liberia: Freeman Challenges Liberia’s US$1 Billion Revenue Story, Says US$400M Is Being “Squeezed” From Economy
World.content:
Liberia’s Economist and Politician Mr. Simeon Freeman

MONROVIA — Liberia’s historic crossing of the US$1 billion domestic revenue mark is being celebrated by the government as a major fiscal achievement.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr

Liberia’s economist and politician Simeon Freeman has raised fresh questions over Liberia’s revenue system, claiming that approximately US$400 million is being squeezed out of the local economy through charges that are not reflected in the government’s budgetary revenue figures.

Freeman said the amount includes payments associated with port operations, terminal charges, shipping companies, tracking fees and other costs incurred when goods enter Liberia.

While acknowledging that international trade taxes account for a significant portion of government revenue, he argued that the broader financial burden imposed on importers and consumers extends beyond what appears in the national budget.

“If you put all of that inflow together, you’re talking about US$400 million that is squeezed out of the local economy,” Freeman stated.

Freeman argues that these additional costs ultimately find their way into the prices Liberians pay for goods and services, particularly in an economy heavily dependent on imports. “By mopping money from the local economy, it makes the cost of goods very expensive,” he said, linking the alleged unbudgeted charges to rising consumer prices and declining purchasing power.

“How much money is circulating out of the pockets of Liberian consumers and businesses through charges that do not appear as direct government revenue in the national budget,” he intimated.

In a pointed economic commentary, Freeman challenged the growing celebration around government’s record revenue performance, arguing that the headline figure alone does not tell the full story of Liberia’s economic condition.

His argument is that government can increase revenue while ordinary Liberians simultaneously become poorer in real terms if the cost of raising that revenue is ultimately transferred to consumers through higher prices. “Every aspect of this budget is mopping money from the local economy,” Freeman said.

“By mopping money from the local economy, it makes the cost of goods very expensive.” The comments come days after President Joseph Nyuma Boakai announced that Liberia had raised more than US$1 billion in domestic revenue during the first nine months of 2026.

The President described the achievement as a historic milestone and said the money was mobilized through taxes, duties, fees and other lawful payments from individuals and businesses. He also said the government intends to ensure that the revenue translates into benefits that Liberians can see and feel.

But Freeman’s analysis challenges Liberians to look beyond the revenue headline.

‘The money is coming from somewhere’

Freeman’s argument rests on a basic economic principle: government revenue does not appear in isolation from the economy, he said

Taxes, duties, fees and other government charges are ultimately paid by individuals and businesses. Where businesses incur higher costs, those costs can be passed on to consumers through higher prices. That, Freeman argues, is the part of the US$1 billion story that deserves greater public scrutiny.

“The government gets the money by mopping and squeezing it from the economy,” he said “What that means is, when tuition goes up, it’s not the school that you blame.” For Freeman, the issue is therefore not whether government should collect revenue.

It is whether the country’s revenue system is increasing the productive capacity of the economy or simply extracting more money from an economy whose businesses and households are already under pressure.

Freeman focused particularly on Liberia’s import-dependent economy

He argued that the official tax figures do not necessarily capture the full range of costs associated with moving goods into Liberia.

According to his analysis, importers face customs-related taxes alongside port, terminal, shipping, tracking and other charges.

The economist contends that when those costs accumulate, they eventually become part of the price paid by consumers. “Something costs one dollar in China, very cheap. One dollar in China comes to Liberia and costs about 10, 15 dollars. Now you understand why.”

Freeman’s specific estimate that approximately US$400 million is being removed from the economy through additional charges is still subject to independent verification. But his broader economic argument is more fundamental: the price consumers pay at the end of the supply chain reflects not only the original cost of the product, but also the taxes, fees and other costs accumulated along the way.

The uncomfortable connection between revenue and prices

Freeman linked government revenue collection to the everyday economic struggles facing Liberians. He pointed to rising transportation costs, food prices, rent and education expenses as examples of the pressure households are experiencing.

“When government mop up the money, they spend it on themselves and not necessarily on us,” Freeman argued.

The IMF has reported that Liberia’s recent revenue performance has been supported by stronger income and international trade taxes, among other sources. It has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a prudent fiscal stance and improving the quality of public spending.

Freeman also turned his attention to Liberia’s debt

He argued that a significant portion of the government’s fiscal resources is already committed to servicing debt.

The FY2026 budget and subsequent fiscal planning have indeed placed substantial emphasis on debt management, while the IMF has continued to monitor Liberia’s debt position as part of its economic program.

Freeman’s concern is that Liberia could find itself in a cycle where government collects more revenue, borrows more money to finance development, and then uses an increasing amount of future revenue to service those obligations.

“You have to keep borrowing repeatedly for every major project,” Freeman said. His broader warning is that revenue growth without corresponding growth in production, investment and household incomes may not fundamentally transform the economy.

President Boakai has argued that the billion-dollar milestone must ultimately translate into tangible improvements in the lives of Liberians.

World.title: Eastern strengthens disaster preparedness
World.content:
Eastern Province Assistant Secretary Clement Chilembo says the province is strengthening disaster preparedness measures to minimise loss of lives and property during natural disasters.

Mr Chilembo said early warning and adequate preparation were critical in reducing the impact of disasters, instead of relying on ad-hoc responses after disasters occurred.

Mr Chilembo was speaking when a joint team from the World Food Programme (WFP) and the National Disaster Risk Management Division (NDRMD) visited him at his office.

Mr Chilembo said early warning systems were important because advance information enabled authorities and communities to prepare adequately for anticipated disasters.

“To be warned is very important, because when you are warned it means you will be able to prepare properly,” he said.

Mr Chilembo said ad-hoc responses were often ineffective and came with several challenges that could result in loss of lives and property.

He said Government has not worked in isolation in disaster management but partnered with reputable institutions, including the United Nations and other cooperating partners.

Mr Chilembo welcomed the involvement of WFP in strengthening disaster preparedness, noting that the organisation had worked with Government for many years to support communities affected by disasters.

He said such partnerships had helped communities understand disasters and access materials and other support to cope with their effects.

Mr Chilembo cited the recent disaster in Lundazi District as a reminder of the need to strengthen preparedness and response mechanisms.

He said training district staff in disaster preparedness would enhance the capacity of authorities to respond effectively to emergencies.

Mr Chilembo said district commissioners and their disaster management committees were functional, while the province also had a Provincial Disaster Management Committee supported by a secretariat and relevant staff.

He said information and skills gained from the workshop would help the province and districts improve their preparedness measures.

Mr Chilembo also stressed the importance of budgeting for disaster preparedness, saying budgets enabled authorities to identify their needs and determine the financial and material resources required.

“At the end of the workshop, people have to make budgets. Budgets are very important because they will tell us what our needs are, the amounts of resources required, be it financial or material,” he said.

He called for a multi-sectoral approach involving Government ministries, departments and agencies, non-governmental organisations and other stakeholders to maximise available resources in disaster preparedness and response.

Mr Chilembo said simple preventive measures, such as securing roofs before strong winds occurred, could help reduce damage to property.

“If we secure our roofs, we will prevent the roofs from being blown off,” he said.

He assured that Eastern Province would use the information and skills gained from the workshop to strengthen preparedness and protect lives and property.

“We will fine-tune our efforts to ensure property is protected, life is protected and even if a wind comes on board, we shall surmount the effects of this particular natural disaster,” he said.

World.title: Govt. urges stakeholder involvement in implementation of occupational safety framework
World.content:
Government says the successful implementation of the new occupational health and safety framework requires the active participation and cooperation of all stakeholders.

Ministry of Labour and Social Security Permanent Secretary (PS), Zachariah Luhanga, says effective implementation of the framework will require adequate institutional capacity, effective coordination and sustained collaboration among stakeholders.

Mr Luhanga said the stakeholders include employers, workers, trade unions, industry associations, professional bodies, regulatory institutions and other cooperating partners.

The media reports that the PS said this in Lusaka today when he officiated at a stakeholder engagement meeting organized by the Occupational Health and Safety Institute (OHSI).

Mr Luhanga said his ministry will continue supporting the Institute

as it expands its physical presence across the country.

He said stakeholder engagement is important in ensuring that occupational health and safety regulations are practical, relevant and responsive to the realities of different sectors.

Mr Luhanga noted that occupational health and safety risks vary across sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, construction, energy, transport, banking, retail and mining.

He said the Ministry, through the Occupational Health and Safety Institute, has therefore placed emphasis on stakeholder participation in the development of proposed occupational health and safety regulations and sector-specific regulatory instruments.

Mr Luhanga has since challenged the stakeholders to continue participating actively and constructively in the development of sector-specific regulations and guidelines in ensuring that safety requirements respond appropriately to the risks, operational conditions and circumstances of different industries.

Mr Luhanga said a safe and healthy workforce is essential for increased productivity and sustainable economic development.

He said Government remains committed to building workplaces where every worker is protected and every employer understands and fulfils their responsibilities.

And Occupational Health and Safety Institute Director General (DG), Martha Chakulimba observed that while the mining sector has made significant progress in occupational safety, small-scale mining remains underserved in occupational health and safety matters.

Dr Chakulimba said Zambia, like other countries, continues to face significant occupational health and safety challenges.

She cited International Labour Organisation and World Health Organisation statistics indicating that about three million workers globally die every year from work-related causes.

Dr Chakulimba said the statistics translate to thousands of work-related deaths every day, underscoring the need for concerted action by governments, employers, workers and other stakeholders.

She stated that the mining sector faces various hazards, including physical risks from rock falls and other mining accidents, as well as emerging risks associated with the use of toxic substances.

Dr Chakulimba observed that while Zambia has made progress in occupational safety, more needs to be done to strengthen occupational health, particularly in the small-scale mining sector.

World.title: Man drowns in Kabompo River
World.content:
A businessman from Manyinga District in North-Western Province has drowned in the Kabompo River.

Kabompo District Commissioner Hubert Chinyanga said the incident occurred on September 20, 2026, at around 16:40 hours.

Mr Chinyanga said, according to a police report lodged by 28-year-old Morgan Dikomeno of Vilembulika Village in Chief Sikufele’s area of Manyinga District, the deceased drowned while swimming in the river.

He identified the deceased as Charles Kambita, a businessman from Malukuchila Village in Chief Sikufele’s area, who is believed to have been aged between 30 and 35.

Mr Chinyanga said Mr Kambita had travelled from Manyinga to Kabompo with four friends, including Mr Dikomeno, to swim in the river.

“The now deceased person came from Manyinga to Kabompo District with his four friends but whilst swimming the deceased person was swept away by the strong current of the river and failed to swim back to safety and drowned,” he said.

Mr Chinyanga said efforts to retrieve the body had so far failed as it had gone underwater.

He said a search party had since been constituted to recover the body.

World.title: Kabwe vendors given October 1 deadline
World.content:
Kabwe Municipal Council (KMC) has given vendors until October 1, 2026 to relocate their businesses to designated markets.

KMC Public Relations Manager Chris Mulaliki said the measure was aimed at restoring order in the Central Business District (CBD) and other public spaces while ensuring that trading activities were conducted in safe and designated areas.

Speaking to the media in an interview, Mr Mulaliki said the council had observed an increase in street vending and trading in undesignated areas, resulting in congestion, obstruction of pedestrians and challenges in waste management, as well as potential risks to public health and safety.

“Vendors should use the remaining period to voluntarily relocate their businesses to designated markets. We will continue engaging vendors and other stakeholders to facilitate an orderly transition,” he said.

Mr Mulaliki said the council had more than 1,000 trading spaces available in gazetted markets across the district.

He warned that the council would, after the deadline, commence enforcement measures against vendors operating in undesignated areas in accordance with applicable laws and council regulations.

“Street vending is illegal under the Local Government Act, read together with Statutory Instrument Number 12 of 2018 on Street Vending and Nuisances Regulations,” Mr Mulaliki said.

He said council police officers would conduct enforcement operations to ensure that vendors returned to designated markets and that illegal temporary structures were removed without further notice.

Mr Mulaliki appealed to vendors, traders and members of the public to cooperate with the initiative, saying the objective was not to prevent people from earning a living but to promote orderly trading, clean surroundings, public safety and a conducive environment for businesses and the wider community.

He also encouraged members of the public to support vendors by patronising businesses operating from designated markets.

Mr Mulaliki said the council remained committed to working with the trading community to promote sustainable livelihoods while maintaining orderly and well-managed public spaces.

Kabwe District Commissioner Lennox Shimwambwa has expressed concern over the failure by Kabwe Municipal Council to work on feeder roads in the district.

Monrovia — South Africa Pushes for Permanent African Seat on UN Security Council

South Africa is leveraging ongoing intergovernmental negotiations on UN reform to advance the African Union's demand for permanent representation. The Security Council currently comprises 15 members: five permanent and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. South Africa maintains that the body must expand to reflect contemporary global realities, specifically addressing Africa's historic absence from the permanent category.

World.title: Nigeria: Central Bank Cuts Interest Rate
World.content:
"It emphasised that the recalibration of the corridor does not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance, but rather an operational reset to enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy and support the transition to an inflation targeting framework," CBN said.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has cut the benchmark interest rate to 23 per cent.

CBN Governor Olayemi Cardoso disclosed the committee's decision at the conclusion of the bank's two-day, 307th Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting, held from 21 to 22 September in Abuja.

This decision followed two consecutive retention of the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 26.5 per cent, holding it in May and July previously, following a 50-basis-point reduction in February from 27 per cent.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Speaking after the meeting, the CBN Governor stated that the committee decided to reset the MPR and recalibrate the policy corridor as an important operational realignment aimed at strengthening monetary policy transmission.

"The committee decided to reset the MPR and recalibrate the policy corridor as an important operational realignment aimed at strengthening monetary policy transmission and reinforcing the primacy of the monetary policy rate.

"It emphasised that the recalibration of the corridor does not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance, but rather an operational reset to enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy and support the transition to an inflation targeting framework," CBN said.

The MPC also adjusted the asymmetric facilities corridor around the MPR to +50/-300 basis points, a move aimed at discouraging banks from keeping idle funds with the CBN and encouraging increased lending into the economy.

Furthermore, the committee maintained the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) for commercial banks at 45 per cent, retained the rate for merchant banks at 16 per cent, and kept the CRR on non-TSA public-sector deposits at 75 per cent for liquidity management considerations.

CBN cut the interest rate amid its continued efforts to moderate Nigeria's headline inflation.

Since CBN maintained the rate in May, inflationary pressure has generally eased, with headline inflation standing at 15.39 per cent in August, down from 15.43 per cent in July, 15.91 per cent in June and 15.93 per cent in May, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).

The rise in inflation recorded in April followed the escalation of the Middle East conflict, which began in February and contributed to higher global oil prices.

However, despite the recent easing in inflation, CBN's decision comes amid a renewed increase in fuel prices across the country, a development that could put fresh upward pressure on the prices of goods and services.

World.title: Kenya: Kenyatta Clears Way for New Jubilee Leadership
World.content:
Nairobi — Former President Uhuru Kenyatta has formally cleared the way for a leadership transition in the Jubilee Party, asking members to accept former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang'i to take his place as the party prepares for the 2027 General Election.

Speaking during the Jubilee Party handover, Uhuru said he would move to a senior advisory role while remaining a member of the party.

He then publicly asked Jubilee members to back Matiang'i, who has already been endorsed by the party as its presidential candidate for the 2027 election.

"Let me take that upper position, to be like a senior advisor there," Uhuru said, adding that he would remain available to guide the party.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He told delegates that once he moved to the senior position, his "younger brother" should take over the position he had been occupying.

"And together with all our Jubilee delegates, let us now go and organize ourselves to give him the work for 2027," Uhuru said.

Uhuru made the message even clearer, directly asking Jubilee members to accept Matiang'i.

"I ask you with respect to accept and welcome him. You agreed that I move to that top position, right?" he told the delegates.

"And agree to welcome Fred Okeng'o Matiang'i to take my place. Will you accept that?"

The crowd responded in the affirmative.

Uhuru described Matiang'i as a young leader from Kisii with the qualities he believes Jubilee needs as it prepares for the next election.

"I see there is this young man from Kisii over there called Fred Matiang'i," Uhuru said.

He described him as a person with wisdom, hardworking and someone who "loves Kenyans" and has "no malice."

Uhuru also urged Jubilee members to begin organising early, saying the political season had already started.

He called for the party to identify candidates for elective positions across the country, including MCAs, governors, senators and MPs, as well as a presidential candidate.

"Let us go and look for a President who will lead us like this," Uhuru said.

Despite stepping aside from the top party position, Uhuru insisted that he was not abandoning Jubilee.

"Even now, me as I am, over there, and I'm going nowhere. I am still a Jubilee member," he said.

He said he would remain involved in the party and use his experience to advise its leadership.

"I want to join hands with you so we can organize ourselves," Uhuru said, adding that he had no interest in political insults and wanted Jubilee to work with other Kenyans.

Matiang'i welcomed the endorsement noting that the moment "is humbling."

Close 

"I am deeply humbled and the best gift that we can give Uhuru is ensure that we keep on with this party and its activities as we head to 2027," he said.

The move follows a High Court ruling that barred retired presidents from continuing to hold formal leadership positions in political parties beyond six months after leaving office. Uhuru had earlier said he was ready to facilitate a lawful handover in line with Jubilee's constitution.

The transition has already triggered competition within Jubilee, with Deputy Party Leader Jeremiah Kioni offering himself for the position of party leader and insisting that the next leader should be chosen through the party's democratic structures.

Uhuru, however, said the process should be about organising the party and preparing for 2027.

"Is it running away that I have run away, or is it organizing ourselves that we are organizing ourselves?" he asked.

He also urged Jubilee members to avoid political insults and instead explain to Kenyans what they intend to do if elected.

"Go and tell Kenyans how you will serve them," Uhuru said.

He added: "A vote is not a marketplace. A vote is a vision."

Expectations are low for breakthroughs when Xi Jinping meets President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C. this week.

If China remains intransigent during the high-stakes diplomacy, it will be time for America to end decades of dialogue with Beijing.

The Trump administration is setting the bar low for the summit. A continuation of last October’s trade truce, reached when the two leaders met in South Korea, is the most that officials are now hoping for. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been talking with a Chinese delegation about an extension. The truce expires November 10.

XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT

The Chinese should be happy with no disruption in the relationship. On Thursday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in the words of China’s Global Times, that "China-US relations have generally moved along the path toward a constructive relationship of strategic stability."

Of course, China wants "stability." The Chinese side, in a stable environment, will be able to continue dangerous and unacceptable conduct, such as selling fentanyl, stealing U.S. intellectual property, engaging in predatory trade practices, supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine, maintaining secret police stations on American soil. And helping Iran kill American service personnel in the Persian Gulf.

TRUMP SAYS CHINA 'SPIES' ON US AFTER REPORT TIES CHINESE IMAGERY TO IRAN STRIKE

China has made its satellites available to that regime for targeting U.S. forces. On March 1, Iran almost certainly used that targeting data to kill six American service members in Kuwait. In July, Iran again relied upon Chinese satellite data to kill three more Americans, this time in Jordan. Washington’s China diplomacy has completely failed.

TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS

It is not hard to see why. American leaders have been pursuing dialogue with China since the early 1970s, when U.S. diplomats literally chased their Chinese counterparts to set up the summit in Beijing between President Nixon and Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong.

America’s ardent desire to maintain dialogue has fed the already inflated sense of self-importance of Chinese leaders. Not surprisingly, this approach over the course of decades has coincided with — and almost certainly been the cause of — a marked deterioration in Chinese behavior.

President Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi in May and made little discernible progress on contentious issues, so what more can be accomplished now?

At some point, the United States needs to lose patience. For one thing, Xi Jinping’s arrogance at the May summit was stunning. On the first day of the event, he publicly mentioned the Thucydides Trap, a reference to a declining hegemon dangerously challenging a rising power. The insult was indirect, but nonetheless unmistakable.

BEHIND SUMMIT SMILES, XI GIVES BLUNT WARNING TO TRUMP OF 'CLASHES' AND 'CONFLICTS'

Even more insulting, the Chinese leader on the first day talked about the "new era," his phrase for the period in which the U.S. has been pushed to the sidelines and China dominates the world. As Charles Burton of the Sinopsis think tank noted, "Xi views himself as the modern heir of China’s lineage of great emperors, so the concept of fair and reciprocal relations with any foreign country is simply absent from his worldview."

Today, Xi is still arrogant, but will arrive in the American capital a diminished figure. That gives Trump leverage, but, on the other hand, it reduces Xi’s room to maneuver.

AMERICA HOLDS THE ADVANTAGE AS TRUMP MEETS XI IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT

NEWT GINGRICH: XI IS COMING TO WASHINGTON. HE SHOULD BRING ONE UNEXPECTED GUEST

There is, at the same time, widespread domestic discontent over China’s stumbling economy and persistent questions about Xi’s health. If all this were not bad enough, Xi is coming off an unsuccessful BRICS summit in New Delhi, calling into question his handling of the country’s affairs.

World.title: Video shows injured man on the ground after ICE mistakenly targets him
World.content:
A man is recovering from injuries he sustained Sunday morning after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him in a Chicago suburb.

In one video verified by NBC News, a Black man is seen sprawled on the street, near a curb, behind a black SUV in Evanston, Illinois. Two agents wearing ICE-style vests are seen standing over him. One has his face covered and his vest reads “POLICE” and the other appears to be pinning the man down to the ground. The man is shouting at them and can be heard saying, “I’m a f------ U.S. citizen.”

According to Evanston police, the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and officers requested an ambulance.

Police said they are investigating the incident, which was filmed by bystanders and gained attention after being posted on social media.

One bystander in the background of the video is heard saying the ICE officers used force against the man. Other bystanders begin shouting at the man on the ground, asking him if he is OK. The ICE officers eventually get in the black SUV and drive off, leaving the man on the ground. The bystanders begin trying to help the man and call Evanston police.

“I saw two agents pinning down a gentleman. They were using very rough force on him, and it looked like they really did hurt him because we had to call 911,” Miguel Angel Olivares, one of the people who witnessed the encounter, told NBC Chicago on Monday.

“When we saw him, he had his jaw swollen and he had a little blood on his shirt. I’m not sure if it was the agent’s or it was his blood,” Olivares said.

In a news release Sunday, Evanston police said they spoke to an ICE agent who said federal immigration officers “had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking.” After the man refused to provide identification, he was “detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention.”

An Evanston police officer reported observing blood on the agent’s hands. The agent said he was injured while attempting to handcuff the individual and declined medical treatment, according to the news release from Evanston police. “Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen. He was released.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that their officers encountered a person who resembled someone they were targeting in an enforcement operation in Evanston on Sunday.

“ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself. ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the DHS statement reads. “DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.”

DHS did not state anything about the injuries the man suffered and why ICE officers did not appear to render aid.

Neither the police nor DHS identified the man who was injured.

Evanston police said they spoke with the injured man at a local hospital on Sunday. They “photographed and documented his injuries” as part of an ongoing investigation into the incident, police said.

World.title: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose of drugs, including fentanyl, coroner says
World.content:
“Heroes” and “Nashville” star Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled an accident caused by the toxic effects of multiple drugs, including fentanyl, officials said Monday.

The Greenville County Coroner’s Office said Tuesday that her “cause of death has been ruled as toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol, and Quetiapine.”

There were no signs of trauma that would have contributed to Panettiere’s death, the release added.

Panettiere, 36, died Aug. 16 at a South Carolina apartment complex where she had been staying. Authorities found her unresponsive after responding to a report of a cardiac arrest.

The Greenville Police Department said there were no signs of foul play during the initial response and investigation. The Drug Enforcement Administration was also investigating Panettiere’s death.

Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was at the apartment complex at the time of her death and showed authorities what a police report described as a “bag of medication” he said she was taking.

An attorney for Hickerson did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on Panettiere’s death. Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, also did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.

In an interview with NBC News last month, a former DEA special agent who probed the overdose deaths of Michael Jackson, Matthew Perry and other celebrities said investigators were likely attempting to reconstruct Panettiere’s final days.

“They will use forensics to exploit her telephone, try to re-create the last two or three days of her life from looking at text messages, looking at phone calls, looking at interaction with people on social media,” said Bill Bodner, a 32-year veteran of the DEA’s field office in Los Angeles.

“Once there’s a timeline of what she was doing before her death, it becomes easier to kind of find where that drug distribution took place that killed her,” Bodner added.

Panettiere’s relationship with Hickerson — an aspiring actor from South Carolina — appeared to have ended in 2020 amid allegations of domestic violence, but her mother told NBC News that they were still seeing each other when she died.

Panettiere detailed those allegations, along with her struggles with addiction and postpartum depression, in her recently released memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning.”

Hickerson pleaded no contest to a charge of injuring a spouse or girlfriend in 2019 in Los Angeles, and he was sentenced to four years of probation, court records show. Panettiere sought a restraining order against Hickerson in 2020, though the outcome is unclear.

In a statement in August, a lawyer for Hickerson reiterated that police found no signs of foul play in Panettiere’s death. The attorney, Sloan Ellis, added that the actor’s death remained under investigation.

“Out of respect for Hayden’s loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time,” Ellis said at the time.

Panettiere began appearing in television commercials as a young child. She landed a breakout role on the NBC sci-fi series “Heroes” and later earned two Golden Globe nominations for portraying an ambitious and volatile country musician in “Nashville.”

In her memoir, Panettiere wrote that her life began to spiral after she had a daughter with Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She began drinking heavily to cope with postpartum depression and Klitschko’s distance, she wrote.

Panettiere eventually checked into rehab and gave Klitschko custody of their child in 2018.

If you or someone you know is struggling with a drug or substance abuse problem, call these numbers for help: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s national helpline is 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357); the National Drug Helpline is 1-844-289-0879; and the American Addiction Centers’ hotline is (866) 464-3073.

World.title: Poll: Most voters say Trump has hurt the economy as competitive midterm election looms
World.content:
“Donald Trump has achieved his goal of making this election about him at a historic level. The problem for Trump and Republicans on the ballot in November is that he has also made history in the highest share of voters who say their vote is in opposition to Trump,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates.

Republicans on the campaign trail are trying to shore up their standing by arguing that Democrats are too extreme to trust with congressional majorities.

But the poll indicates voters are more anxious about restraining Trump: 50% say they’re more concerned that Republicans will go too far in supporting Trump if they keep control of Congress, while 42% are more concerned Democrats will obstruct the president if they win control of Congress. Independents lean 45%-30% toward greater concern that Republicans will go too far supporting Trump.

McInturff acknowledged the challenges for the GOP posed by the political environment, even as the party’s geographic advantages keep Democrats fighting on their turf.

“The issue environment is tilting substantially towards the Democrats,” McInturff said.

Trump’s struggles continue

A majority of voters, 56%, disapprove of Trump’s job performance, including overwhelming shares of Democrats and independents and 16% of Republicans. The share of voters who strongly approve of Trump, 25%, is the second-lowest mark recorded in the NBC News poll across Trump’s first and second terms.

The disapproval rating closely tracks the 55% who say Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, while 26% say they have helped and 18% say they have not made much of a difference. At this point in the 2018 election cycle, more voters said Trump’s policies helped the economy (41%) than hurt (26%).

And the survey suggests some of Trump’s signature economic policies are falling flat.

While Republicans are touting Trump’s signature tax cut and spending measure known as the “big, beautiful bill,” which was enacted in 2025, 42% of voters say they are less likely to support a candidate backing the measure, while 36% say they are more likely to support such a candidate.

Trump’s latest gambit — an announcement at the recent Republican convention that he wanted to issue $5,000 payments to every adult if Republicans keep control of Congress — isn’t garnering much interest. While 21% of voters say they’re more likely to back a candidate who supports Trump’s plan, 46% say they’d be less likely.

A plurality of Republicans say it would make no difference in their vote choice, while Democrats are uniformly against the idea and 45% of independents would be less likely to support a candidate in favor of the plan. Among independents, 13% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate who backs Trump’s plan.

Voters are also continuing to express opposition to the Iran war, with 57% saying they are less likely to support a candidate who supports the war, versus 24% who are more likely to support that candidate. One-third of voters say the war has been worth it, while 62% disagree.

And Democrats also have a 4-point advantage, within the poll’s margin of error, on the question of which party voters say they trust to handle the war with Iran.

Trump has continued to insert himself into the midterms, including endorsing nearly all Republicans in competitive congressional races. But 52% of voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Trump, while 30% are more likely to support a Trump-backed candidate.

Democratic opportunities — and challenges

Clear dissatisfaction with the president opens the door for Democrats as they fight for control of Congress this fall.

Forty-three percent of registered voters say their vote for Congress is intended to signal opposition to Trump, while 27% say they plan to vote to send a signal of support for Trump and 28% say their vote won’t be a signal either way.

Among independents, almost half (46%) see their vote as a signal of opposition to Trump, while just a handful (10%) say their vote is a signal of support for the president.

Democrats have a 1-point lead when voters are asked which party they trust more in dealing with the economy — a result within the poll’s margin of error. It’s the third consecutive NBC News poll with both parties sitting about even on that question. In the same survey just three years ago, Republicans enjoyed a 21-point advantage when it came to handling the economy.

Democrats also have a 7-point edge on controlling inflation, as well as slight leads on dealing with the war in Iran and dealing with corruption — government corruption was the second-most popular choice when voters were asked to rank the most important issue facing the country, with concern about the issue heightened among members of both parties and independents.

The Democratic Party also has double-digit leads on dealing with data centers and dealing with healthcare.

Republicans still hold significant advantages over Democrats on handling crime, border security and immigration, including a 21-point lead on border security. But that is down from the 36-point edge the GOP held over Democrats on the issue in Sept. 2022, after Trump has made aggressive immigration enforcement a hallmark of his second term.

Democrats also have a narrow lead on interest in the election, as well as among party identification. But it’s not all rosy for the opposition party.

The Republican Party is viewed more positively by voters: 36% have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% view the party negatively. On the Democratic Party, voters are split 29%-50%.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America is viewed positively by 22% of voters, as Republicans try to link other Democrats to the left-wing group, which rose in prominence following some major primary wins in the past two years.

One poll respondent — Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old Texan who doesn’t affiliate with either party — told NBC News that he hasn’t plugged into the election yet and is still unsure whom he’ll vote for. But he said his father grew up during the Cold War and that he’s wary of Democrats who describe themselves as democratic socialists.

“Any relation toward socialism or communism in general gives me the ick. It’s like a buzzword that generally just makes me not want to sway in that direction,” he said.

Half of voters say they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who “supports many of the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed policies,” while 31% say they’d be more likely to support those kinds of candidates.

Candidates calling to abolish ICE, a big point of emphasis among progressives, draw similarly unpopular scores with voters.

That said, for all the Democratic infighting over policies like “Medicare for All,” 53% of voters say they would be more likely to support a candidate who favors the policy, while 36% said it would make them less likely to vote for that candidate.

When asked a similar question with slightly different wording to note the healthcare would be financed in part by taxes, 49% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate that backed the policy and 39% say they’d be less likely.

Horwitt, the Democratic pollster, noted that his party “remains in a terrible position as a brand nationally,” even as the poll paints a dismal picture for Trump and Republicans.

“This speaks more to deep dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans than a ringing endorsement of Democrats,” he said. “The party in power does not have a positive story to tell on the major issues of the day: inflation, corruption and the Iran war. Voters are continuing to look for change.”

The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Sept. 11-15 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

World.title: No criminal charges in death of Nolan Wells, grand jury finds
World.content:
A grand jury will not pursue charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said Monday, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teenager this summer.

District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath made the announcement in a video message, saying the grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning it did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime. A partially redacted copy of the grand jury report was also posted to the DA’s Facebook page.

Wells, 18, was with friends celebrating July Fourth and was last seen on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, his family’s lawyer said.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”

The family’s lawyer, civil rights attorney Ben Crump, previously called into question whether race was a factor in Wells’ death, as it appeared Wells was one of a few Black people there that day.

On Monday, Myers McIlrath took direct aim at Crump and his team, saying they also previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.

A picture of Nolan Wells is displayed during his funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs, Miss., on July 20, 2026. Ayrton Breckenridge / USA Today via Reuters

“I’m not suggesting that a grieving mother police the rumors surrounding her child’s death,” the DA said. “What I am suggesting is that the Crump team knew better but did not do better.”

Crump in turn said a statement Tuesday, “This grand jury result leaves us with more questions than answers. Nolan’s family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we.”

“Mississippi’s own pathologist found two bruises on the back of this young man’s head ... An independent autopsy documented traces of blood and recent blunt force injuries to the back of Nolan’s head and his back. To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” he added.

“We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the State of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating,” Crump said. Wells’ parents are expected to make a public address later Tuesday.

The grand jury issued 132 subpoenas and heard from 43 witnesses, and seven people were invited to testify before the panel, according to the partially redacted report.

It was made up of 23 grand jurors from a “cross section of citizens” from Jackson County between 27 and 68 of age, it said. Among them were 13 men and 10 women, including “12 Caucasians, five African Americans, one Asian, two Hispanics, two Native Americans and one individual who preferred ‘other,’” it said.

“The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to ​the death of Mr. Wells,” the report released by McIlrath’s office said.

Wells was last seen sometime in the afternoon of July 4. Friends told police that they had to leave early because their boat started taking on water but that Wells chose to stay and catch a ride back later with others.

The grand jury report found that it was common for people on Horn Island to “socialize on boats and in the water,” and that it was “not unusual or suspicious” for people to return from the island on different boats.

It concluded there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”

Crump and Wells’ family have previously rejected notions that he drowned, saying he was athletic and a good swimmer. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family’s legal team found that the teenager’s cause and manner of death were “undetermined.”

The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.

Wells’ funeral July 20 attracted hundreds of people.

“Your absence has left an emptiness that can never truly be filled,” his mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said at the time. “In a world that can often feel dark, be like Nolan, be the light that brightens the lives of those around you.”

World.title: Senators press Rubio to prioritize release of American journalist held in Iran
World.content:
A bipartisan group of senators is urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to make the release of an American journalist imprisoned in Iran an "urgent priority," warning that his health has deteriorated and his life could be at risk.

In a letter to Rubio obtained by CBS News, Sens. Brian Schatz, Democrat of Hawaii, Republican Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, Democrat Jacky Rosen of Nevada and Republican Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania called on the Trump administration to use "all available diplomatic channels" to secure the release of Reza Valizadeh, a U.S.-Iranian dual citizen and former journalist for U.S.-funded broadcaster Radio Farda.

"With every day of continued detention, Mr. Valizadeh's life is in danger," the senators wrote. "We are extremely concerned that Iranian authorities could take sudden, arbitrary actions to endanger his life."

Valizadeh, 49, has been imprisoned in Iran since September 2024, after returning to Tehran earlier that year to visit his aging parents. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison for "collaborating with a hostile government," a charge tied to his work for Radio Farda and alleged cooperation with the United States. The State Department formally designated him as wrongfully detained in May 2025.

The senators said Valizadeh's health has "significantly deteriorated" at Tehran's Evin Prison and that he has repeatedly been denied medical care, including an inhaler he needs to treat his asthma.

The State Department did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Undated photo of Reza Valizadeh Photo provided by Radio Farda

Valizadeh has previously described worsening conditions inside Evin in recordings obtained by CBS News. In June, he appealed to the U.S. government to secure his release and said he and other Americans detained there were not receiving adequate medical treatment.

The congressional appeal comes just over two weeks after another American designated as wrongfully detained, Kamran Hekmati, was released from Evin Prison on Sept. 5 after serving roughly half of a two-year sentence. Hekmati remains barred from leaving Iran, and the State Department has called on Tehran to lift the exit ban so he can return to the United States.

In July, Dena Karari, a U.S.-Iran dual citizen who was also barred from leaving Iran on allegations of espionage and collaborating with a hostile state, was released and returned to the U.S. after suffering a heart attack, sources told CBS News.

Rubio said in June that the administration raises the cases of wrongfully detained Americans at "every opportunity," calling their release a "highest priority," but he has declined to discuss individual cases, saying that could complicate efforts to free them.

The senators' push comes as the Trump administration weighs its next steps in the nearly seven-month war with Iran, with the conflict and prospects for renewed diplomacy expected to be raised in meetings this week during the U.N. General Assembly in New York.

"Reza deserves the full attention and support of President Trump and the United States government, and he should be released immediately," said Ryan Fayhee, Valizadeh's attorney. "As world leaders gather for the U.N. General Assembly, Iran has an opportunity to demonstrate goodwill through action. The release of Reza would not resolve every issue between our nations, but it could help break a cycle of mistrust that has made it unsafe for Iranian-Americans to visit the country of their heritage," Fayhee said.

The senators described Valizadeh's detention as part of a longstanding pattern by Tehran of targeting journalists and dual nationals, writing that "Iran is not afraid to use American citizens as political pawns."

"We ask that his freedom and welfare be an urgent priority through all available diplomatic channels with Iranian officials," they wrote.

World.title: Even the smallest joys can help prevent suicide, researchers say
World.content:
New research is shedding light on suicide prevention strategies, highlighting that even the smallest joys can help during crisis.

Professor Philip Resnik, of the University of Maryland's Institute of Advanced Computer Studies, said their research started with a public Reddit post. A user had asked "formerly suicidal" people to share what kept them alive and helped them through dark times, and thousands of people responded.

"I realized that not only was this a really remarkable set of people's stories, but it was potentially an important source of data that we might be able to analyze and help people," said Resnik.

He and a team of collaborators conducted computer-assisted analysis of more than 16,000 responses and identified what they describe as four key themes that made a difference for people. The first one they list is concern for others, including a sense of not wanting to hurt loved ones or protecting beloved pets.

Another theme: the appreciation of sensory pleasures or distractions, including TV shows, video games and music.

"I think one of the most interesting things that came out of this was small things can actually have a big effect," said Resnik, whose findings are being published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Positive foresight, or a forward-looking perspective, was another category they identified. It includes things like recognizing the possibility that things might get better in the morning or finding hope in a religious, spiritual or philosophical belief.

The fourth category the study identified was negative emotions including fear or anger.

"This is actually something powerful, and in our minds as clinicians we might miss this," said psychologist Rebecca Resnik, who collaborated with her husband on the project. She said the findings validated much of what she's observed clinically and could help shape future care.

"I now have a much better sense when I'm doing a risk analysis to pay very close attention to your relationship with your pet or the fact that you're looking forward to going to prom," she said.

Dese'Rae Stage, a therapist and survivor herself, said much work remains to be done when it comes to suicide prevention. Stage launched the "Live Through This" project 15 years ago, documenting the personal stories of suicide attempt survivors.

"We definitely were not talking about suicide in any meaningful way back then," Stage said.

Dese'Rae Stage launched the "Live Through This" project to document the personal stories of suicide attempt survivors. CBS News

She believes the new research could be incorporated into crisis training for care providers.

"We do always want to be leading people back to, 'What do you have to live for?' Even if it's the tiniest thing," said Stage. "What's gonna get you through this next moment?"

Stage says it's her two children and her love of music and concerts that help her.

"I keep a list of things that I want to stay alive for and things to look forward to," she said.

She's spreading the word that small joys can be a lifeline.

If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental health crisis, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing or texting "988."

World.title: Do you have enough life insurance? A quick coverage check-up
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Periodically reviewing your life insurance tends to be an important part of a broader financial check-up. Carol Yepes/Getty Images

Life insurance tends to be purchased around a major milestone. Getting married, buying a home or having a child may prompt someone to take out a policy, choose a coverage amount and check the task off their financial to-do list. But while the life insurance policy may stay the same for years on end, the financial picture it was designed to protect rarely does.

Income can rise, mortgages and other debts can grow or shrink and families can take on new financial obligations over time. In turn, a life insurance policy that once seemed substantial may need to cover a much different set of expenses a few years later. On the other hand, some obligations may disappear as the years go by, changing how much protection makes sense.

In turn, periodically reviewing your life insurance tends to be an important part of a broader financial check-up. But rather than focusing on the dollar amount printed on your life insurance policy, it may help to look at what that money would actually need to accomplish if your family had to rely on it. So, how do you do that? That's what we'll examine below.

Find out how a New York Life insurance policy could benefit you today.

Do you have enough life insurance? A quick coverage check-up

There's no single coverage amount that's appropriate for every household. Rules of thumb, such as buying coverage equal to a certain multiple of your annual income, can provide a good starting point, but they don't account for the nuances that make each household's finances different. If you want to ensure that you have enough life insurance, it can help to check the following off your list:

Add up the income your household would need to replace

Start by considering how much of your income other people depend on and how long they would need financial support. If you're the primary earner with young children, for example, your life insurance coverage may need to replace years of income. If your spouse also earns a substantial income and your children are financially independent, the calculation could look very different.

Don't overlook the financial value of unpaid work, either. A stay-at-home parent may not bring home a paycheck, but replacing childcare, transportation and other household responsibilities could carry a significant cost. Those expenses can be worth accounting for when evaluating your coverage.

Compare your life insurance options with New York Life now.

Take inventory of your major financial obligations

You should also look at the large expenses your family could face without you. That may include a mortgage, certain debts, childcare costs, college expenses and final expenses, among other obligations.

The goal isn't necessarily to buy enough insurance to eliminate every future expense. Rather, you want to consider which costs could put the most pressure on your household and which ones you'd want the death benefit to help cover.

This is also where life stage matters. Someone who recently bought a home and had a child may have very different coverage needs than someone nearing retirement with a paid-off mortgage and significant savings.

Subtract the financial resources already available

Your life insurance doesn't necessarily have to shoulder the entire financial burden on its own. Savings, investments, existing life insurance policies and other assets could also help support your beneficiaries.

Suppose you determine that your family would need $1 million to replace income and address major financial obligations, but you already have $250,000 in assets earmarked for those needs. That could have an impact on the amount of additional insurance required.

Be careful about counting assets your family may need for other purposes, though. Draining retirement savings or an emergency fund to cover immediate expenses could create another financial shortfall later.

Check whether your coverage matches your current life stage

Major life changes can alter the equation, even if the amount of coverage you currently have once made sense. In turn, a regular review of your life insurance policy — as well as a check-up after major financial or family changes — can help identify coverage gaps before they become an issue.

For example, marriage, divorce, a new child, a home purchase, a significant raise, a career change or taking responsibility for an aging parent can all be reasons to revisit your policy. Your needs can change in the opposite direction, too. Paying off a mortgage, accumulating substantial assets or having children become financially independent could reduce some of the financial obligations your policy was originally intended to cover.

Consider whether the type of coverage still fits

The coverage amount tied to your life insurance policy isn't the only thing worth reviewing. It's also important to consider whether the type of policy you have still aligns with your goals.

Term life insurance, for example, generally provides coverage for a set period and can be useful for temporary needs, such as replacing income while children are young or covering a mortgage. Permanent policies, including whole life insurance, are designed to remain in force for life as long as required premiums are paid — and according to New York Life, may also accumulate cash value.

That doesn't make one option universally better than another. The right fit depends on what you're trying to accomplish, your budget and how life insurance fits alongside your savings, investments, retirement planning and other financial priorities. Some households may also use a combination of coverage types to address different needs.

The bottom line

Having a life insurance policy in place doesn't automatically mean you have the right amount of protection. Your coverage is designed to support financial needs that can shift substantially as your income, family, assets and obligations change over time, so a policy purchased years ago shouldn't necessarily be treated as a set-it-and-forget-it decision.

By periodically comparing your coverage with the income your household depends on, the expenses it could face and the resources already available, you can get a clearer picture of whether your current policy still fits into your broader financial plan.

World.title: 5 moments from Patrick Clancy's 60 Minutes interview
World.content:
More than three years after the tragic deaths of his three children, Patrick Clancy continues to navigate unimaginable grief as the case thrusts him into the spotlight, bringing public scrutiny and speculation.

Lindsay Clancy's lawyers never denied that she killed her three children. Their argument was that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was not criminally responsible. But that didn't stop online sleuths from scrutinizing Patrick's actions, dissecting his testimony and questioning his character.

The 5-week trial became a national obsession, sparking conversations about mental health, criminal fault and how the medical system fails mothers. The case ended in a mistrial, and prosecutors have yet to determine whether Lindsay Clancy will be retried. Her lawyers have asked a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who sought to convict Clancy and, in another motion, to dismiss the case.

We met Patrick in New York City for a conversation about his grief, his ex-wife's struggles with mental illness, and the social media frenzy surrounding him. Here are some emotional moments from our interview.

Patrick's final moments with son Callan

While 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, tragically died at the scene, Patrick's infant son Callan somehow survived and was airlifted to Boston Children's Hospital.

At first, Patrick didn't have any details about Callan's condition other than learning that doctors were able to get a heartbeat back.

"I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live. And I remember just thinking, 'Just give me one. Just give me one kid, and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I'd tell him about his brother and sister.' And I was holding out hope for that. And then when I got to the hospital, I saw the doctor. I saw the look on her face, and I knew that it wasn't going to be a good prognosis," he said.

Callan's heart kept beating for four days.

"I'm so grateful for those four days that I had with him. And I'm so grateful he hung on," Patrick said.

During those four days, Patrick said he was able to talk to Callan and hold him.

"I said, 'I'm so sorry.' And I got to hold him. I got to lay down next to him. And he died in my arms."

During those hours with Callan, Patrick sat and wrote tributes to each of his three children, typing with one hand while he held his baby's hand with the other. He said he was afraid if he didn't write about them they'd be forgotten.

A panic attack the day the 911 call was played in court

Patrick was the prosecution's first witness. As he took the stand, online influencers quickly began dissecting his testimony and pushing theories questioning his character.

"It's deeply harmful to the legacy of my children. It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health. And it's done real harm to real people, myself included but also others," Patrick said of the viral speculation surrounding the case.

He said the attention has made everyday life more difficult.

"It's painful to see. And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he added.

One of the catalysts for these theories was Patrick's apparent stoicism on the stand.

"Testifying is very difficult," he said, recounting the day his 911 call played in court. He remembered taking a break in the back room right before the call was going to be presented.

"And I went to a back room, and I started having this massive traumatic panic attack. My heart was pounding," he said.

He recalled being put in an ambulance and being offered medication, which he refused.

"I said, "I don't want it, 'cause I want to go back and I want to finish this so I can be done with this." And I went back and I finished the testimony," he said.

"The grief is just so heavy that it makes me quiet"

Patrick said he finds "little reminders" of his children in his daily life, but he also said he makes a conscious effort to keep their memories alive.

"And it's hard sometimes. I've had people say to me, you know, 'Pat, you were really quiet today.' But they don't know the things that are playing over and over and over again in my head. They don't know that the scenes are playing over and over again from that night or that the grief is just so heavy that it makes me quiet," he said.

He tries to hang onto the good memories — like Cora's first plane ride, watching Dawson grab his tool belt to work on a project and sitting in the play pen with Callan.

"When you think about them this way, is it good or is it painful or is it both?" Ross Douthat asked.

"It's both. But I love, I love the memories. I don't avoid the good memories. I really never do. The bad ones I avoid. I really try not to think about them. I mean, it's traumatic and that can be overwhelming. I've never felt like the good memories are overwhelming. I hang onto those," he said.

The treatment that helped him the most

Patrick said he found a treatment that's a "little unusual" called EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) that has helped him heal the most.

The therapy, commonly used to treat PTSD, involves guided eye movements while processing traumatic memories.

"They put you right back in that place that you've been trying to avoid for years. And you face it head-on. And it's unpleasant, but they get you used to dealing with that. And eventually you're better at processing it," Patrick explained.

After several sessions, Patrick said the "waking up screaming" and the "horrible dreams" mostly stopped.

"I mean, it was like a miracle," he said.

How he met his wife, Dr. Rachel Danis

Dr. Rachel Danis, a fertility doctor, says they met in January of 2024 at a run club in New York. They got to know each other over coffee.

At the time, Rachel said she hoped it would simply lead to a good friendship. And that's how it remained for the next few months until Patrick came to one of her races and met her sister, who has Down syndrome.

"There must have been a moment, maybe it was a different moment for each of you, right, where the switch flipped, and you were, like, this is something we're doing," Ross Douthat said.

Rachel said it was the day of a half marathon. After the race, she met Patrick and some other run club friends to celebrate.

"And I think you can tell a lot about someone when they're interacting with a person with special needs," said Rachel, describing Patrick as "really friendly" and "really warm."

"I didn't know at the time, but Pat had taken a candid photo of me with [my sister] Lauren and we were just hugging," she continued, adding, "I just love her so much, and Pat really saw what matters to me."

Rachel and Patrick got married in April of this year in Central Park.
