World.title: Military commander vows fast action on AI and robots, sees 'untapped potential' for Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A top Canadian Forces commander says the military will rapidly buy more low-cost, autonomous and reusable weapons systems and equipment as it faces a rising tide of global threats.

Lt.-Gen. Darcy Molstad, commander of Canadian Joint Forces Command (CJFC), spoke at the Canadian Robotics Council 2026 Symposium on Monday, telling members of Canada's tech industry to stand by for a surge in purchase orders amid a "massive recapitalization of major platforms."

"This industry in Canada has so much untapped potential," the former fighter pilot told a room full of robotics entrepreneurs attending a panel discussion in Toronto. "Your imagination is your only limitation on the use cases for robotics paired with AI."

Molstad's remarks about embracing artificial intelligence-powered military hardware come as world leaders and prominent tech executives debate how to handle rapid advances in AI safely .

Powerful AI models have escaped human control, as was the case in July, when OpenAI agents hacked into a rival firm . Some leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, say the technology is evolving too fast.

Supply depots stuck in the 1980s

While autonomous hardware like drones are frequently associated with front-line combat, Molstad spelled out potential across the military, including medical diagnostic support, supply depot logistics and automated military police vehicle inspections.

"We see MPs [military police] that are inspecting vehicles with a mirror underneath the car. I'm pretty sure that's a use case for a robot with AI integrated to do that — and a lot better than humans can do it," he said.

"Our supply depots are still locked, in some ways, in the '80s and '90s technologies. We do not necessarily need to recreate an Amazon fulfilment centre, but we need to move from the '80s to something in between that is suitable for defence needs."

On the combat side, Molstad said CJFC has already established a list of 399 pre-qualified vendors for the Canadian military's Defence Drone Initiative. He expects more formal requests for proposals (RFPs) will follow as Canada's military leans deeper into new technologies.

"We're closer to a major global conflict than we've ever been in [the] history of our country since the major wars," he said.

"We have to modernize as fast as we possibly can to give our soldiers, sailors, aviators and special operators the tools that they need to be able to deter. Because none of us want to actually fight a war."

Charles Barlow, the CEO of Ottawa-based Robotics Centre, describes his company's drones at the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland. (Katie Pedersen/CBC)

Molstad was joined Monday by Duncan Stewart, a special executive advisor on innovation and industry to the Canadian Armed Forces. Stewart is also a partner at the Business Development Bank of Canada's $200-million tech venture fund, which backs early-stage startups.

"[The] government is a very fickle customer. It's a very tricky customer to deal with from an industry perspective," said Stewart. "Government tends to move very slowly. It tends to be very risk averse, and it tends to buy things in fits and starts."

Stewart added that Canada's traditional military suppliers tend to be large companies, which often lack the agility of the smaller firms he represents. "A lot of the innovation that we're seeing come from the cutting edge, especially in autonomous systems, is coming from small [companies]," he said

Molstad cited the military's Defense Drone Initiative as evidence the government is "doing things differently" now.

"We need to figure out how to get the right industries with security clearances to understand what our concepts of operations are … the threats that we are facing at a classified level, so that you can actually do the work that you need to do to come up with the innovative, novel solutions that we're not thinking about," he said.

In February, Ottawa released its new defence industrial strategy . The plan includes a goal to award 70 per cent of federal defence contracts to Canadian firms within a decade.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the policy will better equip the military, while countering U.S. President Donald Trump's effort to make the United States the arms-maker of choice to allied countries.

'Stand by for G-forces'

Molstad borrowed language from his time flying CF-18s as he told robotics and AI entrepreneurs about the Canadian military's plan to pick up the pace.

"The ex-fighter pilot in me will say, 'stand by for G, stand by for G-forces,'" he said.

"Because when we issue an RFP — the ones that we issued just recently — we're giving five days for you to respond. We're giving you the statutory minimum to respond, because this is how fast we need to move."

WATCH | Quebec will be home to a new facility for military drone research: Quebec will be home to a new facility for military drone research | Duration closed caption 2:25 The federal government is strengthening its defence ecosystem with a new research facility in Mirabel, an off-island suburb of Montreal. Aéro Montréal is spearheading a group of 30 organizations that will receive nearly $30 million from Ottawa over two years to establish and operate the new hub.

Looking ahead, Molstad said the industry can expect "a steady drumbeat of RFPs for robotic and autonomous systems over the course of the next five years."

Earlier this month, Canada and Ukraine signed an expansive 100-year partnership that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones by manufacturers in the two countries.

Carney has said Ukraine's war with Russia marks a turning point in modern warfare, with unmanned weapons systems proving their worth in the hands of Ukrainian soldiers by reaching targets hundreds of kilometres inside of Russia.

Back in Canada, at an isolated location west of Ottawa, Molstad oversaw an exercise last month where dozens of drone manufacturers were put through their paces by members of the Canadian Armed Forces .

"Robotic and autonomous systems are the way of the future," Molstad said Monday. "We have to do it responsibly, with the right policies and checks in play."

World.title: 'Father of Nunavut' has one more fight left: to live in the territory he helped create
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

John Amagoalik is widely known as the ‘Father of Nunavut,’ but after a lifetime advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination he’s now fighting to age in the territory he helped create. CBC’s Juanita Taylor shares his story and explores how it has ignited a broader conversation about Nunavut’s reliance on southern facilities for elder care.

"I'll never go back," John Amagoalik said of an assisted living facility in Ottawa, where he was sent to live by Nunavut's government in February 2025.

The territory's Department of Health transferred him to Embassy West Senior Living after an infection left no choice but to amputate part of his right leg.

"The worst part was the loneliness," Amagoalik recalled in an interview with CBC News as he sat in a wheelchair at his temporary home in Iqaluit with his wife, Evie, on Sept. 7.

"The strange surroundings. That was the worst part, being so far away from home and not ... being able to be with my many grandchildren."

Amagoalik is turning 79 in November and has multiple chronic age-related issues. He also has a difficult time talking.

John Amagoalik, who turns 79 in November, is shown in Iqaluit. The Nunavut government declined his request to provide adequate funding for his care and accessible housing, so he's going to court. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

He's frail, but he's still a fighter.

After a lifetime of struggle that included being forced to attend residential schools and advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination, Amagoalik is in his last fight: to age in the territory he helped create.

"It's been my life," he said, when asked what Nunavut means to him. "And I feel fortunate in being part of it."

'Father of Nunavut'

John Amagoalik is revered as the "Father of Nunavut" for his work spanning over three decades beginning in the 1970s — earning him the Order of Nunavut and the Order of Canada.

Among his many roles, he advocated for Inuit as an adviser with the Tunngavik Federation of Nunavut before it became Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. He was also on the executive council of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in the 1980s, and served as president of what was then the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, now Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami.

Amagoalik holds a photo of himself attending a meeting of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in Iqaluit in 1983. His work over three decades helped lead to the creation of Nunavut in 1999. (Graham Shishkov/CBC)

Amagoalik led the land claims settlement process with Nunavut Tunngavik after ratification in 1993. He also chaired the Nunavut Implementation Commission that designed the public government of Nunavut before the territory was created in 1999.

It's the very government his Victoria-based lawyer and longtime friend, Steve Kelliher, said is now failing him. So he's helping Amagoalik take the Nunavut government to court.

Kelliher, who first worked with Amagoalik in the 1970s formulating Nunavut's future government, said his friend is still as much a force today as he was back then.

But when he and another friend, Mark Stiles of Ottawa — who first met Amagoalik in 1975 while working in the land claims office of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada — visited Amagoalik at Embassy West in March, they felt he needed their help.

Amagoalik, centre, is shown with Georges Erasmus, left, who at the time was national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, and Indigenous rights advocate Louis Bruyere at a news conference in Ottawa in May 1987. (Chuck Mitchell/The Canadian Press)

"I said, 'Well, how do you like it here, John?' And he said, 'I hate it,'" Kelliher said.

So he asked Amagoalik if he wanted help to return home. "He said, 'Do anything to get me out of here, to get me back to Iqaluit.'"

So they did.

First, they delivered a letter to the territory’s health minister, signed by Amagoalik and dated March 31, pleading to return home. Amagoalik claims he never agreed to the move being permanent.

A copy of Amagoalik's letter delivered to Nunavut's health minister in March. (John Amagoalik)

When the minister, Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster, didn't take any action on his request to return home, they formed the John A. Committee and brought in Iqaluit lawyer Anne Crawford.

The committee raised $30,000 for a consultant to develop Amagoalik's plan of care, buy medical equipment and supplies, and pay for eight to 10 hours of daily private home care from personal support workers.

It also secured an accessible unit at a subsidized rate of $2,000 a month that has space for his hospital bed and an elevator. The Amagoaliks' public housing unit has stairs that would be too difficult for him to use.

The committee also arranged air transportation donated by an airline to fly Amagoalik to Iqaluit. On June 12, 16 months after he arrived in Ottawa, he returned home.

Amagoalik’s public housing unit has stairs, making it difficult for him to access his home. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

An uncertain future

But despite all of the hard work to bring Amagoalik back to Nunavut, his future is still uncertain.

The funds raised by the committee were only meant to be for the short term, and Anne Crawford said the money is running out.

"Which we did tell the government at the time, this will not last forever. And therefore, can you talk to us about how and what we can do going forward to continue to support him and live in his home community?"

Anne Crawford, a longtime lawyer in Iqaluit, says Amagoalik is leading the way for Nunavut elders to be cared for in their communities. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

The request to the territorial government for $16,000 a month to cover accommodations in the accessible unit and up to 10 hours a day of support worker care was declined. However, the government can provide a maximum of two hours per week of personal support worker care.

The committee says its research shows that Nunavut was spending about $30,000 a month for Amagoalik’s care at Embassy West.

The Health Department told CBC News that it can't comment on his care in order to protect his privacy. Brewster, the health minister, also declined to be interviewed.

But a communications manager provided a written statement saying the government has not refused to provide publicly funded health care to Amagoalik and that it continues to work in "good faith to support him."

Victoria-based lawyer Steve Kelliher (pictured) and Mark Stiles, friends of Amagoalik, worked to bring him home to Iqaluit and are trying to secure funding from the government for his care. (Submitted by Steve Kelliher)

"So we have no alternative but to appeal to the courts to compel them to do the right thing," Kelliher said, calling the situation "despicable."

"If we've got no money, we'll go beat the bushes," he said. Amagoalik "deserves better. He's earned it. He is an exception. Who treats their leaders like that? Not the Inuit. I don't believe it."

On Sept. 16, two notices of application for judicial review were filed in the Nunavut Court of Justice on behalf of Amagoalik.

"One for judicial review of the assistant deputy minister's letter, the decision not to fund John's care and housing," Kelliher said. "And an application for urgent relief to compel them to do so until the matter is fully heard, which could take months."

Amagoalik and his wife, Evie, embrace. (CBC)

Lack of care facilities for seniors

Amagoalik's care situation is emblematic of a wider problem in Nunavut. The vast territory, which covers a total area of just over two million square kilometres and is home to roughly 40,000 people, has only six seniors' facilities spread across its three regions.

The government says it's expanding two more long-term care facilities in Nunavut.

Currently, 73 elders from Nunavut are being cared for at Embassy West Senior Living, the only out-of-territory facility contracted by the government for more complex needs.

"We don't want to continue seeing our elders getting flown to Ottawa,” said Gloria Uluqsi, president of Nunavut Tunngavik. "I think they can do better. I think we as a team can do better for our elders."

World.title: It's almost the end of September. Where are all the hurricanes?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As of this writing, there have been only six named storms this Atlantic hurricane season, and most of them only lasted a couple of days. So what's going on? Where's all the hurricane activity?

"Normally we have to blame like four or five different things, but this year, I think we really can pretty much put all the blame on El Niño," said Phil Klotzbach, a senior research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University.

"It is a very, very strong event."

It turns out the "super" El Niño that is under way is putting a clamp on Atlantic hurricane activity.

El Niño is part of a natural cycle called the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), involving water in the central Pacific Ocean as well as atmospheric winds.

When the water becomes 0.5 C warmer than average over a particular time frame, it indicates an El Niño event. Water that is -0.5 C cooler than average indicates a La Niña event. The repercussions of these oscillations can be felt around the world.

During a typical El Niño, an amplified polar jet stream often leads to warmer than normal temperatures in much of western Canada during the winter season. (CBC News)

And right now, there is an El Niño advisory, with several models suggesting this could be a historic event.

"The anomalies are getting so strong that we might see stronger than 2.4 C anomaly, which is our historical record that was set back in 1982 and 1983 winter. And we're predicting possibly 2.6 to 2.7 C anomalies," said Lindsey Long, a meteorologist with the Climate Prediction Center at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

"So, a very strong event, [with a] 75 per cent chance of being historical. We have over 90 per cent chance of it being very strong, which is the highest in our category here at NOAA."

WATCH | I've tracked El Niño for years. I've never seen this before: I’ve tracked El Niño for years. I’ve never seen this before | Duration closed caption 3:23 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a "super" El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this "super" El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

The quiet season hasn't exactly been a surprise to forecasters. In May, NOAA forecast eight to 14 named storms and three to six hurricanes. Its August forecast lowered those ranges to seven to 13 named storms and two to six hurricanes.

How does something in the Pacific influence the Atlantic?

How is it that what happens thousands of kilometres away in the middle of the Pacific Ocean influences what happens in the Atlantic?

Long explained that when the sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are higher than normal, they tend to create vertical wind shear in the Atlantic, with strong winds in the upper atmosphere and weaker winds in the lower atmosphere.

"It kind of destroys the hurricane structure that we like to see," Long said. "Hurricanes are very vertical beings."

Tropical Storm Fay (right of centre) is seen in the Atlantic Ocean on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. The storm came very close to being the first named hurricane of the season. (NASA/EOSDIS)

The shear has been so strong that this quiet Atlantic hurricane season could be one for the record books.

"Typically, by the time you get to, say, mid-October, the season is really starting to wind down," Klotzbach said. "So, to use a baseball quote on these — Yogi Berra used to say, 'It's getting late early.'"

He said it's unlikely that we'll suddenly see an uptick, but we might still see one or two hurricanes form.

"I'd be surprised if we end up a season with zero hurricanes, but probably the odds of getting anything substantial out of the deep tropics are pretty low."

However, there's still a chance that one could develop in the warm Gulf of Mexico.

"The Caribbean still has lots of wind shear, so possible formations there are probably low, but in the Gulf of [Mexico] we are seeing less wind shear," Long said. "So there is a possibility for some formation there or off the east coast of the U.S."

Not quiet everywhere

But El Niño tends to have the opposite effect in the Pacific Ocean, creating heightened hurricane activity.

To date, there have been 16 named storms in the Pacific, with another likely to form after publication.

The Atlantic basin almost got its first hurricane this past weekend.

According to meteorologist and hurricane specialist Michael Lowry , Tropical Storm Fay, which formed as a tropical depression on Saturday, reached winds of 112 km/h, falling just short of the Category 1 hurricane wind speeds of 119 km/h.

The Saffir-Simpson hurricane scale gives you an idea of what a Category 5 storm means. (CBC News)

Interestingly, Fay formed significantly farther north than where most Atlantic hurricanes form. Most form around 20 degrees north latitude , while Fay formed around 32 degrees north.

While this El Niño is responsible for the lack of hurricanes in the Atlantic, it's important to note that there have been a few short-lived tropical storms in the Gulf of Mexico that have impacted communities along the coast, including in Louisiana .

This El Niño is forecast to peak in November or December, though it will persist into 2027. What that means for next year's hurricane season is still unknown.

"Typically, the year after an El Niño, you have no El Niño and a warmer Atlantic. So we can't say for sure that it's going to be a busy season next year," Klotzbach said.

World.title: Jenna Timmons-Oikawa wins 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa-based writer Jenna Timmons-Oikawa has won the 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize for her story Wawa Indian.

She will receive $6,000 from the Canada Council for the Arts and a two-week residency in the Leighton Artist Studios at Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity.

Timmons-Oikawa's non-fiction piece was published on CBC Books. You can read Wawa Indian here.

This year's finalists were selected by a jury composed of Claire Cameron, Niigaan Sinclair and Teresa Wong.

"Wawa Indian was a real pleasure to read and a refreshing narrative that took the jury on a dynamic journey. The story is a metaphorical, time-shifting and complicated exploration of identity, contradiction and 'living through history.' At the same time, the narrator's voice is generous and empathic, representing the tenderness of growing up and the tragedy of truth," the jury said in a statement.

"Bringing together past and present, Wawa Indian plays with language, illustrates the complexity of humanity and offers hope to a world built on harm and cynicism."

The story Wawa Indian was inspired by themes of reclamation and renewal, says writer Jenna Timmons-Oikawa. (Tenzin Tsering/CBC)

Timmons-Oikawa told CBC Books that Wawa Indian was inspired by themes of reclamation and renewal. Reclaiming stolen heritage and culture has been an often confusing and sometimes messy human experience, she said.

"It is something that I have been and will be working toward for the rest of my life."

Writing this piece brought to light some feelings I had been holding on to, and brought to my consciousness many things I had been not allowing myself to believe - Jenna Timmons-Oikawa

"It wasn't until last year, when I wrote this piece, that I fully came to terms with, and emotionally understood that, my mom was taken. She wasn't just a gift given to my grandparents, but a stolen person," said Timmons-Oikawa.

"Though I had researched the Sixties Scoop and logically knew what had happened, it still had felt emotionally disconnected from me," she said. "Writing this piece brought to light some feelings I had been holding on to — and brought to my consciousness many things I had been not allowing myself to believe."

Timmons-Oikawa lives on the traditional, unceded territory of the Anishinaabe Algonquin Nation in Ottawa. Her work has appeared or is forthcoming in The Malahat Review, The Fiddlehead and PRISM International, and she was selected as first runner-up for Canadian prose as part of The Temz Review's inaugural "London" Literary Prizes.

She holds a bachelor of arts in creative writing, a diploma in child and youth counselling and spent a decade working with youth in the mental health field.

Timmons-Oikawa joins a long list of writers who have won CBC Literary Prizes, including Lorna Crozier, David Bergen, Michael Ondaatje and Carol Shields.

The CBC Literary Prizes have been recognizing Canadian writers since 1979.

“To have [the judges] select this piece as the winner of the CBC Nonfiction Prize is truly a privilege. I can't thank CBC, the readers and the judges enough for seeing the value and beauty in my story. It was transformative for me to write, and to have it read and honoured in this way by three distinguished Canadian non-fiction writers, is transformative as well. Not enough people get to live out their childhood dreams, and now I am a lucky one of the few."

It was transformative for me to write, and to have it read and honoured in this way by three distinguished Canadian nonfiction writers, is transformative as well. - Jenna Timmons-Oikawa

The other four prize finalists were:

They will each receive $1,000 from the Canada Council for the Arts.

The longlist was selected from more than 1,900 submissions, which are processed by a two-tiered system.

Initial submissions are screened by a reading committee chosen for each category from a group of qualified editors and writers across the country. Each entry is read by two readers.

The readers come up with a preliminary list of approximately 100 submissions that are then forwarded to a second reading committee. It is this committee who decides the approximately 30 entries selected for the longlist, which is forwarded to the jury.

Works are judged anonymously on the basis of the participant's use of language, originality of subject and writing style. For more on how the judging for the CBC Literary Prizes works, visit the FAQ page.

Last year's winner was Laura MacGregor for her story The Invisible Woman.

The 2026 winner of the Prix du récit Radio-Canada is Raphaël Potvin for Points de suture.

World.title: 'What he’s doing is positively un-American': Late-night hosts react to Trump media ban
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jon Stewart, Seth Meyers, Jimmy Kimmel and even — to some extent — the famously "not very political" Jimmy Fallon have built their careers making fun of the U.S. president.

So when Donald Trump announced he was banning news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House last Friday, the late-night television hosts came out swinging in defence of the First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and the press.

Were they outraged? Definitely. Were they funny? You be judge.

"The White House press pool is more of a mess than the reflecting pool right now," said Jimmy Kimmel, whose jokes have landed him in trouble with the Trump administration before.

"What he's doing is positively un-American," he said on ABC's Jimmy Kimmel Live!

"The five networks, including Fox, joined forces to put out a statement saying the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.... Do you realize how far south somebody has to go for Fox News to defend CNN?" he added.

Helipad event offers fodder for jokes

Both Kimmel and NBC host Seth Meyers pointed out how Trump's media ban appeared to backfire when the White House press pool, which usually has eyes on the president at all official events, refused to cover his opening of a new helicopter landing pad.

There were visuals of the ribbon cutting from the White House's own video stream, but there was no microphone there to pick up what the president was saying. All that could be heard was the whirring of the helicopter blades.

"The best is, that sound is always the substance of what Trump is saying," said Meyers.

Yesterday, the Trump administration released a statement reiterating its position that, "White House access is a privilege — not a right" and rejecting claims the media ban undermined reporters' First Amendment rights.

That argument was put to Trump directly by some of the journalists remaining in the White House.

Acting like a diva

Meyers played a clip of Trump's response, saying the president "sounds like an aging Hollywood starlet chewing out a director for cutting her line."

Jimmy Fallon compared him to the host of The Traitors. "He even dressed like Alan Cumming to tell them, 'You're banished from my castle.'"



He also suggested the First Lady wished she, too, would be banished to get away from her husband. "In a related story, Melania just applied to be a reporter for CNN, MSN NOW and Politico," joked Fallon.

On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart focused on Trump's reason for the media ban: his disappointment in the outlets' negative news stories.

Outrage and incredulity

"Have you tried president-ing better?" asked Stewart. "I mean give the press something to work with. Oh, here's a positive story: I never thought my car could take $140 worth of gas in such a small tank!"

Stewart toggled between outrage and incredulity as he replayed footage of Trump justifying his media ban.

"Not for nothing, have we ever had a president just flat out in the Oval Office come out against the Constitution?"

World.content:
Article content

“Jewish Canadians are living in a parallel world,” Herland wrote in his post. “Where police stand guard with guns outside synagogues. And Jewish schools, religious sites and businesses are targeted with bullets. And most Canadians have no awareness or understanding.”

Dedicated police protection has become commonplace at synagogues across Canada, particularly during Jewish holidays, in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks in Israel.

Multiple synagogues in Ontario, and specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years. In March, three GTA synagogues were struck by gunfire in the space of five days — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill, and Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim in North York. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with two of the shootings.

Toronto police were present at Monday’s protest, and kept protesters about five metres away from the door.

Herland noted that the guest speaker was an Australian-born university teacher who lives in Israel, identified by the Song Shul as Mark Regev, former Israeli ambassador to the U.K. A Canadian group called Just Peace Advocates had submitted a complaint demanding that Regev be barred from entering Canada. National Post has reached out to the group for more information.

“His speech was about making peace in the Middle East. Let’s hope that happens this year,” Herland wrote.
