World.title: Brugada, Mamdani swap notes on housing, care systems at U20 mayors summit in New York
World.content:
Mexico City’s public care system and Mayor Clara Brugada’s community center initiative won praise from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during the 2026 Urban 20 Mayors Summit (U20), an annual gathering of mayors from major G20 cities and other metropolises around the world.

Speaking alongside Brugada in New York on Sunday, Mamdani said that Mexico City is a city “that many of us look to for inspiration, especially in how we answer the crisis of care in our economies.”

Gracias, @NYCMayor, por reconocer las #UTOPÍAS de la Ciudad de México como un proyecto para garantizar una vida plena. Una visión de ciudad que pone a las personas y a las comunidades al centro. ¡Es un gusto que este proyecto sea inspirador en las grandes ciudades del mundo! pic.twitter.com/gvZzhVLnF2 — Clara Brugada Molina (@ClaraBrugadaM) September 20, 2026

“When we’re talking about care blocks, we talk about these often within our own administration as an example of what it can look like to deliver for people in our own city,” he said.

Under Brugada’s leadership, the Mexico City government has set up a public care system, a central part of which is the provision of free childcare as well as services aimed at the well-being of seniors and people with disabilities.

Among the government-run centers that offer these services are Unidades de Transformación y Organización para la Inclusión y la Armonía Social (Units of Transformation and Organization for Inclusion and Social Harmony), known as Utopías. These community centers — which also offer cheap meals and a range of recreational, cultural, social and educational facilities — first opened in Iztapalapa when Bruagada was mayor of that Mexico City borough (2018-23) and are now being expanded to other parts of the capital as the city government seeks to offer greater support to primary caregivers, including working mothers.

Brugada is aiming to open 100 new Utopías during her 2024-30 mayorship, while solidifying caregiving as a “public responsibility” rather than a private one.

Mamdani said that “when we talk about Utopías, [there is] the understanding also that we have to be delivering dignity to working people … to ensure they can live lives that are full, lives that are flourishing.”

“And it is such a pleasure to have a fellow mayor here as we do with the mayors of Freetown and Rome who understand that the issues of the working class must be issues at the forefront of our politics,” he said. “And one day I will return to Mexico City, but I don’t know when that is.”

In separate remarks on Sunday, Mamdani said he would like to work with President Claudia Sheinbaum and “any other leaders from across Mexico” to address “global crises.”

“… The crises we face are global crises and that is true for Mexico City, for Rome, for Freetown, for New York City and so many others. And we’ve also watched in admiration of President Sheinbaum’s initiatives and the ways in which she is tackling the same issues of cost of living,” the mayor said.

Brugada draws inspiration from NYC

While Mamdani looks to Mexico City for inspiration, Brugada was herself inspired by New York, a city she said she visited as a young “social activist” in 1987.

In a social media post, the mayor noted that on Monday, she met with Mamdani and “repartidores paisanos” — i.e. Mexicans who work in the Big Apple as deliverymen and deliverywomen for companies such as Uber Eats and DoorDash.

“In Mexico City we will replicate some of New York’s good practices to support those who work in this activity,” Brugada wrote.

She said her government will create “spaces where [repartidores] can rest, recharge their bikes and access bathrooms.”

“We take care of our workers here and there!” Brugada wrote.

En #NuevaYork me reuní con el alcalde @NYCMayor y con repartidores paisanos. Replicaremos en la Ciudad de México algunas de las buenas prácticas de Nueva York para apoyar a quienes se dedican a esta actividad. Como espacios donde puedan descansar, recargar sus bicis y acceso a… pic.twitter.com/NBd5HeccBm — Clara Brugada Molina (@ClaraBrugadaM) September 21, 2026

On Monday morning, the mayor used the New York City Subway to get to her meeting with Mamdani.

“Hello. We’re going on the subway to City Hall where the Mayor Mamdani awaits us,” she said in a video message.

Above the video, Brugada wrote: “On the way to a meeting with the Mayor of New York. We’re continuing the exchange of ideas and experiences about the future of our cities. As in our beloved #CapitalDeLaTransformación [i.e. Mexico City] public transport is what connects and integrates major metropolises … and here we go.”

Brugada: ‘No (affordable) housing, no peace’

During an address at a U20 forum on affordable housing on Sunday, Brugada said that Mexico City would, “of course,” join a global “affordable housing coalition” proposed by Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni.

“I know that many cities present here will [also] join,” she said.

In a video posted to social media, Brugada said that Collboni had made a “very good proposal to build a coalition of cities in favor of affordable housing.”

In the same video, the mayor of Barcelona — a city with serious tourism-related housing problems — said that Mexico City is among the first cities to join “the defense of a fundamental right, as is the right to decent and affordable housing for everyone.”

“This is a fight that all the big cities of the world are in, and I’m very happy that Mexico City together with New York and Toronto … have joined the initiative in order to do big things,” Collboni said.

In her forum address on Sunday, Brugada declared that without affordable housing, there is “no peace,” and spoke about her government’s housing initiatives and the progress made during her mayorship and that of Sheinbaum, who governed Mexico City from December 2018 to June 2023.

“Between 2018 and 2025, nearly half a million people were lifted out of housing poverty in Mexico City. Despite these results, significant challenges remain. As in other cities around the world, the city continues to face a housing shortage, as well as gentrification and the displacement of communities due to speculative dynamics in the real estate market,” she said.

“To address this situation, in Mexico City we have developed the largest housing policy in our history — and one of the policies of greatest reach at an international level as well,” Brugada said.

“The three pillars of this housing policy are firstly, the large-scale construction of social housing; secondly, regulation of the real estate market; and thirdly, we carry this out in partnership with the people through a model of co-management,” she said.

“… We have the goal of building 200,000 … [affordable] homes by 2030,” the mayor said.

“I’m talking about new homes and improved homes. … This means unprecedented progress in reducing the housing shortage,” Brugada said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mass nesting event brings more than 100,000 olive ridley sea turtles to Oaxaca’s Playa Escobilla
World.content:
More than 100,000 olive ridley sea turtles came ashore at Oaxaca’s Playa Escobilla in a single mass nesting event last week, but the spectacle masks a fragile reproductive outlook: As few as 30% to 40% of the eggs may hatch.

According to the newspaper El Universal Oaxaca, 101,500 females emerged from the Pacific Ocean in Santa María Tonameca last Tuesday in a huge, synchronous nesting event known as an arribada.

The sixth arribada (literally “arrival” in Spanish) of the 2026-27 season lifted the season’s running total to more than 465,000 turtles as of last week, according to the paper.

The olive ridley turtle is among the smallest species of sea turtle in the world. They are found primarily in tropical regions, with a nesting season that generally runs from May through February or March.

Playa Escobilla is among the world’s leading nesting sites for the olive ridley, or Lepidochelys olivacea.

The species is listed as endangered in Mexico and faces risks from egg poaching, fishing, destruction of nesting habitat and climate-related events. Conservation efforts are abundant all over Mexico, and volunteer opportunities are many, as detailed this month in Mexico News Daily.

Despite the current large Escobilla tally, Rafael Villanueva Alcázar of the National Commission of Natural Protected Areas (Conanp) cautions that nesting totals do not guarantee a comparable increase in hatchlings.

“It sounds like a lot,” he said, “but it’s actually very low compared to other beaches that have a higher rate of hatchling production.”

Only about 30% to 40% of Escobilla nests hatch, Villanueva said. By comparison, Playa Ceuta in Sinaloa estimates an 85% hatch rate, but it has only about 500 olive ridley nests per season.

No global hatching rate for sea turtle nests could be found, but one widely cited statistic is that roughly one in every 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings worldwide survives to adulthood.

Rising sand temperatures, changes in sand composition, erosion, strong swells and low humidity are among the factors reducing hatching success. Egg theft and other human-caused damage also take a toll.

Conditions can vary sharply between seasons and sanctuaries.

At Morro Ayuta, another major olive ridley refuge on Oaxaca’s coast, a record 1.9 million olive ridley nests were protected and more than 34 million hatchlings were released into the sea during the 2025-26 season.

Guillermo González Padilla, the head of that turtle camp, said those numbers were “unprecedented” thanks to “the rains, the wetter beaches and the fact that the summer’s temperature [in 2025] was ideal for egg incubation.”

(For this season, Morro Ayuta had counted about 135,000 turtles through the start of its third arribada earlier this month, according to Conanp.)

Meanwhile, at Escobilla, conservation work over the past 35 years has helped. Officials set aside a 5-kilometer protected area for nesting during last week’s arribada, and Conanp is monitoring the nesting grounds along with other federal agencies and local communities.

Local participation is critical because available park rangers alone cannot protect the beach from poachers and other threats. Also, according to EDUCA, a Oaxacan community development NGO, locals help strategically relocate eggs — which average 100 per nest — after arribadas.

With reports from El Universal Oaxaca and MeganoticiasMx

World.title: Aeroméxico investigates possible leak of 15 million passenger records
World.content:
Aeroméxico is investigating a possible leak of customer information after the federal Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance (SABG) identified an online user offering to sell a trove of over 15 million passenger records.

However, Aeroméxico said Sunday that it hadn’t identified any compromise of its customers’ financial information.

🚨Detectan posible exposición de datos personales vinculada a Aeroméxico La Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno identificó indicios de una posible filtración de datos personales en un sistema que podría estar relacionado con Aeroméxico. El hallazgo surgió tras detectar,… pic.twitter.com/iSFbFpKhkx — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) September 20, 2026

In a statement, Aeroméxico said that “based on the information available,” it hadn’t identified any “exposure” of its customers’ “financial information,” including details of cards used to purchase flights.

The airline also said it hadn’t detected any compromise of customers’ Aeroméxico account passwords, including those used to access the Aeroméxico rewards program.

“Furthermore, this situation has not created any impact on our operations,” Aeroméxico said.

The airline released its statement after SABG said it had detected that a user of the social media and instant messaging platform Telegram was attempting to sell a 1.1 gigabyte database “supposedly attributable” to Aeroméxico and containing more than 15 million passenger records.

“Within the framework of active forensic monitoring of possible security incidents, the Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance identified signs of a possible exposure of personal data in a system that could be related to Aeroméxico,” the SABG said in a statement.

The ministry said that its monitoring allowed it to locate a Sept. 18 post on Telegram in which “a user offers a database supposedly attributable to Aeroméxico with more than 15 million records,” including — allegedly — the full names of customers of the airline, their e-mail addresses, their telephone numbers and their dates of birth.

The SABG said that it “obtained a sample of 100,092 records” and subsequently identified the names of various people, including those of public servants and public figures.

The ministry said it would “analyze the data obtained” and begin an investigation aimed at determining “the alleged responsibility for the compromised databases.”

Aeroméxico said it would cooperate with federal authorities and report on any relevant developments in a timely manner.

The airline also said it had begun its own “exhaustive investigation” in order to “verify the authenticity and veracity” of the information being offered to “third parties,” determine “its origin” and “establish the reach of any possible impact.”

While the airline said it hadn’t identified any compromise of its customers’ financial information, it advised its customers to stay alert to “unusual e-mails, messages or calls that seek personal or financial information.”

Aeroméxico didn’t say that its systems or databases had been targeted in a cyberattack.

However, hackers have previously targeted both companies and federal and state governments in Mexico. Among the victims of previous cyberattacks are the Ministry of National Defense and state oil company Pemex.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Sheinbaum pledges continued military support as Sinaloa’s cartel turf war shifts to Mazatlán
World.content:
A day after pledging Sunday to keep federal security forces in Sinaloa “as long as necessary,” President Sheinbaum on Monday repeated her conviction that U.S. interference precipitated the cartel turf war plaguing the troubled state. The violence, previously centered in Culiacán and rural areas, has spread south in recent months to the resort city of Mazatlán.

While in Culiacán, the Sinaloa state capital, on Sunday, Sheinbaum said Governor Graciela Domínguez can count on the complete support of the federal government.

Domínguez has been in office for less than a month after being appointed on Aug. 25 to replace Rubén Rocha, who was indicted by U.S. federal prosecutors for alleged links to drug trafficking.

“First and foremost, all federal forces … will remain here for as long as necessary,” she said. “We will not withdraw any element of the Army, the National Guard or the Navy; they will continue to support the governor and, above all, the people of Sinaloa.”

The state has been embroiled in a civil war between factions of the Sinaloa Cartel for two years, becoming what El País newspaper has described as “the biggest political crisis of Sheinbaum’s term.”

As the turf war spread to Mazatlán this summer, the government has deployed thousands of federal troops to the resort city, including 1,000 marines and over 800 Public Security Ministry agents last week. Despite an increase in military presence, homicides in Mazatlán outpaced killings in the larger city of Culiacán in August.

Sinaloa’s economy is facing a historic downturn, driven by severe security challenges and cartel-related violence, leading to a contraction of 4.5% in this year’s first quarter.

On Sunday, Sheinbaum blamed foreign interference for the current situation and then doubled down on that claim during her daily press conference on Monday.

“We don’t want interference from any foreign government in our territory,” she said on Sunday. “Interference generates violence, whereas cooperation for development generates peace.”

Sheinbaum said that before the U.S. “extraction” of drug kingpin Ismael Zambada, the murder rate in Sinaloa was low (“less than one homicide per day,” she claimed). Since then, violence has escalated, producing significant crime rates.

Sunday’s visit was Sheinbaum’s first to the state since the indictments against Rocha and nine other government and law enforcement officials from the state were made public in April.

To address the challenges, Sheinbaum said federal officials would travel in stages to Sinaloa; Security Cabinet officials will visit this week, followed by officials from the Agriculture Ministry.

“There will be no shortage of money to support farmers,” she said, acknowledging that agriculture is the backbone of the state’s economy.

With reports from N+, La Jornada and El País

World.title: After a shootout, authorities rescue 3 kidnapping victims and arrest 7 suspects in Puerto Peñasco
World.content:
Security forces arrested seven people and freed three kidnapping victims during an operation Friday afternoon in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, a popular seaside resort city also known as Rocky Point.

Authorities also seized an arsenal that included more than 40 long guns, approximately 4,000 rounds of ammunition, two Minimi machine guns and a Browning M2 .50 caliber gun, the federal Security Cabinet announced on Monday.

En Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, trabajos de investigación de @fgjesonora, con información del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia de @SSPCMexico @Defensamx1, @SEMAR_mx y @Amicsonora.

En una operación encabezada por @Defensamx1 y @Amicsonora permitieron ubicar un inmueble relacionado con… pic.twitter.com/dtwS2fGtft — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) September 21, 2026

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that three federal agencies and the military joined an investigation by the Sonora Attorney General’s Office (FGJES), supplying intelligence that allowed state officials to identify a property linked to the kidnappings.

As state police and soldiers approached the premises, armed civilians opened fire. The authorities returned fire, eventually outflanking the suspects and containing them.

Three Sonora Investigative Police agents were wounded in the confrontation, none seriously, and three kidnapping victims were freed. Authorities captured seven suspects, including one minor.

The suspects will face charges for attempted aggravated homicide, crimes against public servants, aggravated vehicle theft, criminal association and kidnapping.

After the shootout, the authorities obtained a search warrant and re-entered the property, confiscating the weapons. The search also turned up evidence that was sufficient to merit another warrant that led to two weekend raids on additional properties in downtown Puerto Peñasco.

The sweep of those locations resulted in the seizure of heroin, methamphetamine, loaded magazines, bullet-proof vests, tactical gear and three high-end vehicles which had been reported stolen in the United States.

“We extend special recognition to the three AMIC [the Criminal Investigation Agency] agents who were injured during the attack,” García Harfuch said in a social media post.

A FGJES press release indicated that one of its agents was shot in a lower extremity, while two female agents suffered shrapnel wounds. All three were reported to be in stable condition.

The skirmish came about after several miners reported to police that they had escaped a kidnapping attempt last week, but others hadn’t. State officials alerted federal agencies, who were able to follow the route of the captors and locate a white Chevrolet Suburban truck that had been described by the near-victims.

With reports from La Jornada, Sonora Presente and Eje Central

World.title: Hurricane Polo expected to reach Category 5 as it nears Mexico’s Pacific coast
World.content:
Listen to this article

Hurricane Polo is expected to quickly intensify after forming Monday morning in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Guerrero, with Civil Protection encouraging residents of several states to remain vigilant and follow safety recommendations.

Polo could bring heavy rain, rough surf and tropical-storm-force winds to parts of Mexico this week as it intensifies into a Category 5 hurricane near the coast of Michoacán by Wednesday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center warned.

⚠️ #Polo ahora como #Huracán categoría 1 ⚠️ ◾️Se localiza a 305 km al sur-suroeste de Zihuatanejo, #Guerrero, y a 435 km al sur-sureste de Manzanillo, #Colima

◾️Su circulación refuerza la psibabilidad de #Lluvias de distintas intensidades en Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero… pic.twitter.com/3RRiy2j0PQ — Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil (@CNPC_MX) September 21, 2026

It was centered about 410 kilometers south-southeast of Manzanillo, Mexico, and 322 kilometers southwest of Zihuatanejo at 9 a.m. CST on Monday. As of 12 p.m., it was a Category 1 storm with maximum sustained winds of 129 kph (80 mph).

Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) predicted Monday that Polo would bring heavy rainfall to Pacific coastal regions, potentially raising river and stream levels, triggering flooding and mudslides.

Intense rain is expected over the coming days in the states of Oaxaca and Guerrero (75 to 150 millimeters), very heavy rainfall (50 to 75 mm) in Michoacán, and heavy rainfall (25 to 50 mm) in coastal Jalisco and Colima.

Winds of 10 to 20 kph, with gusts of 30 to 50 kph, can also be expected along the coasts of Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero and Oaxaca. In addition, the storm will bring waves of 1 to 3 meters to Guerrero, Michoacán, Oaxaca, Jalisco and Colima.

Officials urged the public to remain attentive to the warnings issued by Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) and to follow the recommendations of Civil Protection.

The SMN and the U.S. National Hurricane Center established a watch zone from Tecpan de Galeana, Guerrero, to Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, warning that Polo’s trajectory will be “erratic.” It is expected to curve and move parallel to the coasts of Colima, Michoacán and Guerrero.

Farther west in the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Odalys is forecast to become a hurricane by mid-week. It was located over 2,000 kilometers west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula on Monday morning.

In September 2024, Hurricane John hit coastal Guerrero as a Category 3 storm, just one year after Category 5 Hurricane Otis devastated Acapulco, one of Mexico’s main tourist destinations with a population of over one million people, from which it is still recovering.

With reports from AP News

World.title: Bruce Mac Master Snub: Gaviria Calls Colombia’s Government Arrogant
World.content:
Colombia · Politics

Key Facts — What happened Former minister Alejandro Gaviria said on X that the government orders ministers to shun independent business leaders, journalists and executives.

— What the veto is Vicky Dávila of Semana posted on X, citing unnamed government sources, that no minister may meet Mac Master.

— Who is targeted Bruce Mac Master has led ANDI, Colombia’s largest business association, since 2013; its board reconfirmed him on 8 September 2026.

— The catch The government has not confirmed the directive, and no official response to Gaviria has been reported.

— Who else objected Senators Andrés Forero of the Democratic Centre and Ariel Ávila of the opposition Green Alliance both criticised it.

— Why it matters The row comes as ANDI questions health funding in the 2027 budget now before Congress.

A reported order to keep ministers away from the head of Colombia’s main business lobby has drawn fire from a former minister and senators on left and right.

The Casa de Nariño, Colombia’s presidential palace in Bogotá, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Bruce Mac Master, head of Colombia’s biggest business association, is at the centre of a new political row. A reported order barring ministers from meeting him has drawn fire from former minister Alejandro Gaviria.

Without naming President Abelardo de la Espriella, Gaviria called the government “increasingly arrogant, isolated and ineffective”. He made the charge on X, in a post reported by Infobae on Tuesday 22 September 2026.

What the reported veto is

The veto is not about a board seat, a delegation or a commission. It concerns access to the government itself.

The claim came from Vicky Dávila, a former presidential candidate who manages publications at the news magazine Semana. She posted it on X on 21 September 2026.

“Government sources confirm that from now on, no minister can meet Bruce Mac Master, president of ANDI,” she wrote. She added that officials were weighing extending the veto to ANDI board members.

The political news site La Silla Vacía noted that Semana itself had not carried the report. It described Dávila as a kind of spokesperson for the new government.

The Presidency has not confirmed that any such order exists. No official response to Gaviria or to the senators who objected has been reported.

Mac Master has run the National Business Association of Colombia, known as ANDI, since 2013. It groups about 1,500 companies in industry, finance and commerce, according to the news site Las2orillas.

Gaviria’s words, and his stake

Gaviria served as health minister under Juan Manuel Santos and as education minister under Gustavo Petro. His post did not mention De la Espriella by name.

“The order is clear,” he wrote, in The Rio Times’ translation. “Do not talk to business associations, journalists or executives who show any independence.”

“The purpose is also evident: to end dissent, to build by force a kind of artificial consensus,” he continued.

He ended with the line quoted most widely. “The result is predictable: a government that is increasingly arrogant, isolated and ineffective.”

Gaviria has a personal interest in the dispute. His wife, the economist Carolina Soto, withdrew this month from the presidency of the Colombian Chamber of Infrastructure, a construction lobby.

“In view of the opposition my appointment generated, I have decided to decline,” Soto said, as quoted by the outlet Cambio. Infobae reported that she had faced pressure from the government.

The skyline of central Bogotá, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

A board that kept its president

The friction predates this week. Cambio reported on 8 September 2026 that the government had signalled, through various channels, that it preferred a new head at ANDI.

ANDI’s board confirmed Mac Master anyway at a meeting that day. Rodolfo Castillo became board chair and María del Rosario Gómez vice chair, according to Las2orillas.

Earlier, Dávila had written that Mac Master had “zero interactions” with the new president. La Silla Vacía reported that, officially, the two men have no quarrel.

Cambio also described a split over donations for reconstruction in Chocó, a Pacific coast department. Mac Master chose a trust and donors’ board rather than the fund run by first lady Ana Lucía Pineda.

Criticism from both sides of Congress

The reaction crossed party lines. Senator Andrés Forero of the Democratic Centre, the party of former president Álvaro Uribe, objected publicly.

“This is not right,” Forero said. “Business associations’ autonomy and independence is a democratic value that should not be lost.”

He urged the government to reconsider what he called an “inconvenient and alarming decision”.

Senator Ariel Ávila of the opposition Green Alliance went further. He said the president gives no press conferences or interviews and speaks only to “friendly” media.

Ávila also said officials call to demand the heads of journalists and business association managers. He likened the conduct to “any banana-republic authoritarian”.

The health budget in the background

The row lands as ANDI challenges the government on health spending. On 21 September 2026 the association warned about the per-patient payment that funds Colombia’s health insurers.

ANDI said this year’s adjustment of 12.94% would leave a gap of 3.7 trillion pesos (about US$1.16 billion). It had recommended an increase of 15.6%.

That conversion uses the official rate of 3,192.53 to the US dollar for 22 September 2026. The rate is published by Colombia’s Financial Superintendence.

Mac Master argued that the 2027 budget debate in Congress should rest on technical criteria. Infobae read that as criticism of Health Minister Ana María Vesga.

What comes next

For now the dispute rests on a reported directive the government has neither confirmed nor denied. No minister has said publicly whether they will meet the ANDI chief.

The first test will come as Congress debates the 2027 budget. ANDI has already asked for health spending to match the system’s real costs.

More: Colombia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Bruce Mac Master?

He is the executive president of ANDI, the National Business Association of Colombia, a post he has held since 2013. ANDI groups about 1,500 companies from industry, finance and commerce. He was a frequent critic of economic measures under former president Gustavo Petro. The ANDI board confirmed him again on 8 September 2026.

What exactly was vetoed?

Not a seat or appointment. On 21 September 2026 Vicky Dávila, a Semana executive, wrote on X that government sources said no minister may meet Mac Master. The government has not confirmed the directive, and no official response has been reported.

Who is Alejandro Gaviria?

He is a Colombian economist and former university rector. He was health minister under Juan Manuel Santos and education minister under Gustavo Petro. His wife, Carolina Soto, withdrew this month from the presidency of the Colombian Chamber of Infrastructure after what she called opposition to her appointment.

Has the government responded?

No response from the Presidency or any minister has been reported. The criticism has come from Gaviria and from senators Andrés Forero of the Democratic Centre and Ariel Ávila of the Green Alliance.

Sources: Infobae on Gaviria’s post and the reported veto, La Silla Vacía on Dávila’s post and the reaction, Cambio on the ANDI board vote, Las2orillas on the new ANDI board, La República on ANDI’s health funding warning, Colombian open data on the official exchange rate

World.title: Viracopos Power Outage Cancels 26 Azul Flights and Slows Security Checks
World.content:
Brazil · Travel

Key Facts — What happened Part of the passenger terminal at Viracopos, near Campinas, lost power at about 3:10 a.m. local time on Tuesday, 22 September 2026.

— Who was hit hardest Azul, which runs most flights at the airport, said it cancelled 26 flights because of the power failure.

— Why queues built up X-ray scanners at the entrance to the departure area went down, so security checks were done by hand.

— The catch The operator says the backup generator did not work, and knock-on effects on flights could last up to two days.

— What was not affected The runway, aircraft apron, access roads and cargo terminal kept working, according to the operator.

— What travellers should do Check the flight status with the airline before leaving for the airport, as both the operator and Azul advise.

A failed substation and a backup generator that never started left Azul’s main hub in the dark for hours. The airport warns that delays could last for up to two days.

An Azul turboprop near a runway in Brazil, file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

A Viracopos power outage threw Azul’s main hub into disarray on Tuesday 22 September 2026. Queues stretched to the terminal doors as X-ray scanners and flight boards went dark.

Azul, the airline that dominates the airport near Campinas, said it cancelled 26 flights because of the failure. The operator warned that knock-on delays could last up to two days.

Viracopos International Airport sits about 80 kilometres northwest of São Paulo. It is the main hub of Azul and one of Brazil’s leading air cargo gateways.

A substation fails before dawn

The trouble began at about 3:10 a.m. local time, which in Campinas is Brasília time. Aeroportos Brasil Viracopos, the private company that runs the airport under a federal concession, said one substation feeding the check-in hall failed.

What should have happened next did not. The airport has a generator for outages, but it did not work, the operator told g1, the Globo group’s news site.

The concession also said there are three redundancy points meant to prevent this kind of blackout. The link between the three substations was interrupted, and it is investigating why.

Power began to return to the check-in hall at about 6:30 a.m., the operator told the news agency Estadão Conteúdo. Even so, g1 reported that part of the terminal was still on emergency lighting at noon.

The departure boards were dark overnight and came back on at about nine in the morning. The operator had said it expected full power to be restored by 12:30 p.m. Brasília time.

Security checks done by hand

The outage hit the X-ray machines at the entrance to the departure area. Security screening had to be carried out manually, the operator said, slowing the flow of passengers and staff.

During the morning the line for the departure area ran the length of the hall and reached the terminal door. Check-in and baggage drop counters were also crowded, according to g1.

Some passengers were stuck on the other side. Clara Maia, a social media influencer with 3 million followers, said she spent about two hours stuck on board an aircraft.

“There was a blackout and nobody gets in, nobody gets out,” she wrote in a post quoted by g1. At 9:07 a.m. she posted that she had finally got off.

What Azul does. Azul S.A., together with its subsidiaries, provides air transportation services in Brazil and internationally. It is also involved in the cargo or mail; passenger charter; development of frequent-flyer programs; intellectual property owner; travel packages; funding: aircraft financing; and provision of maintenance and hangarage services for aircraft, engines, parts and pieces, aircraft acquisition,…

How many flights were hit

Azul said 26 of its flights had been cancelled so far because of the power failure, and others were delayed. Earlier in the morning the airline had blamed weather in the Campinas region.

Tracking site Flightradar24 showed 26 cancellations and 81 delays at the airport by 1:06 p.m., g1 reported. Not all of those delays were necessarily caused by the outage.

Rival airlines reported little disruption. LATAM said only one of its flights was delayed, a service to Brasília that left 1 hour and 24 minutes late.

Gol said its only departure scheduled for Tuesday morning had operated. The operator said the runway, aircraft apron, access roads and cargo terminal were not affected.

The concession said passengers were still boarding their flights, only more slowly than normal. Because one aircraft flies several legs a day, early delays tend to ripple through the schedule.

Utility says the fault was inside the airport

CPFL Paulista, the power distributor that serves Campinas, said its network was working normally. It said it had registered no problems and received no call for help at the airport.

The fault originated in the airport’s own installations and is therefore the airport’s responsibility, the distributor said. The operator says it is still investigating what caused the failure.

What travellers should do now

Anyone flying through Viracopos this week should check the flight status with the airline before leaving home. Both the operator and Azul have given that advice.

Azul said affected customers are receiving the assistance required by Resolution 400 of Anac, Brazil’s National Civil Aviation Agency. That rule sets duties that grow with the length of a delay.

After one hour, airlines must provide means of communication such as phone or internet access. After two hours they must provide food, and after four hours lodging if needed, with transport.

For cancellations, or delays of more than four hours, passengers can choose a full refund or rebooking at no extra cost. Rebooking can be on another airline, and some trips can be completed by bus.

Keep boarding passes and receipts for any expenses.

The Viracopos power outage is a reminder that a single hub can disrupt a whole network. The operator expects the knock-on effects on flights to last for up to two days.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the Viracopos power outage?

The operator, Aeroportos Brasil Viracopos, said a substation feeding the check-in hall failed at about 3:10 a.m. Brasília time on Tuesday 22 September 2026. It said the backup generator did not work and the link between three substations was interrupted. The power distributor CPFL Paulista said its own network was working normally and that the fault was inside the airport.

How many flights were cancelled?

Azul said 26 of its flights were cancelled because of the power failure, with further delays. Flightradar24 data cited by g1 showed 26 cancellations and 81 delays at the airport by 1:06 p.m. Brasília time. Not every delay was necessarily linked to the outage.

Will my flight through Campinas be affected later this week?

Possibly. The operator said the effects on flights could last up to two days, as delayed aircraft and crews work back into the schedule. Check the flight status with the airline before going to the airport.

What am I entitled to if my Azul flight is cancelled?

Under Anac Resolution 400, airlines must offer communication after one hour, food after two hours and lodging if needed after four hours. For a cancellation you can choose a full refund, rebooking at no extra cost, possibly on another airline, or another mode of transport. Azul said affected customers are receiving this assistance.

World.title: XP ETF Suspension: Brazil Broker Halts New Buys of Six Bond Funds Over Tax Doubt
World.content:
Brazil · Investing

Key Facts — What happened The XP ETF suspension began on Monday 21 September 2026, halting new client purchases of six bond funds run by rivals.

— Which funds AMAB11, DEBB11, LFIN11 and MARG11 from BTG Pactual, GICP11 from Genial Investimentos and NLFA11 from Nubank.

— Why it matters The funds hold company and bank bonds paying the CDI rate; gains could be taxed at 25% instead of 15%.

— Who is not affected Existing holders keep their shares, and trading on the B3 stock exchange continues normally, according to XP and InvestNews.

— The catch The Federal Revenue Service has not said which rate applies, and XP set no date for lifting the pause.

XP, one of Brazil’s best-known brokerages, has stopped clients buying six exchange-traded bond funds run by rivals. The reason is a tax question the Federal Revenue Service has not yet settled.

Reception at an XP Investimentos office, with the firm’s logo and history on the wall; file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

XP Investimentos, a São Paulo brokerage and investment platform, has stopped clients buying six bond ETFs run by rival asset managers. The XP ETF suspension, announced to clients on Monday 21 September 2026, turns on an unsettled tax question.

The pause covers new purchases and transfers into the funds through XP and its sister platforms Rico and Clear. The funds keep trading normally on the B3, São Paulo’s stock exchange.

At stake is whether investors pay 15% or 25% income tax on their gains. That gap can decide whether the funds beat a plain bank deposit.

Which funds are affected

Four of the six are managed by the investment bank BTG Pactual. They are AMAB11, DEBB11, LFIN11 and MARG11, according to Valor Investe, the personal-finance site of the business daily Valor Econômico.

The other two are GICP11, from Genial Investimentos, and NLFA11, from the digital bank Nubank. All six are exchange-traded funds, or ETFs, that track indices of corporate and bank debt.

XP said the funds invest mainly in private credit whose interest follows the CDI plus an extra spread. Its notice cited the lack of “a definitive understanding on the subject” so far.

The pause would last “until there is greater regulatory and tax clarity,” according to the notice quoted by Valor Investe. XP set no end date.

What the CDI is

The CDI is the key benchmark of Brazilian fixed income. It is the average rate at which banks lend to each other overnight.

It moves almost in step with the Selic, the central bank’s policy rate. The Banco Central do Brasil cut the Selic to 13.75% a year on 16 September 2026.

Most Brazilian savings products are quoted as a percentage of the CDI. A bank bond paying “110% of CDI” earns 10% more than that overnight rate.

Because the CDI resets every day, securities tied to it behave like very short-term money. That feature sits at the heart of the tax dispute.

Banco BTG Pactual S.A. provides financial products and services regarding commercial, investments, credit, financing, capital lease, insurance, and foreign exchange portfolios in Brazil and internationally. The company also offers personal investment services for a customized investment portfolio; international banking account services, including debit card, transfer, payment and receipt, and customer support services.…

The 15% or 25% question

Fixed-income ETFs have their own tax table under Law 13,043 of 2014. Gains are taxed at 25%, 20% or 15%, depending on the portfolio’s “average repricing period”.

A fund whose portfolio has an average repricing period of 180 days or less pays 25%. Above 720 days, the rate is 15%.

A Finance Ministry ordinance says a floating-rate bond’s term equals the repricing period of its reference rate, Seu Dinheiro reported. For the CDI, that could mean one day.

That would push the six funds into the 25% bracket, even when the bonds they hold mature years from now. That risk is what led XP to pause purchases.

Anbima, the association of Brazil’s banks and asset managers, backs the lower rate. Its working group says 15% should apply when the underlying bonds carry repricing periods above 720 days.

“The proposal does not seek to create tax benefits,” Anbima said, according to Valor Investe. It said it wants ETFs taxed like the assets they hold, and has put that view to the government.

The Grupo XP logo on a wooden wall; file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

An old fight over Treasury funds

The dispute has happened before. In July 2023, XP halted trading in LFTS11, a Treasury bond ETF run by the manager Investo, over the same doubt.

In February 2024, the National Treasury concluded that such funds reprice every day. The Federal Revenue Service followed, and the rate on those funds rose to 25%, InvestNews reported.

Managers adapted by adding a slice of long inflation-linked bonds, lifting portfolios above the 720-day line. The question now is whether the same one-day logic reaches CDI-linked private credit.

InvestNews asked the Federal Revenue Service for comment on Monday and had not received a reply. InvestNews is owned by the Nubank group, which manages NLFA11.

What it means for investors

The XP ETF suspension changes nothing for current holders, the brokerage said, and they can still sell on the exchange. Brokers withhold the tax when clients sell at a profit, which is why XP carries the risk of charging the wrong rate.

The difference is large. InvestNews calculated that a bond fund earning 110% of the CDI nets only 82.5% of the CDI after a 25% tax.

A bank deposit certificate paying the same 110% nets about 85.2% even at its highest 22.5% rate. That rate falls to 15% for deposits held beyond two years.

ETFs of bank bonds, called letras financeiras, give small savers access to paper that usually demands R$50,000 (about US$9,800) or more. Figures use a rate of 5.11 to the US dollar, the central bank’s PTAX reference for 21 September 2026.

Some bank bonds are sold only to qualified investors, those holding at least R$1 million (about US$196,000). A tax change would narrow the edge the ETFs offer.

Industry split

Some managers say 15% is already practised and that XP created needless noise, Valor Investe reported. Others say the rules are unclear and XP is right to wait.

Bruno Stein, the partner in charge of ETFs at Galapagos Capital, a rival manager, backed XP in an Instagram video. “The brokerage has every right to decide this way, since it is responsible for collecting the income tax,” he said.

BTG Pactual, Genial, Nubank and XP did not comment to Valor Investe. Rival platforms, including those of BTG Pactual, Nubank and Inter, had announced no similar step, InvestNews reported.

Nobody has accused the fund managers of wrongdoing. The outcome now depends on the Federal Revenue Service, which has not said when it will rule.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did XP stop trading in the six ETFs?

No. XP paused only new purchases and transfers into the funds through its own platforms, XP, Rico and Clear. The funds still trade on the B3 exchange in São Paulo. Clients who already own shares keep them and can sell, the brokerage said.

Which ETFs did XP pause?

AMAB11, DEBB11, LFIN11 and MARG11, managed by BTG Pactual; GICP11, managed by Genial Investimentos; and NLFA11, managed by Nubank. All invest mainly in corporate and bank debt paying the CDI rate plus a spread, according to XP.

What is the CDI?

The CDI is the average overnight rate at which Brazilian banks lend to each other. It tracks the central bank’s Selic policy rate, which was cut to 13.75% a year on 16 September 2026. Most Brazilian fixed-income products quote their returns as a percentage of the CDI.

Has the tax law changed?

No new law or ruling has been published. The dispute is over how to apply Law 13,043 of 2014, which taxes fixed-income ETF gains at 15%, 20% or 25%. The rate depends on the portfolio’s average repricing period, and the Federal Revenue Service has not said how CDI-linked bonds should be counted.

World.title: Fitch Chile Rating Stays at A- as Growth Forecast Is Cut to 0.7%
World.content:
Chile · Economy

Key Facts — What happened Fitch Ratings affirmed Chile’s long-term foreign-currency rating at A- with a stable outlook on Friday 18 September 2026.

— Why it held Fitch cited debt below that of similarly rated peers, solid governance and credible macroeconomic policy.

— The catch Fitch held its Chile rating but cut its 2026 growth forecast to 0.7% from 1.6%.

— The debt path Fitch sees debt rising from 41.7% of GDP in 2025 to 42.8% in 2026, then settling near 43%.

— What changed since August In August a Fitch director warned debt above Chile’s 45% ceiling could eventually mean a downgrade.

— Who is cheering The Finance Ministry under Jorge Quiroz said the decision endorses President José Antonio Kast’s fiscal course.

Six weeks after warning that rising debt could cost Chile a notch, Fitch Ratings has left the grade alone. It likes the spending cuts and dislikes the growth numbers.

The doors of Chile’s Finance Ministry at Teatinos 120 in Santiago, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

The Fitch Chile rating is staying where it was. Fitch Ratings, one of three big agencies grading government debt, affirmed Chile at A- on Friday 18 September 2026.

The outlook is stable, meaning no change is expected soon. The same review, however, cut its forecast for Chilean growth this year by more than half, to 0.7% from 1.6%.

The decision landed on 18 September, Chile’s national holiday. The Finance Ministry quickly claimed it as a vote of confidence in President José Antonio Kast, who took office in March.

Why Fitch kept the grade

The A- grade rests on “a relatively solid sovereign balance sheet,” according to the report quoted by the Santiago daily La Tercera. Chile’s debt ratio, Fitch said, is lower than its peers’.

Fitch also cited “Chile’s solid governance and its track record of credible macroeconomic policies,” built on inflation targeting. Those are the strengths.

The weaknesses have not gone away. Fitch listed per capita income that stays low against peers, heavy dependence on commodities, and relatively weak external debt and liquidity indicators.

Spending cuts win praise

The Kast government is running what Fitch called a fiscal consolidation focused on spending cuts. It follows Chile missing its structural deficit targets in 2024 and 2025.

Real fiscal revenue rose 7.0% year on year through July, driven by a strong jump in mining income. Spending fell 0.7%, largely because the state slashed capital investment.

On that basis, Fitch forecasts the headline fiscal deficit narrowing to 1.8% of GDP in 2026 from 2.7% in 2025. It expects a further decline in 2027 on high copper prices and spending restraint.

Fitch also weighed the government’s flagship reconstruction bill, which it said was expected to be enacted in September. It cuts corporate tax to 23% by 2029 and aims to shorten permitting times by 40%.

Fitch described the bill as a possible first stage of labour, capital-market and permitting reforms. “The government’s strong position in Congress should favour the push for these reforms,” the agency wrote, as quoted by La Tercera.

The debt numbers

Public debt held at 41.7% of GDP in 2025, the first year in two decades without a rise, Fitch said. It credited a stronger peso and a copper-driven rise in nominal GDP.

Fitch expects the ratio to reach 42.8% in 2026 and then stabilise close to 43%. That is about 16 percentage points below the 59% median for countries rated in the A category.

The Palacio de La Moneda, seat of Chile’s presidency, seen from the park in Santiago, in a file photograph. (Photo: Chofaska, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)

The government raised its 2026 bond-issuance ceiling by US$6.2 billion to US$23.6 billion in the second quarter. Fitch said the full amount may not be needed, given better fiscal results since then.

From warning to reassurance

The tone is gentler than six weeks ago. On Wednesday 5 August 2026, Todd Martínez, Fitch’s co-head of Americas sovereign ratings, sounded a note of caution in Santiago.

Debt stood at 43.1% of GDP at the end of June, La Tercera reported, near Chile’s self-imposed 45% ceiling. “If debt keeps rising above 45%, I think it could eventually mean a rating downgrade,” Martínez said.

He told the business daily Diario Financiero he doubted a cut in the structural deficit to 1.5% of GDP within five years. He said it was unclear whether the promised US$6 billion in spending cuts would be permanent or temporary.

The formal review now projects debt stabilising near 43% of GDP, below the ceiling rather than drifting through it. With that path, the Fitch Chile rating kept a stable outlook.

The growth problem

Growth is the weak spot. The economy shrank 0.3% year on year in the first half, Fitch said, after shocks to fishing, farming and mining.

Business confidence also suffered as petroleum prices rose, the agency added. Output at Codelco, the state copper giant, fell 7.8% through July, and unemployment hit a post-pandemic high of 9.5%.

Fitch flagged a strong El Niño weather pattern lasting until January 2027 as a downside risk. It expects a public-investment recovery in the fourth quarter to lift the second half.

Fitch is not the first to cut. On 9 September 2026 Chile’s central bank, which sets interest rates, lowered its 2026 growth range to 0.25%-0.75%, from 1%-1.75% in June.

For 2027, Fitch forecasts growth of 3%, helped by base effects, recovering confidence, high copper prices and investment rising 8%.

What it means

For bondholders and foreign investors, the affirmation eases the downgrade risk that Fitch itself had raised in August. Chile keeps its A- grade, and Martínez had said rising debt already cost it two earlier downgrades.

For the Finance Ministry led by Jorge Quiroz, it is a political win. The ministry said the decision “confirms the course of fiscal consolidation” that the Kast government has pursued since March.

For everyone else, the forecast cut is the harder number. Fitch’s 0.7% forecast for 2026 is less than a quarter of the 3% it expects for 2027.

More: Chile coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Fitch decide about Chile?

Fitch Ratings kept its Chile rating for long-term foreign-currency debt at A- with a stable outlook on Friday 18 September 2026. The stable outlook means the agency does not expect to change the grade in the near term. It cited Chile’s lower debt than similarly rated countries, solid governance and credible policy.

Why did Fitch cut Chile’s growth forecast?

Fitch lowered its 2026 forecast to 0.7% from 1.6% after the economy contracted 0.3% in the first half. It pointed to shocks in fishing, farming and mining, weaker business confidence as petroleum prices rose, and lower Codelco output.

Is Chile close to its debt ceiling?

Chile treats debt of 45% of GDP as a prudential ceiling. Fitch put debt at 41.7% of GDP in 2025 and expects 42.8% in 2026, stabilising near 43%. In August a Fitch director warned that debt climbing above 45% could eventually lead to a downgrade.

Who is Jorge Quiroz?

Jorge Quiroz is Chile’s finance minister in the government of President José Antonio Kast. His ministry welcomed the Fitch decision, saying it confirmed the government’s course of fiscal consolidation since March 2026.

World.title: Zuenir Ventura Dies at 95: The Reporter Who Explained Modern Brazil
World.content:
Brazil · Obituary

Key Facts — What happened Journalist and author Zuenir Ventura died of pneumonia at home in Rio de Janeiro on 22 September 2026, aged 95.

— Why it matters His books on 1968 and on Rio’s violence shaped how Brazilians understand the dictatorship years and their divided cities.

— The farewell A public wake at the Brazilian Academy of Letters on Wednesday 23 September, then burial at São João Batista cemetery.

— The best-known book “1968: O Ano que Não Terminou” (1968: The Year That Never Ended), from 1988, inspired the TV Globo miniseries “Anos Rebeldes”.

— The catch The military regime whose harshest year he chronicled had jailed him for three months after its December 1968 crackdown.

— How peers see him Academy president Merval Pereira called him “the journalist we all wanted to be”.

He was jailed by the military regime, wrote the book that shaped how Brazil remembers 1968 and showed Rio its own divisions. Students and colleagues called him “Mestre Zu”.

Rio de Janeiro’s Centro district, home to the Brazilian Academy of Letters, seen around Cinelândia square in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Zuenir Ventura, the Brazilian journalist who chronicled the dictatorship years and Rio’s social divide, died on Tuesday 22 September 2026. He was 95.

The Brazilian Academy of Letters, the country’s leading literary institution, said he died that morning at home of pneumonia. His daughter-in-law, Ana Roditi, told g1 he died in his sleep, without pain.

He worked in Brazilian newsrooms for more than six decades. He also trained generations of reporters as a university teacher.

A farewell at the Academy

His body will lie in state on Wednesday 23 September at the Academy’s seat in central Rio de Janeiro. The wake is open to the public, according to O Globo.

He will then be buried in the Academy’s mausoleum at São João Batista cemetery, in the Botafogo district. He leaves his wife, Mary, and two children, the journalist Mauro Ventura and the editor Elisa Ventura.

He was elected to Chair 32 at the Academy in October 2014 and took his seat in March 2015. He succeeded the playwright Ariano Suassuna, one of Brazil’s best-loved writers.

From house painter to newsroom chief

Zuenir Carlos Ventura was born on 1 June 1931 in Além Paraíba, a small town in Minas Gerais state. His father, José Ventura, was a house painter, and the boy helped him on the job.

At 20 he moved to Rio to study Romance languages at what is now the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. His teachers there included the poet Manuel Bandeira.

He found journalism by accident, as an archivist at the newspaper Tribuna da Imprensa. In 1960 he volunteered to write a piece on the death of Albert Camus, one of his literary passions.

He never left newsrooms again, working at Correio da Manhã, O Cruzeiro, Visão, Veja, IstoÉ and Jornal do Brasil. In 1999 he became a columnist at O Globo.

He also taught for decades at the university’s communications school. His students gave him the nickname that followed him for life: “Mestre Zu”, or Master Zu.

The year that never ended

Brazil had been under military rule since 1964. In December 1968 the generals issued Institutional Act No. 5, the decree that suspended political rights and opened the regime’s harshest phase.

Ventura was arrested that same month and held for three months. He shared a cell with the psychoanalyst Hélio Pellegrino and later said he was not tortured, though always afraid.

Twenty years later he turned that year into a book. “1968: O Ano que Não Terminou” (1968: The Year That Never Ended) came out in 1988.

It told the story of a generation of students, artists and militants who confronted the regime. The book is still reprinted, and it inspired “Anos Rebeldes”, a TV Globo miniseries broadcast in 1992.

Old books on a shelf, in a file photograph. (Photo: Tom Murphy VII / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5)

Chico Mendes, a boy witness and a divided city

In early 1989 he went to Acre, in the Amazon, for Jornal do Brasil. He was investigating the murder of Chico Mendes, the rubber tapper and environmental leader killed in December 1988.

The series won the Esso and Vladimir Herzog prizes, two of Brazil’s best-known journalism awards. It also changed his family.

The main witness was Genésio, a boy of 13 who remained under threat. Ventura took him home to Rio, and the boy lived under his guardianship until he turned 18, g1 reported.

His other landmark was “Cidade Partida” (Divided City), published in 1994. It grew from ten months in Vigário Geral, a Rio favela where 21 people were killed by police in a 1993 massacre.

The book earned a Jabuti, Brazil’s leading literary prize, in the reportage category. Its title became shorthand for the gulf between Rio’s wealthy seafront and its poor hillside communities.

In 2008 a United Nations award named him among five journalists who did most for human rights in Brazil over 30 years. A documentary on his life, “Mestre Zu”, directed by Zelito Viana, was released in 2026.

Tributes from the newsroom

Merval Pereira, a journalist and the Academy’s president, called him “the journalist we all wanted to be”. “Few reach the summit; he was one of them,” he wrote in a statement the Academy posted on Instagram.

Ancelmo Gois, a veteran O Globo columnist, said: “He was a master, a friend. We have lost a great deal,” g1 reported.

The actress Fernanda Torres described him as “this immense man called Zuenir”. The journalist Andréia Sadi wrote that he was one of the most generous people she knew with young reporters.

Fluminense, the Rio football club he supported, also mourned “one of the greatest names in Brazilian journalism”.

His son Mauro posted a photo of his father, O Globo reported. He called him the most generous and welcoming person he had known.

Why Zuenir Ventura mattered

Zuenir Ventura practised what Brazilians call literary reportage: long, patient fieldwork told with a novelist’s ear. He described the job modestly, as gathering raw material for historians.

“Nothing replaces looking someone in the eye,” he told the Brazilian Association of Investigative Journalism in 2008. For foreigners trying to understand Brazil, his books remain among the clearest windows.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Zuenir Ventura?

He was a Brazilian journalist and author, born in Minas Gerais in 1931, who worked for six decades at the country’s leading newspapers and magazines. He wrote “1968: O Ano que Não Terminou” and “Cidade Partida”, two of Brazil’s most influential works of nonfiction, and was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Letters in 2014.

How did he die?

The Brazilian Academy of Letters said he died of pneumonia at home in Rio de Janeiro on the morning of Tuesday 22 September 2026, aged 95. A public wake is being held at the Academy on Wednesday 23 September, followed by burial at São João Batista cemetery in Botafogo.

What is the Brazilian Academy of Letters?

Founded in 1897, the Academia Brasileira de Letras is Brazil’s most prestigious literary institution. It has 40 life members, often called “immortals”, each holding a numbered chair. Ventura held Chair 32, previously occupied by the playwright Ariano Suassuna.

Why is his book about 1968 so important?

It turned one year into the defining story of Brazil’s dictatorship, when a wave of student and cultural protest met the regime’s harshest crackdown. Published two decades later, it shaped how a generation remembered that period and inspired a popular television miniseries.

World.title: LATAM Credit Rating Rises to BB+ as S&P Rewards Its Fuel-Shock Resilience
World.content:
Chile · Aviation

Key Facts — What happened S&P Global Ratings raised LATAM Airlines Group from BB to BB+ on Monday, 21 September 2026, with a stable outlook.

— Why it matters BB+ is the highest speculative grade, one notch below the BBB- level that S&P treats as investment grade.

— What S&P rewarded Strong first-half results despite fuel prices about 80% higher than a year earlier, passed on through fares.

— What S&P expects Adjusted EBITDA of about US$4.3 billion in 2026 and free operating cash flow near US$1.3 billion, per S&P.

— The catch Debt will rise by US$3.5 billion to US$4 billion through 2028 as LATAM adds a net 69 aircraft, S&P projects.

— How far it has come LATAM left US Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 3 November 2022 and returned to the New York Stock Exchange in July 2024.

South America’s largest airline group is now one notch below investment grade at S&P, less than four years after leaving bankruptcy protection.

LATAM Airbus A320-family aircraft at Guarulhos airport, São Paulo; file photograph.

The LATAM credit rating has moved to the doorstep of investment grade. S&P Global Ratings, one of the three big rating agencies, raised LATAM Airlines Group to BB+ on Monday, 21 September 2026.

The previous rating was BB, and the outlook is stable. BB+ is the highest rung of speculative grade, one notch below BBB-, where S&P’s investment-grade scale begins.

LATAM, based in Santiago, is South America’s largest airline group. It runs passenger airlines in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, plus a cargo business.

Why S&P moved now

S&P pointed to “strong performance in the first half of 2026 despite significant market volatility,” according to Investing.com’s account of the report. The volatility was mostly the price of jet fuel.

Fuel prices in the first half ran about 80% above a year earlier, S&P noted. LATAM passed much of that on to travellers, lifting passenger revenue by 27.9% in the second quarter.

Revenue per available seat kilometre, the income earned from each seat flown one kilometre, rose 17.5%. S&P read that as evidence of a resilient business model and a competitive cost base, Times Brasil reported.

The agency had signalled the move. In December 2025 it raised its outlook on LATAM from stable to positive, according to Investing.com Brasil.

At the time, S&P said an upgrade could follow within 12 to 18 months. The conditions were funds from operations above 45% of debt and EBITDA margins comfortably above 20%.

The numbers behind the upgrade

S&P expects LATAM to earn adjusted EBITDA of about US$4.3 billion in 2026. EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a common gauge of cash profit.

The agency also projects free operating cash flow of about US$1.3 billion this year and US$1.9 billion in 2027. It forecasts funds from operations near 50% of debt through 2028.

S&P expects capacity to grow 9% to 10% in 2026, with planes about 84% full. Its EBITDA estimate falls inside LATAM’s own guidance range.

In its second-quarter report of 4 August 2026, LATAM raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance. The new range is US$4.1 billion to US$4.4 billion, up from US$3.8 billion to US$4.2 billion.

Second-quarter revenue rose 27.6% to US$4.18 billion. Net income fell to US$125 million from US$242 million a year earlier, as fuel costs bit.

“Second quarter results clearly demonstrate the group’s structural strength,” said Ricardo Bottas, LATAM’s chief financial officer, in the results statement. Total liquidity stood at US$4.23 billion at the end of June.

A LATAM Airbus A320neo on the taxiway; file photograph.

A bigger fleet, and more debt

The upgrade comes as LATAM spends heavily on aircraft. S&P projects a net addition of 69 Airbus, Boeing and Embraer jets through 2028.

That will push gross debt up by US$3.5 billion to US$4 billion between 2025 and 2028, S&P estimates. It still expects adjusted debt to stay near 1.5 to 1.6 times EBITDA.

Part of the growth is in Brazil, LATAM’s largest domestic market. There it has firm commitments for 24 Embraer E2 regional jets through 2027.

Those jets and eight new routes will lift LATAM’s Brazilian network from 63 to 67 destinations, S&P noted.

S&P kept the rating on LATAM’s secured notes due 2030 and 2031 at BBB-. That rating already sits in investment-grade territory, because bondholders are backed by collateral.

What could go wrong

Brazil is also where S&P sees the most pressure. LATAM’s domestic load factor there fell 1.9 percentage points to 80.7% in the second quarter.

Rival Gol grew capacity 11.7% in the 12 months to July, S&P noted, as summarised by the Brazilian trade outlet Panrotas. Azul, the third big Brazilian carrier, has trimmed its network, Aviacionline reported.

S&P could lower the LATAM credit rating if funds from operations fell persistently below 45% of debt, Times Brasil reported. Weaker margins or thinner liquidity could also trigger a cut.

From bankruptcy to near investment grade

The upgrade caps a long recovery. LATAM filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in New York in May 2020, as the pandemic grounded its fleet.

It emerged on 3 November 2022 with about US$3.6 billion less debt, according to FlightGlobal. Its shares were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in June 2020.

They returned on 25 July 2024 under the ticker LTM, after existing shareholders sold US$456 million of American depositary shares. LATAM received none of the proceeds.

For travellers and investors, a stronger LATAM credit rating mainly means cheaper borrowing for new planes. One more notch at S&P would put the whole company in investment grade.

More: Chile coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What rating did S&P give LATAM?

S&P Global Ratings raised LATAM Airlines Group’s issuer rating from BB to BB+ on 21 September 2026, with a stable outlook. It kept the rating on LATAM’s secured notes due 2030 and 2031 at BBB-.

Is LATAM now investment grade?

Not at S&P. BB+ is the highest speculative-grade rating, one notch below BBB-, where the agency’s investment-grade scale starts. Only the secured notes, which are backed by collateral, carry an investment-grade rating.

Why did S&P raise the rating?

The agency cited strong first-half 2026 results despite jet fuel prices about 80% higher than a year earlier. LATAM raised fares enough to protect cash generation, and S&P expects adjusted EBITDA of about US$4.3 billion in 2026.

Where does LATAM operate?

LATAM Airlines Group is based in Santiago, Chile, and is listed in Santiago and New York. It runs passenger airlines in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, plus a cargo business, and had 383 aircraft at the end of June 2026.

World.title: Colombia Health Funding: Patient Groups Demand US$4 Billion More for 2027
World.content:
Colombia · Health

Key Facts — What happened Pacientes Colombia asked the government on 21 September 2026 for at least 13 trillion pesos (about US$4.07 billion) more for health.

— Who is asking An umbrella movement of more than 200 patient associations, led in public by its spokesperson, Denis Silva.

— What it proposes Keeping the 4×1,000 bank-transaction tax for health, reviewing sales-tax exemptions and taxing online betting and vapes.

— The catch The government plans to phase out the 4×1,000 tax; its filed budget added about 2 trillion pesos (about US$626 million) for health.

— Why it matters Insurers owed hospitals and suppliers 58.06 trillion pesos (about US$18.19 billion) at the end of 2025, the Comptroller’s Office found.

An umbrella group of more than 200 patient associations says the government’s health rescue cannot work without new Colombia health funding. It wants to keep a bank tax the new government plans to phase out.

The entrance of Hospital Engativá, a public hospital in Bogotá, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Colombia health funding needs at least 13 trillion more pesos (about US$4.07 billion) next year, an umbrella group of patient associations says. Without it, the group argues, the government’s new health rescue plan cannot work.

Pacientes Colombia, an umbrella movement of more than 200 patient associations, made the demand on Monday 21 September 2026. It came hours before President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the first phase of his health “plan de choque”, or shock plan.

“It is impossible to implement the shock plan, Mr President, without additional resources,” said spokesperson Denis Silva, according to Caracol Radio. The group wants lawmakers to find the money while the 2027 budget is still being written.

Dollar figures use a rate of 3,192.53 to the US dollar. That is the official rate for 22 September 2026, published on Colombia’s open-data portal.

Who is asking

Pacientes Colombia brings together patient associations from across the country. The political news site La Silla Vacía describes it as grouping more than 200 of them.

It was a vocal critic of former president Gustavo Petro’s failed attempts to overhaul the health system. In July, Silva welcomed the choice of Ana María Vesga, a former head of the insurers’ association Acemi, as health minister.

Silva also said he was sure Vesga would be “the health minister of all Colombians”, Infobae reported.

Where the 13 trillion figure comes from

The group says the 2027 budget adds only about 2 trillion pesos (about US$626 million) for health. It calculates that at least 13 trillion pesos (about US$4.07 billion) more would restore funding to 2022 levels.

The 2 trillion figure matches the Finance Ministry’s own account, according to Forbes Colombia. The ministry says its revised budget gives health about 2 trillion pesos (about US$626 million) more than Petro’s draft.

The group also cites a 2025 health-sector deficit of 58 trillion pesos (about US$18.17 billion). It draws on the latest report of the Comptroller General’s Office, the state audit body.

That report found insurers owed hospitals, clinics and suppliers 58.06 trillion pesos (about US$18.19 billion) at the end of 2025, Infobae reported. That was 26.5% more than a year earlier.

The Capitolio Nacional in Bogotá, seat of Colombia’s Congress, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

How the group would raise the money

The movement’s most pointed idea concerns the “4×1,000”, a 0.4% tax on bank transactions. It wants the tax kept and its revenue earmarked for health for two years.

“Why not think of the 4 per 1,000 for two years earmarked for health?” Silva asked, according to Caracol Radio.

The government wants the opposite: to phase the tax out gradually, Valora Analitik reported on 15 September 2026. Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez told Noticias RCN the cut could not happen overnight.

The group also wants a review of some exemptions from IVA, Colombia’s value-added tax. It estimates that those exemptions cost between 88 and 100 trillion pesos (about US$27.56 billion to US$31.32 billion) a year.

It proposes new earmarked taxes on online betting, vapes, motorcycles and electric vehicles. It also wants existing “healthy taxes” on items such as sugary drinks kept.

A fifth idea is gradual rises in diesel prices, to shrink the deficit of the fuel-price stabilisation fund. The sixth extends the 8.5% employer health contribution to workers earning under 10 minimum wages.

The group says that change alone could raise about 4.5 trillion pesos (about US$1.41 billion). Silva also asked the Finance Ministry to shift unspent money from the social-welfare agency and the Ministry of Equality.

A budget with little room

The group’s demand lands in a tight fiscal debate. On 14 September 2026, Congress’s joint economic committees approved a 2027 budget ceiling of 634.9 trillion pesos (about US$198.87 billion).

The committees have until 25 September 2026 to approve how that money is shared out, Forbes Colombia reported. Lawmakers filed 615 requests to move funds, and the government has endorsed none, according to Infobae.

Instead, the government would move about 3 trillion pesos (about US$940 million) between sectors, Infobae reported. Representative John Edgard Pérez said 2 trillion pesos (about US$626 million) of that would shift from the Finance Ministry to Health.

The health ministry itself asked for 13.9 trillion pesos (about US$4.35 billion) more than the budget filed in Congress. Andi, a business lobby whose members include health companies, cited those figures to press for more money, the trade site Consultorsalud reported.

What comes next

The 4×1,000 change is due in a “Ley Rescate”, or rescue law, that the government plans to present in October. That bill will show whether it accepts any of the group’s tax ideas.

Colombia health funding for 2027 will be settled first in the budget committees, which face a 25 September deadline.

More: Colombia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Pacientes Colombia?

It is an umbrella movement of more than 200 patient associations in Colombia, according to La Silla Vacía. Its public spokesperson is Denis Silva. The group lobbies the government and Congress on access to treatment. It opposed former president Gustavo Petro’s health reform.

How much extra money does it want for health?

At least 13 trillion pesos (about US$4.07 billion) more in 2027, to restore funding to 2022 levels. The group says the 2027 budget adds only about 2 trillion pesos (about US$626 million) for health. On Colombia health funding, the health ministry itself has asked Congress for 13.9 trillion pesos (about US$4.35 billion) more.

What is the 4×1,000 tax?

It is a levy of 0.4% on money moved through bank accounts, hence its name, four per thousand. The government of Abelardo de la Espriella plans to phase it out gradually through a rescue law due in October. Pacientes Colombia wants the tax kept for two years and earmarked for health.

How does this relate to the health shock plan?

President De la Espriella announced the first phase of a health shock plan on 21 September 2026. It targets patients waiting for medicines and procedures. Pacientes Colombia says the plan cannot work without new money for the health system.

World.title: Renan Calheiros Calls Braskem Deal Over Maceió’s Sunken Streets ‘Criminal’
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — What happened Senator Renan Calheiros called Maceió’s 2023 compensation deal with Braskem “criminal” in a TV Gazeta interview on 22 September 2026.

— The deal Braskem paid the city 1.7 billion reais (about US$330 million) and received public land in the evacuated zone.

— The catch The agreement dates from July 2023, and a federal court rejected the state government’s request to review it that year.

— The politics The mayor who signed it, JHC, is running for governor against Calheiros’s son, Renan Filho.

— Why it matters About 60,000 people left five Maceió neighbourhoods after decades of rock-salt mining made the ground sink.

— What comes next Alagoas votes on 4 October 2026, and Calheiros has summoned Braskem’s owners to a Senate committee he chairs.

A veteran senator has revived a three-year-old settlement over a mining disaster that emptied five neighbourhoods. His target is the family now fighting his own for power in Alagoas.

Renan Calheiros speaking from the presiding chair of the Senate in Brasília, in a photograph published in 2016, when he was Senate president. File photograph. (Photo: Wilson Dias/Agência Brasil)
