World.title: Presley Gerber, el hijo de Cindy Crawford, murió de una sobredosis
World.content:
Apenas un día después de su muerte en Los Ángeles se van conociendo las circunstancias del fallecimiento del modelo Presley Gerber, hijo de la también modelo Cindy Crawford y del empresario del tequila y la cerveza Rande Gerber, de 27 años. Según distintos medios con fuentes en la policía, el joven sufrió una sobredosis.

Como se supo al conocerse su muerte, Gerber estaba pasando una temporada en rehabilitación. Ahora, las llamadas realizadas a los servicios de emergencia han dado a conocer los tiempos y lo sucedido. Todo ocurrió en la mañana del domingo, pasadas las nueve y media. En una de ellas alguien pide ayuda desde la calle Berkeley, en Santa Mónica, al oeste de Los Ángeles, donde se encuentra una acomodada instalación para pacientes en rehabilitación, como cuenta TMZ; en ella se escucha hablar de “parada cardíaca”. Otra de las llamadas deja ver que los médicos que acudieron al lugar iban por una sobredosis, según Page Six, que ha tenido acceso al audio. Los médicos acudieron rápidamente al lugar de los hechos, porque Gerber fue declarado muerto apenas 10 minutos después.

“La investigación sigue en marcha y hay poca información disponible”, ha afirmado la oficina del forense del condado de Los Ángeles este lunes a la revista People. “La muerte se declaró a las 9.45 de la mañana del 20 de septiembre de 2026, tras la respuesta de los paramédicos. El Departamento de Policía de Santa Mónica es la agencia legal encargada de dicha investigación”. En cualquier caso, la policía ha afirmado que no hay sospecha de crimen ni de violencia en este caso.

Precisamente el forense del condado de Los Ángeles ya ha completado la autopsia de Gerber, pero todavía no se ha hecho pública, y es posible que aun tarde un poco más.

Durante los últimos años, Presley Gerber se había abierto públicamente sobre su adicción a las drogas. En uno de sus últimos vídeos en Instagram, donde tenía más de 140.000 seguidores (que han aumentado 35.000 tras su muerte), explicó que estaba bajo tratamiento de una sustancia llamada ibogaina que ayuda a controlar la depresión, la ansiedad y también las adicciones. Pero ese medicamento no es legal en Estados Unidos (sí en el vecino México, por ejemplo).

Él mismo afirmó estar “completamente aterrorizado” con ese tratamiento en su perfil. “Mis mantras eran ‘quiérete a ti mismo’ y ‘esta va a ser la última vez”, afirmaba entonces, en marzo. La última vez que se le vio en público junto a sus padres y su hermana, la conocida modelo y actriz Kaia Gerber, fue a finales de mayo en un evento en Los Ángeles.

Presley Gerber, Kaia Gerber, Cindy Crawford y Rande Gerber, en un evento el 20 de mayo de 2026 en Los Ángeles, California. Gilbert Flores (WWD via Getty Images)

Desde que era un adolescente Gerber ha luchado contra las adicciones y los problemas de salud mental. En 2019, cuando no había cumplido los 20 años y no tenía ni siquiera la edad legal para beber, fue detenido por conducir borracho. Entonces ya tuvo que pasar por rehabilitación y cumplir como castigo con unos días de trabajos para la comunidad.

Desde hace un tiempo, los lunes Gerber los dedicaba a su comunidad, con sus llamados Lunes de salud mental (Mental Health Mondays). Por ejemplo , el pasado diciembre habló largo y tendido al respecto, sobre su tratamiento y las dificultades para seguirlo. “Me dan miedo los medicamentos que necesito. Hay un espectro ahí sobre lo intenso que puede ser el síndrome de abstinencia de ciertos medicamentos. Me gustaría que los médicos dijeran: ‘Tómate esto tres veces al día’… pero cada psiquiatra que he tenido, y he tenido 15, me dice: ‘Aquí tienes 20 medicamentos y toma este si te sientes así…’. Y yo le digo como: ‘No, no me des tanta libertad’. Necesito algo de dirección”, relataba a sus seguidores. Su hermana y su madre aplaudían su valentía para abrirse con el público en los comentarios.

Precisamente Kaia habló sobre Presley en una reciente entrevista con la revista Vogue, cuyo número de septiembre protagonizó. “Cuando ocurre algo así en una familia, todo el mundo se ve afectado”, afirmaba, explicando que se alegraba de que su hermano fuera tan abierto con sus dificultades. Según dijo, ver a Presley mostrarse tan abierto sobre su vida le resultaba refrescante. “Durante la mayor parte de nuestras vidas, mis padres han sido muy, muy reservados y no compartían nada; y ahora tenemos a este auténtico maestro, mi hermano, que dice: ‘Voy a mostrarme muy humano ante todo el mundo’. Hay un límite a lo que se puede ocultar al mundo. Y tratar de ocultar algo solo hace que la persona sienta que te avergüenzas de ella”.

Desde muy jóvenes Kaia (dos años menor que su hermano) y Presley protagonizaron juntos campañas de moda y editoriales. Él fue fotografiado para revistas como ICON, y trabajó para marcas como Moschino, Celine, Dolce&Gabbana o, junto a su familia, en campañas para la firma de moda Vuori o la de relojes Omega, aunque en los últimos años estaba alejado de las pasarelas y los grandes eventos.

World.title: Pollo con verduras, aceitunas y limón: la receta que se prepara en una sola bandeja
World.content:
Pollo con verduras, aceitunas y limón: la receta que se prepara en una sola bandeja | EL COMIDISTA

Un plato completo en cuya elaboración solo manchas un recipiente, que se puede hacer en grandes cantidades, y más mediterráneo, imposible

La freidora de aire parece haber venido para quedarse, cosa nada extraña si pensamos en sus ventajas, como la rapidez y la facilidad de limpieza. Sin embargo, el entusiasmo por la novedad no nos debería llevar a relegar a su antepasado más cercano, presente en la mayoría de nuestras cocinas desde hace mucho más tiempo: el horno. Para determinadas preparaciones puede ser más práctico que la satisfryer, trasto muy práctico pero que no lleva muy bien las cantidades grandes de comida.

El pollo con verduras, aceitunas y limón es un ejemplo de uso optimizado del horno. Solo manchas una bandeja o fuente, y para prepararlo solo hay que cortar y mezclar algunos ingredientes, ponerlos en el susodicho recipiente, y tumbarte en el sofá a esperar que el horno haga su trabajo. No solo tiene la ventaja de que ensucias poco, sino que al cocinar todo junto, tanto el pollo como las verduras ganan mucho sabor. Si quieres ver cómo se prepara, mira el vídeo de arriba.

Ingredientes Para 3-4 personas 6 contramuslos de pollo deshuesados y sin piel (8 si son pequeños)

1 calabacín

1 pimiento rojo grande

1 tomate grande o 2 pequeños

1 cebolla morada

50 g de aceitunas verdes

50 g de aceitunas kalamata u otras negras

Perejil u otras hierbas frescas Aliño 120 ml de aceite de oliva virgen extra (unas 8 cucharadas)

El zumo de 1 o 2 limones (unas 4 cucharadas) y un poco de su piel rallada

2 cucharaditas de orégano seco

1 diente de ajo

Pimienta negra

Sal Instrucciones 1. Calentar el horno a 220 ºC (o 210 con ventilador). 2. Preparar el aliño para el pollo. En un bol o un bote con tapa, mezclar el zumo de limón, el ajo rallado o picado fino, el orégano, el aceite de oliva, sal y pimienta negra. 3. Cortar la cebolla por la mitad y luego en gajos gruesos, y ponerla en una bandeja de horno grande. 4. Cortar el calabacín por la mitad longitudinalmente y luego en medias lunas gruesas, y ponerlo en la bandeja. 5. Cortar el pimiento en cuadrados no muy pequeños y hacer lo mismo. 6. Cortar el tomate por la mitad y cada mitad en cuatro gajos, y hacer lo mismo. 7. Salpimentar las verduras. Batir el aliño hasta que esté emulsionado y mojar las verduras con una cuarta parte aproximadamente. 8. Mezclar bien para que las verduras se impregnen y repartirlas para que queden en una sola capa. Conviene asegurarse de que toquen la bandeja para que se doren. 9. Salpimentar el pollo y colocarlo en la bandeja entre las hortalizas, haciendo que toque la bandeja también. Verter el resto del aliño por encima. Consejo Para hacer más hueco, puedes recoger sobre sí mismos los contramuslos, formando una especie de bolas. 10. Introducir la bandeja en el horno, colocándola en el centro, y hornear durante unos 35 minutos. 11. Pasado ese tiempo, añadir las aceitunas y subir la bandeja a la parte alta del horno para dorar durante un par de minutos. Si se dispone de grill, encenderlo vigilando que no se queme. Servir caliente.

World.title: Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
World.content:
The Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.

The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.

The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.

The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.

France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.

The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.

Goals downgraded

The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.

Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.

But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”

Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.

“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.

A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

World.title: Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab
World.content:
Prosecutors have demanded a seven-year jail sentence for a man who blew up a drugs lab in Rotterdam, causing a blast that killed three people and damaged neighbouring flats.

Jalal O., 37, was renting the garage store on Schammenkamp to produce cocaine when it exploded on the evening of January 29, 2024. One of the victims was his 22-year-old cousin, who was working in the lab at the time.

A forensic investigation found that the blast was caused by vats of acetone, used in the production of the drug, catching fire at the back of the building. A neighbouring block of flats was so badly damaged that five homes had to be demolished.

Prosecutors said O. had “allowed financial gain to prevail over the safety of local residents and others”. They said he had sublet the property via a “shady arrangement”.

O. helped with the search for missing neighbours immediately after the disaster, but was arrested a few days later. He told the district court in Rotterdam he found the events “terrible”, but denied that he was using the garage for drug production.

Prosecutors produces messages between O. and his cousin showing steam rising from barrels of acetone, while residents complained of the chemical smells from the building. The prosecution said the defendant’s denials were “totally unbelievable”.

One woman who was evacuated from one of the flats said the explosion had had a devastating effect on her health.

“I have lost part of my hearing, my hair has fallen out and I have lost my teeth through stress,” she said. “I have flashbacks and sleep badly. I have nightmares in which I fall into the fire and burn to death.”

World.title: AP says sharing images from Meta glasses is not allowed
World.content:
Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned on Tuesday that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

“You may not simply share, publish, or use for other purposes photos and videos in which other people are recognisably depicted,” the Dutch Data Protection Authority said in a statement.

“People must be able to walk the streets freely without having to fear that someone is filming them without their knowledge and subsequently sharing the images or posting them on the internet,” board member Katja Mur said.

The group also warned against using the glasses in sensitive locations, like hospitals, courthouses, and religious buildings. It advises those organisations to ban use of the glasses on their premises.

Last month, the consumer watchdog Consumentenbond issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

World.title: Which Dutch city actually fits your budget and lifestyle in 2026
World.content:
Moving to the Netherlands means picking not just a country but also a city, and in 2026 that choice matters more than it used to. Rents in the unregulated sector rose 7.3% nationally over the past year, according to the latest Pararius Huurmonitor, pushing the average to roughly €21 per square metre. But that average hides a lot of variation. Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht, The Hague, and Eindhoven, the so-called G5, each behave quite differently right now, and the gap between them is worth understanding before you commit to a lease.

Here’s how the five compare.

Amsterdam is still the most expensive place to rent in the country by a wide margin, at €28.53 per square metre after a further 5.1% rise this year. That premium buys you the strongest job market for tech, finance, and creative roles, plus the density of international life that draws people here in the first place. An 80m² apartment typically runs €2,300 to €2,500 a month before utilities. If your work is anchored in the city, it’s worth starting your search among the apartments in Amsterdam currently listed.

Rotterdam had one of the sharpest price increases of any G5 city this year, up 10.4% to €22.78 per square metre, and it’s still noticeably cheaper than Amsterdam for comparable space. The city’s pull comes from its modern skyline, its logistics and maritime industry, and an international business culture that doesn’t feel like a smaller copy of the capital. You’ll generally get more square metres for your budget here. Current listings for apartments in Rotterdam are a reasonable place to gauge what that looks like in practice.

The Hague rose 6.5% in price this year to €22.42 per square metre and remains a common choice for people working at the international courts, embassies, or corporate headquarters based there. It has a slower pace than Rotterdam or Amsterdam, more green space, and the coastline is a short cycle away. Neighbourhoods range from the stately Statenkwartier to livelier, more central pockets, so it’s worth browsing a spread of apartments in The Hague before narrowing down an area.

Utrecht climbed 5.9% to €21.61 per square metre and sits at the literal centre of the country’s rail network, which matters more than it might sound. The city has the Netherlands’ largest university, a well-preserved medieval core, and a train commute of 30 minutes or less to nearly any other major Dutch city. That combination of culture and connectivity keeps competition for listings tight. Have a look through apartments in Utrecht to see what’s currently on the market.

Eindhoven posted the second-largest increase in the G5 this year, up 10.0% to €19.55 per square metre, still the most affordable of the five despite that jump. The city runs on ASML, Philips, and a wider “Brainport” ecosystem of tech and engineering firms, which explains why it draws a heavily specialised international workforce. If that’s your field, apartments in Eindhoven are where to start looking.

What this means for your search: In a market this tight, landlords generally expect a gross income of three to four times the monthly rent, and they’ll want to see it upfront. Have your employment contract, recent payslips, and a short summary of your rental history ready before you start applying, since properties in demand can be gone within days. Pararius only lists properties from verified, professional agents, which at least removes one layer of risk from an already competitive process. You can view all listings here.

World.title: Low earners offered €6,000 subsidy to buy used electric cars
World.content:
Low and middle income households will be able to claim up to €6,000 from the government towards the cost of buying a second-hand electric car, three years after the last subsidy was abolished.

Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said the government wanted to make EVs more accessible. Figures published last month showed that only 2% of electric cars and plug-in hybrids were bought by the lowest 10% of wage earners.

People with a pre-tax income of up to €27,533 will be eligible for €6,000 towards the cost of a second-hand electric car, while those earning less than €35,793 will be able to claim €4,000 – provided that they scrap their old fossil-fuel car with a registered dealer.

The amount is intended to reflect the difference in price between second-hand electric vehicles relative to petrol and diesel cars.

A total of €52.4 mln has been made available to fund the scheme, which the cabinet hopes to have up and running by the start of next year following an online consultation.

“It is very important for this cabinet that people with modest means can make the switch to an electric car and enjoy the benefits,” Bertram said.

Falling sales

The government scrapped the last scheme to subsidise purchases of new and used electric vehicles in 2024. Discounts on road tax for electric and hybrid vehicles were also phased out.

In the following year EV sales dropped from 32% of the total market to 26%, with the most popular model, the Tesla Model Y, slumping from 2,000 sales in November 2023 to less than 500 in January 2024.

CBS figures showed that people on the lowest incomes were most likely to buy diesel cars and two-thirds of those in the bottom 20% bought vehicles that were more than 10 years old.

World.title: Dancing bananas are back as social media site Hyves relaunches
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Once the biggest social network in the Netherlands, Hyves has come back online after 13 years.

The “gezelligste platform” in the Netherlands has been relaunched by owners Mediahuis, which hopes to tap into nostalgia and distrust of American social media companies.

First launched by a group of Dutch friends in 2004 who wanted to share photos, Hyves hit its peak in 2010 with 10 million users, more than half of the country’s population.

The same year it was acquired by Mediahuis Netherlands, which also owns the newspapers De Telegraaf and NRC

Users soon began to abandon the site to a new social networking site, Facebook, and by 2013, the site was offline. The games section of the website lived on as Hyves Games.

“Hyves wants to do things differently,” Mediahuis said in a statement. The group promises to keep users’ data within Europe and will not use algorithms to determine what content people see.

The site’s infamous dancing banana will also return.

New accounts will be limited to 10,000 on the first day and 5,000 every day after. Mediahuis hopes to have 1.5 million users by the end of the year.

World.title: Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid
World.content:
A Dutch man whose 14-year-old son died after he was denied medical treatment for Covid-19 has been jailed for 23 years by a court in Belgium.

Rennlhy Manuela covered up the death of his son, Jairon, for eight weeks, refusing to let his siblings enter his bedroom and telling his mother he was out of the house when she tried to visit him.

Manuela, who belonged to a strict Pentecostal sect, refused to consult a doctor when Jairon fell ill at the end of 2021, instead relying on paracetamol, a liquid diet and prayers for his recovery.

The court of justice in Antwerp said Manuela “made his child’s life subordinate to his radical religious convictions”. He was convicted of murder by a jury and sentenced to 23 years in prison, three years more than prosecutors demanded.

The boy died in the night of January 3 and 4 after falling in the bath. When police were called to the house, they found his body underneath a blanket in an advanced state of decay, with traces of ketamine in his blood.

Manuela and his adult housemates had hoped God would answer their prayers to bring Jairon back to life.

Mother raised alarm

Jairon’s mother, Danica, raised the alarm after she contacted the boy’s school across the Dutch border in Tilburg, only to be told he had been signed out months earlier.

She had been denied access to the villa in Turnhout, where Manuela lived with his children and several other members of the religious community.

Four other adults were given sentences of between one and three years in the case. The jury said Manuela had caused “irreperable suffering” by “preventing [Jairon’s] mother and brothers saying goodbye in a humane manner”.

World.title: One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS
World.content:
Water companies have called for PFAS chemicals to be banned in pesticides after a study showed that one-third of people are exposed to high levels of the “forever chemicals” in drinking water.

An analysis by Greenpeace of every postcode in the Netherlands showed that the water in 32% of areas contains PFAS levels that are at least 1.5 times the recommended safe level.

The environmental inspection agency ILT blames the increased use of trifluoroacetic acid in pesticides by agricultural sectors such as potato farming, which has almost doubled in the last two years. The ILT says two tonnes of the chemical end up in the water supply per year.

The highest concentrations are in the provinces of Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Zeeland, with towns such as Zaandam, Purmerend and IJmuiden recording 14.3 nanograms per litre.

PFAS is a collective label for thousands of highly stable chemical compounds that are used extensively in packaging, liquid chemicals and products such as waterproof clothing and non-stick cooking pans.

They are attractive to industry because they are extremely durable, but prolonged exposure increases the risk of cancer, immune system problems, low fertility and damage to unborn babies.

High blood levels

A recent study by the public health agency RIVM showed almost everyone in the Netherlands has unhealthy levels of PFAS in their blood.

Greenpeace compiled a dataset and built an online tool allowing householders to see how much PFAS is in their drinking water, with a map to show the most polluted and least polluted areas.

“We think this information should be available to everyone, so we asked a data analyst to set out clearly how much pollution is in the water per location,” campaign leader Eline Bosman told NRC.

There are strong regional variations, with the northern provinces of Drenthe, Friesland and Groningen showing almost no PFAS chemicals in drinking water.

Patricia van der Linden of Vewin, the association of Dutch drinking water suppliers, said the west of the country drew its water supply from rivers and reservoirs, which are more polluted than water sources in rural areas.

“Ground water contains less pollution than surface water,” she said. “In places where we use surface water for drinking water, we have to take more steps to purify the water.”

Immune system

Although none of the water supplies exceed the legal limit set by the European Union, they are well above the RIVM’s advisory limit of 4.4 nanograms.

The agency lowered the guideline level in 2023 in the light of new information that showed PFAS chemicals have a greater impact on the immune system than previously thought.

Germany, the Netherlands and the Scandinavian nations have been lobbying since February 2023 for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides throughout the EU.

RIVM spokesman Coen Berends told NRC: “We can see that banning individual types of PFAS makes a difference, but really the whole group should be banned.”

Poland has begun paying state benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, has confirmed. Poland was recently ordered to start recognising such marriages by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). Dziemianowicz-Bąk says there are indications that Polish same-sex couples are now travelling abroad to marry so as to gain rights in Poland, where domestic law still does not allow them to form recognised unions. Wiedzieliście, że ZUS wypłaca już pierwsze zasiłki "małżeństwom jednopłciowym" po transkrypcji aktów wydanych za granicą❓❓❓ To już wiecie 👇 pic.twitter.com/W99ymV3T31 — ɐllǝnuɐɯı (@szef_dywizji) September 18, 2026 In November 2025, the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states, finding that failing to do so infringes the freedom to move and reside within the EU as well as the right to respect for private and family life. In light of that ruling, in March this year, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA) ordered Warsaw’s registry office to recognise a marriage conducted by two Polish men in Germany by transcribing it into the Polish civil registry. In May, the Polish government issued a regulation allowing such transcriptions of foreign same-sex marriages to take place nationwide. It went into force in August. However, even before then, some cities had begun transcribing marriage certificates, beginning with Warsaw and Wrocław in May. At the end of August, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski reported that 84 same-sex couples had already transcribed their foreign marriages under the government’s new regulation. All Polish registry offices can now recognise foreign same-sex marriages, after a new regulation went into force. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality warned local authorities they will be breaking the law if they do not comply with the new rules https://t.co/EWGkuvm7EE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 While foreign same-sex marriages can now be entered into Poland’s civil registry, questions have remained as to what that will mean in practice for such couples, especially as domestic law does not recognise same-sex relationships. However, speaking to news service Wirtualna Polska on Friday, Dziemianowicz-Bąk confirmed that “the Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) is already paying the first care allowances to same-sex couples”. Such allowances are paid to someone who is required to provide care for a spouse. The level of the allowance is set at 80% of the recipient’s average salary from the last 12 months, and it is available for up to 14 days per calendar year. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Dziemianowicz-Bąk welcomed the fact that “ZUS, one of the most important institutions, knows and understands that love is love, marriage is marriage, and these rights will be respected”. She is from The Left (Lewica), a junior partner in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and the most enthusiastic supporter of LGBT+ rights. The minister confirmed that her colleague from The Left, Katarzyna Kotula, the government’s plenipotentiary for equality, is “in dialogue with the finance ministry and National Revenue Administration (KAS)” to ensure that same-sex couples who married abroad receive the tax benefits available to other married couples. Dziemianowicz-Bąk also argued that the right-wing opposition and conservative President Karol Nawrocki are unintentionally encouraging Polish same-sex couples to marry by preventing the government from introducing a domestic law on recognising same-sex relationships. In July, Nawrocki vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to obtain certain rights available to married couples, including relating to taxation, property, and access to medical information. However, it would not have allowed same-sex couples to marry or even form civil partnerships. Instead, they would have signed a contract before a notary, formalising their relationship. Yet this step was still too far for Nawrocki, who said that it threatened the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed government bills granting certain rights to unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, for the first time in Poland. He argued that the proposal would have threatened the institution of marriage https://t.co/UXdrNfGfup — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Last week, the ruling coalition attempted to overrule the president’s veto in parliament, which requires the support of a three-fifths majority. However, the vote fell short of that figure after the right-wing opposition voted to uphold the veto. Dziemianowicz-Bąk said that the government’s opponents were “essentially encouraging marriage equality” because they left same-sex couples with only one option to have their relationships recognised: getting married abroad and then having the certificate transcribed into the Polish registry. She told Wirtualna Polska that “we’ve heard indications” that this is precisely what such couples are now doing. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships. Over 62% are now in favour, up from 52% last year and just 25% in 2011, when the question was first asked https://t.co/Y9ydpbwsoU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 However, opposition figures have argued that recognition of same-sex marriages violates Poland’s constitution, article 18 of which says: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” In July, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which has a majority of judges appointed by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, ruled that the government’s regulation allowing the transcription of foreign same-sex marriages is unconstitutional. But the government regards the TK as illegitimate since it contains judges unlawfully appointed under PiS. It therefore ignores the tribunal’s rulings. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Dziemianowicz-Bąk’s announcement that ZUS has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples, Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said that it showed how “the left is ready to trample every law, including the constitution, just to get their way”. “What drives them and what they believe in is ideology, and what guides them is the instinct for domination,” added Bosak, who is also a deputy speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. World.title: Poland’s Catholic church recruits priests from Africa and Asia to stave off vocations crisis
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Marcin Choduń (published in cooperation with Tygodnik Powszechny) With the number of Poles training to be priests falling steadily, Catholic parishes are increasingly looking beyond Europe to fill the gaps. Father Fransiskus Laka will never forget his first day in Poland. When he stepped out of the arrivals hall at Warsaw’s Okęcie (now Chopin) airport in October 1999, he thought he would not last long. Why? The bitter chill in the air. “It was only seven degrees,” he laughs. It is not surprising that the young man from Indonesia was having second thoughts. At home, a cool day meant 25°C. Now, though, having spent 27 years in Poland, no weather fazes him. In the middle of winter, he will sometimes even go out in just a T-shirt to shovel snow or bring wood for the stove. Father Fransiskus has settled in the village of Brzegi, near Zakopane in southern Poland, where he has been parish priest for the last two years. And the mountainous Podhale region it is part of still has long, cold and snowy winters. Father Fransiskus, a Verbite, is not the only foreign Roman Catholic priest working in Poland, where around 70% of the population is Catholic. Their numbers are growing every year in response to the rising shortage of Polish priests. Polish dioceses are increasingly keen to invite young foreigners to study at their seminaries. Poland’s shortage of priests Most of those invited are from Africa. In Kielce, for example, there are currently two seminarians from the Central African Republic and seven from Angola. The Tarnów seminary also trained a priest from the Central African Republic in recent years (ordained as a deacon in the nearby village of Szynwałd in 2024). In the diocese of Ełk, Bishop Jerzy Mazur announced in a letter read out in churches in 2023 that he would be combating the shortage of priests by inviting clergy from Africa to the diocesan seminary. In return for receiving training in Poland, the newly ordained priests were to spend at least a few years working in the region. Previously, the support of retired priests had been sufficient. But, as the shortage grew, the curia even considered reducing the number of services or merging parishes. That was when the idea of seeking help from abroad came about. Just one new priest was ordained in Łódź, Poland's fourth largest city, this year – the lowest figure ever recorded One church figure admits there has been a “dramatic decline” in interest in the priesthood while the head of a seminary calls it a “crisis” https://t.co/QuwKsoPSg3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2023 “Priests from Poland increasingly work for as long as their health permits,” says Andrzej Kobyliński, a priest and ethicist from Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski University in Warsaw. “However, that doesn’t change the fact that, in a few years’ time, we’ll have a staffing shortfall, because Polish seminaries are more and more deserted.” In recent years, a lack of recruits has led to several seminaries merging or closing down. The Wrocław, Legnica and Świdnica seminaries have been combined into one institution – which in reality means the two smaller schools being transferred to the big city. Clerical students in Kalisz have met a similar fate, having to go to Częstochowa to study, while seminarians from Elbląg have been sent to Olsztyn. The seminaries in Łowicz and Bydgoszcz have closed, and education in Drohiczyn and Sandomierz has been suspended. “The changes are happening at such an alarming rate that at present over a dozen seminaries will need to be closed,” says Kobyliński. “Let’s take the Płock diocese. You could say that the students in the seminary there are being put through a mental ordeal.” “Since there are currently 13 seminarians studying in seven year groups, that means that some years are empty or only have one or two people. That causes terrible loneliness. Because how can you survive seven years on your own?” For Kobyliński, the Ełk diocese is a symbol of the changes that are coming. This year, it only ordained one deacon – from Togo, West Africa. A new home in Poland The deacon’s name is Roger and he arrived in Poland a few years ago, along with another prospective priest from Togo who decided to return home for personal reasons. “There are currently seven people studying in our seminary, three of them from Africa. Apart from Roger, we have two more, from Ghana,” says Marcin Maczan, chancellor of the Ełk curia. According to him, however, the presence of African seminarians in Ełk is not only a response to the shortage of priests. “Bishop Jerzy Mazur, who himself spent several years working in Ghana and in the past was the head of the missions committee of the Polish Episcopal Conference, is familiar with the realities of mission dioceses. He knows very well that they can always use help in training priests.” “So these two ideas were combined: training a priest for his home diocese in Africa and his ministry in Poland for eight to ten years after ordination. All in line with the terms of the agreements that the bishop of Ełk made with bishops in Africa,” Maczan says. These agreements vary. Some priests return to their home dioceses shortly after ordination – seminarians from Kielce, for instance. Others remain for many years, such as Father Fransiskus Laka, whose stay in Poland is prolonged by the congregation’s provincial superior every three years. Poland was not his first choice. Shortly before being ordained, each of the clerical students in Fransiskus’s seminary, the Divine Word Missionaries in Pieniężno, northeastern Poland, was supposed to name three countries where they wished to serve. He chose Ecuador, Nicaragua and, in last place, Poland. Usually, one of the first two options is selected, but the provincial superior suggested otherwise. A surprised Fransiskus agreed, and he has never regretted his decision. After spending the first four years in the parish in Pieniężno, he returned to the seminary to become a prefect, responsible for keeping order. In this period, he travelled the length and breadth of Poland to lead retreats in parishes. He then spent seven years as a curate in Chludów, near Poznań, before in 2024 becoming the priest of the parish of St Anthony in Brzegi in the Podhale region. “I arrived on 8 December – so almost immediately I had Christmas pastoral visits to make to parishioners’ homes,” says Father Fransiskus. “They really welcomed me very warmly. They often help me – show me how to light the stove, or leave food outside my door. I learn hard work, humility, patience and faith from them. The mountains are tough terrain – you really need grit to survive.” Poland became home. Fransiskus feels safe here – despite growing hostility towards foreigners, which is particularly visible in the public and online space (foreign ministry statistics confirm that in 2024-2025 the total number of hate crimes reported in Poland increased by more than 50% – from 760 to almost 1,200 cases). “I’ve never yet encountered any hostile behaviour towards me,” says Fransiskus. Although he regularly visits his home island of Lembata, there are many things in Indonesia that he can no longer accept. The organisation of mass, for example: if it is supposed to begin, say, at 7 a.m., worshippers turn up just before 9. They don’t understand why Fransiskus sees this as a problem. Or a bus journey – when the driver passes his house, he’ll usually take a break to have lunch and play with his children. “The passengers wait patiently and no one thinks anything of it,” laughs Fransiskus. The Togolese footballing priest Father Romuald Mawakina Tchilabalo Mozou, from Togo (pictured top), is a newer arrival in Poland. His stay in the country is on the same basis as Fransiskus – an interdiocesan agreement extended every three years. Romuald has only been here seven years, but already speaks impeccable Polish, with barely a trace of a foreign accent. Upon arriving in Poland, he learned the language intensively – for seven months, from Monday to Saturday, seven hours a day. “I knew from the outset that if I couldn’t communicate well with the faithful, I wouldn’t build any relationship with them,” he says. Romuald was born in the village of Kaza, near Sotouboua. His father was a French teacher in the local primary school. And so his first language was French – he only learned Kabije, the ethnic language in northern Togo, in later years. His family is Catholic. And their neighbours? A mixture, just like everywhere else in Togo: the majority are Muslims, but there are also some Catholics and followers of traditional faiths. The proportion of people in Poland who are religious non-believers has risen to a record 14% while those who attend Sunday mass have fallen to a low of 34%. But a large majority of Poles still identify as believers and Catholics https://t.co/2yqrLePAsw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 23, 2024 The Mozou family are very religious. As a young boy, Romuald and his family would pray together daily, and this was what first brought him into indirect contact with Poland: every evening, along with his parents, two sisters and two brothers, he recited Saint Faustina Kowalska’s Chaplet of the Divine Mercy. He also associated Poland with John Paul II – to date the only pope to have visited Togo. Romuald’s great passion has always been football. His dream of a professional career led him to neglect his studies, until his father made things clear: first school, then football. While at high school, however, Romuald started to consider the priesthood. After taking his exams, he began studying in a seminary in Lomé, the Togolese capital. Three years in, the bishop proposed that he go to Poland to study at the seminary in Opole. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 As a dean, Father Romuald gained hands-on experience in Krapkowice. After his ordination in May 2024, he became a curate in Opole (and from August this year he will be based in nearby Ujazd). I ask him how the new parishioners responded to him. “Well, to be honest, they were a little surprised at first,” he laughed. “But that’s hardly surprising – after all, I’m the first priest from Africa to serve in the Opole diocese. They gave me a very warm welcome, though – I’ve never encountered any unfriendly gestures or words from them.” In Poland, Romuald’s childhood passion has been rekindled: he’s playing football again. First for Maciowakrze, a club playing in Klasa B (the eighth tier of the Polish league system), then in Żywocice, in Klasa A. He now plays as a striker for GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory. “I don’t know if I’ll return to my homeland – everything is possible,” Romuald says. “I feel good in both Poland and Togo.” Polish dioceses recruiting in Africa In 2026, 196 priests are to be ordained in Poland – 12 fewer than last year and some 205 down on the figure from 2013. The number of dioceses in which no ordinations took place because of a lack of candidates is growing – seven this year, compared to six in 2025. “We actually have a vocations crisis everywhere in Europe, so we will be looking for priests in other parts of the world,” says Andrzej Kobyliński. “Essentially, we have two areas where we can recruit candidates for the priesthood. Mainly Africa, and possibly India, but the experiences of German and Italian dioceses show that priests from India find it harder to settle in Europe.” “Latin America is not an option, as the Catholic church there is facing its own crisis of a mass exodus to Pentecostal churches,” he adds. “So in the future we will definitely be working intensively with African dioceses. This is an enormous historical change, because it was once Poland and Europe that sent missionaries to Africa.” One of the lads Przywory, a village near Opole, the GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory home pitch. Seven p.m. Training has started. Father Romuald Mozou is a little late, so he rushes into the dressing room. “Romek, you’re doing push-ups as punishment,” laugh his teammates when he appears on the pitch. Everyone calls him by this Polish diminutive – Romek. The team’s coach, Marcin Chudala, admits that the players like to have a laugh at the footballing priest’s expense. “Sometimes we joke when he’s sitting on the bench staring at his phone: ‘What are you doing, Romek – confessing?’ The banter can be cruel,” says the coach. But he also admits that Romek’s presence has left its mark on the team. Less swearing, for example. Even if there is nothing to suggest that Romek is a priest. “We treat him just like one of the lads from the playground,” Chudala says. The original version of this interview can be seen here. Translated by Ben Koschalka. Marcin Choduń is a journalist and translator of German and English. He publishes his articles mainly in Tygodnik Powszechny and Duży Format, a supplement of Gazeta Wyborcza. In 2012, he was nominated for the Grand Press Award in the reportage category for his article “The Blood of a Skinhead, the Blood of a Jew”. World.title: Poland to expand warning siren network along Ukraine border amid Russian attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland plans to have more than 1,000 warning sirens in the eastern Lublin province by the end of the year in response to increased Russian attacks in Ukraine near the Polish border, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński has announced. The Polish government is also working on an application that would use Cell Broadcast technology to turn mobile phones into warning devices, allowing them to function like sirens in a crisis, the minister added. Minister @MKierwinski w Lublinie:💬Budujemy system ochrony ludności niemal od podstaw. W województwie lubelskim na początku 2024 roku było około 30 syren, które można było uruchomić zdalnie. Dziś jest ich prawie 350, a do końca tego roku będzie ich ponad tysiąc. To pokazuje, jak… pic.twitter.com/6uWAgcNrJh — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 19, 2026 Speaking in Lublin on Saturday, Kierwiński said that the region now has almost 350 automatic sirens, compared to just 30 at the start of 2024. The number is expected to triple to over 1,000 by the end of this year. “Jet-powered drones and missiles are increasingly flying near the Polish border” and Poland is therefore “turning to tools designed to counter the associated threats,” Kierwiński said, quoted by news website OKO Press, adding that the government had to build Poland’s civil protection system “almost from scratch”. As part of these efforts, Poland’s fire service, working with the Lublin governor, is now rolling out a project to identify and mark the province’s nearly 3,500 shelters. Last year, Poland launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in the case of an emergency. By the end of the year, Poland also wants to introduce an application that would allow it to “take over” residents’ phones “to function like a siren”, Kierwiński added, without providing any further details. Residents in areas close to the Ukrainian border have heard warning sirens during Russian attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks and received alerts through the state warning system. The opposition has criticised the alerts for not giving residents clear instructions on what to do when the sirens sound. In response, the ministry has stepped up its public information campaign, including a television and social media campaign on emergency preparedness. Additionally, more than 500 fire stations in the eastern Lublin and Subcarpathian provinces held training over the weekend on how to respond to emergency alerts. The sessions were part of a wider campaign that has already involved 630,000 people across Poland. Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats https://t.co/MS0APufAmq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Poland has stepped up preparations along its eastern border following a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation follows a number of incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski described the attacks in the border area as “another escalation” by Russia, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. During his visit to Ukraine last week, Tusk announced that Poland had joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries working together to develop an integrated air defence system for the continent. World.title: Moody’s cuts Poland’s credit rating to lowest level since 2002
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later. Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday. “Large fiscal deficits persist, leading to a material increase in public debt and, together with rising interest costs, weaken debt affordability metrics,” added the agency. It also warned that “fiscal policy effectiveness has weakened”, including a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”. “Political constraints, including the continued standoff between the government and the president and the proximity of the November 2027 parliamentary elections, also limit the scope for meaningful fiscal consolidation,” concluded Moody’s, pointing to Poland’s high social and defence spending. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. However, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, blamed the situation on the government. “They steal, they lie and they burden our homeland with debt,” he wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, we Poles will have to pay for it all.” Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led both Fitch and Moody’s to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Standard & Poor’s, meanwhile, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on the Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. World.title: Poland joins European Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. We are launching a new format – “C8,” the Carpathian Eight – bringing together us and our… pic.twitter.com/tcIupMsBBK — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. World.title: Polish ruling party MP stripped of immunity and detained at request of EU prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds was designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colours offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024.
