World.title: Two North Korea members of Asian Games seek asylum in Japan, report says
World.content:
Two members of North Korea’s delegation to the Asian Games in Japan are looking to seek asylum, South Korea’s Monthly Chosun magazine reported on Tuesday.

Citing a source it identified as an official from Japan’s Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office, the magazine said the two were among a 180-member North Korean delegation attending the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which opened Saturday.

The two North Koreans expressed a preference to seek asylum in Japan rather than South Korea and have communicated their intention not to return home, the report said.

Their identities and positions within the delegation were not disclosed, and it remained unclear whether their reported outreach would ultimately lead to a defection, according to Monthly Chosun.

The magazine said the information was obtained through a source connected to Japan’s intelligence apparatus and linked to the pro-Pyongyang General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, known as Chongryon.

North Korea sent about 180 athletes and officials to the Games, including Sports Minister Kim Il Guk, according to media reports.

Reporters could not immediately reach the Japanese government for comment on a national holiday in Japan.

World.title: At least six dead and six missing in Kanto in wake of Typhoon Dujuan
World.content:
Six people have been confirmed dead and at least six were missing Tuesday morning, after Typhoon Dujuan brought record-breaking rainfall to eastern Japan, triggering landslides, flooding and widespread transport disruptions.

The storm had prompted the Japan Meteorological Agency on Monday to issue its highest-level landslide special warning for parts of the Izu Islands, including Oshima.

The Cabinet Office announced that as of Tuesday, the Disaster Relief Act had been applied to a total of 25 municipalities following the heavy rains brought by Dujuan.

Police, firefighters and the Self-Defense Forces are conducting search operations in Chiba and Kanagawa Prefectures, where a series of landslides struck homes.

In the city of Yokosuka, Kanagawa Prefecture, a 64-year-old woman was pronounced dead after being pulled from her home, which was hit by a mudslide.

About a kilometer away, a couple in their 70s went missing after another landslide struck their home.

Rescue workers clear debris while searching for a missing person at a house hit by a landslide triggered by Typhoon Dujuan in the city of Miura, Kanagawa Prefecture, on Tuesday. | REUTERS

Two other people were also missing in the nearby city of Miura. Mud and debris flowed into the first floor of an apartment building, leaving a woman in her 20s unaccounted for. In another area of the city, one woman is missing after a landslide damaged the building she lives in.

In Chiba Prefecture, a 51-year-old worker died after he and the heavy machinery he was operating fell into a bamboo grove while he was removing mud and debris from a road in the city of Sodegaura. A landslide had occurred around the site, and police are investigating the incident.

In the city of Sanmu, Chiba Prefecture, a house collapsed due to a landslide. A woman in her 70s was transported to a hospital but was later confirmed dead.

Landslides also hit houses at two locations in the Kamogawa, Chiba Prefecture, leaving a couple in their 80s dead and two men, in their 60s and 70s, unaccounted for. In the city of Mobara, also in Chiba Prefecture, a woman in her 80s was confirmed dead after her home collapsed.

Roads around JR Sakura Station in Chiba Prefecture remained flooded across a wide area Tuesday, a day after heavy rain caused the nearby Takasaki River to overflow. Floodwaters were nearly 1 meter deep in some areas, making some residents unable to leave their homes.

In a residential area north of the station near the Takasaki River, several vehicles, including trucks, were stranded with water reaching above their tires, local media reported. Residents could be seen looking out from homes and apartment buildings to assess the situation, while firefighters pulling rubber boats moved through waist-deep water.

Damage to homes has so far reached over 470 buildings in Kanagawa, Chiba, and Ibaraki prefectures.

As of Tuesday afternoon, Typhoon Dujuan was located east of Japan, according to the weather agency. Although the storm has moved over to the Pacific, the agency warned that the threat has not ended because record rainfall had left the ground saturated and rivers swollen.

A car partially submerged in floodwaters after Typhoon Dujuan brought torrential rain to Sakura, Chiba Prefecture, on Tuesday. | REUTERS

In the 48 hours through 1:30 a.m. Tuesday, rainfall reached 832 millimeters — the highest amount on record — in Oshima, part of Tokyo’s Izu island chain. Some 325 mm of rain fell in Tokyo’s Edogawa Ward Rinkai area in the 48 hours through 6:10 a.m Tuesday.

Record-breaking rainfall was also seen in surrounding prefectures. The Sakahata area of the city of Kimitsu, Chiba Prefecture, recorded 476.5 mm of rain in the 48 hours leading up to 1:50 a.m. Tuesday, and the city of Ichihara, also in Chiba Prefecture, recorded 487 mm in the 48 hours leading up to 2:40 a.m.

Landslides can occur even after rain has stopped because of water accumulated in the soil. The JMA urged people in the Kanto region to remain on high alert for landslides on Tuesday and to continue watching out for flooding in low-lying areas and rising or overflowing rivers.

The typhoon also continued to disrupt daily life into Tuesday. Some 42,260 households across four prefectures were without electricity as of 4:30 p.m., according to Tokyo Electric Power Grid, with the vast majority of outages in Chiba Prefecture. Outages were also reported in Kanagawa, Yamanashi and Shizuoka prefectures.

Rail operators also suspended or canceled some services from the first trains Tuesday, including sections of East Japan Railway Co.’s Sobu, Narita and Sotobo lines. Keikyu also suspended services between Kanazawa-hakkei Station and Horinouchi Station, and between Miura-kaigan Station and Misakiguchi Station.

A flooded underpass near Oami Station in Oamishirasatao, Chiba Prefecture, in the early hours of Tuesday. A Tepco worker is assessing the power lines in the area, which was under widespread blackout. | Daniel Traylor

The Haneda area of the capital’s Ota Ward received 261.5 mm of rain in the 48 hours through 6 a.m. Tuesday, the highest amount on record, with widespread flight cancellations affecting Silver Week travelers Monday.

Conditions are expected to improve as Dujuan moves farther from Japan. Sunny skies had been forecast across much of the Kanto region Tuesday. High waves and strong winds remained possible along the Pacific coasts of eastern and northeastern Japan.

Information from Jiji added

World.title: Fake and divisive ads proliferate in Israel’s first AI election
World.content:
In a recent video widely circulated online, Israel’s top justices and its attorney general are seen being dragged by security guards from a chaotic anti-government protest that never took place.

The 33 seconds of emotionally-charged footage was originally posted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a fierce opponent of the judiciary, and triggered an immediate backlash. Critics said it incited violence, while supporters said it was justified because they accuse the leaders of Israel’s legal system of a left-wing plot to stymie the government’s policies.

But the depicted scenes are fake — no such protest took place and the video carries a tell-tale watermark to identify content made using artificial intelligence. Smotrich’s post was just the latest example of a deluge of AI-crafted distortions that are saturating the Israeli information environment just weeks before the country’s most consequential elections in decades.

World.title: As Trump and Xi meet, investors play both sides of AI divide
World.content:
As China and the U.S. race to build separate artificial intelligence supply chains, investors are playing both sides, with U.S. banks fundraising for AI upstarts in China and Chinese money flowing to U.S. tech.

The stakes are sizable, with Wall Street banks acting as book-runners on 19 Chinese high-tech equity capital market deals worth $17.2 billion so far this year, according to LSEG data, accounting for nearly 30% of the sector’s total issuance.

U.S. stocks, particularly semiconductors, are also the favorite destination for China’s outbound mutual funds. The value of U.S. equity held by Hong Kong residents and mainland Chinese has jumped 23% in the past year to top $750 billion, U.S. data shows.

World.title: Indonesia to develop earthquake early warning system with Japan’s help
World.content:
The Indonesian government plans to develop an earthquake early warning system in an effort to reduce damage from temblors that frequently hit the Southeast Asian nation.

Receiving support from Japan, which has already introduced such a system, Indonesia plans to conduct trial runs for the envisioned system in Jakarta and some other regions by 2030, aiming to roll it out nationwide in the future.

Like Japan, Indonesia is located on the Pacific Ring of Fire, so the island country is prone to earthquakes, and damage tends to be severe due to low quake resistance of buildings. More than 140 people were killed in a 7.7 magnitude earthquake that struck off the island of Flores in the province of East Nusa Tenggara in mid-August.

A Japan-Indonesia joint team set up partly using Tokyo’s official development assistance program launched research in three provinces in the western part of Java Island, including the Jakarta capital region, in 2025 under a five-year test project.

It aims to develop low-cost earthquake observation equipment and a system that automatically halts factories and train operations simultaneously with earthquake detection.

The team will also comprehensively consider responses from the occurrence of earthquakes to evacuation, including the compilation of evacuation guidelines tailored to the characteristics of Indonesian buildings and lifestyles in the country.

In addition to radio communication, mosques will be utilized to inform residents of earthquake early warnings.

Specifically, quake warnings will be issued through loudspeakers at mosques used for playing the Adhan call to announce the start of Muslim prayers. Muslims account for some 90% of Indonesia’s population.

Dr. Andi Eka Sakya, senior researcher at the Indonesian government-affiliated National Research and Innovation Agency and the Indonesian head of the joint research team, was visiting Japan when a powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on July 28.

Noting that there was no panic after measures people should take to ensure their safety were shown on television following an earthquake early warning, he said, “This is the one that we actually would like to replicate.”

Once Indonesia’s earthquake early warning system is realized, Japan would consider the possibility of supporting the introduction of similar systems in other countries. Japan also aims to improve its own system by accumulating know-how through the operations of foreign systems.

Japan’s earthquake early warning system was introduced in October 2007, providing quake information on TV and radio and through smartphones.

World.title: National security and the stakes of ‘technology sovereignty’
World.content:
The technologies that increasingly determine national security are being developed not only by governments but by private companies and universities. This creates a dilemma for liberal democracies like Japan: How can governments secure strategically important technologies without undermining the autonomy and innovation of the private sector?

Investment in dual-use technologies — those with both civilian and military applications — is increasingly seen as an efficient way for states to acquire critical capabilities. But because these technologies are often developed outside government, securing them requires more than technological capacity. It requires a way to govern dispersed capabilities without stifling them.

This is the challenge of technology sovereignty. Countries increasingly speak of AI sovereignty, digital sovereignty and data sovereignty. Technology sovereignty provides a broader framework for understanding these efforts.

World.title: Vietnam’s President To Lam says Hanoi ‘very close’ to inking U.S. trade deal
World.content:
Vietnamese President To Lam said his nation is “very close” to a trade deal with the U.S. as he pledged to buy more high-tech goods like aircraft to narrow the trade gap ahead of talks with U.S. administration officials in New York.

“One of the issues we need to discuss with U.S. leaders, particularly the U.S. president, is how to expedite negotiations toward an agreement on reciprocal, balanced and equitable tariffs between the two countries,” Lam, Vietnam’s top leader, said in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Monday.

“Vietnam exports align with U.S. demand without competing directly with U.S. products,” said Lam, who is also Communist Party General Secretary. Vietnam wants to import more U.S. items to support industrial production, although certain policy constraints persist on the U.S. side, the president said.

World.title: Seoul’s green space is a battleground for its mayor and South Korea’s president
World.content:
A showdown over green space is pitting South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is trying to address a national housing crisis as his approval ratings slump, against Seoul’s mayor, who is pushing to create a huge park in the capital.

For Mayor Oh Se-hoon, the planned open area is needed to address Seoul’s “greenery deficit,“ which requires cleanup of the 300-hectare site to address environmental flaws.

Oh said he would not surrender “a single centimeter” of the capital’s largest planned park to the apartment towers that Lee wants to build as surging home prices batter the president’s popularity.

World.title: CUHK economist apologises over talk that examined women ‘marrying for money’
World.content:
A prominent economist at the Chinese University of Hong Kong has apologised after he analysed women “marrying for money” in a talk on campus that led students to accuse him of making gender-biased remarks.

The backlash erupted shortly after Terence Chong Tai-leung, an associate professor of economics, delivered his talk about how to invest in one’s life at the university’s bi-weekly assembly on Tuesday.

According to posts on social media platform Threads, slides presented by Chong included one titled “Economics of Partner Choice” that contained the heading: “The Cost-Benefit Analysis of Women Marrying for Money.”

The content sparked outrage among students, who accused the academic of reducing women’s partner criteria to purely material gain, with critics slamming the framing as gender-biased, objectifying and unfair.

World.title: Hong Kong workforce to shrink by 20,000 yearly as key sectors face shortages
World.content:
Hong Kong’s workforce is forecast to shrink by around 20,000 a year until 2028 despite measures to import labour and talent, with shortages remaining most acute among skilled technical workers.

A government report on manpower projections on Tuesday found that although the labour shortfall would narrow to 130,000 by 2028, down by nearly a third from the original estimate of 180,000, the city would continue to face critical manpower challenges across key sectors.

“Due to economic transformation, the adoption of AI [artificial intelligence] and various talent and labour importation measures, the predicted manpower shortfall in 2028 will narrow to 130,000, but most critical industries, especially innovation, aviation, construction, city operations and healthcare, still face a manpower crunch,” said Ho Kai-ming, the acting secretary for labour and welfare.

“The adoption of AI is expected to accelerate and companies are likely to take a more cautious approach when hiring for entry-level positions. We believe demand for these roles will ease and some clerical jobs will undergo restructuring. Overall, fresh graduates and middle-aged clerical staff are expected to be most impacted.”

World.title: Committee to investigate Hong Kong district councillor’s sex crime conviction
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities have appointed a five-member supervisory committee to investigate the conviction of a district councillor for having sex with a 13-year-old girl 15 years ago.

Yuen Long district councillor Sei Chun-hing, 39, is the first elected officeholder to face possible imprisonment for a criminal offence since Beijing’s 2021 electoral overhaul, which restricted candidates to those vetted as “patriots”.

The offence is punishable by up to five years in jail..

World.title: Hong Kong on way to securing green fuel supply to safeguard aviation hub status
World.content:
Hong Kong risks losing its status as an international aviation hub if it fails to secure a reliable, credibly certified supply of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the head of the government’s think tank has warned.

Stephen Wong Yuen-shan, head of the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit, made the remarks at the Sustainable Aviation Futures China Congress on Tuesday, days after the government set out its fuel strategy in the city’s first five-year plan and policy address amid mounting global competition.

“It is a question of whether Hong Kong can remain an international aviation hub as the economics and rules of global aviation change,” he said.

He added that future demand for SAF was increasingly being driven by policy rather than voluntary action, with the European Union and the United Kingdom introducing mandates and Singapore and Japan setting their own targets.

World.title: Fatal dog attacks trigger safety fears in Hong Kong. Here’s how to protect yourself
World.content:
The death of a cyclist in a suspected canine attack in Hong Kong’s Yuen Long on Saturday night has sparked fierce discussion on social media, with users sharing similar encounters and debating how to stay safe.

The woman was discovered along Pok Wai South Road in the early hours of Sunday. She had suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with the wounds to her head and neck believed to have been fatal.

Nearly a month earlier, a 33-year-old dog handler was found dead near her pet training centre in Ta Kwu Ling after being mauled by a canine.

To help residents stay safe, the South China Morning Post has spoken with canine behavioural experts and dog rescuers to share essential safety tips.

World.title: Hong Kong to bar firms with integrity offences from building renovation lists
World.content:
Hong Kong building maintenance consultants and contractors prosecuted or convicted of integrity-related offences in the past three years will be excluded from pre-qualified lists set up for owners undertaking renovation projects, the development minister has said.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on Tuesday that applications to join the lists – covering inspection consultants, supervision consultants and building works contractors – would open next Wednesday and close on October 23. The lists would be set up by the end of the year, she added.

Linn told the Legislative Council’s development panel that the lists would be reviewed every two years, as authorities tightened oversight of integrity standards.

“If they are convicted of integrity-related offences, they will be removed from the pre-qualified lists immediately,” Linn said.

World.title: Hong Kong bans caterer from importing workers for year over local hiring breach
World.content:
Hong Kong’s Labour Department has terminated Kwai Chung-based catering firm Happy Up Corporation’s application to import workers after it failed to meet the required local hiring ratio.

The company has also been barred from applying to import workers for a year.

A department spokesman said on Tuesday that the administrative sanctions had taken immediate effect under the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme (ESLS) following an application previously submitted by the company.

He added that following an investigation, the department found the company had breached the scheme’s requirements by failing to maintain the required ratio of two local employees for every imported worker.

World.title: Stand News editor had no intention of harming national security, court hears
World.content:
A former acting chief editor of the now-defunct Stand News was fulfilling his duty to publish articles and had no intent to undermine national security in Hong Kong, his lawyer has said while appealing his conviction for sedition.

A panel of High Court justices pointed out on Tuesday that the presiding trial judge had ruled Patrick Lam Shiu-tung’s decision to run material containing false information from interviewees had the seditious effect of inciting hatred against authorities.

They noted the point was among the grounds for the appellant’s earlier conviction.

In August 2024, Lam was found guilty of a joint conspiracy charge of publishing and reproducing seditious material along with former editor-in-chief Chung Pui-kuen and Best Pencil (Hong Kong), Stand News’ holding company.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019055/Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.title: Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019055/Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.content:
From preparing restaurant-worthy meals and repairing cars to programming robots and operating drones, young people from around the world will put their skills to the test in Shanghai this week at the largest WorldSkills Competition yet.

The event opens Tuesday with a record 1,385 competitors from 68 countries and regions, marking its first edition on the Chinese mainland. Often dubbed the “Skills Olympics,” the biennial competition will see participants vie for medals across 64 disciplines, ranging from traditional trades to advanced manufacturing and emerging technologies.

Unlike conventional sporting events, WorldSkills tests competitors on their ability to perform practical tasks drawn from the workplace. Participants generally must be under 22, although the age limit extends to 25 for some disciplines, and have between 15 and 22 hours to complete their assignments. They can compete only once in their lifetime.

In cooking, competitors must plan menus, prepare and plate dishes, and serve them on time while meeting food safety standards. Automobile technology contestants diagnose and repair vehicle faults, while robot systems integration contestants assemble and program industrial robots to perform automated tasks. This year’s debut unmanned aerial systems discipline tests skills in building, testing, and maintaining drones.

It’s one of seven disciplines added this year to reflect changing labor-market demands, with the others including dental prosthetics, digital media interactive design, intelligent security technology, rail vehicle technology, retail sales, and software testing.

Chen Yujie, deputy director and researcher at the Vocational and Skills Research Office of the Chinese Academy of Labour and Social Security, told state agency Xinhua that WorldSkills regularly adds, merges, or eliminates disciplines to keep pace with industry changes. Chen added that even established disciplines update their technical standards and competition content.

The inaugural competition, held in Madrid in 1950, featured just six disciplines — fitting, pattern making, turning, electrical installations, milling, and cabinetmaking — and 24 competitors from two countries.

This year’s opening ceremony will take place Tuesday evening at the Shanghai World Expo Cultural Center. The roughly 90-minute event centers on the mortise-and-tenon joint, a traditional Chinese woodworking technique.

Competition begins Wednesday and runs through Saturday at the National Exhibition and Convention Center, where roughly 300,000 square meters of space has been converted into workshops ranging from professional kitchens to drone-flight zones. Some 400,000 visitors are expected over the four days.

Admission is free, but visitors must reserve a time slot online. Once inside, they can watch competitors at work from just a meter away or try their hand at practical skills. Some events, including beauty therapy, hairdressing, and restaurant service, will also recruit members of the public to take part.

The event will also host the WorldSkills Conference, bringing together more than 2,000 delegates, including 50 government ministers, to discuss issues such as AI’s impact on labor and green development.

China joined WorldSkills International in 2010 and made its competitive debut the following year in London. From 2011 through 2024, Chinese competitors won 93 gold, 41 silver, and 28 bronze medals, along with 71 Medallions for Excellence. China topped both the gold-medal table and overall team rankings for four consecutive editions.

China will field competitors in all 64 disciplines this year, with vocational-school teachers and students making up more than 60% of its delegation, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security.

(Header image: South Korean mechatronics competitors prepare for the 48th WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai, Sept. 21, 2026. Xinhua)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.title: China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.content:
China’s men’s basketball team has suffered its second-worst defeat in its history at the Asian Games, calling into question the coach’s abilities and the team’s training methods.

On Sunday, China lost 70-79 to Iran, two days after it lost 77-97 to Japan, host of this year’s Games, its second failure to reach the finals and its largest-margin loss in men’s basketball at the tournament. The country finished fourth, one place higher than at the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon — its worst result ever.

China has claimed eight Asian Games titles, with its most recent gold coming in 2018. Since then, China has failed to win the title.

Head coach Guo Shiqiang said the team fatigued toward the end of the tournament, noting that only nine players were available for rotation partway through the Games due to injuries. He also said the team’s younger players lacked major tournament experience and had struggled to play consistently, and that “the team had failed to execute its pregame tactical plans.”

China’s unusually long training and competition period this summer has been a focus of criticism. The team spent around 140 days in camp before the Games, domestic media reported. Internationally, teams typically spend only one to three weeks at training camps, widely considered to be intensive and demanding.

Criticism has also centered on Guo, 51, a former starting point guard for China’s national team who began coaching the team in 2006 and became head coach in 2009. After leaving the team to coach locally in 2010, he returned as head coach in 2024, and led China to a runner-up finish at the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup.

Critics have questioned Guo’s tactical approach. Against Iran, China’s defense focused heavily on protecting the net rather than the court’s three-point line, leaving space for their opponents to take jump shots and make three-pointers. The team also struggled to secure rebounds in both its matches against Iran and Japan.

Others criticized Guo’s offensive strategy, arguing that he relied too heavily on the backcourt, that players became isolated at crucial moments, and that his in-game player selection was overly conservative.

The defeats have prompted broader discussion about whether China’s traditional approach of requiring athletes to spend a large portion of the year in training camps can keep pace with changes in the sport, particularly the increasing emphasis on spacing, perimeter shooting, and shooting efficiency.

“Everyone on our team has worked extremely hard this summer,” Guo said in a post-game interview with domestic media. “Every member of the Chinese men’s basketball team has put in a tremendous amount of effort.” His comments sparked widespread backlash online, with many arguing that the team’s prolonged exhaustion from training camp caused the poor results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Jiao Boqiao (left) of China blocks a shot by Mohammad Jamshidi of Iran during the men’s basketball bronze medal match between China and Iran at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 20, 2026. Andy Cheung/Getty Images/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.title: Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.content:
YUNNAN, Southwest China – Growing up in a remote mountain village in Yunnan province near China’s southwestern border with Vietnam, Zhou Lifang had only ever seen clouds from below. In late July, on her first flight, the 16-year-old saw them from above.

“I thought clouds were transparent because (my) textbook said clouds are made of water vapor,” she tells Sixth Tone. “But I didn’t expect them to be like a white wall. The clouds you see from the ground are in pieces, but from the sky they are one big mass.”

Lifang and her 14-year-old twin sisters, Zhou Lixin and Zhou Liyi, were among 145 students from Yunnan taking part in “Mountain-Sea Bond,” a four-day program in Shanghai that included reunions with parents working in the city.

The sisters are among China’s “left-behind children,” who remain in their home communities while their parents migrate for work, often placed in the care of grandparents or other relatives. China had 9 million such children in 2022, according to the 2023 Rural Education Development Report.

Born in Kunming, Yunnan’s provincial capital, the sisters have lived for more than a decade with their grandparents in a village in Malipo, a county in the Wenshan Zhuang and Miao Autonomous Prefecture roughly 400 kilometers away by road. Their parents, Zhou Yuneng and Zhang Shunfen, now work in Shanghai, where Zhou drives for a ride-hailing service and Zhang sorts groceries at a supermarket warehouse.

Smartphones have long allowed Zhou and Zhang to remain involved in their daughters’ lives from afar. They check in, offer advice, and try to mediate fights between the sisters. But they can see and hear only what the girls choose to share, and cannot always persuade them to talk.

Asked how well she knows her daughters now, the mother says they all like drawing, then pauses. “Close to zero,” she admits. “I don’t really know what they like anymore.”

After more than a decade of parenting largely by phone, Zhou and Zhang would spend two weeks sharing a 20-square-meter room in Shanghai with their daughters, their longest stretch together since the girls went to live with their grandparents.

On her own

Before the sisters left early that morning, their grandmother, Kuang Tianzhen, 64, tucked 50 yuan ($7) into each girl’s pocket, twice their usual weekly allowance. Rumors of scams in their border village had made her uneasy about the journey.

“Where will you stay in Wenshan?” she asks, the prefecture’s seat. “This is all reliable, right?”

After the neighbor’s car carrying them disappeared from view, their grandfather, Zhou Shucheng, 72, sat brooding outside the house for at least half an hour, staring down the rain-soaked road and gently petting the tabby cat his granddaughters had adopted.

Four hours later, the sisters arrived at a hotel in Wenshan for a predeparture meeting with participants from surrounding villages and counties. They would spend the night there, then continue to Kunming the next day for the flight to Shanghai.

“Are you Zhou Lifang’s parents? Have your three children arrived yet?” a trip organizer asks over the phone.

“I am Zhou Lifang,” she replies. “We’re already here in the lobby.”

Lifang was the only child in the tour’s WeChat group; everyone else was a parent. She had followed instructions about when and where to meet and confirmed the arrangements for all three sisters.

Inside the hotel’s meeting hall, grandparents sit beside children waiting to register while organizers address the crowd from the stage.

Elders are heard asking “Where should I sign?” and “Do I fill this part in?” At the line marked “guardian,” some pause, unsure whether to write their own names or those of the children’s parents in Shanghai.

One grandmother checks her granddaughter’s schoolbag, rebraids her hair, and films her on her phone. When organizers ask the adults to leave, she goes downstairs, then turns back and slips inside again.

Lifang sat quietly on one side of a wide pillar, her twin sisters on the other. Unlike many of the children around them, the sisters had arrived without a grandparent.

The sisters began attending boarding school around age 6. When home, they helped with farm work and tended the family’s wood-burning stove. Before they had smartphones of their own, they called their parents using their grandmother’s phone or a public telephone at school.

At 12, Lifang went alone to a hospital near her school for a tuberculosis screening while her mother guided her through the process over a video call.

“Sometimes I felt pretty helpless,” she says. “I would ask adults passing by for help and follow their directions.” On other visits, her mother advised her to follow a classmate who knew the hospital better.

When the village prepared to allocate plots of collectively owned farmland, Lifang took the call and passed the information to her grandmother. During school vacations, she tidied the twins’ room and called her mother when she needed money or help handling her sisters.

Her grandfather divides farm work and allowances equally among the three girls. But when they argue, he tells Lifang, “You’re the older sister. You’re the eldest. You should give way to them.”

The twins usually side with each other against Lifang, and a stray remark can set off a fierce argument. From Shanghai, Zhang tells her, “If someone hits you, whether it’s your sisters or your schoolmates, you should hit them back.”

Lifang sometimes goes into a room and locks the door instead. “Then they can’t come in,” she says. “They’ll play a game, and after that, everything will be fine.”

She has repeatedly asked her parents for a room of her own. When she wants to be alone, she sometimes sits on a swing her father built on the rooftop. On a nearby window, smiling faces the sisters traced with their fingers years ago remain visible beneath layers of dust.

“Sometimes I wish I could be the younger sister, not the older one,” Lifang says.

Close to zero

When the twins moved to the village at 3, they sometimes cried for their mother. Their grandmother would carry one of them outside and point toward Kunming, along the road winding over the mountain.

“I’d hold her for a while and tell her that her mother was there,” Kuang recalls. “Then she’d stop crying. They’re good girls, easy to coax.”

Their father had tried to leave the twins in the village a year earlier. He drove them there when they were 2, but couldn’t bear to leave them and took them back to Kunming.

By 2015, private kindergarten in Kunming cost 1,800 yuan ($250) per child per month, meaning fees for all three would have consumed 5,400 yuan of the couple’s roughly 6,000-yuan monthly income.

The family was also hundreds of thousands of yuan in debt after rebuilding the village house and paying hospital bills for the grandfather and one of the twins, who had spent several weeks in neonatal intensive care with meningitis. Because the girls lacked local household registration, or hukou, enrolling them in Kunming’s public schools was difficult.

For the next decade, their parents remained in Kunming, making the six-hour drive to the village every month or two for a weekend or holiday.

Years of installing wood floors damaged both of Zhou’s knees. The work required him to squat and sometimes kneel. “After every shift, I would get off my scooter and walk stiff-legged,” he says. In 2025, chronic arthritis forced him out of construction, and the couple moved to Shanghai, approximately 2,500 kilometers away.

When the sisters missed their parents, Lifang says, they video-called them. “Mom and Dad would always say they only had a few more days of work and would be back to see us soon.”

Over time, however, the girls stopped asking when their parents would return for good. “They used to say, ‘Mom, I miss you,’” Zhang says. “Since I moved to Shanghai, I hardly ever hear that anymore.”

In 2023, the couple installed a camera at the gate of the village house, primarily for safety. It lets them check on the grandfather and see when the girls return from school. They chose not to install one in the girls’ bedroom.

“I just feel that girls, after all, need some privacy,” Zhang says.

The mother also bought her daughters smartphones with large screens to make video calls easier and placed few restrictions on how they used them.

“Kids today are different from us back then,” she says. “Digital devices aren’t just for studying anymore. They have access to so many things on their phones. I don’t restrict them too much.”

The twins often decline their parents’ calls or hang up after a few sentences. Sometimes, one answers while playing on the computer, points the phone’s camera at the ceiling, and keeps playing.

Asked why, one of the twins says, “Just because I don’t have the patience.”

Every time this happens, Zhang just smiles and rarely lets her temper show.

“I feel that if I push too hard, I lose the right to speak,” she says. “I’m afraid they’ll think, ‘You didn’t raise me. You weren’t there when I was small, and now you want to tell me what to do.’ So sometimes I can’t be too direct. I have to be careful how I put it.”

When Lifang and the twins argue, the parents try to settle their disputes by phone, usually scolding both sides. Each girl comes away believing that she alone has been blamed.

“That’s because of the distance and what a phone call can’t do,” the mother says. “If it were face to face, a few sentences would clear it up.”

Unlike the twins, Lifang video calls Zhang almost every day and has her saved in her phone as “Dear Mom.” But she seldom calls Zhou. “Dad is quite busy driving day and night, so I rarely call him,” Lifang says. “I’m afraid of interrupting his work. I feel like I’m not close to him because he’s too strict.”

Even with Zhang, much of Lifang’s life remains outside their conversations. At school, some classmates seek her out for tarot readings, calling her “Master Zhou.” Others mock the way she speaks, comparing it to barking, and give her insulting nicknames.

Lifang spends nearly every break between classes drawing. She draws when she feels happy, angry, or embarrassed, and says it helps her relax. She keeps one sketchbook, which she rarely shows others, for times when she feels low.

One drawing shows a figure with its arms crossed and an X over its mouth. In the background, Lifang has written, “What if speaking is also a fault?”

“All I can do is draw them as ugly monsters,” Lifang says.

She closes the sketchbook.

“There are some words I cannot show,” she says. “Cannot.”

In another sketchbook, Lifang has created Yumeng, a cheerful girl from the sea who grows increasingly troubled as she tries to save a city from destruction. “Why should I, who am already living such a miserable life, have to save others?” the character asks.

Lifang also has a circle of friends her parents know little about. She met them through a nonviolent multiplayer game she describes as “healing.” Unlike the competitive games her sisters prefer, it lets players explore different settings, build homes and farms together, and talk.

“Besides my best friend at school, they are the most important friends in my life,” Lifang says.

Before boarding the flight to Shanghai, Lifang sent them an update: “I’m boarding now, so I can’t reply to your messages. I’ll send you some amazing pictures later.”

Under one roof

Two days after reuniting privately with their parents, all three sisters stepped onto a stage in matching pale green T-shirts and brand-new canvas shoes their mother had prepared before their arrival. “Mountain-Sea Bond” organizers had chosen the family for a letter reading at the Aug. 1 reunion ceremony.

Standing between the twins, Lifang began reading, with Zhang beside her daughters and Zhou watching from the audience.

“Before, I never understood why you were always away and could not be with us,” she reads. “Only on this trip, after coming to Shanghai where you live and work, did I truly understand how hard you work and how much you have given.”

When Lifang finishes, the audience applauds, and Zhou begins to sob. As the sisters come down from the stage, he pulls the twins close and continues crying until his face turns red. The twins’ eyes fill with tears.

“You don’t see your children often,” he says after regaining his composure. “And then suddenly you realize they have grown up all at once.”

After the ceremony, the family go to Jing’an Joy City, a Shanghai mall the sisters had long wanted to visit for its anime shops. Lifang taught herself to draw manga and now takes commissions through an app from clients across China, earning several dozen yuan per drawing. She hopes to attend one of China’s leading art academies, though she usually tells adults she wants to become a civil servant like her older cousin.

The program ended that day, but the sisters remained in Shanghai for the rest of their two-week stay. All five shared a one-room, 20-square-meter unit with a private bathroom and an induction cooker in one corner.

Zhou and Zhang had moved there at the beginning of the year, hoping the girls might eventually join them in Shanghai. Before the trip, Lifang had assumed the move had made her parents’ lives easier.

“Now that Mom and Dad work in Shanghai, the conditions are better, and the work is a little easier,” she says.

Zhou no longer installs floors, but his ride-hailing shifts often last at least 12 hours. “If you work less, you can’t make enough,” he says. “You drive for 11 or 12 hours, come back, charge the car, make something to eat, then sleep. The next day, you get up and repeat it. That’s the job.”

Zhang works similar hours sorting groceries at a supermarket warehouse and has no regular weekends. Sometimes they go an entire day without seeing each other awake; one leaves breakfast behind before the other gets up.

During the visit, Zhou took another week off from driving, while Zhang continued working. The parents would not allow the girls to go out alone in an unfamiliar city.

Before leaving Yunnan, Lifang says, “I want to help my mom sort groceries at the supermarket warehouse.” In Shanghai, she often accompanied Zhang to work, while the twins remained in the apartment.

One night, Zhang returned late from work and began tidying the room. One of the twins ran over and hugged her.

“Mom, I feel like you’ve worked so hard,” Zhang recalls her saying. The girl then began to cry.

“I feel like she’s really growing up,” Zhang says.

Despite all five sharing one room, the sisters argued less during the visit. Disputes that had been difficult to settle over the phone rarely became as heated in person, Zhang says.

Even before his daughters arrived, Zhou had been considering returning to Yunnan after another year in Shanghai.

“Whatever happens, I should go back and do whatever work I can, as long as we are by their side,” he says.

But Zhou has taken no steps toward moving and cannot say what work he might find near the village. Its karst terrain leaves little room to expand farmland, and 796 of its 2,172 residents work elsewhere, according to a village official.

Zhou and Zhang each earn about 8,000 yuan ($1,120) a month in Shanghai, though Zhou can make more by taking fewer days off. Returning would mean giving up the income that had drawn them farther from their daughters.

During their stay in Shanghai, the sisters called their grandmother about once a week. One day at a café, a blue parrot perched on Lifang’s shoulder. She has long wanted one like it, and blue is her favorite color. Lifang immediately called Kuang on video.

“Grandma, look what’s on my shoulder,” Lifang says. “Isn’t it impressive?”

“Behave yourself,” Kuang replies. “Where are the twins?”

“They went with Mom to work.”

“When will you come back?” Kuang asks. “How are you getting home?”

“Dad says he’ll drive us back next weekend,” Lifang says. “My school starts early.”

Editor: Apurva.

The Shanghai Small and Medium-sized Enterprises Technology Talent Introduction Service Center has organized six such reunions since 2024. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019049/China Tells E-Commerce Apps to Stop Selling Loans
World.title: China Tells E-Commerce Apps to Stop Selling Loans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019049/China Tells E-Commerce Apps to Stop Selling Loans
World.content:
As young Chinese increasingly borrow through food-delivery and e-commerce apps, Chinese payment institutions, apart from banks, will no longer be allowed to list financial products such as loans and credit services among payment options at checkout, according to a new national policy set to take effect later this month.

The new measures, announced in April by the People’s Bank of China and seven other government departments, will take effect on Sept. 30. The rules also require companies to clearly state when they are selling financial products and bar bundled “buy now, pay later” financial services as a default option at checkout.

Companies must also direct users to financial institutions’ own platforms to purchase credit products, rather than third-party platforms; provide prominent risk reminders that must be read before purchase; and must either provide an option for customers to turn off algorithmic recommendations or algorithms that do not take into account their personal characteristics. Only financial institutions and certain authorized accounts may market financial products online.

In recent years, platforms ranging from food delivery and e-commerce to video streaming and online travel have begun offering installment-payment options at checkout, making it easier for consumers to access credit without undergoing traditional bank credit assessment or acquiring a credit card.

These services are usually provided by the platforms themselves or through third-party financial institutions, and encourage users to access loans through default selections, prominent placement of credit options, or discounts tied to activating consumer-credit products.

Sixth Tone found that on Black Cat Complaint, a mediation service launched by tech company Sina, hundreds of thousands of customer complaints about such credit services have been lodged. Complaints ranged from credit services being activated without customers’ knowledge, difficulties canceling services, disputed interest charges, and aggressive debt collection and personal information leaks when payments were not met.

“The core purpose of the new rules is to draw a clear boundary between payment tools and credit and wealth-management products, while better protecting consumers’ rights to know and to choose,” Dong Ximiao, director of the Shanghai Institution for Finance & Development, told domestic media.

As of Friday, the topic had garnered more than 42 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many users expressing support for the policy.

On Tuesday, customer service representatives from e-commerce platforms including Alipay, Meituan, Douyin, and JD.com told domestic media that their per-month payment plans will remain available.

Several platforms have begun to clearly identify credit service providers and separate credit services from regular payment methods. For example, Alipay’s online consumer credit service Ant Credit Pay is now listed under a separate “Credit” section.

However, some platforms still place credit options alongside or above regular payment methods. A check by Sixth Tone on Monday found that when placing a food delivery order on Meituan and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, credit-related options still appear alongside regular payment channels. Default selections and discounts encouraging their use also remained.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: iStock/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019031/From Paris to Hangzhou: The $9m Quest to Return China’s Lost Encyclopedia
World.title: From Paris to Hangzhou: The $9m Quest to Return China’s Lost Encyclopedia
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019031/From Paris to Hangzhou: The $9m Quest to Return China’s Lost Encyclopedia
World.content:
Over six centuries, the Yongle Encyclopedia has all but disappeared. Commissioned by the Ming emperor Zhu Di and compiled by more than 3,000 scholars, it once contained over 11,000 volumes on science, poetry, philosophy, medicine, and law. Today, less than 4% survives — fires and foreign invasions consumed the rest.

So when Weng Lianxi at Beijing’s Palace Museum received word in 2020 that two volumes would be auctioned in France, he was skeptical. Fakes were common, and with the pandemic grounding most international flights, he was unable to fly out to inspect them firsthand.

The researcher had only 39 JPEG images, a lifetime of handling ancient books, and a set of exacting criteria for the type of binding and paper used in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). The photos checked every box, and the sellers were descendants of a French naval officer stationed in China in the late 1800s.

Convinced of their authenticity, Weng contacted businessman and book collector Jin Liang, who ultimately secured the volumes at auction for 8.12 million euros ($9.31 million), 1,600 times the starting price. This June, Jin donated them to the China National Archives of Publications and Culture (CNAPC).

Yet the journey of these “national treasures” from a Parisian attic, where they had sat unread for 140 years, to their new home in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, was anything but simple.

Cultural compendium

Weng first heard about the auction at Beaussant Lefèvre & Associés from a friend in June 2020, but he didn’t get his hopes up. “So many purported volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia have emerged in recent years, and so few have been real,” he explains.

The original work was commissioned in 1403. After a first draft failed to meet his expectations, Zhu Di — aka the Yongle Emperor — ordered eminent scholars and calligraphers from across the realm to assemble and compile knowledge, “grouped by category and organized by rhyme.”

The final version approved in 1407 consisted of 22,877 manuscript rolls across 11,095 volumes, with between 370 million and 450 million Chinese characters, according to estimates by various academics. The book was first stored at the Ming Palace in Nanjing, which served as the nation’s capital from 1368 to 1421. It was later moved to the Forbidden City in Beijing, now the Palace Museum.

After a fire in 1557, the Jiajing Emperor ordered that the encyclopedia be reproduced, creating what’s known as the “Jiajing copy.” All known surviving volumes come from this edition.

The two copies were kept separately at the Forbidden City’s Belvedere of Embodying Benevolence and the nearby imperial archive, Huang Shi Cheng. When the Ming dynasty eventually fell in 1644, the belvedere was burned down, and the fate of the original became a mystery.

Between 1723 and 1735, the Jiajing copy was moved to the elite Hanlin Academy, just east of the Forbidden City. However, Qing dynasty inventory records from 1794 show that 1,154 volumes were already missing.

With the imperial court consumed by conflict with foreign powers as well as internal strife, fewer than 5,000 volumes remained by 1875. Within the next 25 years, nearly all of the Yongle Encyclopedia had been lost, largely because of corruption among Qing officials and looting by the invading Eight-Nation Alliance.

China today holds just 241 volumes, including the two purchased by Jin, with most housed at the National Library in Beijing.

Weng, a senior member of China’s Ancient Books Preservation and Conservation Association, says what first caught his attention in 2020 was the volumes’ provenance. “According to the collector, they were passed down through the family,” he says. “One ancestor was a French naval officer who had close connections with several Chinese officials in the 1870s and received many gifts, including these volumes.”

But what mattered most was determining their authenticity.

Having seen genuine excerpts from the ancient encyclopedia, he was confident he could easily spot a fake up close. But with many air routes suspended because of the pandemic, traveling to Paris wasn’t an option. He could only base his judgment on 39 photos taken by a friend in France.

First, Weng examined the volumes using conventional authentication criteria. The Yongle Encyclopedia uses wrapped-back binding, a traditional Chinese method in which a hard cover is added for protection after the pages are bound. The cover, made of high-quality xuan paper and silk, has a book label comprising blue silk under a smaller layer of yellow silk, and a manuscript roll label in the upper-right corner carrying indexing information.

Pages measure 50.3 centimeters by 30 centimeters, with a text frame of roughly 35.5 centimeters by 23.5 centimeters and hand-drawn border lines on all four sides.

“All these text frames had to be drawn by hand. To ensure speed and quality, line spacing was controlled using pinpricks,” Weng says, explaining that the compilers would pierce a stack of paper before drawing the lines.

In addition to the binders’ fine craftsmanship, another way to verify authenticity is through the display text. The Jiajing copy was written entirely in red and black ink, with the main text in Ming ministerial-style script.

To fix errors and omissions, the transcribers used a splicing technique that involved cutting out the erroneous section with a knife at a 45-degree angle and applying a patch, carefully aligning the paper’s fibers. Repairs are only visible when held up to the light.

Over about two weeks, Weng forensically examined each photo for clues and ultimately determined the volumes were real. Soon after, he called Jin, his longtime friend. “I told him there were no problems with the books. We just needed to prepare the money,” he recalls.

Pearls of wisdom

With the sale fast approaching, Jin, a textiles tycoon in his late 50s from Zhejiang’s Taizhou City, immediately set aside 100 million yuan ($14.9 million) of his personal finances. “That figure came from discussions with experts,” he says. “More importantly, it was all I could afford.”

On July 7, 2020, he used three phone lines to call the French auction house, just in case one got disconnected. The bidding began at 11:10 p.m. Beijing time, an hour later than scheduled because of the larger-than-expected turnout.

The starting price was just 5,000 euros. “We learned that despite taking China’s growing economic prosperity into account, the auctioneers expected a final sale price of only 200,000 euros. They obviously underestimated the value of these two volumes,” Jin says.

After the first round, bidding had already reached 4 million euros.

“Things started to slow down after it reached 5 million. Once it reached 6 million, I thought that was it, because people started to become a bit hesitant, and it finally ended at 6.4 million,” he says. With VAT and commission, the final price came to 8.12 million euros.

Jin immediately called his friend Weng to give him the good news.

“People and books are brought together by some kind of fate,” muses the entrepreneur. “When I was bidding for these volumes, if it hadn’t been for the transportation difficulties caused by the pandemic, many experts from around the world could have attended and recognized their authenticity at a glance. The government would also have arranged for experts to authenticate the volumes and applied for funding to make the purchases.”

However, purchasing them had been the easy part. Now Jin had that challenge of getting them back to China.

The first obstacle was France’s export review process for cultural property. Jin believes that, as the Chinese government was paying close attention to the matter, the French Ministry of Culture became “extra cautious.” The businessman had to apply twice to get an export permit.

When approval finally came almost five months later, China’s cultural and customs authorities and security transportation agencies drew up a plan for the volumes’ return. “We received considerable guidance from the National Library of China and the CNAPC,” Jin says. “We had to carefully consider the process to avoid any errors.”

In early 2021, employees from China Shipping Group accompanied the relics from the auction house’s storage facility in central Paris to the city’s Charles De Gaulle Airport, where they were loaded onto a China Eastern Airlines flight to Shanghai.

After clearing customs, the volumes were initially stored at the bonded warehouse in the Shanghai Free Trade Zone before being entrusted to Hangzhou’s Zhejiang Library for safekeeping.

On July 30, 2022, the CNAPC opened specialized storage facilities for ancient books in Beijing and Hangzhou, as well as Xi’an, capital of the northwestern Shaanxi province, and Guangzhou, capital of the southern Guangdong province. The new volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia were deposited at the Hangzhou CNAPC soon after.

At the official donation ceremony in July this year, Jin expressed relief at having this weight lifted from his shoulders and joy at safely returning two “national treasures.”

“If they had remained in a private collection, their true value wouldn’t be fully realized,” he tells Jiefang Daily. “The CNAPC has done extensive research on these volumes. That’s why I donated them to the institution. … books are simply a vessel for research.”

Jin has donated 3,337 items to the Hangzhou CNAPC, but the Yongle Encyclopedia is “so important, so precious,” he says, describing it like a giant gene bank preserving thousands of years of Chinese civilization.

In terms of content, this monumental work contains a vast number of lost texts from the Song (960–1279) and Yuan (1279–1368) dynasties, and informs researchers on manuscript production in the Ming era.

“Unlike the ‘Complete Library of the Four Treasuries’ compiled in the Qing dynasty, which strictly adhered to Confucian principles, teasing out all the materials that were irrelevant or fell outside the content, the Yongle Encyclopedia showed far less parochialism,” says Zhang Pu, deputy director of the Hangzhou CNAPC.

The Ming-dynasty book provides a wealth of firsthand materials for research, everything from a prescription by a physician in the central Hunan province to detailed rules for the game pitch-pot.

“There are just so many things to look into,” says Zhang, whose team has already published eight theses on the new volumes and discovered 22 previously unknown poems. “Every one is like a pearl left behind by history.”

Reported by Li Chuyue.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Li Yu; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.
