World.title: Azerbaijan, Djibouti review bilateral relations, regional security
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. On the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA 81, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan Jeyhun Bayramov discussed with Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Djibouti, current state and prospects of Azerbaijan-Djibouti relations.

This was stated in a publication by the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry on its X page.

"The sides reviewed the current state and prospects of Azerbaijan-Djibouti relations, stressing the importance of sustained high-level contacts and political dialogue.

Particular attention was given to expanding cooperation in trade, economy, education and humanitarian affairs making effective use of existing opportunities.

Coordination and mutual support within the UN, OIC, NAM and other multilateral platforms were also discussed.

Azerbaijan’s preparations to host the OIC Summit in 2027 and its upcoming OIC Chairmanship were also touched upon during the meeting.

Ministers also discussed evolving security situation in the broader Middle East and emphasized the importance for reducing tensions and resolve the situation peacefully," the ministry reported.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan ready to contribute $10m to Issyk-Kul preservation fund
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Kyrgyzstan is ready to contribute $10 million from its state budget to a special international trust fund for the preservation of Lake Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said, while addressing the UN General Assembly.

“To confirm our intentions with concrete actions, we are ready to contribute $10 million from the state budget to this fund,” Japarov said.

He called on the United Nations, international financial institutions and donor countries to support the initiative to establish the fund.

According to Japarov, Lake Issyk-Kul is facing significant climate-related pressures. Its water level has declined by nearly 14 meters over the past 170 years, while the rate of decline reached 7 centimeters per year over the past five years.

He noted that only around 30 of the 101 rivers that historically flowed into Issyk-Kul now flow year-round.

More than 30% of the Tien Shan's mountain glaciers, which are among the lake's main water sources, have melted over the past 70 years, according to the president. Around 20% of this decline occurred over the past seven to 10 years.

Japarov said the changes pose a threat to the region's biodiversity and the economic stability of hundreds of thousands of people.

“We are not asking you for help. We are proposing a joint global partnership to preserve this unique natural resource of planet Earth,” the Kyrgyz president said.

World.title: Japarov proposes UN registry to track implementation of resolutions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov has proposed establishing a permanent public registry within the UN General Assembly to track member states' implementation of resolutions and commitments, while addressing the UN General Assembly.

“First of all, it is necessary to create, within the framework of the UN General Assembly, a permanent public registry of the implementation by Member States of resolutions and commitments undertaken,” Japarov said.

According to him, the registry should systematically record and verify the level of implementation of adopted decisions and require regular reporting by Member States in line with established standards.

The proposed mechanism should also provide analytical reviews by sector and region while ensuring transparency and equal access to information for all states, he said.

Japarov proposed that the registry be administered by the UN Secretariat with the assistance of independent experts.

He also called for a phased response mechanism in cases of systematic non-implementation of UN decisions, including official notification, consultations, the deployment of a monitoring mission and consideration of the issue at a plenary meeting of the UN General Assembly.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan to join UN Security Council for first time
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Kyrgyzstan has been elected to the UN Security Council for the 2027–2028 term for the first time in its history, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said while addressing the UN General Assembly.

“The support of 142 Member States not only confirms Kyrgyzstan's readiness to contribute to international affairs but also demonstrates the growing role of Central Asia in international relations,” Japarov said.

According to him, membership in the Security Council is not a privilege or an award for Kyrgyzstan, but a major responsibility.

“Kyrgyzstan firmly adheres to international law, justice and the protection of human rights, and supports the multilateral system based on mutual respect, balance of interests and responsibility toward future generations,” the president said.

Japarov also called for reform of the UN Security Council.

He proposed granting Africa two permanent seats on the Security Council and Latin America one permanent seat, noting that Africa has a population of more than one billion.

He also said that the requests of some developed countries seeking membership in the Security Council should be considered.

World.title: President Erdoğan voices hope for lasting peace between Azerbaijan, Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan addressed the situation in the S. Caucasus, expressing his desire to achieve lasting peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

President Erdoğan declared his support for the peace process between the two countries

“We desire a lasting peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia. We appreciate and support the political will demonstrated by the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, and the Prime Minister of Armenia, Nikol Pashinyan, toward a peaceful resolution.”

Erdoğan noted that Türkiye is also resolutely continuing the process of normalizing relations with Armenia.

During his speech, the Turkish president also noted that the Organization of Turkic States has developed and become a model platform for regional cooperation:

“Year after year, the Organization of Turkic States has developed and become a model platform for regional cooperation,” Recep Tayyip Erdoğan stressed.

He noted that the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, to be held in Ankara on October 30, will open up new opportunities and horizons for the organization.

World.title: €12B for Middle Corridor: Azerbaijan's efforts boost route's importance for EU
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. The European Union’s decision to mobilize up to 12 billion euros for the development of the Middle Corridor has become one of the most notable signs of this route’s growing importance for European transportation and trade policy. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, delivering her annual State of the Union address, announced a new international connectivity project designed to directly link the South Caucasus and Central Asia to the European market.

“Today, I can announce a new international project in the field of transport connectivity. It will directly connect the South Caucasus and Central Asia to the European market, what we call the Middle Corridor. Through the Global Gateway, we intend to attract up to 12 billion euros in public and private investment. Our goal is to diversify routes, triple trade flows, and significantly reduce cargo transit times by 2030,” she stated.

In response to a Trend's inquiry, the European Commission clarified that the announced amount includes both public and private investments. At the same time, officials in Brussels expect that collaboration with partner countries, international financial institutions, and the private sector will secure more than 12 billion euros in investments for the corridor. Thus, this is not merely a matter of financing a single transport route. The EU effectively views the Middle Corridor as part of a broader system for diversifying trade links, designed to make supply chains between Europe and Asia more resilient, faster, and more predictable.

It is precisely in this context that Azerbaijan’s role stands out. Geographical location alone does not make a country a transportation hub. For the Middle Corridor to become attractive to international business, it was necessary to transform Azerbaijan’s location between the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus, and Türkiye into a functioning multimodal system.

In recent years, Azerbaijan has consistently invested in its railway, port, road, and logistics infrastructure. Key elements include the Baku International Commercial Seaport, the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars Railway, the Caspian Fleet, logistics centers, and the modernization of the railway network. The modernization of the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars line is of particular importance here. Upon completion of the project, the line’s capacity was increased to 5 million metric tons per year. This allows the Azerbaijani section to be viewed not merely as a potential link in a future route, but as infrastructure designed to handle growing transit traffic.

Port infrastructure is also developing in parallel. According to data from Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Digital Development and Transport, from January through July 2026, container throughput at the port of Alat grew by 20% year-over-year, reaching 72,370 TEU, while dry cargo transshipment increased by 82%, reaching 1.4 million metric tons. This is of fundamental importance for the Middle Corridor, as its competitiveness is determined not by a single section of the railway or a single sea crossing, but by the ability of the entire chain to operate in sync.

The main result — not just kilometers, but also time

For a shipper, a geographically short route does not necessarily mean an attractive route. Delivery times, cost, predictability, and the ability to track the shipment throughout its journey are of decisive importance. That is why digitalization has become Azerbaijan’s next area of focus.

The country is implementing electronic transport and transit tools, including e-TIR, e-CMR, e-Permit, and e-CIM/SMGS electronic waybills. A “Single Window” information system has also been created—a digital logistics platform designed to speed up document processing and simplify interaction among participants in the transportation process.

Azerbaijani authorities note that, thanks to infrastructure and digital reforms, the transit time for cargo along the China-Europe route—which stood at 38–53 days a few years ago—has been reduced to an average of 12 days.

It is precisely these changes that are transforming the Middle Corridor from a geographical alternative into a commercially more predictable route. In essence, Azerbaijan is working to reduce one of the main risks for shippers: uncertainty.

The growth in freight volume indicates that demand is already taking shape. According to data from the Kazakhstan Railway Company, 44,200 TEU were transported via the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route in the first eight months of 2026, including 419 container trains from China. Compared to the same period in 2025, container traffic volume increased by 58%, and the number of container trains rose by 84%. At the same time, route participants are already discussing increasing the number of container trains from China to 600 in 2026 and to 800–1,000 in 2027.

For Azerbaijan, this means the need to develop not only its own segment but also to coordinate the entire supply chain — from the Caspian ports to the Caucasus rail lines and onward access to the European market. This is precisely why the Azerbaijan Railways’ work on tariffs, attracting return cargo, coordinating with ports and partners, and efforts to more actively reach out directly to shippers in the European market are of particular importance. This is an important stage: while the initial focus was on attracting Chinese and Central Asian cargo, the route’s participants are now striving to ensure a more balanced flow in both directions.

Azerbaijan is reducing the fragmentation of the route

One of the long-standing challenges of the Middle Corridor is that it passes through several countries and includes rail, maritime, and road segments. Therefore, the efficiency of the entire route depends not so much on any single country as on the coordinated actions of all its participants. In this regard, Azerbaijan is striving to serve not only as a transit territory but also as one of the coordination hubs.

Infrastructure modernization is accompanied by negotiations on tariffs, digitalization, border procedures, data exchange, and the synchronization of transportation systems. The TITR working group, which includes railway administrations, ports, shipping companies, and logistics firms from the countries along the route, is now discussing not only infrastructure construction but also specific issues related to its joint operation.

Why has the Middle Corridor become more important for Europe right now?

The EU’s growing interest in this route cannot be separated from changes in global trade. Following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, European companies and institutions were faced with the need to diversify transport routes between Europe and Asia. Disruptions to traditional maritime supply chains, including the situation surrounding the Red Sea, created additional pressure. As a result, the issue of supply chain resilience has moved beyond the scope of transportation policy alone. For Europe, having multiple alternative routes has become a key component of economic resilience.

At the same time, the Middle Corridor has one important advantage: it connects China and Central Asia to the European market via the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus, and Türkiye. Its development therefore addresses several EU objectives at once: diversifying routes, strengthening trade ties with Central Asia and the South Caucasus, and reducing dependence on specific transport routes. The European Commission explicitly links the new initiative to the need to diversify routes, triple trade flows, and reduce transit times by 2030.

In January 2026, the European Union and Azerbaijan agreed to strengthen cooperation within the framework of the Global Gateway, including in the areas of transportation, digital, energy, and trade connectivity. At that time, with the participation of the EBRD, work began on a feasibility study for the Nakhchivan Railway as part of the broader Trans-Caspian transport connectivity initiative. Thus, the current decision to mobilize up to 12 billion euros does not appear to be an isolated step, but rather a continuation of the European interest in regional connectivity that was already taking shape.

TRIPP could add another level of connectivity to the corridor

The development of new transportation links in the South Caucasus is another contributing factor.

In this context, the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) deserves special attention. The document describes TRIPP as a route intended to promote regional integration and trade development. For the Middle Corridor, the significance of TRIPP lies primarily in the potential expansion of the South Caucasus’s transportation network. It is precisely this network effect that is particularly important for the EU: the corridor’s value increases as it ceases to be a single, fixed chain and transforms into a system of interconnected routes.

In recent years, Azerbaijan has consistently expanded its infrastructure capacity, modernized its rail and port facilities, developed its Caspian Fleet, digitized transit procedures, and participated in coordinating the activities of the route’s participants.

The result was a combination of several factors that are particularly important for European businesses: shorter transit times, increasing throughput capacity, digitalization, the expansion of multimodal capabilities, and a gradual improvement in the predictability of shipments. According to data from the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport, the total volume of transit cargo through Azerbaijan from January through July 2026 exceeded 9.1 million metric tons, reaching its highest level in the past five years. At the same time, shipments along the East–West Corridor grew by 16.5% year-over-year. This points to a significant shift: Azerbaijan is no longer merely offering the EU a geographically advantageous location. It is establishing the infrastructural and institutional framework that enables this location to serve the interests of international freight flows.

This is precisely why the European initiative, worth up to 12 billion euros, represents a logical next step.

Brussels is effectively shifting from supporting individual elements of transport connectivity to attempting to scale up the entire system — from Central Asia through the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to the European market.

For Azerbaijan, this represents both recognition of the work already done and a new challenge. The more European and Asian cargo that flows along the route, the higher the demands on its speed, cost, and reliability.

Consequently, the next stage in the development of the Middle Corridor will no longer be determined solely by infrastructure construction. The route’s competitiveness will depend on how successfully the countries involved can harmonize tariffs, digital systems, border procedures, and maritime and rail transport, as well as ensure traffic flow in both directions. It is precisely this transition from a separate transit route to a unified, predictable, and interconnected system that explains why the Middle Corridor is now becoming one of the priority areas of European connectivity policy.

World.title: Trump weighs 'big decision' on Iran, rejects AI push in major UN speech
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has used a speech at the UN to portray "American power" as the solution to the world's problems, defending his ongoing war with Iran and declaring he now had to decide whether to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic.

Mr Trump also said the US would reject any international scheme to put controls on artificial intelligence — just a day after 22 world leaders, including Australia's Anthony Albanese, signed a statement calling for global guardrails.

Mr Trump's address, delivered six weeks before the US's midterm elections, amounted to a pushback against growing criticism that his administration's actions abroad were harming the US and creating a more destabilised and dangerous world.

"We're reasserting American power, including American military power, where necessary, in our region and around the world, to create a safer future for all of us," Mr Trump said.

"While others have talked, I have acted," he said.

" While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. "

As the war with Iran approaches the eight-month mark with no end in sight, Mr Trump said he was facing a "big decision": Strike a deal that allowed Iran to rebuild, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".

The UN is needed now more than ever When Anthony Albanese and Penny Wong attended the UN General Assembly 12 months ago, it felt like something significant might be happening. This year, things feel like they will be a bit more... prosaic.

"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations?," he said, as a representative for Iran's delegation sat stony-faced in the audience.

"But I believe we'll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election."

Mr Trump suggested Cuba was the US's next target, predicting its communist dictatorship "will fall", but also saying "let's see what happens" in negotiations with the US. His comments prompted a walk-out by the Cuban delegation.

He also used his address to predict, as he has repeatedly in the past, that he would end the Russia-Ukraine war soon.

"It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand," he said.

Renaming AI and rejecting regulation

On the dangers of AI, which Mr Trump has been downplaying as a "hoax", he conceded there was a need to "be careful", but said: "The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now."

The comment represents a rejection of a global body proposed by a coalition of middle power nations, including Australia, in a statement signed on the sidelines of the summit yesterday.

Mr Trump said he was ordering the US government to start referring to "artificial intelligence" as "super intelligence" in all official documents.

"The use of the word 'artificial' makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake and it is not fake," he said.

"It's actually amazing."

The term "superintelligence" is already defined as an advanced form of artificial intelligence that exceeds human capabilities.

Some experts have warned superintelligence represents one of the greatest risks AI could pose to humanity, and US politicians including independent senator Bernie Sanders have proposed a ban on its development.

Mr Trump was one of the first heads of state to address the UN General Assembly high-level week, the UN's annual gathering of world leaders in New York.

He is expected to hold a series of sideline meetings after his speech, including with gulf state leaders whose countries have borne the brunt of Iran's retaliatory missile and drone strikes.

Mr Albanese will address the body later this week.

World.title: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose of Fentanyl and other drugs
World.content:
Actor Hayden Panettiere died from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, a coroner in South Carolina has declared.

The 36-year-old was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16.

Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home.

According to a statement from the Greenville County Coroner’s Office, a combination of fentanyl and its chemical by-product, alongside the anti-anxiety medication alprazolam, a muscle relaxer and a drug used to treat major depression and other serious mental health disorders.

The office did not include further details from the autopsy report in its initial release.

Kasey Kitchen, a publicist for Ms Panettiere's family, told The Associated Press “the investigation is still ongoing and the case is complex".

Hayden Panettiere and her brother Jansen, who died in 2023. (AP Photo: Dan Steinberg, file)

Greenville Police confirmed Tuesday, local time, that their investigation into Ms Panettiere's death is continuing.

Paramedics attended Ms Panettiere's apartment after a 911 call and performed CPR and other advanced resuscitation efforts for more than 40 minutes before she was declared dead.

The autopsy found no signs of trauma that could have contributed to her death, Greenville County Coroner Mike Ellis said in a statement.

The police report released after her death listed medications Ms Panettiere was taking, but drug names were redacted.

Early fame brought success and struggle

Ms Panettiere soared to fame in the TV shows “Heroes” and “Nashville.” In her memoir “This Is Me,” released in May, she described lifelong scars from her early fame.

The autobiography acknowledged her addiction to alcohol and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014.

Heavyweight boxing world champion Wladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere share a daughter together. (Reuters)

Family struggles and tragedy were also outlined in the memoir, her parents’ marriage was strained and eventually ended.

Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023, at age 28.

Domestic violence endured

Ms Panettiere also talked about her long relationship with Brian Hickerson and allegations the aspiring actor physically abused her.

He was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse, and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner.

Mr Hickerson served 45 days in jail and was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management and alcohol rehabilitation sessions.

A judge was recently asked by Mr Hickerson to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours, the request was denied.

Influence of acting roles on mental health

Ms Panettiere was one of two children to former soap opera star, Lesley Vogel and Skip Panettiere, a former New York City fire captain.

The actress rose to fame in childhood, beginning screen work in commercials and soap operas. (Reuters: RMP/ELD/ME)

She acted in commercials and soap operas, including the troubled character Lizzie Spaulding on “Guiding Light.”

In Ms Panettiere's memoir she wrote the traumas her character endured, from being kidnapped to killing her mother’s boyfriend, led her to associate “catastrophe with adoration.”

The actress also said she experienced a cycle of using alcohol and drugs to cope with depression and anxiety, attending rehab in 2015 and 2020.

“I was the one who put myself in the first treatment centre. I was drowning,” Ms Panettier said in a 2023 interview with Women’s Health magazine.

AP

World.title: Sri Lanka convicts 15 men over deadly bombing that killed two Australians
World.content:
A Sri Lanka court has convicted 15 men over the deadly 2019 Easter Sunday bombings that killed more than 260 people, including two Australians.

The bombings, considered the deadliest in Sri Lanka's recent history, were carried out on three churches and three luxury tourist hotels.

Australians Manik Suriaaratchi and her daughter, Alexendria, were among those who lost their lives when a bomb exploded inside a church in Negombo, just north of the capital, Colombo.

The attacks by Islamic State-inspired terrorists also injured more than 500 people.

St. Sebastian's Church in Negombo was damaged in one of the blasts in Negombo. (AP: Chamila Karunarathne)

Sri Lanka's High Court convicted 14 of the 24 men accused of being directly involved in attack on charges including murder and conspiracy to commit terrorism.

The three-judge bench read out its decision on Tuesday after a five-year trial.

Nine of the men were acquitted, while one other was found guilty of only some of the charges, the court said.

In 2021, authorities filed more than 23,000 charges against the suspects accused of planning or inspiring the attacks.

None of those believed to have directly participated in the attacks are alive.

Sentencing will take place at a later date.

Sri Lanka's military stands guard at the front of St Anthony's Shrine which was damaged in a blast. (Reuters: Dinuka Liyanawatte)

Sri Lanka president vows to pursue penalties for those responsible

Sri Lanka's President, Anura Kumara Dissanayake had pledged to hold those responsible for the wrongdoing to account when he was elected two years ago.

In July a former police chief and a former defence ministry official were sentenced to death for failing to prevent the bombings.

Sri Lanka sentences officials to death over bombing that killed Australians The 2019 Easter Sunday bombings on churches and luxury tourist hotels killed more than 260 people, including two Australians.

The court heard then that an Indian intelligence agency had weeks earlier alerted Sri Lanka to a possible suicide attack by Islamist extremists, but authorities failed to take action.

While former police chief Pujith Jayasundara and former defence ministry secretary Hemasiri Fernando were sentenced to death, Sri Lanka has not carried out the death penalty since 1976, and the pair was expected to serve a life sentence instead.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Vulnerable residents feeling 'distress' as Mildura power outage drags on
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A power outage in the north-west Victorian city of Mildura is set to enter a third day, raising concerns for the elderly, residents reliant on medical devices and domestic violence survivors.

Power has been out for almost 3,000 residents and businesses since a ute crashed into a critical power pole at nearby Birdwoodton about 6.30am on Monday.

Just before 7pm Tuesday, electricity distributor Powercor said the expected timeframe for "the majority of the network" to be restored had been extended from Wednesday afternoon to midday Friday.

Among those without electricity are 24 supported accommodation homes run by Sunraysia Residential Services (SRS).

SRS CEO Marian Luehman said many affected were elderly or living with a disability, who relied on electricity to power equipment and undertake everyday tasks.

Marian Luehman says outages cause anxiety for the elderly. (Supplied: Sunraysia Residential Services)

"Prolonged periods without power can be distressing and isolating," she said.

"Uncertainty around restoration timeframes can add further anxiety, particularly for those already facing health or personal challenges."

Ms Luehman said the situation highlighted a need to strengthen emergency response arrangements for vulnerable residents, who needed support accessing generators, alternative accommodation, transport assistance and targeted welfare checks.

An anxious wait for victim-survivor

Sarah, a victim-survivor of domestic violence whose name has been changed to protect her privacy, said the outage had caused anxiety, because it meant her home security cameras were not operating.

"[Previously, the perpetrator] would park across the road. Some nights he would be standing in the shadows of a tree watching my house," Sarah said.

"[The cameras] alert me to any activity around the boundaries of my property and they give me a feeling of safety.

"I spent quite some time not being able to shower or sleep in the dark unless I had someone there to ensure I was safe. The cameras helped me a great deal."

Victoria Police said it was sorry to hear about the impact on a victim of domestic violence, and told "anyone who feels threatened by the presence of someone at their home, or anywhere else for that matter, to call Triple Zero immediately".

Police will not respond to alarms

Mildura police Acting Inspector Daron Hulls urged residents to "remain calm" and "check on [your] neighbours".

Acting Inspector Hulls said Victoria Police had increased patrols around the impacted area, but would not be responding to alarms until power was restored.

"For security, we encourage [residents] to obviously manually lock their doors and their windows, especially if they've got automatic systems in place there," Acting Inspector Hulls said.

"[People] need to be aware of alarms because we won't respond to an alarm or a security system that's been triggered by power failures."

In the case of a break-in, Acting Inspector Hulls said victims would need to contact police and may be required to submit extra evidence.

"We'll have to rely on some other supporting information, such as phone calls or observations," he said.

Outage extended to Friday

Powercor spokesperson Jodan Oliver said crews were prioritising regular welfare checks for about 130 residents living with life support apparatuses.

He said the outage was an "unusual one".

Many Mildura shops are closed as the power outage continues. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

"The different circuits on that pole, one was very high voltage and we have low voltage as well, which connects people's homes," he said.

"We're checking with customers' properties whether [that high voltage] has entered into people's wiring, switchboards … and potentially caused damage.

"So we're really keen on people to make any reports to us of any damage they notice at their homes and their switchboards, appliances not working."

Powercor has set up an information station outside the Alfred Deakin Centre in Mildura. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

A relief centre has been set up at the Benetook Room of the Alfred Deakin Centre at the corner of Deakin Avenue and Twelfth Street.

Chargers are available for residents' devices, as well as information from Powercor, Mildura Rural City Council and local police.

World.title: US attacks Australia's 'opt-out' algorithm law in rare intervention
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Trump administration has made an extraordinary public intervention into Australia's debate about its proposed digital duty of care, warning the Albanese government that the policy would be "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech".

It called for the Australian government to exclude US social media companies from its plans to give users the option to opt into algorithmic recommendation feeds — a decision that would effectively neuter the law, removing the biggest platforms from its application.

The rare public rebuke took the form of a response to a consultation on the draft digital duty of care bill, which would force platforms to take actions to mitigate and respond to harms caused by digital platforms.

The submission, published by the US Embassy today, said Washington had "serious concerns" about how Australia would decide what counts as "foreseeable harm".

This comes with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese currently in the middle of a United States trip to promote his government's tech policy agenda at the United Nations General Assembly.

His support for international AI regulation and his government's teen social media ban have increasingly earned the ire of the Trump administration.

Washington objects to harm rules and feed mandates

In the submission, the US government said it was concerned by what it described as rigid, one-size-fits-all design requirements.

Such mandates, it argued, would push platforms to demote sensitive or controversial topics to comply, reducing the reach of independent journalists and other voices.

"The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship," the submission said.

Communications Minister Anika Wells and the federal government are developing digital duty of care laws. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

It put a number of questions to the Australian government, including how Australia would define "harm" and "risks", how they would be adjudicated, by whom, and whether platforms or users could appeal. It also asked about the role of the eSafety Commissioner and impacts on privacy.

While it is common for governments to express their views on other countries' policies, those views are usually communicated through private channels.

It is exceedingly rare for a foreign government to make a direct, public intervention into a domestic debate like this.

The US government's hostility toward the digital duty of care was signposted earlier this month in a statement from White House spokesperson Kush Desai to the Guardian Australia.

He said President Donald Trump had warned other nations against imposing "digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America's leading technology sector".

Warning Australia's tech policies could spread elsewhere

The submission argued forced changes to mitigate Australia-specific risks could change how users everywhere, including Americans, experienced the platforms.

If other jurisdictions adopted conflicting duty-of-care mandates, platforms could face incompatible design requirements not technically or commercially scalable in parallel, it said.

Australia's teen social media ban inspired a number of other countries to introduce, or pledge to introduce, similar restrictions.

Earlier today, it was reported by Politico Australia that the American industry body representing American tech companies had joined in a High Court challenge to Australia's teen social media ban.

The group, NetChoice, described it as "the most extensive prohibition on youth access to social media in force in any liberal democracy".

The digital duty of care draft shows how the government plans to create a legal obligation for online services, including social media, gaming and other platforms, to create a safe experience for users through its design.

The Albanese government said it would use this law, if passed, to force platforms like Facebook, Instagram and TikTok to send users a pop-up offering a choice between a personalised algorithmic feed and a feed limited to accounts they follow.

Communications Minister Anika Wells last week downplayed the White House's warning as "broad" and said she had not directly received such a warning from a US representative.

When asked about the US government's intervention, Ms Wells's office and the US Embassy both declined to comment.

World.title: Teen tells court of 'painfully real' impacts of explicit deepfake images
World.content:
A teenage girl who had sexually explicit deepfake images of her shared online has told a court that, although fake, the images have had a "painfully real" impact on her.

William Hamish Yeates, of Netherby, appeared in South Australia's District Court today for a pre-sentence hearing after he pleaded guilty to two counts of creating or altering sexual material without consent earlier this year.

The 20-year-old was the first person in Australia to be charged under federal laws introduced in 2024 to combat the rise of deepfake pornography.

The offending, which occurred between October 2024 and February 2025, involved the creation of sexually explicit deepfake images and videos of his victim that he shared online.

The now-19-year-old woman was supported by more than a dozen family members and friends as she delivered her victim impact statement to the court.

"For a long time, I've carried the shame of something that was never my fault. Today, I'm here to give that shame back to the person it belongs to," she told him.

"I want to make it very clear, these images of me were fake but the impact they had is painfully real."

William Yeates has previously pleaded guilty to two counts of creating or altering sexual material without consent earlier this year. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

In her statement, the teenager said the first time she saw her graduation picture was on a pornography website.

"Knowing that my graduation photo was taken and used with such a corrupt context has been one of the hardest things for me to process," she said.

"The first time I saw my actual graduation picture was on a pornography website beside altered videos of me with my full name and school attached to it.

"Every time I now see that photo, I feel sick.

"You took a memory that was supposed to represent achievement, friendship and happiness and turned it into something so painful."

The 19-year-old said the discovery of Yeates's offending resulted in the "darkest period" of her life but said she would not let it define her.

"Despite everything I will refuse to let what you did to me define me forever," she said.

"I am not your victim, Will. I am a survivor.

" You tried to reduce me to an image on a screen, but I am so much more than that. "

Yeates read an apology to his victim in which he said the harm he caused the girl was "unintended".

"My actions were repulsive and will continue to plague my mind for as long as I breathe," he said.

Exposure to explicit online content

Yeates's defence barrister, Jane Powell SC, told the court that a psychologist had diagnosed the 20-year-old with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and that a report mentioned a diagnosis of compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (CSBD).

She said he developed "a sense of an obsession" with the victim.

The victim made her impact statement in South Australia's District Court today. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Ms Powell also told the court that in the lead-up to his offending, Yeates began engaging in "communities" on the social media platform X, formerly Twitter, "where everyone was in the same mindset".

"It was very common to post nude images of women in such communities," she said.

" His exposure to that content made him think that sharing photos of women in a sexually derogatory manner was OK. "

Ms Powell also told the court that Yeates had been introduced to Andrew Tate online, who she referred to as a "hateful, misogynistic individual".

Tate is a well-known social media influencer, self-described misogynist and alleged rapist.

"Mr Yeates found himself conflicted in some ways but still attracted to that platform … in the months and year leading up to the offending," Ms Powell said.

She asked the court not to sentence Yeates to time behind bars as it would "weigh heavily" on his mental health.

However, a prosecutor from the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions (CDPP) opposed Ms Powell's submission and said a term of imprisonment would be the only appropriate sentence due to the "extremely insidious" nature of the "serious conduct".

William Yeates, right, did not comment as he left the Adelaide Magistrates Court alongside his lawyer, Tim McGrath. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

"One might be able to accept, on the one hand, that there was a desire to belong in this deplorable community of the Andrew Tate manosphere but that is not an exclusive motivation for this offending when one looks at the content that he was posting," she said.

"Two things can be true, which is: he wanted to belong, but he also wanted to degrade and humiliate the victim online."

The prosecutor said a sentence of imprisonment would work to deter others from committing similar offences.

"The nature of this offending is significant, it is prolific and it is online and it is growing," she said.

"A sentence in this matter has to deter particularly young men from engaging in this type of behaviour."

Yeates faces a maximum penalty of seven years behind bars and will be sentenced next month.

World.title: Teen jailed over home invasion that traumatised Melbourne family
World.content:
Last August, Kai Li and his family were jolted awake just before 4am.

Intruders had jumped the fence and were using garden shears to smash a downstairs window.

Seconds later, Mr Li was face-to-face with five of the masked group.

Some were armed with machetes, and the Children's Court later heard they had no hesitation in using them.

During the aggravated home invasion, Mr Li fought desperately to protect two children, his wife, his grandparents and a nanny inside.

Mr Li's wife and grandparents were assaulted but Mr Li's injuries were the most severe.

He was stabbed 11 times in the face and upper body before the intruders allegedly stole the family car and fled the Kew home.

Mr Li was left with permanent damage to his eyesight and his family remains traumatised.

Today, one of Mr Li's attackers was jailed for two years and nine months after pleading guilty to aggravated home invasion, assault charges and a raft of other car theft crimes.

Victims' lives changed 'forever'

"What happened to my family has changed our lives forever," Mr Li told the ABC this afternoon.

"I never imagined that something like this could happen in our own home."

Mr Li said his case was emblematic of "weaknesses" in the legal system and called for stricter bail laws and tougher sentences for violent crime.

"I hope both the Australian government and the Victorian government will introduce policies that genuinely improve community safety, so that families like mine do not have to experience this again," he said.

In sentencing the 17-year-old attacker, Judge Jack Vandersteen said the home invasion was a "grave violation".

Not only had the judge considered the police report and Mr Li's victim impact statement, he also viewed footage of the incident which was captured on a baby monitor in the home.

"The screams, the threats, are evident. The fear of the occupants was palpable," he said.

"A home should be a place of safety."

A teenager will spend nearly three years in jail for his role in the violent Kew home invasion. (ABC News)

Prosecutors did not allege the 17-year-old directly caused Mr Li's injuries but argued he was part of the broader plot to storm the home.

The teenager said he had taken drugs and alcohol before the attack and said the incident remained "a bit of a blur".

He had written an apology letter, committed himself to reform while in youth detention and had the support of his family and church community, the court heard.

Invasion occurred before new laws passed

The aggravated home invasion occurred before Victoria's "Adult time for Violent Crime" laws were passed.

It meant the case was not automatically transferred to the County Court, where judges have the power to impose the same sentences on children as they do for adults.

Under the new regime, a child guilty of aggravated home invasion could be sentenced to life in prison by the County Court, however the judges have not yet come close to imposing such a devastating sentence.

The maximum penalty the Children's Court can set is four years in youth detention.

Mr Li said he was grateful to the local police officers who handled his case, and said politicians needed to tackle the issue of repeat violent youth offenders.

"What families need is not symbolic measures, but policies that actually address the problem and give ordinary residents a greater sense of safety in their own communities," he said.

Two others charged with breaking into Mr Li's home remain before the courts.

Police are continuing to hunt for two more people.

World.title: 'Sophistication' spat over foot traffic decline in Adelaide CBD
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A sharp decline in foot traffic in Adelaide's CBD has prompted a prominent property industry lobbyist to take a swipe at the city council, which he has accused of lacking "sophistication".

But the lord mayor has staunchly defended the council's approach to CBD visits, and hit back at those she said "don't understand the city is a complex beast".

According to Adelaide City Council documents citing Kepler Analytics data, there were 138.8 million foot traffic visitors in 2023, before the figure dropped to 130.6 million in 2024 and 122 million in 2025.

A month-by-month dashboard, published by the Adelaide Economic Development Agency, shows 13.9 million visits were recorded citywide in the month of July 2023, before the figure fell to 10.9 million in July 2024.

In July 2025, there were 10.2 million visits and, in July of this year, 9.6 million visits.

Rundle Mall is the city's main shopping strip. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Executive director of the state's Property Council, Bruce Djite, blamed factors including car parking, which he said was having a deterrent effect on visitors.

"This is what happens when you have — with all due respect — Adelaide city councillors who are very nice people but unfortunately lack the sophistication required to attract people into the city on a regular basis," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"We have a council that is at war with car parking without an alternative solution.

" When you're ripping out car parks and putting in bike lanes, you make it increasingly difficult for anyone who needs to travel into the CBD to get there, do their shopping and get home. It's too inconvenient. "

Bruce Djite said parking and a lack of housing were deterrents to visitors. (ABC News: Dan Taylor)

Mr Djite said a more significant factor than parking was housing, and he accused the council of failing to make best use of its building stock, more of which, he said, should be converted for residential use.

"What they need to do is have more residential in the city," he said.

"They could put some of their underutilised buildings to the development sector, so they could have professionals come in and deliver the residential supply that's required in the CBD."

Adelaide Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith rejected Mr Djite's criticisms, but said she did not wish to "have a discussion about people's character".

"I'm not into criticising him for his sophistication — that's not my style," she said.

Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith says Adelaide has a strong record on affordable parking. (ABC News)

Cr Lomax-Smith said foot traffic figures were partly reflective of demographic changes.

"More people are working from home now than there were five years ago, and it's taken a while for the foot traffic to recover after COVID. There's been a bounce back," she said.

" Clearly people don't understand the city is a complex beast — we have retail, we have nightlife, we have all sorts of professional services and we've had a growth in business activity in the city. [There are] more businesses now than ever before. "

Cr Lomax-Smith said CBD parking in Adelaide compared favourably with other Australian capital cities, and added that the council's housing strategy was paying dividends.

"We've had an increase of 3.5 per cent in our residential population in the last year, and that's the largest increase of any council area in South Australia," she said.

Foot traffic has decreased in Adelaide's CBD. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Rundle Mall tailor Joseph Uzumcu said he had not noticed a decline in passers-by, and said his business was "doing incredibly well".

"People point fingers at other outside effects of why people are not coming into the city," he said.

"We've got to realise the population of Adelaide is [smaller than elsewhere].

"We're not Sydney, we're not Brisbane."

World.title: At UN, Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran but predicts deal after midterms
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump At UN, Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran but predicts deal after midterms Michael Koziol September 23, 2026 — 2:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Donald Trump told world leaders at the United Nations that he was weighing whether to annihilate Iran to end the war, but predicted the two countries would reach a peace deal after the US midterm elections in November. The US president also rejected what he called a “globalist scheme” to regulate AI – which Australia has joined – and said the US would officially rename artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in a bid to rehabilitate the concept’s image. Donald Trump said he had a “big decision” to make about whether to annihilate Iran. Dominic Lorrimer Trump said the change would be made on all US government documents regarding AI, and he hoped the world would follow suit. “It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don’t – we’re going to find out pretty soon.” Trump’s speech to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday morning (US time) was less combative than his effort last year, when he lectured the world about the climate change “hoax” and told his global counterparts their countries were “going to hell” thanks to mass migration.



While the president revisited those topics in passing, he focused on opposing AI regulation and defending the war against Iran, which has now lasted nearly seven months. The war had severely weakened the Islamic theocracy in Tehran, he said, which has lost its entire navy and is suffering from inflation that eclipsed 300 per cent. But a deal to end the conflict collapsed, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps continues to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump addressing the General Assembly. Bloomberg “I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations? But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election. Because it doesn’t make sense for them not to.



“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m no running. I did that already, and won in a landslide. I’ll be here for two-and-a-half years. The Republican Party is running [in November’s election] and I’ll be helping them. But I am not running.” Trump said he gave no credence to the midterm elections at all when it came to deciding what to do about Iran. “It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.” Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the UN floor for the opening session. Dominic Lorrimer The speech came a day after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – who is also in New York for UN leaders’ week – joined counterparts from Canada, Europe and elsewhere in calling for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. The declaration called for a UN-style international organisation that would set standards and oversee AI use.



Trump’s rejection of this “globalist scheme” reflects his belief that any regime to regulate the sector would cede control to China, the US’ main rival to AI dominance. “I am not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” he told the UN General Assembly. “Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter or how great or how daunting that challenge may be.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio and First Lady Melania Trump listen as President Donald Trump addresses the UN. Dominic Lorrimer As he did last year, the US president used the platform to attack elements of the UN itself – including UNESCO and the Human Rights Council – and its “far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”. Trump also lashed out at the International Criminal Court, which he called a “rogue institution” and “an evil group of people”. The ICC – which the US has never been a party to – has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is due to deliver his own address to the UN on Thursday.



Related Article Updated

AI ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons When the US president turned his attention to Cuba, branding it “an absolutely failed state” that would soon collapse, the Cuban delegation in the audience walked out of the room. Earlier, as he entered the UN building, Trump briefly stopped to speak to reporters, and targeted CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins. CNN was one of three news outlets Trump banned from the White House last week. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump said. “You should not be here. You said you weren’t going to cover me, you shouldn’t be covering me.” Like other news organisations, CNN received credentials from the UN to cover the General Assembly.

World.title: Lachie Neale out of grand final in sensational tribunal ruling
World.content:
Lachie Neale is sensationally out of the grand final after the AFL tribunal upheld his one-match ban for striking and gave the veteran Lion a stinging rebuke for the off-the-ball incident.

Not even Neale’s exemplary record of avoiding suspension in 320 AFL matches for Brisbane and former club Fremantle saved him from losing his shot at the Lions’ hat-trick of premierships.

Lachie Neale copped an initial one-game ban for the gut punch. The suspension was upheld. Fox Footy, Getty

The tribunal was highly critical of Neale, who they accused of giving “inconsistent” evidence about his clash with Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan. Brisbane desperately tried to have the impact downgraded from medium to low, allowing Neale to be fined instead and to be able to face Fremantle at the MCG on Saturday.

“It is relevant that this strike occurred nowhere near the ball, was not affected in or around the play, and because Ginnivan did not see Neale coming from behind or the side until the very last moment, he had no expectation of being struck until it was too late to meaningfully defend himself,” said tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson, KC.

Loading

In a compelling case that tested the AFL’s crackdown on “gut punches” and whether a player such as Neale should be granted leniency after 15 AFL seasons without a suspension, the 33-year-old copped the full wrath of the tribunal.

“Neale jogged towards Ginnivan and formed the immediate intention to swing his arm forcefully at Ginnivan, and that is what he did,” Gleeson said.

“We have listened carefully to Neale’s evidence.

“But we find that it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video, and to that extent, we do not accept it.

“There is no doubt in our minds that this should be graded as medium impact.

“While Ginnivan was not injured and did not appear to suffer any significant pain or discomfort, the blow was forceful and knocked him off his feet.

“He immediately doubled over in a manner more consistent with a more-than-negligible blow having landed.”

Brisbane had tried to argue that Neale’s strike on Ginnivan wasn’t a “classic punch in the guts”. Neale relied heavily on his argument that his conduct constituted a “body check” instead of a strike on Ginnivan.

While the Lions prepared an argument that it was a case of low impact instead of medium, they were equally prepared to rely on Neale’s good record to constitute “the exemplary and compelling circumstances” allowing him to have his one-match ban waived.

“It’s relevant there’s a grand final on the line,” said Neale’s advocate, Adrian Anderson.

“This is potentially the most important match of Lachie Neale’s career. It could be a defining moment in the career if he’s to miss a historic opportunity to play in a three-peat grand final.”

Lachie Neale at training on Tuesday. Getty Images

Anderson continued: “If you’ve had 15 years of being a great example for young players and not getting suspended and playing the game like Lachie Neale does, it’s something deserving some credit for him if he does have a lapse, even if it’s an intentional minor lapse.

“He one of the best and one of the fairest players to have played the game.”

But the AFL was adamant that Neale should be penalised for an incident “a long way off the ball”.

The AFL’s counsel, Andrew Woods, KC, strongly argued that it was an intentional act.

“You take into account the medical report ... it does confirm that he [Ginnivan] required immediate on-field assessment by a doctor,” Woods said.

“It was off the ball. It was a long way off the ball.

“Ginnivan wasn’t expecting it. He couldn’t expect it … he wasn’t braced, and he took the full impact.”

Loading

Anderson, however, said Neale’s action was a “body check”.

“We respectfully submit that when you have a careful [examination of the footage and Neale’s testimony] … this was not a strike with the left arm.

“It was a body check, primarily with the body and shoulder.

“It’s not a classic punch in the guts.

“At the very most, the contact [on Ginnivan] from that left arm is negligible, or such a level to classify it as low impact.

“There is not a frame of this vision where you see a fist in Ginnivan’s torso.“

Neale was asked if he knew what was at stake when he targeted Ginnivan. Specifically, he was asked if he knew that by committing a reportable offence during the game, he risked missing a grand final.

“I don’t think I’ve ever thought about that during a game of football, about the consequences of a report. I’ve just tried to play as fairly as possible and stick up for my teammates,” Neale said.

Neale explained that he clashed with Ginnivan because he was unhappy with the Hawk’s treatment of Eric Hipwood seconds earlier.

“For me, I was very close to the incident between Jack [Ginnivan] and Eric Hipwood ... where it seemed that Jack ... gave him some jumper punches,” said Neale.

“I didn’t feel that that looked great.

“I went to show my disappointment in that action, and ran past Jack and body check, bump him and felt that my shoulder made contact with his body and shoulder first.

Neale faced questions whether Ginnivan would have known he was approaching.

“You can see him [Ginnivan] look a step or two before I make impact,” Neale said.

The Lion confirmed that it was an off-the-ball clash. “No, the ball is not in the area,” Neale said.

Neale said he spoke to Ginnivan ahead of the tribunal.

“I spoke to Jack this morning on the phone,” Neale said.

“He [Ginnivan] said it felt more like a bump [or a] body check [rather] than a strike.

“He said my body force made him go to ground.”

When Neale was running away from the incident, the veteran Lion explained why he gestured with a diving motion.

“I felt that Jack might have taken a dive to get a free kick, and that was why I was indicating a diving action,” Neale said.

“He [Ginnivan] had a bit of a smile on his face, but didn’t say anything.”

World.title: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose, coroner finds
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose, coroner finds Jeffrey Collins September 23, 2026 — 12:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Actor Hayden Panettiere died from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, a coroner in South Carolina said on Tuesday (US time). Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home. Hayden Panettiere, pictured at the world premiere of Scream VI in New York in 2023, died last month. AP Photo/Evan Agostini According to a statement from the Greenville County Coroner’s Office, a combination of fentanyl and its chemical byproduct, as well as the anti-anxiety medication alprazolam, a muscle relaxer and a drug used to treat major depression and other serious mental health disorders, were found in Panettiere’s system. The office did not include further details from the autopsy report in its initial release.



Asked for comment on the coroner’s report, Kasey Kitchen, a publicist for the family, told The Associated Press that “the investigation is still ongoing and the case is complex”. Greenville Police confirmed on Tuesday their investigation into Panettiere’s death is continuing. Related Article Vale Hayden Panettiere’s final battles: Mysterious pain and trouble with an ex Paramedics responded to Panettiere’s apartment last month after a 911 call and performed CPR and other advanced resuscitation efforts for more than 40 minutes before she was declared dead. An autopsy found no signs of trauma that could have contributed to her death, Greenville County Coroner Mike Ellis said in a statement. The police report released after her death listed medications Panettiere was taking, but the drug names were redacted.



Panettiere soared to fame in the TV shows Heroes and Nashville. In her memoir This Is Me, released in May, Panettiere described lifelong scars from her early fame and acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. Panettiere rose to fame in the TV series Heroes, before landing roles in Nashville, Scream 4 and the Bring It On series. Getty She also endured family struggles and tragedy. Her parents’ marriage was strained and eventually ended. Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023, at age 28. Panettiere also talked about her long relationship with Brian Hickerson and allegations that the aspiring actor physically abused her. He was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse, and he pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner and served a short time in jail due to the case. He was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous sessions.



Hickerson completed the terms and recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours; that request was denied. Panettiere was one of two children born to Skip Panettiere, a former New York City fire captain, and Lesley Vogel, a former soap opera star. She acted in commercials and soap operas, including as the ever-troubled Lizzie Spaulding on Guiding Light. In This Is Me, she wrote that the traumas her character endured, from being kidnapped to killing her mother’s boyfriend, led her to associate “catastrophe with adoration”. Loading She then played a cheerleader with supernatural powers in Heroes, which propelled her to fame in 2006. By 2015, Panettiere was playing a brash country upstart opposite Connie Britton on Nashville, which aired on ABC for four seasons before being cancelled and revived on CMT. She did her own singing in the show, which scored some hits on country charts, spawned US tours and earned Panettiere two supporting actress Golden Globe nominations.

World.title: ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalAI ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons Rob Harris Updated September 23, 2026 — 12:05am ,first published September 22, 2026 — 2:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres says artificial intelligence demands the “same sense of urgency” as nuclear weapons did, warning that technology “without accountability” threatens humanity. Addressing the UN General Assembly, Guterres noted that developers were now “pulling the alarm” and said governments “must assume their responsibilities”. He called for co-operation and common safeguards on AI, adding that the UN was a good place to work on this. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres delivers an address at the headquarters in New York. AP Photo/Seth Wenig Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese echoed the rallying cry for world leaders to unite on efforts to protect people from the risks of artificial intelligence, saying in a speech that no country can manage the technology’s growing risks alone. Australia was among a group of 22 signatories to call for new international safeguards on AI at the United Nations on Monday, amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks.



The prime minister joined colleagues, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to call for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the opening Ceremony of New York Climate Week on Monday. Dominic Lorrimer The declaration warned that capable AI systems have already been seen circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorised access to real-world systems. “Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks,” the statement said, which was also co-signed by Ireland, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. It called for a UN-style international organisation that would set standards and oversee AI use.



The leaders stopped short of calling for a halt to development, instead arguing that AI’s potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen economies should be preserved while stronger controls are imposed. Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it “AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control,” they said, insisting that it must be developed and used in accordance with international law. Its release comes ahead of Thursday’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI expected to be a major topic of discussion. Guterres called for the AI superpowers to start a dialogue on the technology’s future.



“Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity. To establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and co-operation,” Guterres said, referencing the US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War. “At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognise the need to manage shared existential risks,” he added. Loading Following the declaration from other world leaders, Trump said that US law enforcement agencies like the Department of Justice would regulate artificial intelligence risks if necessary, but emphasised his primary goal was to encourage its development. Downplaying potential dangers, Trump argued against stifling AI growth, comparing its future impact to the Industrial Revolution and the internet. He maintained the US must protect its edge over China while fostering both AI and superintelligence.



“We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way!” Trump wrote on social media. Related Article Opinion

AI Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Albanese has cited Australia’s role in shaping international rules for AI as a key plank of its bid for a seat on the UN Security Council. He said he hoped for a positive meeting between Trump and Xi. Addressing the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI, Albanese will say the risks posed by increasingly capable systems will cross borders and require countries to work together on common standards. “And no country can manage these risks alone,” he will say. “We must come together.”



Albanese will argue countries can seize and share the opportunities created by AI while developing common standards to protect children and communities. “We can develop clear shared expectations and common guardrails,” he will say. The US and China are locked in a race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, while Washington and Beijing have resisted calls from industry figures including Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the development of frontier models amid warnings that humans could lose control. Neither the US nor China are part of the new declaration. The declaration calls on AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory testing before systems are deployed and independent assessments by qualified evaluators given sufficient access to identify risks. Governments and regional organisations are also urged to develop common standards, strengthen transparency and share reports of serious AI safety incidents.



Albanese said AI had the potential to improve lives, strengthen the economy and productivity, and advance science and medical breakthroughs, but “humans need to be in control of it”. Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates He said he had played a central role in the statement through conversations with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who initiated the declaration along with Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. The leaders want countries across all regions to have access to the scientific expertise, technical capacity and trusted evaluation needed to assess advanced AI systems. The declaration also calls on UN member states to explore creating an international institution that could set standards, enable verification and convene governments when AI systems cross agreed capability thresholds.



The group warned that efforts to control frontier AI should not widen the gap between countries with access to the technology and those unable to benefit from its advances. At a separate business event with Macquarie, Albanese will argue Australia is being recognised internationally for moving early on emerging challenges. “I think the world is seeing Australia as a smart, adaptable and successful middle power, succeeding because we’re not afraid to get ahead of the curve on the issues that matter to the future,” he will say.
