Air New Zealand

AsureQuality Ltd

Fisher & Paykel Healthcare

New Zealand Customs Service

Department of Conservation

Royal New Zealand Airforce

Access Community Health

Deloitte

Ministry for Primary Industries

World.title: Company size makes no difference to workplace safety, report finds
World.content:
A new report by a business leaders group says the size of a company has nothing to do with workplace safety.

Major law changes to kick in from April include removing the need for small firms to manage risks that are not critical.

Critics say this will create a two-tier workplace safety system, with big firms held to higher standards.

The Business Leaders' Health and Safety Forum said the government and companies needed to acknowledge size does not matter.

"The 20-worker threshold separates small businesses from large ones, but it does not separate safe workplaces from unsafe ones," said report author and economist Shamubeel Eaqub in a statement.

"When we looked at the injury rate by different sizes of firms and industries we found no consistent pattern - so there was no evidence that small firms were somehow less risky than larger firms," he told RNZ.

The law changes made things murkier, he added.

Big health and safety law changes kick in from next April. 123rf

The report summed up the state of workplace safety saying the country was improving but too slowly.

It said some of the riskiest industries were improving fastest but mental wellbeing was one area consistently getting worse.

The system must be better coordinated to cut rates of harm much higher than in Australia or the UK, it said.

"New Zealand has extensive health and safety regulation but lacks sufficiently clear stewardship and coordination across the system," said forum chief executive Francois Barton in a statement.

Eaqub said NZ had comparable regulation to those two other countries but they had much better experiences. Applying rules in a way that made sense was the key.

But the report said the workplace safety system made it hard for firms to figure out what rules applied to them as there was no public register of approved codes, which numbered more than two dozen.

"If a firm cannot easily find the codes that inform it [our] system is falling short."

Screengrab / Facebook

The lack of follow-through was demonstrated by regulations to keep plant machinery safe, slated for improvement since 2021, but still not done, it added.

"The Health and Safety at Work Strategy 2018-2028 sets direction to 2028 but still has no delivery mechanism, performance measures or oversight of its own.

"We need better regulatory practice, not more law."

Eaqub said it was good more resources were being put into inspections by Worksafe but "we can't inspect our way to improvement" because inspectors could not be everywhere.

The report estimated workplace harm cost $5.5 billion a year.

Among the encouraging signs were improvement in core safety practices, greater worker engagement and greater grasp of risks across supply chains, said Barton.

World.title: Environment Southland rejects request for data centre review
World.content:
Environment Southland says it can't proceed with a request to review consent for a major data centre.

Development of the $5 billion Datagrid AI factory is underway at the Makarewa site, with consents to draw up to 600,000 litres of groundwater a day.

Datagrid has since said it cut its expected water use by 70 percent, and the centre would run primarily on rain water.

Southland Sustainable Resource Coalition requested Environment Southland review Datagrid's consent for water take and use.

File photo. In a fiery public meeting on 19 August 2026, Southlanders hit back at promises of a scaled-back Datagrid factory - vowing to continue fighting the $5b development. RNZ / Katie Todd

Environment Southland general manager strategy & regulation Hayley Fitchett said a consent may be reviewed in certain circumstances, including where it was necessary to ensure limits set in a regional plan could be met.

"In this case, the company's consented operational water take is less than 10 percent of the limit set in the Proposed Southland Water and Land Plan."

Environment Southland's resource consents relate to discharges to air and land, taking water, and a small wetland.

World.title: Canterbury council may declare nitrate emergency over
World.content:
Canterbury regional councillors will vote on Wednesday on a proposal to declare the region's controversial nitrate emergency over.

This time last year the council voted to declare an emergency as nitrate levels climbed across the region, with council and private water supplies seeing levels inch towards - and in some cases breach - the national drinking water standard of 11.3 milligrams of nitrate per litre of water.

The notice of motion, proposed by former councillor Vicki Southworth, included the declaration of emergency, a recognition the council should "take a leadership role" to urgently address the issue of groundwater pollution, and requested staff provided workshops for the incoming council on the scale, causes, and impact of nitrate pollution.

It also sought advice on the costs for private bore users and councils to treat nitrate pollution or find alternative sources, as well as options to reallocate costs so "nitrate polluters contributed to the costs of nitrate removal from drinking water".

At the time, Agriculture Minister Todd McClay called the declaration "gimmicky", while Federated Farmers deemed it unhelpful and politically motivated.

In a report to be presented to the council on Wednesday, staff recommended councillors vote to recognise the work that had been done so far responding to the notice of motion, and agree not to have staff carry out the investigation into how to pay for nitrate contamination treatment.

Further, staff suggest the council's Drinking Water Action Plan provided "sufficient response" to the notice of motion, delivering on the council's statutory responsibilities, and that the notice of motion could now be resolved.

Agriculture Minister Todd McClay. RNZ / Mark Papalii

A regional council spokesperson described the Drinking Water Action Plan as "a collation of various workstreams" which "captures the work we are doing in the drinking water space".

Greenpeace programme director Niamh O'Flynn criticised the council's reliance on the Drinking Water Action Plan, which she said "did not sufficiently address the fact that rural Cantabrians cannot guarantee the safety of the water coming out of the taps".

She said it was deeply concerning the council was proposing resolving the notice of motion.

"A few discussions by the council didn't magically make the problem of nitrate pollution coming out of people's taps and polluting our rivers go away, and I think ECan [Environment Canterbury] have a bare minimum responsibility to keep telling the truth about the situation in Canterbury, which is that there is indeed a nitrate emergency."

O'Flynn noted the regional council had consented tens of thousands of extra cows for the region this year alone.

"Where does it stop and how can we say a nitrate emergency has been solved when it's very clearly going to get worse from here?"

Figures obtained by the Green Party under the Official Information Act showed the regional council had granted consents for an extra 57,000 cows in 2026.

Between 1990 and 2022, Canterbury's dairy herd increased by more than 1000 percent, to well over a million cows.

The staff report found treatment systems to remove nitrate from drinking water cost between $3000 to $5000 for a whole-house system, plus annual maintenance costs.

The report said surveys found a lack of awareness among private bore users and of a need for them to "understand" their source water and to test and treat, and that cost was less of an issue than raising awareness.

It was "ridiculous" to place that responsibility on individual bore owners O'Flynn said.

Greenpeace programme director Niamh O'Flynn. Supplied

"If you have no control over the amount of pollution that's going into your bore, how can you bear the responsibility for dealing with the problem at the other side?

"We live in a country where most people think everyone should have clean drinking water coming out of their taps. Environment Canterbury are responsible for protecting source water, from preventing pollution getting into source water in the first place."

But in any case "awareness doesn't magic pollution away".

"Awareness doesn't stop the industry in your region polluting your drinking water, and awareness certainly doesn't put an extra couple of grand in your bank account so that you can keep your family's drinking water safe."

Federated Farmers president Colin Hurst said the group welcomed the proposal to dismiss the notice of motion, calling it a "cheap political stunt".

But he said it was important to understand in more detail what was causing the problem.

"Sure, farming is part of the issue. It's also some of the irrigation practices have been changing ... There's a number of reasons causing this.

"The key thing is we need to understand the trends. Is it getting worse? Is it getting better or is it staying the same? So I'm not quite sure if we understand that completely yet."

Hurst said farmers were a lot more attuned to understanding nitrate issues and making reductions in nitrogen, as well as other practices such as fencing off waterways.

"It's not exactly an easy topic to understand, but certainly there's no question too much nitrogen is not good for the environment," Hurst said.

Federated Farmers president Colin Hurst. Supplied / Federated Farmers

Forest and Bird regional conversation manager Nicky Snoyink said the proposal to declare the nitrate emergency notice of motion resolved was very premature.

"There's nothing to show that anything is actually improving.

"It's all very well to have a drinking water action plan but that's all it is ... there's no actual data to show that anything is improving so you know they haven't addressed the elephant in the room which is dealing with the pollution limits in the plan that will actually achieve the desired freshwater outcomes and clean up our drinking water."

Snoyink said the declaration should not be altered until studies showed decreasing nitrate levels.

"The numbers don't lie. We need the actual evidence to show that things are changing before they remove the nitrate emergency.

"We not only have more and more dairy cows being consented to go out onto the Canterbury Plains ... we not only have no evidence that things are getting better, we also have more dairy cows being consented."

The costs of treating nitrate pollution needed to lie "where the pollution is coming from, which is largely the dairy industry in Canterbury", Snoyink said.

Forest and Bird regional conversation manager Nicky Snoyink. RNZ / Conan Young

Environment Canterbury's most recent groundwater report showed 59 percent of monitored sites had worsening levels of nitrate in 2024, and 10 percent had breached the drinking water standard.

The 2025 groundwater report was not expected to be released until next month.

In the largest study of its kind, released last year, GNS Science confirmed Canterbury had the highest percentage of elevated groundwater nitrates in the country, following testing of 3800 rural drinking water samples from private wells between 2022 and 2024.

Researchers identified nitrate-rich cow urine as a primary cause of contaminated groundwater.

The study found more than 21,200 people nationwide could be drinking water contaminated with nitrate above the legal limit while more than 100,000 people could be drinking water above half the legal limit - one in three rural homes.

New Zealand's nitrate limit of 11.3 milligrams per litre is based on 1958 World Health Organization guidelines specifically for preventing infant death from methaemoglobinaemia or blue baby syndrome.

Emerging research has pointed to health risks at far lower levels.

New Zealand's nitrate limit is 11.3 milligrams per litre. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

In 2021, the College of Midwives advised members to tell women on private bores to get their water tested, and for pregnant and breastfeeding mothers to switch to bottled water if nitrate levels were over 5mg/L.

A 2021 analysis by Victoria and Otago universities found a potential link with bowel cancer at levels as low as 0.87mg/L.

A 2026 study of more than 750,000 New Zealand births found higher nitrate concentrations in drinking water were associated with small but consistent increased risks of pre-term births at levels well below the current legal limit.

The study also found the risk of pre-term birth increased by about 1 percent for each milligram a litre (mg/L) of increased nitrate levels, and comparing births from areas where nitrate levels were very low (close to zero) to those with the highest levels in the study (over 5mg/L) showed a starker jump - around an 8 percent increase in pre-term births.

In June RNZ revealed the Ministry of Health had quietly launched a review into the health effects of nitrate in drinking water.

The outcome was expected to be public by the end of the year.

Earlier this month, regional councillors heard from water regulator Taumata Arowai, which suggested there may need to be a long term nitrate limit to accompany the current short term acute limit.

World.title: Education Ministry whistleblower claims OIA subversion not an isolated incident
World.content:
The person who leaked a video of an Education Ministry official apparently attempting to subvert the Official Information Act (OIA) claims it was not an isolated incident.

The ministry insider, who RNZ has agreed not to identify, also revealed that they and other ministry staff were repeatedly asked to delete the word "Aotearoa" and other Māori terms from draft curriculums - but the instructions were deliberately verbal and never put into writing.

The person said they were speaking out because they had "had a gutsful".

"I was just so over the dishonesty and the toxicity of the workplace," they said.

The Education Ministry did not address the claims directly in a response to RNZ but Education Minister Erica Stanford said the source of the information was ideologically-driven.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405403556112

Stanford said there had been no attempts to circumvent the OIA and denied Māori words were reduced in the curriculum.

"We considered Article 3 of the Treaty throughout the process of updating the curriculum ... as a result, there is vastly more Māori content across the refreshed curriculum," she said in a statement.

The claims are the latest in a series of leaks from the Education Ministry, many of them to RNZ, in the past couple of years.

They have included internal documents and emails and Budget-sensitive information - the latter prompting an urgent injunction and an investigation.

The person behind the latest revelations told RNZ the video recorded last week was not the first time staff had been instructed not to write things down, it happened about six or seven times a year, but it was one of the most brazen.

"It was probably worded the worst, but the others have been a bit more subtle and more careful," they said.

The footage originally given to the New Zealand Herald and later obtained by RNZ showed senior Ministry of Education official Catherine Law telling staff not to put in writing that they were responding to feedback from the Education Minister's office, reminding them it was "OIA-able" - referencing the Official Information Act.

"What we do not need is anything in response in writing that shows that this stuff has gone backwards and forwards between them and us," Law said.

"It's just really important.

"As far as anyone's concerned it's just feedback from me."

Law was seconded from her role as principal of Avonside Girls' High School to lead work on the secondary school curriculum.

The person who provided the footage told RNZ: "There was 30-odd people on the meeting and to say, brazenly, 'this is not an official channel, it's not the official bags going across to the minister's office'...

"If it's not a formal process, then we shouldn't be doing it," they said.

Senior Ministry of Education official Catherine Law. RNZ / Niva Chittock

They said some ministry leaders would often give verbal instructions after meetings with ministers and some liked to give the impression they were chummy with Stanford and their instructions therefore had to be followed.

They said senior leaders repeatedly asked staff verbally to make changes and refused to put their instructions in writing even when asked.

"Like changing ākonga into student or kaiako into teacher," the whistleblower said.

"Māori terminology like manaakitanga and kaitiakitanga - the number of times they've been in and out of the curriculum document is just ridiculous. It's wasting millions of dollars of work with all of this roundabout, in-and-out, not making your mind up."

They confirmed that "Aotearoa" - which RNZ had observed was not used once as a synonym for New Zealand in any of the final curriculum documents - had been deliberately removed.

They said the term "Aotearoa New Zealand" was used by writers as the default term for this country, but proofreaders and educators were later told to remove it unless it was part of a name.

"I think there was a verbal explanation of: 'We can't legitimately say when that word was introduced and it's history, so we've got to take it out'," the insider said.

When RNZ queried the absence of the word last month it received the following response: "The curriculum is called The New Zealand Curriculum, and references within it generally use New Zealand. This approach has been taken to keep the terminology consistent throughout the document."

Though recently-published curriculums did include Māori terms, teachers last year warned there were fewer of them.

The ministry insider said in their opinion the curriculum was a white-washed, 1980s-style curriculum that sidelined brown people.

"They didn't have to swing to such a vastly Westernised, whitewash view. It's just too ideological. It's too extreme," they said.

They said ministry leaders had not attempted under previous governments to keep instructions from the minister's office off the official record, or refuse to put instructions to staff in writing.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Stanford said in a statement draft curriculum documents were supplied to her office as part of normal business.

"As part of the normal process, the seconded education staff member checks for spelling mistakes, duplication, plain language, any obvious errors and asks questions to ensure the papers are of an acceptable standard before I review them," she said.

"All of the processes we have followed comply with the OIA, there has been no attempts to circumvent the OIA."

Stanford said the insider's description of the curriulum demonstrated they were ideologically-driven.

"The updated curriculum strikes an appropriate balance between ensuring all young New Zealanders have access to clear, knowledge-rich learning and reflecting the unique history, languages, cultures, and identities of Aotearoa New Zealand," she said.

The Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid said in statement: "We've been clear that the comments in the video don't meet the Ministry's expectations for transparency, record-keeping or compliance with the Official Information Act.

"We're addressing the specific matter directly and have initiated an internal review to provide assurance that this was an isolated incident."

She said the curriculum had to meet the needs of all young New Zealanders.

"That includes te reo Māori and Māori perspectives, alongside the language, knowledge and concepts that reflect the diverse students in our schools. The Ministry stands by its curriculum work and takes responsibility for the advice and material it produces.

"Working with ministers as advice and curriculum material are developed, and implementing government decisions, are normal parts of our role. That doesn't change the Ministry's responsibility for its advice or its record-keeping obligations.

World.title: RMA replacement laws pass in Parliament
World.content:
The two laws replacing the Resource Management Act (RMA) have passed their third reading in Parliament.

The RMA is being superseded by the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill.

The government said the reforms were "the most significant overhaul" of New Zealand's planning system in more than three decades, and would make building infrastructure easier, faster and more affordable.

But opposition parties have warned the changes could make the system more unworkable, and dilute environmental protections.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said scrapping the RMA was breaking free from a system that had stifled economic growth.

"We are restoring the freedom for New Zealanders to shape their own futures by using property as they choose, a once in a generation shift towards growth, choice and prosperity," he said.

At the heart of the reforms were enjoyment and use of people's own land, he said, labelling that "the Kiwi dream".

Bishop said the Opposition had painted property rights as "some evil, right wing plan".

Labour's Rachael Brooking said the inclusion of regulatory relief scheme (that would see landowners compensated by councils for changes that affect them) would either cause chaos and great expense for ratepayers, or see councils give up on environmental protections.

"This [reform] will lead to a big, muddy mess ... it will not improve efficiencies, and it will not improve the cost burden on the public," Brooking said.

A Labour government would not flip-flop on the reform - rather, make amendments, she said.

The Greens' environment spokesperson Lan Pham said the laws would allow untold harm to human health and the environment.

"With the passing of these bills, Aotearoa is in a new era of environmental exploitation at the hands of polluting industries," she said.

Pham said the government had ignored official advice, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment and 75 percent of submitters.

The ACT party is claiming victory, saying National had in the past been against RMA reform but ACT had never run from the massive job of replacing it.

Infrastructure spokesperson Simon Court said the old system "let every Tom, Dick and Harry say no" to building projects.

World.title: Alleged kidnappers accused of impersonating police officers
World.content:
Two Bay of Plenty youths were detained by three people allegedly pretending to be police officers and driving a former police car.

The three people have been charged with multiple offences, including kidnapping, indecent assault and impersonating police after the "traumatic" incident last Sunday.

Acting Detective Senior Sergeant Ash Clements said the two youths were detained on Sunday 13 September by two men and a woman who had presented themselves as police officers and appeared to be driving in an unmarked police car.

Clements said one of the men had a 2017 black Holden Commodore, which had been a police vehicle and had been stripped of all police equipment and markings before being sold at auction.

He said parts of the car had been allegedly re-fitted with off-market lights to make it look an unmarked police car.

"The occupants of the vehicle were in plain clothes - not police uniform, were not wearing police body armour, and were portraying themselves as detectives. This, paired with the imitation police vehicle, is more than enough to trick an unsuspecting person."

A 34-year-old man was arrested yesterday over this incident and prior reports of impersonating police. He has been remanded in custody, and faces charges of impersonating personnel, indecent assault, intimidation, two counts of kidnapping, and five counts of impersonating police.

A 19-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman were also arrested today. The 19-year-old has been charged with indecent assault, two counts of kidnapping, and two counts of impersonating police, while the woman faces kidnapping charges.

"Detaining a person under false pretences and without the proper authority amounts to kidnapping, which is an extremely serious offence in addition to impersonating police, and we take this offending seriously," said Clements.

"This was a traumatic incident for the victims involved.

"Anyone who doubts that they are speaking with a real police officer is urged to ask for their police issued ID, and if you still have concerns, call 111 immediately and a police communicator can identify the officer for you."

World.title: Man dies after fight in Lower Hutt last month
World.content:
A man critically injured in a fight in Lower Hutt last month has died in hospital.

Police were called to Waterloo Road on Sunday 30 August, after reports of a brawl in which a number of people were hurt.

A 45-year-old man was arrested after he handed himself in at the Wellington Central Police Station.

He was charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and striking with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

World.title: NRL's hardest job a family affair for Rob Toia
World.content:
Marking Herbie Farnworth is just about the hardest job any centre can have in rugby league, but Roosters flyer Robert Toia will not have to do it alone.

Friday night's preliminary final will be a family affair for the 22-year-old in more ways than one.

As a Redcliffe junior and one of 10 siblings, Toia cannot even begin to count how many friends and family he will have in the stands at a sold-out Lang Park, but he is sure to have some kin close at hand for his battle with Farnworth.

"Me, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong, we're all related," Toia said.

"We're cousins through our grandparents. Me and Salesi have always known since we were young, but Siua we only found out last year.

"[Redcliffe] is home. It's always felt like home, and every time I play at Lang Park, it's the stadium with the best atmosphere."

Toia and Wong discovered they were related last year. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Wong will line up at second row alongside Toia on the Tricolours right edge, against Farnworth and Toia's State of Origin teammate Max Plath, and both know what to expect from the fires of "The Cauldron".

Toia made his Queensland debut there after just 10 NRL games last year, while Wong is in the midst of his fourth finals campaign in as many years.

Foketi has been a later starter, only securing a place in the run-on side in recent weeks, but the three have been close ever since they lived together in the Roosters academy house as boys.

Around that same time, the trio played in a junior grand final against a Penrith side containing future Dolphins kingpin Isaiya Katoa, who will be a target for Foketi on Friday night.

The miracle wins that made Isaiya Katoa Isaiya Katoa prepares for his NRL semifinal debut as the prince of the game's playmakers and four years ago it was a series of brilliant finals performances that birthed his budding legend.

A bustling run from the 20-year-old knocked Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes out of last week's semifinal after just 75 seconds and proved why he is a danger man even among a team with as much strike as the Roosters.

"I'm so proud of him. Everything is God's timing, because he was battling and playing Cup in the beginning of the year, but he got an opportunity and took it with both hands," Toia said.

"He's one of the best backrowers in the comp."

But as big a job as the Dolphins face with containing Foketi, Toia has an even more difficult one on his hands as he tries to put a saddle on Farnworth.

The Englishman has proven he is the best centre in the world several times over, if not one of the best players overall.

Farnworth leads the NRL in tackle breaks with 161, a full 44 ahead of the next best centre, and is first among all players for offloads with 75.

Farnworth is the best centre in the world and enters the prelim in terrific form. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

He is first among centres for runs, run metres and post-contact metres and is fresh off a magnificent showing in the Dolphins' 26-16 win over the Warriors that has them one win away from their first-ever grand final.

Toia has the size and athleticism to hold his own in any battle — in that star-making Origin debut last year, he held his own against no less than Latrell Mitchell — but Farnworth still shapes as a challenge that will go a long way towards deciding whether the Roosters can progress to their first grand final since 2019.

"You see the tackle-busting ability he has, but his work rate is underrated. He's always involved, on the offensive side and the defensive side," Toia said.

"I think pressuring him, shutting him down, getting my D movements right and hopefully, I can stop him from doing what he does best."

Toia comes into the match in imperious form of his own. He has scored in both the Roosters' finals matches and, along with Mark Nawaqanitawase, was the club's chief destroyer in last week's win over Cronulla.

The highlight was a massive fend on KL Iro that sent the rugged Sharks centre, who normally defends like someone taught a bicep muscle how to tackle, fully airborne.

It is a measure of how much Toia has continued to improve this season after claiming rookie of the year honours last year and a reminder that the best is yet to come, something the Tongan international believes is just as true for his team.

"I got a bit lucky there," Toia said.

"The boys just put me in the right spots and I was just moving for them.

"It's the best feeling [winning]. It's been frustrating for a lot of the year, we haven't been able to produce our brand of game, so it was good to show a glimpse of that.

"I feel like we still haven't played 80 minutes of Roosters footy."

World.title: Chimney colours unveiled for Norwood SANFL victors amid TV ratings boost
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Norwood Football Club's colours have been unveiled atop the Brickworks chimney to celebrate its SANFL Grand Final win in what was the most-viewed game since a modern rating system began.

The total national television audience on Sunday was up 16 per cent on 2025 numbers to 109,700, which included 93,500 broadcast TV viewers.

It also included 16,100 viewers from broadcaster video on demand (BVOD), which was up 52 per cent.

The VOZ ratings, which started in 2022 and combine both broadcast TV and BVOD, found that 87,500 viewers of broadcast TV viewers were from Adelaide, along with 12,800 of those streaming online.

The Norwood and Sturt colours will stay atop the Hoffman Kiln until the end of season 2027. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The broadcast ratings were exceptional, broke every record for the last five years," SANFL executive Darren Chandler said.

"And when you compare those to what's happening in Western Australia and Victoria, we've absolutely blown it off the charts."

SANFL kicking TV goals SANFL crowds are continuing to climb each year after COVID-19 restrictions put a dent in numbers

Football commentator Mark Soderstrom said 71 per cent of South Australian televisions switched on were tuned into the decider between Sturt and Norwood, which drew 38,250 spectators to Adelaide Oval.

The WAFL Grand Final, on the other hand, drew 19,210 people to Perth Stadium, continuing a four-year decline in crowds, while the VFL Grand Final drew just 12,941, the first time the league had attracted more than 8,000 fans in seven years.

A time-honoured tradition

The annual winners and runners-up of the SANFL grand final have been displaying their colours atop the 1913 Hoffman-designed kiln at Thebarton since the start of the decade.

The much-loved ceremony of nearly 70 years had to be moved from its previous home chimney at the West End Brewery after the facility was closed by its owners, Lion, in 2021.

Redlegs supporters came out to celebrate their team's 2026 premiership win. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Redlegs coach Jade Sheedy, who was a premiership player for Sturt in 2002 when he won the Magarey Medal with teammate Tim Weatherald, also coached Woodville-West Torrens in back-to-back premierships in 2020-21.

He told the crowd of Redleg supporters at Thebarton that when the siren blew on Sunday and Norwood beat Sturt 87 points to 73 after a final-quarter comeback, he thought he was "still in a dream for 15 minutes".

"I guess it was two years of building something pretty special, and to come together in the last 30 minutes and to believe in that, and to kick five goals three to one point in the last quarter showed how much the group had grown and that's what I'm most proud of," Sheedy said.

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and coach Jade Sheedy were still celebrating on Tuesday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said the team had not changed "too much structurally" since they lost the preliminary final by two points in 2025 but had "increased the belief in how we play".

"We just fell short in 2025, but we took a lot of learnings from that and a lot of confidence reviewing how we were playing our footy," he said.

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle payed tribute to the Redlegs at the chimney ceremony. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle attended the ceremony on behalf of the runners-up.

"I think we can all agree that Sunday was a great spectacle, and it was a great  for the competition and the league across the country," he said.

He said Norwood were "deserved winners" as the "most consistent team all year".

World.title: NRL grand final loses headline act for pre-match entertainment
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL says it is prepared to have no pre-match entertainment at its grand final this year after talks broke down with Australian artist Tones And I.

Instead the league is offering to increase funding to grassroots competitions with the money set aside for a pre-game performance.

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

The move would be a stunning break from tradition — the grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop-star Teddy Swims last year.

Teddy Swims performed at last year's NRL grand final. (Supplied: NRL)

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'Landys said the total cost of such performances ran close to $1 million and that the plan for grassroots funding was one he had been mulling for sometime.

V'Landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league — they don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'Landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones and I broke down.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred the NRL's insistence that Tones and I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

"You spend money to get outcomes and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league," V'Landys said.

"I'm a fan of Tones and I. She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction.

"We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act."

Peter V’landys (right) says the league has decided it would prefer to spend its money elsewhere. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The grand final hosting rights are bid for by state governments across the country. New South Wales holds the rights now, but it is not clear if the minister for sport or the premier were consulted over the matter.

Neither office has replied to requests for comment.

NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'Landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

World.title: Lachie Neale to miss grand final after AFL tribunal decision
World.content:
Brisbane Lions star Lachie Neale has failed in his attempt to overturn a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan at the AFL tribunal and will miss Saturday's grand final against the Fremantle Dockers.

Neale's "gut-punch" on Ginnivan means the former Brisbane co-captain has played his last game for the Lions, as the team seeks a second premiership three-peat in club history.

The appeal, held remotely with Neale watching from Queensland, took more than two hours, with deliberations going for close to two and a half hours.

Neale's counsel, Adrian Anderson, argued that the dual-Brownlow-winner's case was not a strike, rather a bump or body-check. He said if it was ruled a strike, that it was of "negligible impact" and if the Tribunal disagreed then there were "exceptional and compelling circumstances" to justify a ban being overturned.

Neale gave evidence that he had watched Ginnivan come together with Brisbane's Eric Hipwood, ending up lying on the tall forward and giving him several jumper punches.

He said he went over to "express his disappointment", and collided with him shoulder-first.

But the Tribunal did not accept his version of events.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, told the Tribunal that Neale was running away from the direction of the ball to confront Ginnivan.

"Neale is running ... he has time to decide what he is going to do," Woods said.

"It's not a football act. It's a forceful arm, you really see this with respect to the vision, that swinging towards the opposition player."

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC, told Anderson the incident was "well off the ball, not in play" and not a strike that happened during a grapple of scuffle.

Anderson argued that Neale's long and honoured career (320 games) without suspension was worthy of making an exception to the ban.

"The primary (argument for exceptional and compelling circumstances) is he is one of the best and one of the fairest to have ever played the game," he says.

However, the Tribunal disagreed.

"Having carefully reviewed the evidence and listened to Neale’s explanation, we find that this was a forceful blow, delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand," Gleeson said delivering the verdict.

" When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts. We are comfortably satisfied that this is what occurred. "

Gleeson said that after consideration, the panel did not feel there were exceptional circumstances to overturn the ban.

"The purpose of the [gut-punch] guideline is to stamp out this very sort of conduct. Neale ignored it, and he knew the consequences,' he said.

"Even Neale's outstanding record does not render a one-match suspension for that act inappropriate or unreasonable."

Look back at how Tuesday night's proceedings unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Diamonds name Klau for Constellation Cup squad
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Diamonds netballer Sarah Klau has retained her spot in Australia's Constellation Cup squad after pleading guilty to assault.

Klau was included in the 14-player squad named on Tuesday, less than a week after the goalkeeper was sanctioned by Netball Australia (NA).

The 31-year-old was handed a $5,000 fine and a two-match ban — suspended for 12 months — by the sport's national governing body.

Klau fined after unprecedented assault charge Diamonds defender Sarah Klau is handed a $5,000 fine and a suspended two-game ban after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the incident prior to the Commonwealth Games.

Klau had fronted Downing Centre Court earlier this month, facing a common assault charge.

She had allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub in Sydney's eastern suburbs when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.

The NSW Swifts player had reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match a day after an ongoing leg injury ruled her out of the remainder of the Super Netball season.

Klau, who has represented Australia on 67 occasions since her Diamonds debut in 2019, failed to disclose the matter to NA before the Commonwealth Games in July, resulting in the sanctions.

Sophie Dwyer also retained her spot in the Diamonds squad, looking for a chance to find redemption after missing an after-the-siren shot in the Commonwealth Games semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Constellation Cup First Test: October 18 (Auckland)

Second Test: October 21 (Christchurch)

Third Test: October 25 (Sydney)

Fourth Test: October 28 (Melbourne)

Dwyer was left on the bench in Australia's bronze-medal win over England in Glasgow.

The core of coach Stacey Marinkovich's squad remains the same from the Games, with Jo Weston unavailable for selection.

Jessie Grenvold, Amy Parmenter and Donnell Wallam return to the side after travelling to Glasgow as reserves.

Grenvold is yet to make her Diamonds debut after earning her maiden call-up in May following a breakout season in defence for the Melbourne Mavericks.

The Constellation Cup begins on October 18, with the Diamonds travelling to Auckland to take on the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds squad: Kiera Austin, Courtney Bruce, Sophie Dwyer, Sophie Garbin, Matilda Garrett, Jessie Grenvold, Georgie Horjus, Sarah Klau, Cara Koenen, Kate Moloney, Amy Parmenter, Jamie-Lee Price, Donnell Wallam, Liz Watson
