World.title: More votes than three entire clubs: How Nick Daicos won the Brownlow
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coming into the night, the 2026 Brownlow Medal count held little intrigue about who the winner would be.

Few — if any — in the footballing world thought there was anyone who could seriously challenge Nick Daicos for the award.

But there was still one person who was in shock: Daicos, himself.

"I can't believe I'm the Brownlow medallist to be honest," Daicos said at the award ceremony in Melbourne.

The count was close until about the halfway mark, before Daicos pulled away from the pack as the season progressed.

With his 47 votes last night, Daicos has earned more votes in the last four years than any other player has in any five-year period.

Daicos earned more votes than three entire clubs. He collected 63 per cent of Collingwood's votes for the evening.

He racked up record after record: the most votes in one year, most consecutive games with three votes (six), the most games with three votes (13).

It wasn't just a win, it was domination.

With the win, Daicos joins Tom Mitchell, Gary Ablett Jr and Ben Cousins as father-son selections who have claimed the Brownlow Medal (Jobe Watson's 2012 victory was rescinded).

Daicos time

Plenty has been written about what makes Daicos special.

Coaches and opposition players talk about his elusiveness, vision and ability to make something out of what seems like nothing.

And then there is his competitiveness.

"He hates losing," Magpies great Scott Pendlebury said.

"Especially at table tennis. Whenever we travel on the road, he always tries to get a re-match."

That competitive drive is often what turns good into great, and great into legendary.

But words pale into insignificance compared to watching the best of Daicos in full flight.

Players like Daicos stand out due to the highlights they create.

Teams spend more time trying to get Daicos off balance than any other player in the competition.

It hasn't seemed to have an effect yet.

No matter what teams throw at Daicos, he still has an unerring habit of getting the ball and letting his imagination run wild.

That drive was forged from his early days as a player, often being one of the slightest on the field when he played up in age at both the Greythorn Falcons and the Kew Rovers.

When Daicos moved to Carey Grammar for year 10, he was thrust immediately into the first team to compete in the prestigious APS football competition.

His teammates were no slouches either, with Daicos playing alongside the likes of Noah Anderson and last year's Brownlow medallist, Matt Rowell.

No player in the AFL was more important in getting his team in scoring positions than Daicos was this year.

Daicos thrived at winning the ball when no-one had clear control.

He has an innate ability to track the ball before anyone else, working smarter and not harder.

Daicos also has a scary ability to render his direct opponents as traffic cones.

The Magpies look to get Daicos the ball as much as possible, and he repays them with territory.

Few can match his combination of skill, speed and footy intelligence.

Although Collingwood fell short this year, hopes are higher for 2027 with additional reinforcements.

Family zone

Throughout football's history, geography has shaped the make-up of teams to a great extent.

Teams recruited from specific regions. The fortunes of clubs rose and fell based on the growth of different geographic areas.

Urban expansion fuelled Hawthorn's rise, while weak and depopulating zones condemned other clubs to near extinction.

There was one exception to the geography-based dictation of the footy landscape: the sons of former players.

The father-son rule was introduced in 1949 to ensure players such as Ron Barassi could continue on the legacy of their fathers at their clubs regardless of geography.

These days, the role of geography has inverted and it now dictates where all the father-son selections are.

The family zone for Victorian footy now runs through south-east Melbourne.

This was the former recruiting area for Hawthorn, otherwise known as the Family Club.

The ranks of father-son selections are littered with schools and clubs based in the most desirable parts of Melbourne, often far from the origins of their fathers' careers.

For example, the Silvangi and Daicos offspring played their junior footy at the Greythorn Falcons.

That's only a stone's throw from Collingwood captain Darcy Moore's junior club of Ivanhoe.

Nor is it far from where Mitchell or Watson first honed their craft.

The eastern side of Melbourne has increasingly become a powerhouse in junior footy as well, with Sandringham, Oakleigh and the Eastern Ranges dominating the AFL's Talent League in recent seasons.

Brownlow's changing face

A major change took place to the fabric of the Brownlow Medal this year.

Umpires gained access to a select group of 17 statistics before voting. Daicos excelled in several of these measures.

This may rob part of what made the Brownlow so special.

Umpires have a unique perspective. They're also party to the intangibles, such as on-field demeanour, respect and sportsmanship.

This year's votes aligned more closely to the results of the AFL Coaches Association award than ever before, according to Wheelo Ratings.

Coaches pore over key numbers throughout their games and now umpires can rely on some of the same figures to adjudge best afield as well.

Supplying data may condition umpires to discard insights gleaned in the heat of the action, turning them instead into just another spin on the same cold distant observations.

Defenders are already suffering even more than they traditionally do, while midfielders, who often accumulate high "count" stats, get a larger share of the spoils.

Rucks also outperformed their expected output this year, likely benefiting from the inclusion of hit-outs.

This will likely serve to further intensify a growing trend towards vote concentration in disposal-accumulating midfielders.

The leaderboard for career-long average votes is strewn liberally with current players, with previous leaders Haydn Bunton and Graham Moss only playing the prime vote-earning part of their careers in the VFL.

If this trend continues, Daicos will soon break Patrick Dangerfield and Ablett Jr's record for most career votes, at least until the next star enters the scene.

But all of that is for the future.

All that is important now is that the inevitable ascension of Daicos to the pinnacle of the game has taken place.

World.title: Formula 1 agrees to shorter races in 2027
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Formula 1 has approved a 15 kilometre reduction in official race distances starting next season.

The change means the total distance will be cut from 305 to 290 kilometres.

The Formula 1 Commission finalised the decision in London.

"In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps," a statement read.

Aussie F1 GP loses season-opening honour Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

The power unit regulations favour increased engine power over hybrid electrical output.

To better handle rain delays and red flags, the commission has also abolished the strict three-hour overall event cap.

While the two-hour maximum of active racing time remains, the change gives organisers flexibility to complete full race distances.

Another objective ‌is to give spectators the best possible chance ‌to enjoy a full race when disruptions occur.

Practice sessions will also gain added flexibility to extend following stoppages.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Lions 'praying' Neale gets off but confident they will cope if ban stands
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Lions players are confident they can cover the potential absence of Lachie Neale in the grand final, with the two-time Brownlow medallist facing a one-match ban.

Neale and the Lions will challenge the suspension at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday evening.

The 33-year-old has been charged with striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

If the suspension is upheld, Neale will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

Lions teammate Jarrod Berry said it would be a blow to lose Neale.

But he said the Lions were equipped to overcome any adversity.

"One of our best traits is being able to deal with that [adversity]," Berry said.

"We do it well and there's no point putting energy into it until we know the result.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

There is damning vision showing Neale guilty of the behind-play strike and numerous precedents this season of other players being banned for one match for similar incidents.

But the Lions are set to argue the suspension should be downgraded to a fine.

They will cite a fresh clause that allowed Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury to avoid a suspension in March.

Clause that could save Neale The Brisbane Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Pendlebury was given a one-match ban for rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

He was found guilty by the tribunal but the sanction was downgraded to a $3,000 fine due to "compelling and exceptional circumstances", a clause open to the tribunal that will be central to Neale's case.

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record.

"However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances."

The Magpies successfully argued the clause applied to Pendlebury, who had never previously faced the tribunal in his storied 21-year career.

Neale also has not previously appeared before the tribunal in his 320-match career.

He is also a dual Brownlow medallist and premiership captain, plus a four-time All Australian.

Geelong coach Chris Scott does not agree with the provision.

"Seriously, when we're starting to say, 'There's a rule for you because you've done good things for the game,' it's almost implying that other people haven't done a good job," Scott said on Fox Footy.

But Scott added: "I know his record is exceptional, but aside from that, I just like to see them play.

"I actually think that's going to be hard to defend personally, but my hope is that he does play."

AAP

Tech.title: Apple is reportedly working on a Whoop-like fitness tracker
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is working on a new fitness tracker with a screenless design, similar to the one made by Whoop, according to a report from Bloomberg. A prototype of the device reportedly has “a thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module.”

The device is in an early stage of development and likely wouldn’t arrive before 2028 if Apple decides to release it, Bloomberg reports. In addition to Whoop’s lineup of 5.0 bands, the company also sells MG — or “medical grade” — variants with a built-in EKG feature. The bands are designed to be worn continuously, as they offer more than 14 days of battery life.

As pointed out by Bloomberg, Apple has added several features already offered by Whoop to its new Apple Watch Series 12, including continuous heart rate tracking. Apple’s Health app also now has a “readiness score” used by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop, which is supposed to tell you how “ready” you are to work out based on several factors, along with an estimate of your biological age.

Tech.title: Andreessen Horowitz is launching an ‘academy’ with no homework and partnerships with Palantir, Google, and Meta
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) is creating an “academy” positioned as a pipeline for young people to build or join a Silicon Valley startup. The “Horowitz Andreessen Academy” will launch with 10 partners, including Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe, along with $42 million in funding led by a16z. While billed as a “highly selective school,” it does not grant any degree or accreditation. Instead, students will attend short classes led by tech figureheads, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as “co-ops” that give students roles at tech companies.

To partake in the one-year program, students will have to move to San Francisco and arrange their own housing, according to the academy’s FAQ page. Students are promised more than $50,000 in compute credits and a $5,000 travel and research budget offered by a16z. The announcement says they’ll have “no traditional grades, tests, or homework,” but will “learn from Silicon Valley’s most storied founders and operators in short, high-impact classes and spend the rest of your time working and exploring.”

The academy seems like the latest attempt by Silicon Valley’s billionaires to “fix” America’s education system by creating their own. Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos have all poured money into starting their own schools, while a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz have been critical of colleges. Last year, Andreessen reportedly called Stanford and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology “political lobbying operations fighting American innovation” in a group chat with White House officials and tech leaders, according to The Washington Post.

The Horowitz Andreessen Academy will be free for its first one-year program in the fall of 2027. It will only accept 50 students and is designed mainly for recent high school graduates.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches Claude Opus 5.5 with stricter safeguards for cybersecurity
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic says its new Claude Opus 5.5 model comes with stronger safeguards in the wake of recent rogue AI hacking incidents. In an announcement on Tuesday, Anthropic says Opus 5.5 comes with improvements to certain risky behaviors, including attempts to escape the company’s testing sandbox.

It’s the first model released by Anthropic after CEO Dario Amodei announced plans to “pace the frontier,” or slow down AI development. In recent weeks, several AI companies, including Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, have reported that their AI models escaped containment and hacked third-party companies during testing.

Anthropic says Opus 5.5 is the “strongest performing” model on the company’s most comprehensive alignment test. The model, which is cheaper and more efficient to run than Opus 5, will come with safeguards similar to the ones offered by Anthropic’s more advanced Fable 5.1 model. That means Opus 5.5 will re-route certain cybersecurity-related requests to the less powerful Opus 4.8, while biology-related requests flagged by its safeguards will go to Opus 5.

Opus 5.5 also matches the performance of Fable 5.1 “on most work,” and was tested by outside partners, including Frontier Design and METR, before release. The company also plans to launch Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 in the coming weeks.

Tech.title: Rivian’s R2 beat its own climate goals four years early
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rivian always planned for its all-important R2 vehicle to be less expensive than its pricey R1 predecessors, but also less polluting. The production process for the R2 would rely on more renewable energy, and the vehicle itself would feature more recycled and biodegradable materials than the models that came before it. With this and a few other tricks, Rivian set the target to achieve a 50 percent lifetime carbon reduction for the R2 by 2030.

Today, the company released its 2025 impact report outlining its sustainability progress for the year. The main takeaway is that over the entire lifespan — everything from production, driving, and eventually recycling — the R2 Performance generates only half the greenhouse gas emissions of Rivian’s original 2022 R1 vehicles. And it did it four years ahead of schedule.

Halving the lifecycle footprint of a flagship vehicle is relatively easy if the vehicle is a tiny, stripped down model or impractically expensive. The R2 is neither of those. It’s a mass-market SUV designed to appeal to the broadest section of customers. The fact that Rivian was able to deliver lower lifecycle carbon emissions on a vehicle like the R2 — and 58 percent lower lifetime emissions than a comparable gas-powered vehicle — is pretty impressive.

In a blog post about the report, Rivian attributes the accomplishment to a relentless focus on aerodynamics, weight, efficiency, and materials. The company went to some extreme lengths to ensure it wasn’t using your run-of-the-mill rubber and plastic for the R2.

Photo: Anthony Tahlier / The Verge

For example, some of the surface material is made from “paper industry waste sourced from responsibly managed Nordic forests” — a sentence that may make more than a few eyes roll, but has resulted in fewer lifecycle emissions. The R2’s floor mats are made from 99 percent ocean waste. The frunk and trim are 85 percent post-consumer recycled material. The resin cell trays for the battery packs are 100 percent recycled. And so on.

Rivian’s climate progress stands out in an industry that has largely walked away from electric vehicles, as government-backed incentives have been rolled back and consumer interest has waned. Rivian expects to deliver approximately 70,000 vehicles in 2026 driven largely by the R2, which would represent a big jump from about 42,000 vehicles delivered last year.

Rivian also formally published its own AI guidelines as part of its impact report, emphasizing safety, fairness, data privacy, transparency, and quarterly oversight by an executive AI Governance Committee. The company affirmed its commitment to develop “AI systems that are ethical, emphasizing ‘doing the right thing,’ and promoting a sustainable future.” Rivian is making big moves in AI, developing robotaxis for Uber and planning to introduce an unsupervised, “eyes-off” autonomous driving system for consumers as early as next year.

Tech.title: Trump says the US is officially renaming AI to ‘super intelligence’
Tech.content:
The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globallist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. Here and after officially called “super intelligence,” changing the name, and that the use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake.

It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing. But we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports. From this point forward, all of the United States documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, super as opposed to artificial. So it’s super intelligence. In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence—SI. That’s, uh, let’s see if that does. It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don’t, we’re gonna find out pretty soon.

Super intelligence. Every major new technology brings challenges, and super intelligence is… no exception. Yet. the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming — a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead. These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster.

Same group of people. This is the group. That came up with. The Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax. Climate change, open borders. Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this. And now I say, whoever wins…SI. Whoever wins super intelligence wins. That’s the group that wins. And we’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else.

We’re going to keep it that way. We’re going to keep it very, very straight and very strong. I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. Many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself. And we will be very careful, and that’s why we have a Department of Justice that…. we’ve already used it having to do with this very subject, and used it very powerfully.

Everything worked out very well and very quickly, and other law enforcement bodies that will rein things in if we have to do that. But we will only encourage super intelligence. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in. We’re going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice.

The United States leads the world in super intelligence and will continue to do so safely and responsibly. Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be. Freedom was not a gift that Americans want easily after 250 years, and it is not one that we will ever, ever, ever, ever surrender.

Tech.title: Xbox is barely Xbox anymore
Tech.content:
Xbox has become a shell of its former self — and things are only getting worse. As part of its planned cuts impacting around 3,200 workers, the company announced today more changes that will further dilute the brand. Studios are being consolidated, others are on the brink of being closed altogether, and Xbox’s most iconic franchise, Halo, is being moved to a new developer. The future of Xbox looks more uncertain than ever.

Similarly, Obsidian is being moved out from Xbox Game Studios and under Bethesda Game Studios, where it will refocus on the Fallout franchise, and all of Microsoft’s casual games, like Minesweeper and Solitaire, are moving under Candy Crush developer King. Meanwhile Playground and Turn 10, the studios responsible for Fable and Forza, are merging into one.

This is all part of the Xbox “reset” outlined by new CEO Asha Sharma, which kicked off with 1,600 employees being laid off in July, with 1,600 more planned over the following fiscal year, leaving many employees in an awkward state of limbo. A pair of studios were also spun off from the company, with both Double Fine and Compulsion going independent. Today’s layoffs are part of that second wave that was previously announced.

The reason for all of the changes, according to Sharma, is to eventually become a company that reaches “more than a billion people each day,” a nearly impossible goal that will be especially challenging to pull off given all of the cuts. The plan is to focus on known hits like Minecraft, Halo, and Candy Crush, while eschewing everything else and reevaluating just how much the company is investing in its Game Pass subscription service.

“For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place,” Activision president Rob Kostich said in a statement. “It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community.”

Image: Xbox Game Studios

Some of today’s moves, like expanding King and focusing more on franchises like Halo and Fallout, fit into that framework. But they also yet again raise a question that has plagued Microsoft’s gaming division for the last few years: What even is Xbox?

Once upon a time it was clear: It was a console business that also developed and published exclusive games for the platform. But as Microsoft attempted to expand, particularly by spending billions of dollars to turn Game Pass into a Netflix for games, the brand was diluted. The console became increasingly unimportant, and as for exclusives, well, it’s hard to follow just what the plan is for those. Despite some superficial rebranding, the case for Xbox isn’t any clearer now.

Today’s changes make that even more pronounced. Xbox Game Studios was once a sprawling organization of game developers creating titles for Game Pass and the various Xbox consoles. But after waves of layoffs, closures, and spinoffs, there isn’t all that much left under the umbrella. Today it consists of just a handful of studios like Gears of War developer The Coalition and Wasteland studio InXile. And the fate of these teams feels increasingly precarious. What happens to The Coalition after Gears of War: E-Day launches next month? History suggests it won’t be anything good. After all, Halo Studios just released a well-received Combat Evolved remake in July, and now it has been reduced to a “small team” that “will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market.”

Xbox still plans for a future in the hardware business through whatever “Project Helix” ends up being. But when it comes to games, Xbox is mostly just Activision Blizzard and Bethesda now. Almost all of its most notable new games are coming from these subsidiaries, all of which were acquired for billions of dollars, initially to boost Game Pass. Recently, these companies have announced far-off titles like Fallout 5 and StarCraft in an apparent attempt to show that everything is okay while the broader Xbox business is embroiled in chaos.

And now we have Activision making Halo games. It’s a further signal that Xbox is attempting to make its franchises as big as possible — Activision managed to do just that with the annual juggernaut that is Call of Duty — but also a sign that the traditional Xbox brand is less important than ever. And that’s something no amount of capital letters will change.

Tech.title: Xbox is merging its Forza developers into a single studio
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is uniting its two Forza developers into a single studio today, as part of a massive restructuring of Xbox. Playground Games, which develops Forza Horizon, and Turn 10 Studios, creators of Forza Motorsport, are merging together to focus on Forza Horizon and Fable.

“Playground and Turn 10 will come together as one studio focused on the Forza and Fable franchises,” explains Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty in a memo. “These two studios have been technological, creative, and franchise partners for over a decade, and today’s changes will formally move their work into one team.”

The closure of Turn 10 Studios leaves big unanswered questions around the future of Forza Motorsport, and whether Microsoft will ever return to the franchise or simply focus on Forza Horizon instead.

More than 70 people at Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10 Studios were laid off last year, in a move that hit the vast majority of the studio. Over the past year, Turn 10 Studios has essentially been maintaining Forza Motorsport, and now those who remain will be moving over to Playground Games to work on Forza Horizon and Fable.

The Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios changes are part of a larger reorganization of Xbox today. Activision is taking on the Halo franchise, alongside Sea of Thieves developers Rare and World’s Edge, the studio responsible for Age of Empires. You can read more about the latest Xbox shake-up right here.

Tech.title: Microsoft is laying off 268 Xbox staffers and Ninja Theory may close
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is laying off around 260 Xbox employees today, as part of an ongoing “reset” of its gaming business. 1,600 Xbox employees were impacted by layoffs in July, with Xbox CEO Asha Sharma describing the cuts as “the most significant restructure in Xbox history.” Today’s layoffs are part of the 3,200 roles that were previously confirmed to be impacted over the course of Microsoft’s 2027 financial year (which ends in June 2027).

“We are eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer,” says Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty in a memo. “The actions completed since July, inclusive of the studio divestitures, bring us roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring. I am deeply grateful for what our colleagues have built, and I know how difficult today will be for those leaving and the teams around them.”

The Xbox restructuring also includes Microsoft selling off four Xbox studios as part of its significant gaming cuts. While two studios, Double Fine and Compulsion Games, have already gone independent, deals to sell off Ninja Theory have fallen through. As a result, Microsoft is now proceeding with a consultation period to close the studio, unless the company can find another buyer.

“Unfortunately, two separate agreements for Ninja Theory fell through,” explains Booty. “We will now begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while continuing to explore other paths forward.”

The deal to sell off Undead Labs is still proceeding, and Booty says it has “now successfully transitioned on similar terms” to Compulsion and Double Fine. Xbox is also still in consultations over the future of Arkane and the Blade game, in accordance with French labor laws. “Consultation with Arkane remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year,” says Booty.

Today’s Xbox layoffs are also part of a larger reorganization of Xbox today. Activision is taking on the Halo franchise, alongside Sea of Thieves and World’s Edge, the studio responsible for Age of Empires. You can read more about the latest Xbox shake-up right here.

Tech.title: Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 with lower prices and Fable-level performance
Tech.content:
Anthropic’s newest model, Opus 5.5, was released on Tuesday, setting a new state-of-the-art in coding and knowledge work performance, according to the company. Opus is the most capable and expensive tier in Anthropic’s three-tier Claude lineup; Sonnet sits in the middle, while Haiku is the fastest and cheapest. Notably, Anthropic says, the release outpaces the larger Fable model in many benchmarks and succeeded in a number of informal tasks that Fable failed to complete.

The new model is also significantly cheaper than its predecessor. Output tokens will be charged at $20 per million tokens for Opus 5.5, compared to $25 for the previous model. Other metrics have similar price drops. The model is also faster to run, reflecting an overall drop in the compute required to serve it.

The new version also makes significant changes to how Opus communicates, with the Opus 5.5 less likely to use jargon and more likely to put important information at the start of its messages.

The launch comes just two months after the release of Opus 5 on July 24. According to the announcement, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, which are the next tiers in the line-up, will be released “in the coming weeks,” with similar performance improvements.

Anthropic says that Opus 5.5 is comparable to Mythos in its biology and cybersecurity capabilities, so its release is subject to the same safeguards as the company’s Fable model. Those safeguards limit how much the models can be used to discover exploits in compiled programs or developing recognizable biological weapons, among other tasks.

Opus 5.5 is Anthropic’s first model release since CEO Dario Amodei embraced calls to pace the frontier, deliberately slowing down progress on AI capabilities to match the rate of progress on alignment.

“I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence,” Amodei wrote in a post earlier this month, “not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.”

Opus 5.5’s safety training was broadly similar to its predecessors, with alignment testing and pre-release evaluation by outside organizations like METR and Frontier Design. But Anthropic emphasized that more advanced training and evaluation systems were already being prepared for future models, including improved security and monitoring systems.

“As AI becomes more capable, public policy should play a larger role in making sure the systems people rely on are safe. That capacity takes time to build, and we’ve started to put the infrastructure in place to support it,” the blog post reads. “We expect to share more details on these efforts soon.”

Tech.title: Stolen passwords are exposing America’s water providers to hackers
Tech.content:
New security research has found that well over a thousand U.S. water and wastewater providers are exposed to hacks due to malware that’s capable of stealing their employees’ passwords and active logged-in sessions.

The findings by cybersecurity defense firm SpyCloud underscore how water providers and other critical infrastructure can be compromised with relative ease amidst a wave of hacks targeting the water supplies of dozens of communities across the United States.

While password-stealing malware is not new, the research highlights how stolen passwords offer hackers an easy route to break into an organization’s network without using AI tools.

SpyCloud said it built a database of more than 66,000 public-facing systems that are registered with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, amounting to 10,000 organizations. The company found password-stealing malware had swiped passwords and credentials from 1,787 organizations, or nearly two in 10 providers they checked. The firm noted at least 250 organizations had credentials exposed that appeared to allow access to their operational networks and remote-access systems, which control the physical pumps and water flows.

The analysis covered an unnamed metering tech provider, which had a device on its network that was infected with password-stealing malware. The malware stole reams of credentials, including passwords for 167 U.S. utility companies that rely on the metering tech provider.

SpyCloud Chief Investigations Officer Jason Lancaster said in the post that this single breach handed criminals the keys to access “a hundred otherwise unrelated organizations.”

Password-stealing malware, also known as infostealers, allows hackers to steal a person’s stored passwords as well as the session tokens that are used to keep them logged in. These session tokens can allow a hacker to log in as if they were the legitimate user, and can often bypass multi-factor authentication systems. Hackers regularly trade stolen credentials in order to obtain passwords or session tokens for accessing specific organizations.

This research comes weeks after a spate of hacks targeting water providers around the United States, which the U.S. government has privately tied to Iran-backed hackers. SpyCloud said it found no evidence that those Iran-linked hacks relied on stolen passwords. In those cases, the signs point to security weaknesses, such as manufacturer-set default passwords, in the mechanical switches and physical controllers used by critical infrastructure, SpyCloud said, echoing earlier findings from U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA.

Rather, the researchers note that stolen passwords are a major source of access to “whoever wants to buy or find it,” in parallel to the known security risks with critical infrastructure tech. Lancaster said that the water-sector “has to hold both stories at once.”

Tech.title: Noble Carbon will show how it’s making EV charger installs painless at TechCrunch Disrupt
Tech.content:
Plenty of people want to buy electric vehicles, but not everyone is prepared to shell out for an upgrade to their home’s electrical service just to add an EV charger. The worry is reasonable. One study found that upgrading things like electrical panels (that box in the garage or basement that delivers power throughout a home) can more than double charger installation costs.

Rather than rip out the old panel, Noble Carbon has developed circuit breakers that can take the headache out of installing an EV charger, or a heat pump or an induction stove for that matter.

The Pittsfield, Massachusetts, startup is one of 200 startups in this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield, a pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in October in which 20 finalists will present on the main stage.

Noble Carbon’s breakers can adjust how much electricity they deliver to an EV charger in real time, allowing the chargers to squeeze into otherwise at-capacity panels.

Electrical panels in people’s homes are typically designed to handle absolute peak usage, something that might happen only “a handful of hours per year,” Spencer Fields, Noble Carbon’s head of marketing, told TechCrunch.

For example, if someone is hosting family for a holiday, they might find themselves simultaneously using the water heater, air conditioning, oven, and several TVs, all while every light is on in the house. The rest of the time, the electrical panel has room to spare.

Jared Lebos explains how Noble Carbon’s breakers work to Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey Image Credits:Josh Qualls, Director of Photography, Office of Governor Healey

In that scenario, Noble Carbon’s smart breakers would turn down the power flowing to the devices they control, essentially guaranteeing that the entire house doesn’t draw more power than the panel can provide.

“In order to avoid a main panel upgrade, you really only need control on your three to six largest loads [the biggest power-drawing appliances],” Fields said.

Co-founder and CEO Jared Lebos was inspired to create the product after experiencing rolling blackouts in his home country of South Africa. He worked with Andrew Crane, the company’s co-founder and CTO, to turn it into reality.

The result is a breaker that fits into existing slots in a home’s electrical panel and, according to the company, takes less than five minutes to install. Some of the startup’s employees have been testing the breakers in their homes for more than a year, and the product is now undergoing evaluation for UL certification, a widely recognized electrical safety standard.

Noble Carbon currently is partnering with the utility Eversource to install its breakers in up to 200 multifamily units in Massachusetts.

Tech.title: AstroForge is putting AI in command of its next spacecraft
Tech.content:
Fly to an asteroid, land on it, make no mistakes: If only it were that easy.

When NASA sends spacecraft to explore the solar system, they build in redundancy and automation. But much of the work is done by teams of flight controllers communicating with the vehicle from Earth. The OSIRIS-REx mission, which rendezvoused with an asteroid in 2018, had 100 operators on each eight-hour shift.

But resources like that aren’t available to startups, so AstroForge, which is developing technology to mine asteroids, is turning to AI. The company has developed an autonomous control stack for its spacecraft called “Solo,” a transformer-based model made in-house.

AstroForge plans to fly its first autonomous spacecraft in 2027 on the first rocket launched by Stoke Space. That mission will be backed by NASA and is expected to gather scientific data about the sun.

That would be an accomplishment: Most spacecraft autonomy depends on traditional control algorithms due to concerns about the unreliability of neural networks. The first use of a neural network to control a satellite’s positioning in orbit took place just last year.

AstroForge, founded in 2022 and backed with $56 million in venture funding, has launched two prototype spacecraft, both of which suffered anomalies that prevented them from achieving most of their mission objectives. In 2025, its Odin spacecraft was launched into deep space, but the company had difficulty communicating with it. There are a limited number of antennas on Earth big enough to transmit to spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles away, and the windows of time in which to do it are small.

Ultimately, AstroForge couldn’t gain control of Odin, but the experience spurred it to consider alternatives: Could it put sufficient intelligence onboard the spacecraft for it to solve its own problems?

“Would that have been recoverable with all the data on the spacecraft? I don’t know, but I can tell you nothing onboard tried it, and I would love something onboard to try if the spacecraft is unrecoverable at launch,” Matthew Gialich, AstroForge’s co-founder and CEO, said.

“The trade for me is: Do I go build my own ground network, which is going to cost [around] $200 million to put up five dishes around the world and then do operations on it, or do I try to remove it with a model?”

Armand Awad, AstroForge’s head of flight software, said the company decided to leverage the advances in transformer models driven by the frontier labs. It created a stack that includes traditional control algorithms, models trained on test data for specific subsystems like power generation or navigation, and an overall intelligence layer trained on about 2,500 sensors in the spacecraft.

“I’m not saying I’m going to make general spacecraft autonomy or general autonomy for the world,” Gialich said. “I’m making a constrained autonomy at a very low sensor input, following the basic training of a transformer model.”

In theory, the agent in control of the spacecraft will perform tasks like anomaly resolution. Awad imagines it realizing that it has lost track of its position in space, correlating a power anomaly to issues in its star tracker, and fixing the whole thing — “probably turning it on and off in this case.”

The company’s third vehicle, DeepSpace-2, is currently set to launch alongside Intuitive Machines’ third moon mission, expected to head for space by the end of 2026. Solo will be onboard that vehicle, flying in “shadow mode,” so AstroForge’s engineers can put it through its paces before the Autonomy-1 mission.

Will this truly be an AI agent operating an independent spacecraft?



“I don’t plan on flying radios that can receive from Earth on Autonomy-1,” Gialich said. “We have to go all in right now. The team’s probably going to talk me into it by the time we fly it. But right now, I’m telling them no radios.”

Tech.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Aaron Edsinger brings Hello Robot’s Stretch 4 to life onstage
Tech.content:
Robots that walk, talk, dance, and perform backflips make great videos. But can they close the blinds? Help someone eat? Scratch an itch?

For people with severe mobility impairments, those everyday tasks can mean greater independence. And they’re exactly the kinds of jobs Hello Robot designed its home-assistance robot, Stretch, to tackle.

The Robot Built for Real Life, Not a Demo Reel.” The live demo takes physical AI out of the lab and puts it to work alongside people, showing what’s possible when usefulness, safety, and accessibility drive robot design.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

The timing couldn’t be better. Stretch 4 launched in May, and its first production run was already sold out when TechCrunch caught up with Edsinger in June. While much of the robotics industry is focused on humanoids, Hello Robot is taking a different route: a compact robot on wheels with a telescoping arm designed to navigate human spaces and perform useful tasks.

Want to see what physical AI can do when usefulness drives the design? See Stretch 4 in action on the Real World AI Stage. What does it take to build a useful robot?

Stretch 4 doesn’t need legs to get around. It rolls. It doesn’t need two arms to pick things up. Its single telescoping arm reaches out to grab and manipulate objects. The robot is compact enough to operate in spaces designed for people and equipped with the sensors, perception, and contact sensitivity needed to work around them.

Those design decisions become more meaningful when you see what people are doing with the technology. Users with severe mobility impairments who use Stretch technology can feed themselves, close blinds, and even scratch an itch. TechCrunch recently profiled one user with quadriplegia who has used Stretch to help him drink a protein shake, handle his glasses, and brush his teeth.

That’s a very different measure of progress from a slick demo video. At Disrupt, attendees will get to watch Stretch 4 work live and hear how Hello Robot is approaching physical AI for environments where robots and people share the same space.

Meet the roboticist behind Stretch

Aaron Edsinger has spent his career building robots designed to work with people. Before co-founding Hello Robot, he founded Meka Robotics and Redwood Robotics, two robotics companies acquired by Google in 2013. As robotics director at Google, Edsinger led the business, product, and technical development of two of the company’s central robotics investments and worked with senior leadership to help define its broader robotics strategy.

His expertise covers virtually the entire robot product design stack, from human-robot interaction and UX to mechanical and industrial design, manufacturing, software architecture, real-time control, robotic arms, hands, and humanoids. That experience now comes together at Hello Robot, where the goal isn’t to build a robot that looks the most human. It’s to build one that people can actually use.

Stretch 4 is Hello Robot’s latest step toward that goal. The company says the new generation was shaped by six years of customer feedback and comes with a full-stack, open source software platform for researchers and developers working on robotics and embodied AI.
