Tech.title: TikTok’s US arm joins Lantern, a cross-platform child safety initiative
Tech.content:
Eight months after it was spun out of TikTok, the social media platform’s U.S. unit, known as TikTok USDS Joint Venture, is joining Lantern, a cross-platform child safety program launched by a group of tech companies.

Lantern, launched in 2023, helps social media companies work together to securely share signals of harmful behavior and content in order to identify bad actors as they move across platforms. Members in the program include Google, X, Snap, Twitch, Anthropic, Meta, Discord, Microsoft, Apple, Roblox, Reddit, and more.

“Cross-platform collaboration is essential to identifying and disrupting child sexual exploitation and abuse, and TikTok USDS JV’s participation will help strengthen coordinated enforcement across the wider tech ecosystem,” Lantern’s director, Marc Leone, said in a statement.

It makes sense for TikTok USDS to join Lantern, given most of its competitors are already participants in the program. Through 2025, Lantern says that participant companies have shared over 2 million signals of potentially violating behavior.

As legally required of U.S.-based companies, TikTok’s U.S. venture has been reporting to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)’s CyberTipline when it becomes aware of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and other threats to children’s safety. The company is now also committing $2 million to NCMEC’s efforts to modernize its CyberTipline.

“This investment will help NCMEC deploy advanced search, automation, and analysis tools to detect harm sooner, cut manual processing times in half, and accelerate actionable reports to law enforcement when a child’s safety is on the line,” TikTok said in a press release.

This NCMEC project is expected to take three years and $10 million, with partners like AWS, Microsoft, and Palantir also contributing resources.

Tech.title: Rabbit Is Back, This Time With an AI Agent App
Tech.content:
Jesse Lyu doesn't think the Rabbit R1 was a flop.

Lyu's gadget was among the first in the gold rush to create dedicated AI hardware that acted as a virtual assistant. You could speak into the R1 and ask it to complete tasks for you—book an Uber; order food on DoorDash. After a buzzy launch at CES 2024, it earned scathing reviews. All the agentic stuff on the R1 just didn't work that well. WIRED gave it a 3/10.

Since those early days, the capabilities of AI assistants have vastly improved, and now the tech is all the rage. So Rabbit is banging the drum again.

On Tuesday, Rabbit announced OS3, a standalone “agentic operating system” designed to run across multiple screens. It also arrives as a software update for the company's R1 gadget, though you don't need an R1 to use it. Instead, you can access OS3 through a desktop browser, Telegram on your phone, or even iMessage.

It’s a striking pivot for a company that once championed the handheld hardware over smartphone apps, but the environment for this type of software has ripened.

Agents that handle tasks for you are all anyone in Silicon Valley talks about. Meta's new Muse agent was just banned from crawling Amazon to shop on a user's behalf using a virtual machine. Lyu smirks as he brings it up, saying, “We've been through all of this a year and a half ago,” calling back to the R1's controversial use of a virtual machine to execute app actions on your behalf. So was Rabbit just too ahead of the curve?

Lyu says from a monetary perspective, the Rabbit R1 was tremendously successful, especially considering the company doesn't offer a subscription for its AI features, unlike many competitors. He claims the company delivered more than 100,000 of the orange-red, Teenage Engineering-designed gadgets worldwide, with return rates of less than 5 percent, and earned roughly a 45 to 50 percent margin on the hardware.

Jesse Lyu, CEO and founder of Rabbit. Courtesy of Rabbit

"Internally, from an engineering perspective—we didn't make the wrong bet," Lyu says. “I think the challenge is really being extremely limited in resources, team-wise and money-wise, compared to other AI studios that raised billions of dollars.” He says Rabbit has raised around $60 million in total and currently employs 15 people.

But after dismal reviews upon the R1's launch, the company had to make tough decisions. Rabbit decided against expanding the team and chose to stay lean, but things were dire around this time last year. A planned launch in India was stymied by regulations, putting the company in financial strain, so much so that a handful of employees went on strike and claimed they weren't getting paid. Lyu says he respected their decision, adding that the company secured more funding and is on stronger footing. “There are no issues with the company's health,” he says.

Lyu says the team decided not to rush into new hardware, and instead focused on delivering software updates to polish the R1 experience—to date, Lyu says Rabbit has deployed around 50 updates in the past year and a half. He points to a dedicated Discord community of more than 12,000 users that provide feedback on what new features to add to the R1, like opening up the hardware. For example, you can integrate OpenClaw or Hermes AI agents into the R1 instead of using Rabbit's proprietary models.

Tech.title: Viture’s Vonder Glasses Are Meant to Map Your Mind
Tech.content:
David Jiang, cofounder and CEO of smart glasses company Viture, tells me about how he used to yell at his kid.

His 10-year-old son played tennis. During tournaments, Jiang says he had a habit of shouting and criticizing his son’s mistakes as he played. He wanted to apply pressure to make him succeed—it was the way he’d been taught to raise kids, after all. It made sense.

But then, unprompted, his smart glasses sent him a message. The AI assistant in his company’s newest wearable had picked up on what he was doing, recognized that his behavior wasn’t helpful, and messaged him about what he should do differently. Stop shouting. Stop criticizing. Just be there, be present, and show that you support your son. That worked, Jiang says, and being called out like that has supposedly made him a better father and improved the relationship with his kid, all thanks to his yet-to-be-released Vonder AI glasses.

“I didn't know this until Vonder could find my pattern,” Jiang says. “This is not only a tool that can summarize your life, but also a tool that can help yourself to be a better person.”

Viture, a San Francisco-based company known for its plug-in virtual display glasses, announced its first pair of spectacles with no virtual display on Tuesday. The glasses instead look remarkably like normal glasses, but aim to map out your memories, ideas, and goals and plop them on a digital vision board, all without embedded cameras.

Now co-headquartered in California and Beijing, Viture has made glasses like the Viture One and the Viture Beast—wearable face computers that connect via USB-C cable to a device to project its screen right before your eyes. The company's products have primarily targeted gamers or anyone interested in big-screen entertainment. They work well for that purpose, but their chunky design means they fall short in comfort and fashion.

The new glasses are a bit of a pivot. They're called Vonder, you know, like “wonder” but with a V, and they don't have cameras. The glasses' arms feature mics and speakers that can play music, dictate map directions, and let the wearer make phone calls. Vonder also features a built-in AI assistant that combines the top large language models. It can trigger OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, or even DeepSeek. Based on the task’s complexity, Vonder AI will source the answer from whichever model is the quickest and most economical.

Tech.title: Adobe Premiere, One of the iPhone’s Best Video-Editing Apps, Is Now on Android
Tech.content:
It's easy to add your footage, then opt for the mini editor or the full editor. The former lets you easily trim or replace your footage, and even choose a filter to apply a specific color style to all of your clips. You can export directly to YouTube Shorts without leaving Premiere. The full editor gives you a multitrack timeline for more granular edits, like layering text, music, and effects.

Several AI tools are on board, like Enhance Audio, which can boost the subject's voice and cut background noise. If you want to add a voice-over, you can speak into your phone's mic and see your footage in real time so it all matches up. Adobe says the app has Firefly-powered AI features, like Generative Fill, Image-to-Video, and Generate Sound Effects. However, these require generative credits, aka a subscription, if you run out of your monthly allotment.

Some features are still “coming soon,” like the Continue Editing function so you can wrap up an edit on desktop after starting it on mobile, or support for Adobe Fonts.

Uniquely (for an Adobe product), you do not have to log in or subscribe to Adobe's creative suite to use Premiere on Android. Like the iOS version, the app is free to use.

“What we're seeing with a lot of mobile apps right now is that there are these huge barriers to entry to using it for the first time,” Snowden says. “We really wanted to get away from that, and I think part of the accessibility and simplicity of the app—the onboarding process is part of that—and we just want to get people in and using it."

Tech.title: AI Models Built From Rat Brains Just Got Closer to Reality
Tech.content:
A biological computing startup that uses neural patterns from rat brain cells to build artificial intelligence just got a major boost from Amazon.

Starting Tuesday, select Amazon Web Services customers will gain access to The Biological Computing Company’s “rat brain” AI model as part of a limited preview. The startup’s technology is specifically designed to improve AI for generating videos. Both Amazon and The Biological Computing Company, which goes by the acronym TBC, says they expect the tech to roll out to all AWS enterprise customers soon.

“We figured out a way to code information, like images for example, to the biological material,” says TBC cofounder Alexander Ksendzovsky. “We then observe how the biology processes that information, and then we build a tool that mimics that process.”

This is not the first biologically-derived computing platform that Amazon has made available in its marketplace, says Deap Ubhi, global director of technology for startups at Amazon Web Services. Ubhi says the cloud-computing giant also works with Cortical Labs, an Australia-based company that combines lab-grown neurons with silicon chips to help companies process data. (It calls its products WAAS, or “wetware as a service.”) Cortical Labs also sells a multi-thousand dollar “biological computer,” a low-power device designed for use in laboratories that can supposedly keep neurons alive for six months.

TBC takes a “pragmatic approach,” says Ubhi, which is part of why the company appealed to Amazon. Rather than taking big swings or trying to reinvent the transformer, the core architectural unit of large language models, “they’re working within existing standards of the generative AI space and saying, ‘How can we make the current visual models more efficient?’” he explains.

Tech.title: GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS Review (2026): Cinema-Quality Action Cam
Tech.content:
For example, GoPro sent a Laowa 7.5-mm lens for me to test with. When HyperSmooth is on, that's the equivalent of shooting with a 23-mm lens on a full-frame camera. With HyperSmooth off, it becomes a 20-mm lens. I bring this up mainly because if you want to go really wide on the ILS, you'll need a very, very wide lens (fisheye lenses are probably your best bet).

Now for the downside to the ILS: There are no electrical contacts, which means lenses that rely on electronic focus or aperture control probably won't work. For example, my all-time favorite MFT lens, Panasonic's original 20-mm pancake, won't work on the ILS because there's no manual aperture ring.

Your best bet is to stick with fully manual lenses that have a mechanical aperture ring. There aren't many, but there are enough with quality glass to cover a good range of focal lengths. GoPro's Abe Kislevitz put together a nice collection of lenses that he has tested with the Mission 1 Pro ILS, along with his recommendations for various shooting scenarios. Be aware that the camera is sold body-only, and so far, we haven't seen any bundles from GoPro or resellers that include a lens.

And yes, you have to manually focus. I could drop some jokes here about kids today not knowing how to do it, but the truth is, I shoot vintage manual-focus lenses all the time on my Sony A7R II. While I've shot sports and wildlife with these lenses and had a pretty high success rate, I struggled to focus on the ILS.

The problem with focusing on the ILS is the small screen. It's hard to see, not just in bright daylight. It's just really small. There is focus peaking, which uses color banding to indicate what's in focus, but it can be hard to see exactly where it ends, and I've learned from my Sony not to fully rely on peaking.

You can zoom in to get very precise focus, which is what I do on the Sony, but again the small screen makes it hard to see. Worse, for filmmakers especially, you have to have the camera at eye level to focus it well, which limits your shooting ability (or you get to contort into all sorts of weird poses). I would love to see the next Mission 1 Pro ILS get a tilting screen; it's not waterproof anyway, so it doesn't seem like there would be a need to reengineer. GoPro no doubt would suggest using the app on my phone, as it does make it considerably easier to focus, but then you need a cage, and then a handle, and at that point most of the Mission 1 Pro ILS' size advantage is gone; you might as well get a Panasonic GH7, which has an even larger sensor.

Ultimately, while focusing on the small screen is challenging, using a phone or other external monitor sidesteps that issue (and is what pro filmmakers do anyway), but the inability to control the lens iris electronically feels like a bigger limitation since it eliminates a significant number of lenses. It would be nice to see a future Mission 1 Pro ILS support at least electronic connectors for aperture and manual focusing on lenses that require it.

Shooting With the Mission 1 Pro ILS

Once you get past the hurdle of manual focusing, there's a lot to love about the ILS footage. Testing it reminded me more than anything of the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera from several years ago. I can't believe this tiny little thing can match the quality of those early Blackmagic cameras.

Tech.title: The UK Government Faces a Reckoning Over Palantir
Tech.content:
When Andy Burnham sat in his office in Manchester as the regional mayor, building an unrivaled power base on Britain’s left that ultimately catapulted him into the prime minister’s office, he did so in the only region of England that refused Palantir access to its data.

Now, as Burnham enters his first parliamentary session as British leader, Palantir could prove to be his first major test in office, as sources in Westminster tell WIRED the prime minister is under significant pressure from his new colleagues to break the company’s contentious contract with the National Health Service. The dispute could become the first major crisis of Burnham’s premiership, with those sources saying pressure is mounting on him to decide the future of Palantir’s growing role across the British state in the coming weeks.

Palantir currently holds contracts worth around £670m in the public sector, including major deals in health, defence, and policing. The largest—a £330m contract to manage healthcare data on the NHS Federated Data Platform—is the one Palantir opponents have opted to focus on. Reports circulated during Labour’s leadership election that Burnham would block Palantir, but they were swiftly cut down in follow-up reporting. Campaigners are now pushing for Burnham to use a break clause in Palantir’s contract with the NHS, which would see the deal end in 2027.

Burnham’s government and the Labour Party he leads are fractiously split on the issue. On one side, leading officials and parliamentary veterans argue cautiously in favor of the provider. On the other, Labour’s left-leaning grassroots and influential backbench MPs are pressuring the government to end the relationship, and in the process begin a huge schism with the company.

The government has so far obfuscated in response to an official petition asking for people to be able to opt out of Palantir’s FDP, after it got 10,000 signatures, saying only that the government would consider it in future policy making. A similar, non-official petition calls for Palantir to be removed from the NHS entirely and has already reached 177,000 signatures.

Growing public opposition to the company has put the government under real pressure to reduce Palantir’s role in the British state. WIRED spoke to three Whitehall sources who believe that, if the deal is to be broken, a decision to do so would need to be made in the next few weeks.

“Given the need to hire an alternate provider or make a decision to move the contract in house, any decision to tear up the contract would need to be done by the Autumn,” one Whitehall source tells WIRED. “Otherwise the government would risk botching any changeover.”

Many of the supporters who secured Burnham’s position in Downing Street are natural Palantir skeptics who come from the soft left. Intrinsically wary of privatisation, they want to see the firm’s role reduced or removed entirely from British politics.

Beyond the inner circle, opposition to Palantir is organised and loud, including many members of the Socialist Campaign Group, a faction within the Labour Party, who are on the whole more experienced MPs. Burnham supporters like Rachael Maskell have vocally opposed Palantir.

Maskell has highlighted her own work as an NHS clinician to justify her opposition to the company in a parliamentary debate in April. During a debate on Palantir’s FDP in February, she said: “This US spytech company is now deep into the data of our NHS and of course patients across the country. I know as a former clinician in the NHS, trust is key. If you do not have the confidence and trust of your patients, that results in people having worse health outcomes. So in the interest of our constituents' health, I urge the government to end this contract.”

Tech.title: Everything You Know About Political Violence Is Probably Wrong
Tech.content:
It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.

In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”

Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.

But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”

What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.

What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.

Courtesy of The New Press Buy This Book At: Amazon

Bookshop.org

Books-A-Million If you buy something using links in our stories, we may earn a commission. This helps support our journalism. Learn more.

Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?

America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.

Tech.title: Is a Home Security System Subscription Worth It? (2026)
Tech.content:
No one wants to worry about a break-in. But no one wants to end up paying fees every month just to check their video doorbell feed or find out their window was broken, and most smart security systems (even the original ones that weren't touted as smart!) rely on your fear to have you paying month after month for the promise of catching burglars and stopping intruders for you.

These systems do work, and they can give you a lot of peace of mind. This comes with a hefty price tag, though, and plenty of people would be more than happy with a system they build themselves sans monthly fees. If you're not interested in a system that will call the police or fire department if you don't respond fast enough to something that turns out to be minor, or don't want to have strangers looking through your security cameras at your property, I'm here to help with that.

This guide collects a handful of our favorite smart home security accessories that won't paywall you left and right, and will give you local storage options for video so you aren't locked into the cloud. This way you can build the system that works for you. Here's everything I recommend if you want smart home security without the subscriptions.

What Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?

Smart security systems can look like whatever you want, in my opinion, but there are a lot of starter kits you've probably seen. Smart-home brands like Abode and SimpliSafe have starter packs you've likely seen before with motion sensors, door sensors, and security hubs that sound an alarm when one of those sensors is triggered.

But smart home security can go way beyond that. Most systems let you add on cameras and even video doorbells to monitor movement around your home and catch people at your door who shouldn't be there. (This is also a handy way to know when it’s a package delivery or another random salesperson.) These systems are usually modular and customizable, whether you DIY or go with a brand. Overall, the goal is to protect and monitor your home through motion sensors and video feeds.

Home security brands usually have various subscription options and some kind of self-monitored, subscription-free tier, but you usually lose out on a variety of features to encourage you to subscribe.

What Do Smart Home Security Systems and a Subscription Get You?

I remember running into the issue of paywalled features for the first time a few years ago when I was testing Abode's smart lock. I liked the lock, but I woke up to unclear notifications that happened in the dead of night. Had the lock been hacked? Had it sensed itself being manually opened when we were asleep? There was no way to tell because Abode’s base level would only tell me the lock was interacted with without explaining how. I signed up for the Abode membership that day to be able to review the events, and luckily it was just a loss of Wi-Fi connection and reestablishment that happened within a minute of each other. Crisis averted.

The main thing that subscription services paywall is video storage, which allows you to review past events at your home. Sometimes it can also be notifications, whether that's the type of notification or the ability to review notification history. What is or is not paywalled largely depends on the brand and its offerings. Professional live monitoring, however, is almost always paywalled, whether that's an agent calling police when an alarm has been triggered or an agent reviewing flagged footage (e.g., motion alerts) to either notify you of a situation or call emergency services on your behalf. That’s one thing you can't DIY—if you’re on vacation or otherwise not able to call police if there's an issue, you're out of luck.

Base stations from home security companies like ADT, SimpliSafe, and Vivint will act as a smart-home hub to connect and control sensors and other devices, and be able to sound an alarm. It might have a keypad that you can use to arm and disarm the system too.

Tech.title: I Tried Breville’s $300 Slot Toaster That Watches Bread So It Doesn’t Burn
Tech.content:
A toasted slice of bread is a simple pleasure and is often the subtle touch a meal needs. That’s one reason the humble toaster remains a mainstay in many kitchens, even in the age of air fryers.

Toasters typically achieve doneness using time and temperature. The recently launched Breville Eye Q 850 Auto Toaster swaps those imperfect elements for a more modern approach. The Eye Q uses a pulsing internal sensor to watch the color of the bread as it toasts, only finishing when it hits the perfect result, at least in theory.

I put it to the test to see if this $300 high-tech toaster lives up to its promise. While I generally think it does, I noticed a few things worth considering before you splurge. Let’s dig in.

What makes the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster different?

An optic sensor seems like a good way to ensure your toast always reaches the right doneness without tweaking settings between batches. John Carlsen/CNET

At first glance, the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster looks like any other high-end toaster — my test sample featured a matte black brushed stainless steel case and a ceramic top portion. But the real magic happens when you start the toast cycle. The Eye Q lowers the bread, and a green light inside the toaster starts flashing. This Eye Q Optic Sensor reminds me of something you’d see on fitness trackers, but instead of tracking a pulse, it monitors the bread’s visual doneness.

The sensor is only in the left-side slot, so you can toast a single slice, which I think is very helpful. Importantly, the toaster won’t run without something inside, which is a great safety feature. Like most premium toasters, this Breville unit uses a motorized lift to lower and raise your bread. It won’t pop up with a spring-loaded mechanism as on a typical toaster. It will, however, play a little chime at the beginning and end of each toasting cycle — the volume is adjustable, so you can turn it off or up depending on your needs.

I found the controls fairly intuitive once I figured out how to activate each mode, like timer mode. John Carlsen/CNET

Five buttons on the unit start/stop the toasting process, adjust the doneness, toggle bagel and English muffin modes, and trigger a feature called A Bit More. Most notably, the start button selects the operation: One press toasts normal bread, a long press does the same for sourdough, and two presses switch on the timer mode for things like Pop-Tarts.

I’m a huge fan of the power cord storage slot on the bottom of the unit, which holds the cord when you need to put the toaster away. This saves you from having to wrangle the cord another way. The crumb tray is completely removable, making the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster fairly easy to clean out. However, the tray isn’t dishwasher safe, so you’ll need to wipe off the old crumbs with a cloth instead. I doubt there’s much else to say about the tech in this toaster without digging into its performance, so let’s jump into my tests.

My time with the Breville Eye Q

Hitting the A Bit More button is an excellent way to finish toasting if it’s not quite perfect. It’s also a good option for folks who want to reheat forgotten toast that sat in the toaster too long, though you should expect it to get even more done. John Carlsen/CNET

Unlike an air fryer, a toaster isn’t a particularly versatile kitchen appliance. It makes toast, more toast, and the occasional Pop-Tart or frozen waffle. So this simplifies my testing, allowing me to focus on a few different types of bread — white, brown and sourdough — in addition to Pop-Tarts and frozen French toast (something I’ve long used my toaster to reheat).

I had a few problems with most of what I toasted. Aside from the darkest setting being a bit much for my usual preference, both white bread and sourdough turned out well across all of the doneness settings. I really liked the results for the sourdough using the corresponding setting, which was nice and crisp, despite not showing as much visual browning. I’m confident that the Eye Q Auto Toaster is perfectly suited for light-colored breads.

I can’t say the surface of the toast always browns evenly—one side generally gets less toasting than the other —but I’m happy with the results. John Carlsen/CNET

However, dark brown bread threw a curveball. The lowest setting was way too crispy, and I had to cancel the toasting on the second-lowest after smoke appeared. I’d previously tested some of the same dark bread in the toaster without issues, so it’s possible my continuous toasting session somehow threw off the accuracy for darker bread. I can’t say whether this would be a long-term issue, but it’s something to watch out for.

Beyond my tests with sliced bread, Pop-Tarts showed that the Timer Mode requires a little more attention and experimentation to get the results you want. At one point, I accidentally used the Auto Mode on Pop-Tarts, and they came out overdone, but not burned, so it’s probably best to stick to the timer or a low setting for toaster pastries. Reheating frozen French Toast went fairly smoothly, but I set the timer too short and had to retoast until the center was nice and hot. I imagine the experience would be similar for frozen waffles.

Should you buy the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster?

If the choice came down to getting a toaster or an air fryer for $300, I’d choose the air fryer. John Carlsen/CNET

I’ll say it outright: the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster is a fantastic toaster, but the $300 price tag is out of reach for budget-conscious households. If you want a more affordable standalone toaster, I recommend something like the $40 Cuisinart CPT-122, which has been a reliable workhorse in my home for years.

Similarly, you might check out the Breville BTA720XL, a solid mid-range model for around $110, even though it’s Breville’s most affordable option. That said, if you use a toaster daily and can afford something in the premium category, it’s worth considering, especially compared with the disappointing $450 Revolution Cooking R180 Connect Plus Smart Toaster.

Tech.title: How to Make Air Fryer Fries Taste Exactly Like Deep-Fried
Tech.content:
Deep-frying at home isn’t rocket science, but it does present a challenge: what to do with all that oil afterward. This oil reuse routine is worth considering, but if you’d rather not manage a pot of boiling oil, an air fryer is your next best option.

Air fryer fries, even frozen grocery store fries, come out surprisingly good, but they don’t reach the heights of their deep-fried counterparts. Air-fried fries typically come out drier with a less even crisp than ones submerged in hot fat. Perfectly edible, but we can do better.

7 Best Air Fryers, Out of 20 Tested See at CNET

To bridge the gap, an air fryer specialist shared his tips for taking fries from mediocre to the crispy, golden ones you’d get from a restaurant. Best part? No hot oil, no cleanup hassle, no standing guard over a deep fryer. Just perfectly crisp fries ready in 15 minutes or less.



Air fryer fries that taste exactly like deep-fried

Air fryer fries are already an easy snacking win. As I learned from an air fryer expert, they can be way better. Pamela Vachon/CNET

In the age of TikTok, it can be hard to trace the origin of certain hacks, but the method was shared with me by Andreas Hansen, founder and CEO of Fritaire, whose tumbler-based model is especially ideal for this French fry preparation, since it both aids in the texturizing of the exterior of the fries and precludes the need to shake several times during air frying.

The Best Frozen Fries to Cook in an Air Fryer, Tested by CNET See at CNET

A little investigation revealed that Chef Joshua Weissman is frequently credited with bringing attention to the method, but even in his video he gives a shoutout to Chris Young, whose video predates Weissman’s by over a year, and who credits Heston Blumenthal for inspiring the “triple-cooked” method, and so on, and so on.

Regardless of the actual origin of this hack, I’m taking their collective wisdom and applying it to french fries, since the method was specifically developed for thick-cut fries, which, I’m sorry, are steak fries, and not at all the same thing.

What you need for mind-blowing air fryer french fries

Here’s everything you need for the best air fryer fries of your life. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a majority of what is needed here probably already exists among the various compartments of your kitchen, the supplies you’ll need to gather are:

Frozen french fries (I’m using straight cut, not thick/steak fries)

Large bowl with lid for shaking

Microwave-safe bowl

Microwave

Air fryer

Duck fat, goose fat or beef tallow for best flavor

Salt

Step 1: A quick soak

A quick soak removes excess starch from the frozen potatoes. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Completely counterintuitive to the idea of crunchy fries is the notion that you must first make them soggy, but that is indeed what is recommended.

Straight from the freezer, soak the fries in warm water for 30 seconds to remove some of the starch on their exterior. (30 seconds to 1 minute is recommended for thicker-cut fries.) This is phase one of the “roughing up” process that will eventually create small micro-pockets of additional surface area on the fries, allowing the air fryer to really get a good crisp going.

The goal here is to keep the interior of the fries frozen, so set a timer to prevent over-soaking.

Step 2: Shake vigorously

Yep, now we’re really going to rough up the fries. After draining the soaking water, shake fries vigorously for another 30 seconds or so. The fries should be soft enough just on the exterior to add some texture, but not fall apart entirely. If they do, you’ve soaked too hard in the first step.

The more little craters you can add to the surface of the fries, the more area there is for the air fryer’s air to circulate, giving an unparalleled crisp.

Step 3: Nuke for 5 minutes

Before we go for the big crunch, we’re softening the insides a little. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Before we actually get crunchy, though, things are going to get even softer first. Using a microwave-safe dish with a lid, par-cook the fries for 5 minutes. Since I was using thinner fries, I hedged my bets and went with 50 percent power, but still cooked for the full 5 minutes.

Both Weissman’s and Young’s videos use a plastic container for both soaking and shaking, but we know better than to do that. So long as we’re being extra with this french fry preparation, let’s switch out for a glass or ceramic container, OK?

This par-cooking stage steams the interior of the fries. If you’ve ever found air-fried fries to be hollow, this is the antidote. The unexpected bonus of this step is that microwaving the fries releases a satisfying french-fry aroma.

Unsurprising step: Following the microwave par-cooking, proceed airfrying as normal by placing the fries in a shallow layer in the air fryer and cooking at 400 degrees Fahrenheit for about 12 to 15 minutes (longer for thicker fries), shaking once or twice during the process to ensure all surface areas have access to the circulating air. The goal is golden brown with edges just starting to brown, so that the fries are crispy but still pillowy soft on the inside.

Step 4: Season with cooking fat

Use a drizzle of duck fat to send your fries’ flavor soaring. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While certain items get a little dousing in fat before being cooked in the air fryer, here we’re just using cooking fat as a seasoning, allowing the already-crisped fries to absorb the oil for both texture and flavor.

But not just any fat. For best results — since you’ve gone this far, why not go all the way — look to rendered animal fat such as duck fat, goose fat or beef tallow for a rich flavor boost. Salt to your liking, and voilà: air fryer french fries that are actually kind of fried.

Hungry for more? Learn how to deep-clean your air fryer in three easy steps and see how much less energy it uses than a wall oven.

Tech.title: Can Bambu Labs 3D Printer Success Translate to a Standalone Laser? I Believe It Can
Tech.content:
If you’re into 3D printing and have been around for the last few years, the name Bambu Lab will be familiar to you. Its products often top best 3D printer lists, including ours, and the company has helped bring genuine plug-and-play standards to in-home 3D printing.

Today, Bambu Lab has announced the R1, a standalone CO2 laser engraver designed to integrate seamlessly into your existing ecosystem. The R1 is available today for a base price of $2,500. I’ve spent some time with it — though not enough for a full review — and so far it’s been a great experience.

A standalone laser with Bambu finish Bambu Lab R1 $2,500 at Bambu Lab

While the R1 looks nothing like a 3D printer, it does have a design language that’s easily identifiable as Bambu Lab’s. The light gray plastic casing is well-fitted, and the interior metal frame feels solid when you move the machine. The LEDs in the back around the CO2 gas chamber highlight the interior and you can see the laser pulses through the rear glass as it works on your material.

Even the molding around the power button exudes a high-quality finish, making the R1 feel like a consumer product you would have in your home office rather than a workshop. The optional riser fits right into that aesthetic, too, and makes the laser-and-riser combo feel like one continuous piece.

The finishing touches, like this power button, show an effort to make things beautiful.

According to Bambu Lab’s press release, the company has brought what it’s learned from 3D printing to the R1, using a lot of its excellent acceleration algorithms and hardware to reduce ringing and other artifacts that occur when cutting or engraving at high speed. Bambu Lab has also used its vision encoders to make sure the cameras on the R1 accurately represent the material on the bed.

This is often an issue with larger lasers, as the fisheye lens can distort images at the edges, making the cuts off-center or overlap in weird ways. If you’re trying to cut around an existing image, this can lead to cutting failures that cost you time and money.

Why make a standalone laser cutter?

Cutting through 3mm plywood is a breeze with the R1.

Bambu Lab has already dabbled in laser cutting. The H2D and H2S both have laser configurations that work OK, but a two-in-one solution will always be a compromise. If you use the laser side of the H2D for too long, eventually the soot and buildup will compromise its ability to 3D print correctly. By creating the R1, Bambu Lab can potentially compete in a space that doesn’t look too kindly on two-in-one devices.

The R1 is a 55-watt CO2 laser, instead of the diode laser that was used in the H2D. The big difference between the two is the amount of materials you can work with. The CO2 laser can’t cut metal, or even etch it well (unless the metal is painted), but it can cut and engrave just about anything else.

I’ve only managed to play around with acrylic, wood and cardboard so far, but the R1 will etch on glass, cut through wood and clear acrylic without any issues. The list of what you can cut with a CO2 laser is long, and with the optional riser and conveyor system, you can go from a 600x300mm cutting area to a 600×3,000mm area, increasing the scope of your projects even more.

Being able to cut clear acrylic and etch on glass is a CO2 laser’s biggest asset, and the R1 does an excellent job. You can often see charring on clear acrylic when it’s not done right, but the settings for the R1 through its Bambu Suite software keep everything well in check. It even has a tracing feature that can take an image of the object on the bed and create a cutting sequence to cut around. It’s quite impressive.

First impressions

The CNET logo always looks good in red

Bambu Lab has a track record of making its first product a good one, and so far, the R1 meets that standard. From the testing I’ve done, this machine is competent, well-made and easily integrates with the great Bambu Lab infrastructure, using the Bambu Handy app and the Makerworld website to help you find projects.

As with all Bambu products, setup took minutes, and the R1 includes multiple calibration tools that make getting started a breeze. The company has long tried to lower the barrier to entry for 3D printing, and it is clearly doing the same with laser cutters.

Xtool, WeCreat and Glowforge have long dominated the consumer and small business space for laser engraving. Some new competition from a proven crafting company can only be good for us all.

Tech.title: I’ve Been Waiting for a Coffee Maker With No Plastic in the Brew Path. Caraway Just Delivered
Tech.content:
Over the last two or so years, I’ve been slowly swapping out the plastic in my kitchen for better alternatives to avoid as many microplastics as possible. I use glass Pyrex for storage, bamboo utensils for cooking, a wooden cutting board for all of my slicing and dicing, glass dishes and reusable, stainless steel water bottles. But there was still one thing I knew for a fact contained plastic: my coffee maker.

Although I haven’t removed every single piece of plastic from my kitchen, I was extra cognizant of my coffee maker because every time it’s used, boiling water goes over the plastic and into the coffee. No, I don’t put my morning beverages under a microscope, but I feel like there’s a good chance that microplastics are leached during this process. And it seemed unavoidable, because every single drip coffee maker I’ve used has had plastic either in the basket where the coffee grounds are placed or on the carafe lid.

So when I learned that Caraway was entering the appliance scene with a drip coffee machine that has absolutely no plastic in the brew path, I had a sneaking feeling that it would end up being my favorite coffee machine ever. Two weeks into having it in my kitchen, I can say I was right.

Trying out Caraway’s new coffee maker

I was already familiar with Caraway through the brand’s ceramic-coated cookware, so I wasn’t surprised to find an exceptionally sharp-looking appliance when I opened the box. Aesthetically pleasing kitchenware is what the brand is known for after all. The design, the color, the quality of the build — all of it made a great first impression. Even the removable cord is thoughtfully designed, but I had to make sure it functioned as well as it looked.

The brew basket is stainless steel, and it comes with a reusable stainless steel coffee filter, too. The glass coffee carafe holds up to 10 cups, and although there’s silicone around the lid, the part that comes into contact with your hot coffee is stainless steel. All of those pieces are dishwasher safe.

The coffee only comes into contact with stainless steel. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

There is only one knob on the coffee maker, which helps it keep its sleek look. It controls the brew, clean and start/stop options. After the coffee is finished brewing, it stays warm in the carafe for up to an hour and a half.

You can twist the knob for brew or clean and push it for start or stop. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

No plastic, no rogue grounds

After using it multiple times, it has consistently made great coffee with no grounds in it, so the reusable coffee filter was a success, too.

Although it’s simple in design, there are nice details throughout, such as a matte finish, a tall, glass carafe and the blue light that illuminates when you pour water into the reservoir.

If you like to schedule your coffee ahead of time, though, you won’t be able to do so with this appliance. There are no extra buttons for scheduling or digital screens, which is partly why this appliance looks so chic.

After the coffee is finished brewing, the stainless steel filter can be rinsed out and reused next time. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

I’m loving this coffee machine for many reasons, but the biggest one is that it solves a problem I’ve been focused on for a while. As we continue to learn more about microplastics and their potential impact on our health, I’m becoming more cautious about how often my food and drinks come into contact with plastic.

Before this launch, if I wanted to avoid plastic when making coffee, a pour-over was the main option I saw. Caraway’s new coffee maker not only keeps plastic out of the brew path but also offers the convenience of a drip coffee maker — and looks great doing so.

The Caraway Coffee Maker is now available for $495 in cream, stone, midnight and clay colors.

Tech.title: Adobe Brings Its Premiere Video Editing Mobile App to Android
Tech.content:
Adobe is bringing its flagship video editing program to Android phone owners. The Android Premiere app is now available to download from the Google Play Store, the company announced on Tuesday.

Premiere is the mobile app version of Adobe’s flagship video editing software. It first became available on iOS last year, and now, Android phone owners will be able to edit their videos on the go, too. The app is designed to be compatible with all manner of Android phones, including foldables like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8. And as a nice perk for foldable fans, you can edit videos with the phone closed and opened up — the multitrack editing timeline and preview video are visible in each configuration.

Adobe has long been the industry standard for professional content editing software, from filmmakers to marketers and photojournalists. But over the past decade, as seemingly everyone has become a content creator, the company has faced increased competition from cheaper, more user-friendly services like Canva, CapCut and Instagram Edits. Premiere and the long-awaited Photoshop mobile apps are one way Adobe is trying to remain competitive.

As the demands on content creators keep rising, mobile apps are an increasingly popular way for creators to keep up. Some creators, particularly in India and Brazil, are adopting a mobile-only editing workflow, Diksha Kuhar, Adobe’s director of product marketing for Premiere, told me.

You can download the app for free from the Google Play Store. You don’t need an Adobe account or subscription, unless you want to use Adobe’s Firefly AI editing features or cloud storage, which may prompt you to 

The Android app was designed to work for aspiring creators and professionals. Beginners can scroll through the app’s library of templates and be guided through creating their own version. Popular tools such as enhance audio are available on the new mobile app, letting you clean up messy audio by enhancing speech and removing background noise. You can also directly publish your videos as YouTube Shorts from Premiere, like how you can directly publish Instagram Reels from Edits, thanks to a partnership between Adobe and YouTube.

In my experience using the Premiere iPhone app, I found it to be a relatively easy, quick way to edit videos. The auto-captioning is particularly useful. You can download videos free of watermarks, and there aren’t any ads clouding the app. (At least not for now. Never say never.) But don’t go in expecting the full bulk of the desktop app’s editing tools. If you need to do meticulous editing on longer videos, you’re probably still best off using Premiere on a laptop or desktop.

Tech.title: Apple’s MLB Dodgers Live Broadcast Was Shot With iPhone 18 Pro Max
Tech.content:
iPhone 18 Pro Max units were spread strategically around the field of Dodger Stadium for the first Apple TV broadcast shot with iPhones that didn’t have sports lenses.

It was a beautiful night for a ballgame last Friday at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles — and some of the footage seen by viewers at home came right out of the phone in their pockets.

That’s the iPhone 18 Pro Max in their pockets, if they happened to be one of the serious fans who bought one when it went on sale Friday. Apple’s latest iPhones have video upgrades with physical aperture blades and new modes, which fans watching the Dodgers take on the San Francisco Giants saw for themselves: Out of the 30 cameras shooting footage of the game, 14 were iPhone 18 Pro Max units.

Several iPhone 18 Pro Max units were tucked into custom-made protective cushions to catch the game — and hopefully survive any unlucky foul balls rocketing their way. David Lumb/CNET

Ahead of the game, Apple brought members of the media, including me, to Dodger Stadium to see the setup, which would record footage for Apple TV Plus’s final broadcast of the Friday Night Baseball game. As soon as I stepped from the stands out onto the field, I found the first of these iPhones on a tripod just inside the dugout, pointed at the field. Considering the phone had only been released to the public that morning, it didn’t surprise me that the phone case for mounting it on the tripod read “iPhone 17 Pro Max.”

A total of three iPhone 18 Pro Max units were arranged behind the plate — two on either side slid into protective padding and one atop the pitch speedometer cameras.

Our tour continued behind the home plate, where iPhones were slotted into custom-made, heavy padding on the backstop and perched above the tower of pitch clock cameras. Others were placed in the visitors’ dugout, posted on the right-field foul pole and positioned toward the field from either team’s bullpens.

One perched on the wall above right-center field was on a gimbal, nicknamed “the robo” and manually controlled from the broadcast center, was positioned to capture outfielders rushing to the wall and reaching over to rob home runs. And one was carried out in the stands to get live fan reactions during the game.

The Ronin gimbal-mounted iPhone 18 Pro Max setup, seen in profile, perched just in front of right-center field, ready to catch game-making plays at the wall — and the crowd reaction behind it. David Lumb/CNET

Apple had its first live iPhone-shot broadcast of a Major League Soccer game back in May, but around half of the fifteen iPhone 17 Pro Max units were bolted onto large, professional-grade telephoto lenses. At Dodger stadium, all the iPhone 18 Pro Max units are shooting from their lenses alone. It’s a way to show off the differences in video capabilities on the premium phones, especially under the challenging conditions of night-time baseball games that start in daylight and end under stadium lights, explained Dylan Ashbrook, director of content and brand development for Apple Sports.

“The new 48MP Fusion Main camera gives us even more versatile video capabilities, and the variable aperture on the Main camera gives us another tool for managing exposure in-camera, giving us more control over the look of the game as conditions change,” Ashbrook said.

Apple didn’t go into detail on the sixteen other cameras that shot the game, but presumably, they were conventional cameras with powerful telephoto lenses to capture plays up close. But the iPhones were chosen to capture angles that those hefty cameras couldn’t — because unlike them, nine of the iPhone 18 Pro Max units weren’t connected by cable wire to pipe in their live footage to the broadcast center. They sent it over wireless 5G — in the middle of the game.

An iPhone 18 Pro Max was positioned in visitor and home bullpens to capture close plays near the edge of the outfield. David Lumb/CNET

Live-streaming footage over 5G for a professional MLB broadcast

While five of the iPhones sent their footage through fiber cable to the broadcast center, nine sent theirs over a private 5G network, which T-Mobile set up ahead of the game. Apple tested the network and was confident there wouldn’t be any latency — in theory, it would be able to switch to any of the 14 iPhones around the stadium at any time.

Not needing a bulky cable to send broadcast footage freed up Apple to place the iPhones in many more locations. That behind-the-plate setup only required Apple to get specially made backstop cushions (which met MLB safety standards) with small slots to slide an iPhone 18 Pro Max into, rather than arduously rebuilding the whole setup with wire connections. Not needing wires also enabled the free 360-degree movement of the gimbaled setup on the outfield wall.

It also means most of Apple’s setup for the game is intentionally temporary. When I asked the company’s representatives touring us around the field why they hadn’t put up an iPhone on the left-field foul pole, they noted that they could easily switch around the layout for the next game — including adding more gimbaled iPhones on the outfield wall, which they’re particularly excited about.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max mounted above the speedometer — and cameras to capture spatial video. David Lumb/CNET

There’s one downside to the freedom of wireless iPhones: They won’t be plugged in to charge while they’re shooting video, which often drains the battery quickly. Since the iPhone 18 Pro Max units were shooting in 4K (which was later scaled down to 1080p in the broadcast center), and were streaming their footage to the broadcast center over 5G wireless, I was concerned about whether they’d last a whole game. While recent rule changes have shortened baseball games (last year’s average was around 2 hours and 40 minutes, according to MLB.com), that’s still a long stretch of continuous video.

Yet when I asked, Apple wasn’t worried. It was confident the iPhone 18 Pro Max units would last the whole game, no problem. (That’s also confidence that the phones wouldn’t overheat while recording video; temperatures topped out around 82 degrees F the day of the mid-September game).

This iPhone 18 Pro Max unit is mounted inside the home team’s dugout, sitting alongside the World Series Champion players of the Dodgers. David Lumb/CNET

Apple’s likely right to feel secure that the iPhone 18 Pro Max wouldn’t run out of battery while shooting the games. The company never gives out exact capacities for the batteries on its iPhones, but has said that its latest and biggest phone should get last 30 hours on a full charge. In his review, CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland got about a day and a half of casual use before hitting 0% on the battery, and on a more intensive day of use, had 14% charge left just before midnight.

I caught some of the game’s broadcast on Apple TV Plus, and while most of the broadcast stuck with the views that most viewers are familiar with (and were likely shot by conventional cameras) like looking over the pitcher’s shoulder toward the batter and bleacher-positioned zoom-ins on big plays, I did notice some iPhone footage snuck in there.

Some of these were vantages at the field level of players and pitchers locked in to the game, but the biggest screentime came from the iPhone wandering around the stands getting the true fan experience. For viewers at home, this was definitely a new vantage from the seats they wished to be in, surrounded by jovial comrades adorned in Dodger blue.

Tech.title: There’s a Simple Reason Your Latte Foam Stinks. This $10 Tool Is the Fix
Tech.content:
As an engineering and math student, the technical side of coffee-making always appealed to me as much as the part where I get to drink it. I’ve become quite adept at pulling the perfect shot of espresso and executing a meticulous pour-over setup, even deep in the wilderness.

Latte art is another story. More often than not, I’d undo a carefully pulled shot with over-steamed milk, topping it off with a shapeless splash of dairy instead of the pluff of semifirm foam I was after. After enough failed attempts, I decided latte art just wasn’t in my skill set. Even so, I wanted that cafe-quality texture, so I went looking for a fix that didn’t rely wholly on technique.

Turns out, a simple and cheap instant-read thermometer is the difference maker I needed. An analog or digital thermometer (mine’s the former) eliminates a whole lot of guesswork. While the milk swirls and hisses, I can check the temperature and pull away the steam wand at the exact right moment. No longer do I venture into stiff, overheated foam or flat, watery dairy; my milk coffee tastes just right.

A thermometer guides the milk steaming process

A simple instant-read thermometer turned out to be the difference maker for my latte art. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Several tools can be used to aerate milk: simple handheld models, dedicated heated milk frothers and steam wands integrated into espresso machines. A thermometer can help with all three setups; I use it with my espresso machine. The steam wand rapidly creates vapor, producing velvety, satisfying milk.



The downside? A powerful boiler system steams fast. My model heats the vapor nearly instantly, then integrates it into the milk through four holes in the wand. In 30 seconds, the dairy goes from cold to aerated. A few moments longer, and the emulsion breaks into runny milk and stiff foam. Not pretty and not delicious, either.

Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Baristas often suggest halting the steaming process when a milk pitcher turns too hot to the touch. Truth be told, I’ve found such subjective guidance misleading. To my fingers, the pitcher turns excessively warm early in the steaming process. I used to hold on too long to compensate, which scalded the milk. A thermometer provides a welcome technical metric instead of this sensory step.

The Best Espresso Machines We Tested See at CNET

I simply clip the tool onto the side of my milk pitcher, then watch the degrees steadily climb. Now the steaming process has a visual rhythm. I can focus on rolling the milk to create abundant microfoam. Then, once the temperature reaches exactly 149 degrees Fahrenheit (65 degrees Celsius), I know I’ve frothed the milk enough. This single tool provides practical guidance for the steaming process.

Don’t neglect proper frothing technique

Whether or not you use a thermometer, you still need good technique for dense foam.

Chris Monroe/CNET

Using a steam wand requires the right approach — a thermometer won’t address every mishap. To get foam with small, suspended bubbles, submerge the frothing tip at the ideal depth. The goal is to create a vortex of spinning milk, which signals uniform aeration. If you place the wand too deep in the liquid, it won’t introduce enough air, yielding a runny result. Too high up, and the bubbles get too large, occasionally even sputtering out of the pitcher.

I introduce the steam wand at an angle and just barely submerge it to kickstart this rolling motion. Once the milk has expanded enough to form a layer of foam on top, I submerge the wand deeper into the dairy, ensuring aeration throughout the pitcher.

The process is easy to mess up. Steam wand placement takes trial and error. Even when the resulting milk reaches 149 F (65 C), latte-art-quality foam isn’t guaranteed. The thermometer helps, though. I’ve learned to switch from surface aeration to the milk body at 104 F (40 C). Milk frothing requires focus on several processes in parallel — a thermometer helps keep track of everything at once.

Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Art is subjective. Well-aerated milk is not

Even with a pitcher full of perfectly foamed milk, there’s still more to producing latte art. Tracking milk temperature didn’t miraculously take me from blobs to elegant, layered hearts. My latte aesthetics still err on the simple side, with continued trial and error regarding design. The height, speed and even angle of how milk is poured all affect what appears on top of the espresso.

After the thermometer, though, I can pour shapes with confidence. The white foam stays contained on the top layer of the coffee—no liquid consistency spills across the cup. With properly textured dairy in hand, I can focus on making designs.

Good frothing isn’t only about visuals, either. Foaming milk to the proper temperature brings out dairy’s intrinsic sugars, which meld with the bold notes in espresso. Texturally, it has a silky mouthfeel, even when the latte art looks bad. Properly frothed milk heightens the espresso, rather than diluting it.

Adjust the temperature per milk type

A thermometer makes experimenting with nondairy milk easier. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

I prefer whole milk for my coffee — its fat content creates a thick, stable microfoam. Other dairy options offer their own advantages. If you’re after a dryer foam — say for a traditional cappuccino or an espresso macchiato — consider skim milk. The leaner consistency turns meringue-like when frothed, perfect for dolloping atop a cup. Skim milk scalds quickly. A thermometer is even more handy here; I’d pull the pitcher away at 140 F (60 C) when steaming skim milk.

The same adjustment applies to the best milk alternatives, too. Although many plant-based milks struggle to produce microfoam, barista-grade oat milk works for latte art. Like skim milk, I’ve noticed this dairy replacement froths swiftly. Steam too long, and you get quite a dry foam (useful for cappuccinos). Not enough heat, and this less stable emulsion falls apart. When a thermometer is in the pitcher, there’s less estimating involved. With my machine, I pull away oat milk at an even lower temperature than skim milk — around 131 F (55 C).



A thermometer makes experimenting with the many types of milk easier. Steaming tempo varies widely depending on both the liquid and the frother. Each setup has its own nuances. With an attached thermometer, though, it’s easier to replicate good results. When you reach the ideal consistency, it’s helpful to write down the temperature to build confidence as you go.

Tech.title: Epson Expands Its Home Theater Projector Line
Tech.content:
Epson’s LS11000 laser-lit 4K projector, with a wide zoom range and excellent image quality, debuted in 2022. Rather than replace it with a new model, the company has expanded the line with newer, cheaper options.

All the new projectors are 4K and lit by lasers, including the LS11000. The LS11000 remains in the lineup with a $4,500 retail price, which appears to be a stealthy increase from its longtime price of $4,000.

Also read: Best Projectors of 2026

LS5000

Epson

At the bottom of the range is the $2,000 LS5000, which Epson says can produce 2,500 lumens. The company’s brightness claims tend to be fairly accurate, though usually only in a mode that sacrifices some image accuracy. The projector will have two HDMI inputs and a throw ratio of 1.32 to 2.15, which the maker says lets you place the device about 11.5 feet away for a 120-inch screen. Like the other models in the line, the LS5000 lets you connect Bluetooth headphones for movie nights without disturbing others in the house. It also has manual lens shift, while only the flagship LS11000 offers motorized lens shift.

LS6000

Epson

For a bit more money, the $2,200 LS6000 bumps the claimed brightness to 3,400 lumens. That’s higher than the LS11000, though Epson rates the LS6000 and its other new projectors as having lower contrast ratios. Otherwise, the LS6000’s features are basically the same as the LS5000’s.

The price is right in the range of several great recent DLP projectors. Epson projectors typically have better color, but a worse contrast ratio due to their LCD-based design. It’ll be interesting to see how they compare, and we’ll find out soon in our testing. But given the small price difference, I bet most people will go for the LS6000.

LS7500

Epson

The LS7500 is a little different. It’s a short-throw variant with a slightly higher brightness rating of 3,500 lumens. The throw ratio is 1.0-1.3, which Epson says requires a distance of 8.8 feet — about 106 inches — to produce a 120-inch image. So perhaps shorter throw would be more accurate. By comparison, the BenQ TK705STi I reviewed earlier this year needs only 83 inches to produce the same size image.

Because all these new models are intended for dedicated home theaters, the longer distance required by the shorter-throw variant seems reasonable. It’s likely designed more for smaller rooms than for a traditional short-throw setup.

Lasers coming your way

The new LS models start shipping later this month. We’ll be getting one in for review soon.
